10118-the-folk-lore-of-plants:
T. F. Thiselton-Dyer published this handbook in 1889, gathering plant lore from Britain and the wider world. He set aside strict botany to ask what people believed about plants: their powers, omens, and sacred ties. The book sums up a field that had grown fast in late Victorian years.

Chapters cover plant worship, witchcraft, demon lore, fairy lore, love charms, dream plants, weather signs, proverbs, and folk medicine. Each topic gets short, clear examples drawn from many sources. Readers get a handy, wide survey of how plants entered myth, magic, and daily custom.
10484-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-03:
John Lord published this third volume of Beacon Lights of History, on ancient achievements, treating governments and laws as the first great work of Greece and Rome. Lord, author of The Old Roman World, traces law from Oriental and priestly codes through Lycurgus, Solon, and Cleisthenes to Roman tribunes, senate, and empire.

The Twelve Tables, Roman lawyers like Gaius, Paulus, and Ulpian, and Justinian's Code, Pandects, and Institutes fill the survey. Marriage, property, contracts, courts, and crimes show law shaping daily life. Readers get a readable, old-style history of ancient law, through institutions rather than battles alone.
10489-an-english-garner-critical-essays-:
J. Churton Collins introduced this 1903 volume of An English Garner, gathering critical essays and literary fragments from Professor Arber's eight-volume Garner of 1877 to 1890. Thomas Seccombe rearranged the texts, classified them for the first time, and filled gaps with fresh matter. Old spelling is mostly modernized for ease.

Pieces include Wilson's Art of Rhetoric, Sidney's letter to his brother, Meres's Palladis Tamia, Dryden's Essay of Dramatic Poesy, and Ellwood on Milton. Advice to a young reviewer and lives of Addison add variety. Readers get a rich, scholarly sampler of English criticism from 1554 to the nineteenth century.
1050-the-dark-lady-of-the-sonnets:
George Bernard Shaw imagines William Shakespeare slipping out to meet the Dark Lady of his sonnets, only to find Queen Elizabeth herself in the way. In one witty act, the playwright, the lady, and the queen trade barbs about love, fame, and the stage, while a watchman guards the door.

Shaw uses the joke to argue his own case: that Shakespeare's plays, not his poems, are his true monument, and that the Dark Lady was a real, dark-eyed woman of the court. The play is short, bright, and full of Shavian paradox. It delights readers who know the sonnets and enjoy a sly literary game.
10582-for-luncheon-and-supper-guests:
Alice Bradley, head of Miss Farmer's School of Cookery in Boston, wrote For Luncheon and Supper Guests in 1923 for hosts who liked to entertain. The book offers ten menus and more than one hundred recipes, suited to company luncheons, Sunday night suppers, afternoon parties, picnics, tea rooms, and small inns.

Each menu comes with notes on what to prepare the day before, so a hostess need not spend the whole party in the kitchen. Hot dishes cooked at the table and simple, fresh foods get special attention. Readers today will find both working menus and a charming record of how American entertaining looked in the 1920s.
10597-four-early-pamphlets:
William Godwin published these four early pamphlets in 1783, before his famous works on political justice. Godwin, then a young writer, treats the Rockingham party's coalition with Lord North, instructions to a statesman, an account of a seminary, and a herald of literature. The pamphlets show a mind already keen on politics and reform.

The defense of the Rockingham party opens with a claim that the reign will give posterity noble materials for history, as science spreads and luxury breeds irresolution. Each pamphlet argues in plain, earnest prose. Readers get a rare, early Godwin, useful for students of radical thought before the French Revolution.
10671-the-botanic-garden-part-2-containi:
Erasmus Darwin's Botanic Garden, part two, The Loves of the Plants, appeared in a second edition in London in 1790. The poem teaches botany by dressing plant reproduction in the language of love, with Flora at play with Cupid on its frontispiece. Philosophical notes explain the science behind the verse.

Darwin's stated aim is to enlist imagination in the service of science, leading readers from loose poetic images to stricter reasoning. The poem recommends the study of plants to ingenious readers in graceful couplets. Modern readers get a delightful oddity: real botany taught through myth, wit, and verse.
10744-men-women-and-ghosts:
Elizabeth Stuart Phelps published Men, Women, and Ghosts in 1869, a book of stories mixing daily life with the uncanny. Its contents include "No News," "The Tenth of January," "Night-Watches," "The Day of My Death," "Little Tommy Tucker," "One of the Elect," and "Kentucky's Ghost." Several first appeared in Harper's Monthly and other journals.

Phelps writes of women, work, loss, and second sight with sympathy and a touch of the supernatural. Her ghosts often carry moral weight rather than mere fright. Readers get a notable collection from a leading American woman writer, blending realism with ghostly tales.
10747-chantecler-play-in-four-acts:
Edmond Rostand, author of Cyrano de Bergerac, wrote Chantecler as a play in four acts, here in Gertrude Hall's 1910 translation. Its cast is a farmyard: Chantecler the cock, Patou the dog, the blackbird, peacock, nightingale, game-cock, turkey, hens, and a host of woodland creatures. A manager's prologue opens the play with three knocks.

Chantecler believes his crow calls up the sun, and the play turns on pride, love, and the gap between belief and truth. Rostand writes in rich, witty verse, full of animal character. Readers get a famous, fanciful drama about art and self-deception, beloved on stage and in reading.
10834-the-history-of-insects:
The History of Insects, printed and sold by Samuel Wood at his Juvenile Book-store in New York in 1813, taught children about creeping things. Its opening pages drill the alphabet in large and small letters, with the long s forms of the day, before verses on insects keeping a half year's sleep beneath a filmy web. A text from Genesis heads the book.

The volume mixes primer and natural history, made for the schoolroom and the nursery. Its quaint type and simple verse mark an early American children's book. Modern readers get a rare survival of how insect lore and ABCs were taught together two centuries ago.
10901-three-young-knights:
Annie Hamilton Donnell wrote this short boys' story about three farm lads on holiday in New England. Jot, Kent, and Old Tilly finish haying, earn five dollars apiece from Father Eddy, and set off on their own, calling themselves knights. Bicycles, country houses, and a night locked in a strange room give their fortnight its adventures.

Good humour and fair dealing carry the boys through scrapes, and older neighbours treat them with kindly tolerance. Donnell keeps the tone sunny and the lessons light: work earns freedom, and friends look out for one another. Young readers meet a vanished rural world of hay mows, Sunday peace, and small-town neighbours, told in simple, warm prose.
1105-the-sonnets:
William Shakespeare's 154 sonnets sing of love, time, and fame in fourteen-line poems of unmatched craft. Some praise a young man of beauty, some scold a dark lady for faithlessness, and many brood on how verse alone can cheat age and death. The sequence moves from praise to jealousy to hard-won calm.

The poems play with puns, paradox, and plain feeling, and lines like "Shall I compare thee to a summer's day" have entered common speech. Scholars still debate who the persons were, but the poems need no key. They stand as the finest sonnet sequence in English.
11068-the-spirit-of-the-age-or-contempor:
William Hazlitt wrote this collection of contemporary portraits, opening with Jeremy Bentham, William Godwin, Coleridge, Irving, Horne Tooke, Scott, Byron, and many others. Hazlitt says Bentham, little known in Westminster where he lived, was better known in Europe and best in Chile and Mexico.

Later portraits cover Wordsworth, Malthus, Gifford, Jeffrey, Brougham, Eldon, Wilberforce, Southey, Moore, Leigh Hunt, Elia, and Geoffrey Crayon. Hazlitt writes with sharp, personal judgment, praising intellect and mocking pretension. The book remains a classic of English criticism, giving vivid, opinionated sketches of the leading minds of the early nineteenth century, by a contemporary who knew many of them.
11121-the-bracelets:
Maria Edgeworth published this 1850 tale, The Bracelets, or Amiability and Industry Rewarded, with illustrations from original designs. Mrs. Villars, a lady of accurate understanding and steady temper, educates twenty young persons in a beautiful retired part of England. Her pupils are good and gay, emulous but not envious, since her praise rewards merit and her blame follows ill conduct.

Each year a small honorary prize rewards successful application, and this year the prize is a bracelet bearing Mrs. Villars's picture, needing no gold or pearls to give it value. The foremost candidates are Cecilia and Leonora: Cecilia active, ambitious, and vain, Leonora contented, temperate, and proud. A pedlar's china figure of Flora, crowned with roses, later tempts Cecilia. Edgeworth's tale rewards industry and amiability over vanity.
11140-rollo-at-play-or-safe-amusements:
Jacob Abbott wrote this volume of the Rollo series, revised by the author and published in Boston in 1855. Rollo at Play joins thirteen companion volumes, from Rollo Learning to Talk through Rollo's Philosophy of Sky. Abbott tells parents that the stories aim to entertain while cultivating children's thinking powers, reading, and gentle manners.

Six stories follow Rollo in the woods, catching a squirrel with a steeple-trap, watching a halo round the moon with Lucy, weathering a freshet, blueberrying with old Trumpeter. In the freshet story, Maria wins the turn to ride to town with her father and visit a caravan of animals. Abbott's tales mix play with moral reflection, a formula that made Rollo a fixture of nineteenth-century children's shelves.
11232-bullets-billets:
Bruce Bairnsfather's 1916 memoir, Bullets and Billets, recounts his service on the Western Front from landing at Havre through Plugstreet trenches, mud, rain, and flooded dugouts. Chapters follow his battalion to billets, a transport farm, a Christmas lull shared with German soldiers, and leave in London, with cartoons' humor breaking through the grim routine. Bairnsfather, already famous as a cartoonist, writes in the voice of his drawings.

The book's tone is wry rather than heroic: soldiers endure, grumble, and joke, and officers muddle through. Its value lies in that ordinariness, a firsthand account of trench life before the war's later bitterness set in. Readers of First World War memoirs will recognize it as a classic of the early war years.
11413-the-refugees-a-tale-of-two-contine:
Arthur Conan Doyle's Refugees, a tale of two continents, follows Huguenot exiles from Louis XIV's France to America. Part one, In the Old World, moves through Versailles, the king's cabinet, the dungeon of Portillac, and the scaffold, as the Catinat family flees persecution. Part two, In the New World, sails on the Golden Rod to Quebec, the inland waters, Sainte Marie. A stockade, with notes on the Huguenots' dispersion and on Louis, Maintenon, and Montespan closing the book.

Conan Doyle writes historical romance with the same pace as his detective fiction. The novel's two continents mirror each other: court intrigue in France, frontier survival in Canada. Readers of historical adventure will find it among his most substantial non-Holmes novels.
11559-renaissance-in-italy-volume-3-of-7:
John Addington Symonds, in the third volume of his Renaissance in Italy, does not retell the history of Italian art work by work. He aims instead to show how the arts stood toward the wider Renaissance: first bound to medieval Christianity, then freed from church control, then free at the height of the classical revival.

Painters such as Filippino Lippi, Botticelli, and Perugino are judged against that arc, with close looks at Madonnas, angels, and the grief in a woman's face. The volume is a study of art and culture together, not a catalogue of pictures.
11661-the-piper-a-play-in-four-acts:
Josephine Preston Peabody's 1910 play in four acts sets the Pied Piper story in Hamelin on the Weser in 1284. The cast lists the Piper and strolling players, the burgomaster Jacobus, the syndic Kurt, and townsfolk from cobbler to smith.

Act one plays in the market place, act two inside the Hollow Hill and at the crossways, and acts three and four return to the crossways and market place. Barbara dances alone, circling slowly, as Michael the sword-eater watches and tries to save her. The play retells the old legend as a drama of town, children, and a piper's bargain.
12047-legends-of-the-madonna-as-represen:
Anna Jameson's Legends of the Madonna, as Represented in the Fine Arts, appeared in a corrected and enlarged Boston edition in 1881. It came from Houghton, Mifflin and Company at the Riverside Press, Cambridge, and treats the Virgin Mary in art. A publishers' note explains that Jameson had kindly consented to prepare for this edition the series of Sacred and Legendary Art, but died before she could fulfil her promise.

Jameson reads paintings, sculptures, and mosaics for their stories: the Annunciation, the Nativity, the sorrows and glories of Mary, as artists from Giotto to Raphael imagined them. Her book taught Victorian readers to see pictures as narratives, and it remains a classic introduction to Marian iconography for gallery visitors.
12269-wee-macgreegor-enlists:
J. J. Bell published Wee Macgreegor Enlists in 1916, a wartime comedy about a Glasgow family sending its boy to war. Bell created Wee Macgreegor, a Scots laddie, in earlier stories, and here the boy grows toward soldiering.

Chapters run from arms and the maid through breaking it gently, first blood, the ring, and uniform, to Mrs. McOstrich entertaining, a tea party, and conscience and a cocoa-nut. Family, sweethearts, and aunts fuss over enlistment, training, and letters home. The Scots dialect is thick, and the humor is domestic rather than martial. The book shows how wartime Britain laughed at home-front worry, while taking the war itself seriously underneath.
1240-the-playboy-of-the-western-world-a-:
J. M. Synge's comedy opens in a Mayo village pub, where Christy Mahon arrives claiming he killed his father, and the locals, charmed by his tale, make him a hero. Girls court him, men toast him, until his father turns up alive and the hero's shine fades fast.

The play's rich, poetic speech and its mockery of hero-worship caused riots at its Dublin premiere in 1907. Synge drew the tale from Aran island lore. The comedy remains a landmark of Irish theatre, funny, lyrical, and sharp about how crowds make and break their idols.
1241-the-well-of-the-saints-a-comedy-in-:
J. M. Synge's comedy tells of Martin and Mary Doul, a blind old couple who live happily by a holy well. A saint restores their sight, and they find the world ugly and each other plain. When their sight fades again, they choose blindness and contentment over a sighted life of scorn.

The play's irony is gentle and sharp: seeing, in Synge's hands, brings not wisdom but vanity. The dialogue sings with the speech of the west of Ireland. The comedy remains a gem of the Irish stage, funny, lyrical, and quietly sad.
12474-write-it-right-a-little-blacklist-:
Ambrose Bierce's 1909 handbook, Write It Right, aims to teach precision in writing. Good writing, Bierce says, is clear thinking made visible, and precision is its point of capital concern. The writer must choose the word that accurately expresses his mind, and exclude words that denote or connote something else.

Quintilian's rule guides the book: write so the reader not only may, but must, understand. Bierce attacks bloated dictionaries that gather every metaphorical and unrelated meaning, and insists on a word's actual, serviceable sense. The little blacklist that follows is sharp, dogmatic and quotable, a satirist's guide to plain, exact English.
12559-the-automobile-girls-at-washington:
Laura Dent Crane's 1913 Automobile Girls at Washington, or Checkmating the Plots of Foreign Spies, follows the series heroines to the capital. A frontispiece shows a fat Chinese gentleman regarding a heroine. Chapters run from a chance meeting and cabinet day to Mr. Tu Fang Wu, the Chinese embassy, sub rosa dealings, arrest, Mollie's temptation and the White House.

Bab's discovery, a confession, Barbara's secret errand, a foolish girl, grant no favours, a white veil, a tangled web, Harriet in danger and foiled plots follow. Crane writes brisk girls' adventure, mixing motoring, mystery and patriotism. The book is a period girls' series tale, lively, innocent and fond of Washington.
12560-port-o-gold-a-history-romance-of-t:
Louis J. Stellman's 1922 history-romance, Port o' Gold, tells of San Francisco's argonauts, dedicated to the city of his adoption and rebirth. An opening illustration shows sunlight scattering fog into luminous shapes above a splendid, impalpable city, hinting at destiny. Stellman watches day break over roofs and towers, mirrored by the bay.

Gold rush, fire, rebuilding and romance follow, as fortune seekers build a city from tents and ships. Stellman mixes history with invented lives, in a lyrical, boosterish manner. The book is a love letter to San Francisco, fond of its fog, gold and grit, and it captures the argonaut myth as the city told it to itself in the 1920s.
12596-the-purple-heights:
Marie Conway Oemler's 1920 novel, The Purple Heights, follows Peter Champneys of Riverton, South Carolina, and Paris. His mother Maria, Chadwick Champneys called the god in the machine, Emma Campbell, and Anne Champneys, née Nancy Simms, called Cinderella, surround him. Chapters run from The Red Admiral and The Promise to At Grips with Life, The Soul of Black Folks and The Purple Heights itself.

Cinderella, price-tags, a dear dam-fool, a grandmother's house, swan feathers and kismet mark a story of class, race and ambition in the South and beyond. Oemler, author of Slippy McGee, writes in a warm, Southern manner. The novel offers a romance of rising, falling and finding a place, with the purple heights as its image of hope.
12687-the-title-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Arnold Bennett's 1918 comedy The Title is set in one well-furnished West End sitting room over three days around the New Year. The Culver family gathers for dinner while a newspaper article, signed Sampson Straight, stirs secrets about who really writes it. Father, mother, daughter Hildegarde, and son John all have a stake in the truth.

Much of the fun comes from unmasking: the father works out, step by step, that his clever daughter is the hidden author. Bennett uses the puzzle to poke at honours, press fame, and family pride. The play reads briskly, with short scenes and sharp talk throughout.
12750-the-stolen-bacillus-and-other-inci:
H. G. Wells's Stolen Bacillus and Other Incidents, Methuen 1895, dedicated to H. B. Marriott Watson, gathers stories mostly from the Pall Mall Budget, with two from the Pall Mall Gazette and one from St James's Gazette. Wells notes that a third story was reprinted by the Observatory, and The Lord of the Dynamos by the Melbourne Leader.

Contents run from The Stolen Bacillus and The Flowering of the Strange Orchid through In the Avu Observatory and Triumphs of a Taxidermist. A Deal in Ostriches, Through a Window, Temptation of Harringay, The Flying Man, The Diamond Maker, Aepyornis Island, Davidson's Eyes and The Lord of the Dynamos follow. Wells writes early science fiction and fantasy, witty, inventive and dark. The collection shows a young master finding his range.
12753-the-legends-of-king-arthur-and-his:
Sir James Knowles retold the Arthur legends for young readers in this 1862 volume, dedicated by permission to Tennyson, then Poet Laureate. Knights, quests, enchantments, and betrayals follow in clear, storybook prose, with pictures by Lancelot Speed. Tennyson's own Idylls had spurred Knowles to try the tales.

Inside, Arthur deals with Morgan le Fay's plots, sends a rich mantle back as a grim gift, and watches knights like Accolon fall to wounds and treachery. The book keeps Malory's shape while smoothing his language for family reading. It remains a friendly doorway into Camelot, the Round Table, and the Grail quest.
128-the-arabian-nights-entertainments:
Scheherazade tells tales night after night to delay her death, and her stories fill this volume. Andrew Lang's Arabian Nights Entertainments, selected from the Longmans edition, gathers the merchant and the genius, the fisherman, and the three calenders. Sindbad's seven voyages follow.

The little hunchback, the barber's brothers, and other tales of Bagdad complete the set. Lang's plain retelling keeps the wonder without heavy ornament. Readers meet genies, viziers, and sailors in quick succession. The book serves as a friendly door into the Nights. Lang's selection suits family reading while keeping the tales' danger and delight intact.
12850-a-philological-essay-concerning-th:
Edward Tyson's philological essay on the pygmies of the ancients, edited with an introduction by Bertram C. A. Windle, asks what truth hides in old tales of tiny peoples. Tyson gathers legends and travellers' reports, with help from scholars like Turner, Haddon, and Topinard, and debts to De Quatrefages's book on pygmies. The preface warns the account is selective, not exhaustive.

Notes on fairy folk living among rocks and hills, and wood trolls dwelling in thick forests, show how small peoples were imagined across Europe. Tyson tests myth against early anthropology with care. The essay interests readers of folklore, classics, and the history of science.
12881-mrs-budlong-s-christmas-presents:
Rupert Hughes wrote Mrs. Budlong's Christmas Presents in 1912 as a comedy of small-town giving and getting. Christmas morning in Carthage brings remorse for gifts given, withheld, and received, with everyone forced to exclaim over trivial presents. Mrs. Budlong, once snubbed, suddenly finds callers crowding her house like a daily reception.

Overflow meetings fill the den where she keeps furniture too poor for the parlour, while old calls long unreturned are paid up with enthusiasm. Hughes mines humour from pride, envy, and social climbing. The book offers a light, sharp Christmas satire in the author's popular style.
12974-christmas-entertainments:
Alice M. Kellogg compiled Christmas Entertainments for children aged five to fifteen, with fancy drills, acrostics, motion songs, tableaux, short plays, and recitations in costume. New songs to old tunes, a Christmas-bell drill, a snow brigade, and plays like Mr. St. Nicholas and Christmas Waits fill the contents. Contributors include M. Nora Boylan and Ella M. Powers.

A play scene brings Father Christmas, Jack and Jill with their pail, and Simple Simon meeting a pieman, while a song recalls a naughty child grown good through Christmas teaching. The book served schools and churches planning holiday shows. It remains a charming period source for children's Christmas performance.
13-the-hunting-of-the-snark-an-agony-in-:
A bellman leads a mismatched crew on a voyage to catch a creature called the Snark. Lewis Carroll's Hunting of the Snark tells the quest in eight fits, or cantos. The crew includes a baker, a beaver, a barrister, and a banker.

Carroll's preface defends the poem's nonsense with mock-serious logic. The hunt mixes sea charts, rules of five, and jokes about the beast's habits. The final fit warns that some Snarks are Boojums, whose sight makes the viewer vanish. The poem remains a favorite of nonsense verse. Illustrations and stage versions followed, keeping the crew's strange voyage alive for new readers.
13050-the-easiest-way-representative-pla:
Eugene Walter's play The Easiest Way, in the Representative Plays series, opens with the author's own low view of it. Walter said a good play needs uplift in thought, and his play has none; only the old agent is worth much, and the rest portray a sordid life. A first-night audience at the Stuyvesant Theatre disagreed, and the play became a hit.

Laura, the heroine, is torn between a lover who asks her to give up her kept life and struggle honestly, and the comforts she knows. She promises to stick to the right thing, yet the play keeps pulling her back. Walter's frank portrait of kept women, agents, and stage life made the play famous, and infamous, in its day.
1306-seven-men-excerpts:
Max Beerbohm, the wit and caricaturist, offers excerpts from Seven Men, his book of mock biographies: six imaginary writers and one real one, each sketched with irony, invention, and perfect prose. The pieces blend fact and fancy until the reader cannot tell which is which.

Beerbohm writes with a dandy's polish and a satirist's eye, and his fake lives are funnier than many real ones. The excerpts give the flavor of a minor classic of English wit. They suit readers who like literary games played beautifully. Beerbohm's fake lives are funnier than many real ones.
13089-the-making-of-arguments:
J. H. Gardiner, formerly assistant professor of English at Harvard, published The Making of Arguments in 1912 as a textbook for students. Gardiner defines argument as writing or speech meant to make others take your view of a case. He notes that exposition and argument have no certain line between them, since even Huxley and Arnold slip into proof.

Later chapters teach how to frame a proposition, pick four or five main issues, and throw out the rest when space is short. Gardiner warns that fifteen hundred words vanish fast once evidence is stated in detail. The book is a clear, practical rhetoric, built for classrooms and debates, and it still reads as sound advice for any writer with a case to make.
13424-honoring-parents:
A short Boston tract of 1851, prepared for the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society, teaches children to honour parents under the fifth commandment. Obedience, cheerful and prompt, is the first duty named. But the writer adds a second test: a child can also make others respect his father and mother by his own conduct.

Stories carry the lesson. A boy stands up for his parents, a Sabbath school gathers with hymn and prayer under a teacher called Miss H., and Willy, given a bright picture book, meets unkindness from Henry with quiet patience. The tract is brief, direct, and meant to be read aloud to young scholars.
13430-a-librarian-s-open-shelf-essays-on:
Arthur E. Bostwick, a librarian writing in 1920, gathers essays first printed in journals and read to library meetings. He asks whether readers really read, what makes people read, how book titles change, and what fiction is good for. Selective education, modern teaching methods, and the value of association all get their turn.

Browsing earns a careful defence, so long as it stays occasional and does not crowd out steady reading and study. Other essays range wider, into American government, where a president holds more power than many kings yet can be removed by elected representatives. The collection shows a working librarian thinking about books, schools, and citizens together.
13515-bracebridge-hall-or-the-humorists:
Washington Irving's Bracebridge Hall, subtitled The Humorists, gathers sketches of an English country house and its people. The hall, the busy man, family servants, the widow, lovers, family relics, an old soldier, Ready-Money Jack, bachelors, wives, and story-telling fill the first volume, with falconry, hawking, and St. Mark's Eve among its customs.

A stranger in a ruff and overshadowing hat, buried among books in the library, draws Antonio's curiosity, while rooks quarrel, plunder, and brawl over timber in the rookery during building season. Irving writes with gentle humour about English country gentlemen, their servants, books, and pastimes, in a book meant to be read slowly, sketch by sketch.
13535-selections-from-five-english-poets:
Mary E. Litchfield edits selections from five English poets for school readers in 1902, with introduction and notes. Dryden opens with A Song for St. Cecilia's Day, Gray follows with his Elegy in a Country Churchyard, and Goldsmith offers The Traveller and The Deserted Village.

Burns gives The Cotter's Saturday Night, and Coleridge closes with The Ancient Mariner. Litchfield presents Dryden as the link between Milton, last of the Elizabethans, and Pope, chief poet of Queen Anne's age. Goldsmith's lines on laws grinding the poor while rich men rule the law show the moral edge of his verse. The book teaches poetry through brief lives and clear notes.
13677-beautiful-thoughts:
A small devotional book of 1892, arranged by Elizabeth Cureton from the writings of Henry Drummond, the Scottish preacher and author of The Greatest Thing in the World. Short passages are set out day by day through the year, each drawn from Drummond's books on natural law, love, and the Christian life.

The selections press a simple point: faith should show in conduct, self-denial buys the larger good, and the laws of nature and of spirit run together. Cureton chose them to help a friend enjoy Drummond's longer works, and the book reads as a bedside companion rather than an argument. It captures a Victorian habit of daily reading meant to steady the reader's temper and aims.
13709-wolfville-nights:
Alfred Henry Lewis returned to his Arizona mining town in this 1902 collection. Wolfville Nights gathers tales told at night by cowboys, gamblers, and old-timers. Faro Nell deals bank, Colonel Sterett hunts a panther, and Dave Tutt shows his strange ways. Ghosts, Apaches, and Tucson Jennie all get their turn.

Lewis writes in rich Western speech, with humour and a touch of menace. Each story stands alone, yet the same voices and places recur. Gambling halls, ranches, and desert trails set the scenes. The tales celebrate craft, nerve, and quick wit. They also show the harsh codes that governed frontier towns. Fans of Western yarns will enjoy the pace and talk.
13755-how-to-see-the-british-museum-in-f:
W. Blanchard Jerrold published this guide in London in 1852. It plans four visits that cover the British Museum's main rooms in order. Each visit lists what to see, from stuffed animals and birds to Egyptian, Greek, and Roman antiquities. Later visits take in manuscripts, prints, medals, and the reading room.

Jerrold writes for visitors with limited time and no expert help. He names star objects and tells readers what to skip. Short notes explain animals, gods, and historic figures as the tour moves on. The guide captures the museum when its galleries were still new and crowded. It also works as a period piece, showing how Victorians learned from public collections.
1378-the-land-of-footprints:
Stewart Edward White's 1913 travel book records a long safari through East Africa, from the coast into game country. White writes about camps, porters, hunts, and the peoples he meets. He opens by sorting travel books into honest records and tall tales, promising his own to be of the honest kind.

The narrative follows the trail day by day, with notes on animals, landscapes, and the work of keeping a large party fed and moving. Its tone is that of a sportsman and observer rather than a naturalist. It is a vivid period picture of African travel before the age of easy roads.
13894-the-great-adventure-a-play-of-fanc:
Arnold Bennett wrote The Great Adventure, a play of fancy in four acts, in 1913. Ilam Carve, an illustrious painter, longs to escape fame. His valet Albert Shawn takes his place, and confusion follows. Dr. Pascoe, journalists, dealers, and an American millionaire crowd the plot. Scenes move from Redcliffe Gardens to the Grand Babylon Hotel and Putney.

Bennett turns identity into comedy: the false painter charms, while the real one watches. Janet Cannot, a widow, adds romance and sharp talk. A joke about pneumonia as a mercy in hot weather shows Bennett's dry wit. The play satirises art, fame, and London society. It remains a light, clever piece from Bennett's middle years.
13943-political-pamphlets:
George Saintsbury edited Political Pamphlets in 1892 for the Pocket Library of English Literature. The volume gathers short pieces by one writer or on one class of subject. Contents include Halifax's Letter to a Dissenter, Defoe's Shortest Way with the Dissenters, and Swift's Drapier's Letters to tradesmen and shopkeepers. Later pamphlets follow in the same vein.

Saintsbury's series also covered tales of mystery, political verse, and Defoe's minor novels. The pamphlets show English political argument from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Halifax urges healing without sharpness, while Defoe and Swift attack with irony. The collection suits students of political prose. It offers sharp, short classics in one volume.
14095-the-thirteenth-chair-a-play-in-thr:
Bayard Veiller's 1922 play in three acts stages a séance that turns into a murder inquiry. A medium named Rosalie, speaking in a child's voice, moans of a man far away, bad people, and pain like a knife burning in the back. A voice calls for Ned, and a knife appears sticking in the ceiling. Spencer wants to tell Ned about letters, and the room tightens with dread.

Police work follows the spirits. Inspector Donohue suspects Rosalie of finding what his men could not, orders her searched, and keeps her from speaking to anyone. She answers that she found comfort and faith that the innocent would come to no harm. Veiller, a master of stage thrills, balances supernatural chills with detective logic. Audiences loved the trick: a ghost story that solves a crime without ever quite proving the ghost.
14246-mercadet-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Honoré de Balzac's comedy Mercadet, first staged in Paris in 1851, sets its scene about 1845 in a speculator's house. Mercadet, his wife, their daughter Julie, clerk Minard, friend Verdelin, and creditors fill the cast. Justin the valet, Thérèse the maid, and Virginie the cook open the play dusting a drawing room, while debts pile behind the mirror.

Credit itself becomes the plot. Mercadet begs Verdelin for a fortnight of opulence, confessing his wife and daughter lack clothes and his plate sits in pawn. A dinner for a future son-in-law needs a thousand crowns and a borrowed dinner service. Suitor De la Brive boasts an estate of sand wastes and firs worth thirty thousand francs, mortgaged for forty-five thousand. Mercadet admires the trick: good to make toothpicks, he jokes, and part of the ocean besides. Debt, bluff, and marriage bargain for laughs throughout.
14359-macmillan-co-s-general-catalogue-o:
Macmillan and Company printed this general catalogue of works in history, biography, travel, and belles lettres. Each entry gives a short account, with a note of critical praise where the firm had it. The history section alone names many writers, from Baker and Bryce to Gladstone, Guizot, and Kingsley. Biography, travel, and letters follow in the same plain style. The book served buyers and librarians who wanted a guide to the firm's list.

Readers can trace the firm's taste through its chosen names: explorers, statesmen, churchmen, and men of letters. The catalogue groups books by field, so a buyer can find histories beside lives and travels. Short notices tell what each book covers and why it won praise. The volume doubles as a record of the firm's publishing and as a shopping aid. It still helps readers map what a great London house thought worth printing.
1443-two-poets:
Two Poets opens Balzac's Lost Illusions trilogy in the provincial town of Angouleme, where Lucien Chardon, a handsome young poet, and his friend David Sechard, a printer, dream of fame and fortune. Lucien's sister Eve binds the pair, and Lucien's love for a local noblewoman pulls him toward Paris.

The novel studies ambition in a small town: printing presses, paper mills, and salon gossip all shape a young writer's fate. Lucien's gifts and vanity carry the seeds of his later fall. It is a rich, detailed start to Balzac's great story of literature, money, and illusion.
14448-cromwell-a-drama-in-five-acts:
Alfred B. Richards wrote this five-act verse drama, printed in London in 1852, around Oliver Cromwell and the men who made and unmade the English republic. Cromwell dominates the stage, with John Milton as his secretary.

Parliamentarians, royalists, soldiers, and plotters argue over kingship, regicide, and the army's power, while a young lover's intrigue runs beside the politics. The play stages debates rather than battles, and its blank verse aims for grandeur. It is a mid-Victorian attempt to bring the Civil War's central figure to the stage. The play never held the stage for long.
14908-recollections-of-bytown-and-its-ol:
William Pittman Lett recalls Bytown, the early name of Ottawa, and its old inhabitants in an 1874 volume printed by the Citizen company on Sparks Street. His introduction jokes that no book can be complete without a preface, and admits he never meant to publish these reminiscences beyond a few hundred lines.

Friends desirous of having them in compact shape changed his mind, not any ambition of his own to write a book. What follows is local memory: streets, people, shops and incidents from a frontier town growing into a capital. Lett writes with humour and affection, and the book remains a first-hand source for early Ottawa life.
15298-sword-and-crozier-drama-in-five-ac:
Indridi Einarsson's Sword and Crozier, a drama in five acts translated from Icelandic by Lee Hollander, appeared in Poet Lore in 1912. The cast pits Botolf, bishop of Holar, against Kolbein Arnorsson the Young, chieftain of Iceland's north quarter, aged thirty-four. Helga his wife, Salvor the woman physician, and henchmen fill the stage.

Old Kolbein Kaldaljos, steward of the bishopric, his son Brand of Reynistad, and their households widen the feud between church and sword. The play draws on medieval Icelandic strife, with bishops, chieftains, and beggars in conflict. Theatre lovers will find it a rare, stark sample of Icelandic drama.
15400-renaissance-in-italy-volume-1-of-7:
John Addington Symonds's Renaissance in Italy opens with The Age of the Despots, in an author's edition printed at New York in 1888 and dedicated to John Beddoe. A Machiavelli motto on idle princes and vile arms fronts the work. Symonds notes that each volume aims to stand complete, though all form one study of Italian culture.

Despots, city states, and the arts of power fill this first volume, with wars, courts, and civic life in vivid narrative. Symonds writes as a Victorian humanist, learned and lyrical. Students of the Renaissance will find the book a classic, if dated, gateway to Italy's fierce, brilliant age.
15468-lectures-on-popular-and-scientific:
The Earl of Caithness published these lectures on popular and scientific subjects in London in 1879, in a second enlarged edition with Trübner. Delivered at various times and places, they aim to bring science to general audiences, in plain language, with facts a listener could carry home. The contents list eight talks.

Coal and coal mines opens the set, calling coal one of England's greatest blessings and a cause of its wealth, with yearly values in the millions. Other lectures cover science applied to art, thrift, past and present means of communication, the steam engine, attraction, and oil from linseed. A closing hodge-podge mixes lighter matter. The book shows Victorian popular science at its earnest best: useful, moral, and proud of British industry.
15517-acetaria-a-discourse-of-sallets:
John Evelyn, author of the Kalendarium and famous for his Diary, wrote this discourse of sallets, first published in 1699. This edition, printed in Brooklyn in 1937 by the Women's Auxiliary of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, reprints the first edition faithfully, keeping old spelling and punctuation, with a few plain errors corrected. The old-style long s is kept.

Evelyn treats salads as a serious art: herbs, oils, vinegars, and the health of green foods, in the learned style of a Restoration gentleman. A publisher's note warns that much flavor is lost if the book is scanned too hurriedly, and that Latin and Greek were then the gauge of a man of letters. Evelyn, friend and contemporary of Pepys, writes with less sparkle but more gravity. The discourse remains a classic of English food writing.
15621-the-story-of-jack-and-the-giants:
This story of Jack and the giants, published in London in 1851 by Cundall and Addey, is illustrated with thirty-five drawings by Richard Doyle, engraved by G. and E. Dalziel. A frontispiece shows Jack killing the giant Cormoran by stratagem of a pit, and a title page shows Jack listening to stories of giants and fairies. The book retells the old English tale in a handsome Victorian edition.

Pictures trace the plot: the giant comes, Cormoran carries off his booty, shepherds panic, justices present Jack a sword and belt, and a Welsh giant offers deceitful civility and pudding. Jack measures legs with a giant, alarms his three-headed uncle, delivers a lady from an enchanter, and is dubbed a knight by the king. The tale is a classic of English folklore, told for children with Doyle's lively, detailed drawings.
15744-the-gay-lord-quex-a-comedy-in-four:
A comedy in four acts by Arthur W. Pinero, a leading London playwright of the late Victorian stage. Pinero built his fame on witty society plays that tested manners, money, and reputation. Lord Quex, a gay blade with a past, faces a new love and an old scandal at once. The play ran as polished drawing-room comedy, with brisk dialogue and carefully staged confrontations.

Quex must choose between a respectable match and the claims of a woman from his earlier life. A duchess, a young lover, and a sharp-tongued friend press him from all sides. Pinero keeps the tone light while the stakes stay real: honour, gossip, and marriage. The comedy still plays well as a study of how a charming man tries to outrun his own record.
15762-side-lights:
A set of essays by James Runciman, issued in London in 1893 with a memoir by Grant Allen and an introduction by W. T. Stead. Runciman, a journalist and critic, wrote short, sharp pieces on books, morals, and London life. John F. Runciman edited the volume after the author's death. T. Fisher Unwin published it as a tribute and a sampler.

Topics run from letter-writers and the decline of literature to ill-assorted and happy marriages. Runciman writes on the hopeless poor, waifs and strays, stage children, and the values of labour. Public and private morality, past and present, get a frank comparison. The essays keep a humane, combative tone, siding with workers and children against cant. Together they preserve a vivid critic's view of late Victorian England.
15788-waste-a-tragedy-in-four-acts:
A tragedy in four acts by Harley Granville Barker, issued by Sidgwick and Jackson in London in 1909. Barker, actor, director, and playwright, wrote political drama for a thinking audience. Waste opens at George Farrant's house in Hertfordshire, on a summer Sunday evening, with Mrs. Farrant at her piano. The play then follows ambition, love, and scandal in high politics.

Henry Trebell, a rising politician with a great reform in hand, risks all on a secret affair. When scandal breaks, his career and his cause fall together, and no apology can save them. Barker writes with cool, modern prose, letting talk and silence do the work of fate. The play remains a sharp study of how private acts wreck public hopes.
15878-the-stepmother-a-drama-in-five-act:
A drama in five acts by Honore de Balzac, first presented in Paris at the Theatre-Historique on May 25, 1848. Balzac, the great novelist, turned his hand to the stage with this tale of a general's house. The scene is the chateau of General de Grandchamp near Louviers in Normandy, in 1829. Persons of the play fill a full page of the text.

Comte de Grandchamp, a Napoleonic general, lives with Gertrude, his second wife, and Pauline, his daughter by his first wife. Eugene Ramel, a state's attorney, Ferdinand Marcandal, and Doctor Vernon stir the plot. A stepmother's power, a daughter's honour, and a father's pride collide. Balzac's drama shows his novelist's eye on stage: strong passions, sharp talk, and a house divided.
16221-the-spirit-of-youth-and-the-city-s:
Jane Addams of Hull House, Chicago, published The Spirit of Youth and the City Streets with Macmillan in 1909, reprinted here in 1930. Dedicated to Louise de Koben Bowen, president of Chicago's Juvenile Protective Association, the book opens with youth in the city and the wrecked foundations of home life. Addams, author of Democracy and Social Ethics, writes from settlement work among immigrant children.

Her chapters argue that city streets starve young people's need for play, adventure, and beauty, driving them toward dance halls, gangs, and trouble. The remedy lies in parks, playgrounds, and supervised joy. The book remains a founding text of youth work and urban reform, humane and practical.
16225-music-as-a-language-lectures-to-mu:
Ethel Home, headmistress of Kensington High School, published these lectures for music students with Oxford's Clarendon Press in 1916. Her chapters cover the training of the music teacher, organizing musical work in schools, voice production and songs, the sol-fa method, and first lessons in ear training. Sight singing, time and rhythm, dictation, harmony, composition, transposition, and piano teaching follow.

Home writes for a young woman fresh from school who has added special music training and now faces a classroom. Her advice is practical, orderly, and encouraging, with hints for taking a lesson and leaving a training department. Music teachers and students will still find her clear, schoolroom-wise guidance useful.
16250-tristan-and-isolda-opera-in-three-:
Oliver Ditson's edition of Wagner's Tristan and Isolda gives the opera in three acts with a full story synopsis. Act one brings Tristan, a valiant Cornish knight, carrying Isolda, princess of Ireland, as a bride for his uncle King Mark. Though he loves her, a blood feud makes him hide it, until Isolda tries to poison them both and her maid Brangaena swaps the draft for a love potion.

Act two finds Isolda wed to Mark yet meeting Tristan in secret, until betrayal by Melot and Mark's bitter reproaches drive Tristan to provoke a fight. The synopsis lets readers follow Wagner's great love tragedy without a score. Opera lovers and newcomers alike will find this a clear guide to a towering work.
16261-some-chinese-ghosts:
Lafcadio Hearn's Some Chinese Ghosts, copyright 1887 by Roberts Brothers, gathers retold Chinese legends chosen for weird beauty. Hearn dedicates the small volume to his friend Henry Edward Krehbiel. Krehbiel was the musician who coaxed Chinese wanderers in America to play the serpent-bellied san-hien and the shrieking ya-hien. He also got them to sing the jasmine-flower song Mohli-hwa. That musical friendship frames the tales.

Hearn's preface cites Scott on the supernatural, appealing to emotions widely and deeply sown among people. The ghosts that follow are tender, eerie, and strange, never merely frightening. Readers of folklore and ghost stories will find a slim, beautiful classic of East-West retelling.
16410-the-life-story-of-insects:
George H. Carpenter, a Dublin zoology professor, tells the life story of insects in this short Cambridge manual of 1913. Growth and change, sucking insects, the move from water to air, and the inner and outer changes of transformation fill the chapters. Larvae, pupae, seasons, and the deep past close the account, with a gnat's transformation as frontispiece.

Carpenter writes for general readers, with clear prose and helpful pictures. The book makes metamorphosis vivid without heavy science. Young naturalists and curious adults will find it a fine short guide to the insect world and its wonders.
1649-ferragus-chief-of-the-de-vorants:
Honoré de Balzac opens his story of the Thirteen, a secret band of powerful men in Paris under the Empire. A young officer follows a mysterious beggar and stumbles on a hidden past. The trail leads to Ferragus himself and to Madame Jules Desmarets, whose quiet married life hides an old loyalty that could ruin her.

Balzac builds the plot from watched streets, intercepted letters, and whispered meetings. The suspense rests on what a husband will do when he learns his wife keeps a secret. In Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation, the tale reads as both a Paris mystery and a study of how one buried fact can undo a household.
16510-essays-on-education-and-kindred-su:
Herbert Spencer's essays on education, collected in Everyman's Library with an introduction by Charles W. Eliot, ask what knowledge is of most worth. Intellectual, moral, and physical education each get a full essay, followed by pieces on progress, manners, the genesis of science, laughter, and the origin and function of music.

Spencer argues from science and evolution, urging useful learning over mere bookish drill. The essays first ran as review articles in the 1850s and 1860s, and they shaped Victorian debates on schools. Readers of education history will find a bold, plain-spoken thinker still worth arguing with.
1664-songs-for-parents:
John Farrar's Songs for Parents offers rhymes for children, dedicated in verse to Barbara, Ted, Wink, and Dick, the last of whom would rather fish than read rhymes. Songs of Desire, Summer Explorer, and spring pieces follow, with verses meant to be read aloud in nurseries and at bedtime.

Farrar writes with lightness and affection, and his songs suit small listeners and their parents alike. The book is slight and sweet. It is a period children's verse collection, charming for its dedication and its easy, singable rhymes. The verses are made to be read aloud at bedtime.
16655-artist-and-public-and-other-essays:
Kenyon Cox gathers essays on art in this 1914 Scribner volume, with thirty-two pictures. Artist and Public leads, followed by Millet, The Illusion of Progress, Raphael, Two Ways of Painting, The American School, and Augustus Saint-Gaudens. Millet's Goose Girl fronts the book, with the Sower, Gleaners, and Spaders among the plates.

Cox writes as a painter-critic, defending craft and tradition against mere novelty. His essays are clear, firm, and beautifully illustrated. Readers of art criticism will find a classic American voice, arguing that art must serve both maker and public.
16698-the-king-s-arrow-a-tale-of-the-uni:
H. A. Cody tells a loyalist tale in this 1922 novel, dedicated to his ancestors who reached the St. John River in May 1783. Chapters open with cannon roaring, come and take it, and Cupid's arrow, then warnings, bow-strings, and storms. Plotter councils, King's Rangers, smoke signals, and tempered punishment follow, through wilderness and desperate straits.

Cody writes of the loyalist flight and settlement with warmth for his forebears. The tale mixes love, war, and frontier hardship. Readers of Canadian historical fiction will find a stirring story of loyalty, exile, and new homes on the St. John.
16728-a-catechism-of-familiar-things-the:
Benziger Brothers issued this enlarged 1881 school and home book in question-and-answer form. It tells the past of common things and the steps that led to their finding, with short notes on key facts of nature. Recent tools and gains of the day get plain, simple treatment, and hard words are defined where they first appear.

Teachers and parents used it to give children plain facts about the world they touched each day. Inventors and men of science get short lives, and the tone stays clear and direct. The book now reads as a window on what 1800s schools thought every child should know about tools, nature, and daily life.
16892-samuel-rutherford-and-some-of-his-:
Alexander Whyte gave these lectures on Samuel Rutherford and some of his correspondents at St. George's Free Church in Edinburgh, issued by Oliphant, Anderson and Ferrier in 1894. The first lecture, Joshua Redivivus, opens with a small vellum book of Rutherford's letters, printed in 1664 for folk put to suffering for Christ. Rutherford was born in south Scotland in 1600.

Whyte sets Rutherford beside Goodwin, Leighton, Baxter, Owen, Bunyan, and Howe, all born within a generation. He reads the letters as seraphic, full of faith under pain. The book suits readers of Scottish church history who want Rutherford's circle, his letters, and his suffering faith in a warm, scholarly voice.
17055-the-submarine-boys-trial-trip-maki:
Victor G. Durham's second Submarine Boys book, from 1909, follows Jack and his mates as they prove themselves as young submarine experts. The Pollard, their boat, faces a rival, a missing crew scare, and a crash hurled by Mr. Melville, while Farnum stock rises and falls with each trial. A race for prizes, a mutiny scare, and a practical sea joke fill the middle chapters.

The boys serve in the cause of peace, not war, and their trials test nerve, skill, and fair play. Durham writes in brisk, boyish prose with plenty of shop and sea detail. Young readers who like early tech adventure will enjoy this tale of a new machine and the lads who learned to run it.
17188-buccaneers-and-pirates-of-our-coas:
Frank R. Stockton's 1897 book tells pirate tales of American coasts for young readers, with pictures including pirates climbing a man-of-war like twenty-nine cats. Chapters cover bold buccaneers, masters and pupils in piracy, Peter the Great, a pearl pirate, and the surprising adventures of Bartholemy Portuguez. A pirate who could not swim and a pirate author add humor to the set.

Stockton writes in clear, lively prose, mixing history with yarns of raids, escapes, and treasure. The book suits boys and girls who like sea adventure without gore. It remains a classic first pirate history, where daring deeds and odd characters carry each short chapter.
17203-witchcraft-and-devil-lore-in-the-c:
John Linwood Pitts's 1886 book prints transcripts from Guernsey Royal Court records on witchcraft and devil lore, with an English translation and a historical introduction. The set covers the witches' sabbath, the devil's ointment, three women burnt for heresy, Jersey ordinances, hangings, pricking of witches, and torture in Guernsey and Scotland. Confessions of Collette Du Mont and Marie and Isabel Becquet follow.

Pitts dedicates the book to Edgar MacCulloch, Bailiff of Guernsey, whose research lit the island's old constitution. Trials from 1563 to 1634 close the record. Historians of witch trials will find a sober, source-based book on a dark chapter, told from court papers rather than legend.
17218-the-black-cat-a-play-in-three-acts:
John Todhunter's Black Cat, a play in three acts, was first acted at London's Independent Theatre, at the Opera Comique on December 8, 1893. Todhunter's preface notes critics praised it, some with reckless enthusiasm, and objected that its tragic ending seemed tacked on to a comedy. He answers that the end was foreseen from the start, with tragedy implicit in the subject itself.

The play was not performed again after that special audience, which makes this text a rare survival of the Independent stage. Its mix of comedy and fate suits readers of late Victorian drama. Theatre historians will value a short, curious play where a light start darkens into a symbolic close.
17448-the-auld-doctor-and-other-poems-an:
David Rorie, a medical doctor, gathered these poems and songs in Scots, the speech of lowland Scotland. The title piece, The Auld Doctor, leads a set that includes The Crambo-Clink, The Lum Hat Wantin' the Croon, The Pawky Duke, Macfadden and Macfee, Tam and the Leeches, and The Howdie. Several pieces had first appeared in student magazines and medical journals.

Rorie opens by refusing grand, lofty verse about higher things, and his poems keep to plain, comic, and local ground instead. Doctors, patients, country folk, and student life supply the humour, all in broad Scots. Readers get a lively corner of Scottish verse, best read aloud, where a doctor-poet turns daily life into song.
17463-great-violinists-and-pianists:
George T. Ferris published this small book of lives of great violinists and pianists in 1881 with D. Appleton and Company. His note warns that the title may mislead, since he makes no attempt to cover the immense field of executive music. He calls attention only to those musical celebrities universally recognised as occupying the most exalted places in violin and pianoforte playing, landmarks in the history of music.

Readers get short, vivid portraits of the great players, chosen for fame rather than completeness. The book suits music lovers who want the leading names and their stories in compact form. Its selections show which players Victorians held highest.
1756-uncle-vanya-scenes-from-country-lif:
A retired professor named Alexander Serebrakoff comes back to the country estate his first wife's family kept for him, bringing a young wife and a long list of complaints. Vanya, who has run the estate for years, and Sonia, the professor's daughter, watch their work and their hopes shrink under the old man's complaints and demands.

The play turns on unspoken love, wasted years, and the question of whether anything can still change. Chekhov gives no villains and no rescues, only people who talk past each other and then return to their ledgers. Its final scene, with Sonia urging Vanya to endure, is one of the most quoted endings in modern drama.
17581-the-romancers-a-comedy-in-three-ac:
Edmond Rostand wrote this comedy in three acts, Les Romanesques, translated by Barrett H. Clark and published in 1915. Rostand, born at Marseilles in 1868, ranks among the most brilliant dramatic poets of modern times, in the judgment of the edition's introductory notes. The play was first performed in Paris at the Comedie Francaise in 1894, with considerable success.

Its delicacy and charm revealed the true poet, and the deftness of its plot handling won praise. Readers get a light, romantic comedy of young lovers and parental scheming, in Clark's readable translation. The play suits readers of French drama and of Rostand beyond Cyrano.
17926-fians-fairies-and-picts:
David MacRitchie wrote Fians, Fairies and Picts in London in 1893, restating a theory he had pushed for a dozen years. He held that fairy lore in the Highlands kept a dim memory of a real, small, dark people who once lived in caves and earth houses.

The book opens with underground galleries in the isles, then turns to the tales of J. F. Campbell and the old Pictish folk. MacRitchie argues, with charm and care, that stones and stories can speak of lost tribes. Modern scholars now doubt his case, but the book stays a lively, learned look at how folklore may hide real history.
17944-the-house-of-rimmon-a-drama-in-fou:
Henry Van Dyke wrote The House of Rimmon as a drama in four acts, put out in New York by Scribner's in 1908. The scene is Damascus and the hills of Samaria in 850 B.C., and the cast joins kings, priests, soldiers, and prophets of the old Bible world.

Benhadad rules Damascus, Rezon serves as high priest of Rimmon, and Naaman leads the armies, with Elisha the prophet of Israel set against them. A captive maid of Israel, Ruahmah, stands at the heart of the play. Van Dyke's verse drama asks how faith and power meet, and it reads as a stately, old-style stage piece on an ancient tale.
17964-olympian-nights:
John Kendrick Bangs wrote Olympian Nights in 1902, a comic fantasy in which a modern man climbs Mount Olympus and finds the gods living like grand hotel guests. Bangs had already sent a house-boat to the Styx, and here he turns the same jest on the Greek gods.

Chapters take the hero to shelter, an elevator boy, a valet, the Olympian links, the dining room, the zoo, and the palace of Jupiter. He meets a doctor named Aesculapius and gods who talk trade, sport, and gossip. The book is light, witty fun, a spoof of both myth and modern life, best read as a clever holiday from grave books.
18013-representation-of-deities-of-the-m:
Dr. Paul Schellhas wrote Representation of Deities of the Maya Manuscripts, printed by Harvard's Peabody Museum in December 1904, in a second revised edition. Selma Wesselhoeft and A. M. Parker turned the German text into English, with Schellhas revising the translation.

The paper, with one plate and sixty-five text pictures, seeks to name the gods drawn in the Maya books, so students can read the glyphs aright. The Peabody Museum chose it as the first in a line of short, key translations. It is a learned, early study of Maya religion, still useful for students of the ancient American books.
18285-tales-from-the-hindu-dramatists:
R. N. Dutta, late headmaster of the Metropolitan Institution at Bowbazar, Calcutta, retold tales from the Hindu dramatists for English readers. J. S. Zemin, professor of English literature at Bishop's College, revised the volume, published at Calcutta in 1912 by B. Banerjee and Company. Dutta, author of The Boy's Ramayana, dedicates the book to Justice Ashutosh Mookerjee of Calcutta.

The tales draw on classical Indian drama, turning stage plays into prose stories that keep their plots, characters, and morals. Readers who know the Ramayana from Dutta's earlier book will find a companion here: gods, kings, lovers, and sages in stories shaped for the stage and now retold for the home. The volume serves as an entry to Sanskrit drama without demanding a scholar's training.
18364-my-war-experiences-in-two-continen:
S. Macnaughtan wrote this memoir of war work on two continents, drawn from service with ambulance and relief units in the First World War. The volume opens in Belgium, with Antwerp, Dr. Hector Munro's Flying Ambulance Corps, Furnes railway station, work under difficulties, the spring offensive, and last days in Flanders. A middle part tells how the message was delivered at home.

A third part carries the writer to Russia and the Persian front, where the war took a different shape. Macnaughtan writes as a woman worker near the fighting, not as a general: stations, wounded, shortages, and long journeys mark her pages. Readers get the war from the ambulance side, in Belgium first and then in the east, where distance and hardship tested every plan.
18598-stories-of-achievement-volume-iv-a:
Asa Don Dickinson edited this fourth volume of a series on people who rose by hard work, first printed in 1916. It holds ten short life stories, from Jean Jacques Rousseau and Robert Burns to Charles Dickens, Louisa May Alcott, and Helen Keller. Each sketch draws on its subject's own words and early setbacks.

Readers meet a farm boy turned editor in Horace Greeley, a factory boy in Dickens, and a country parson's daughter in Charlotte Bronte. Later sketches follow Jacob Riis, Henry George, and William Rideing through poor jobs and rejected work. Together they give an easy first look at how skill, grit, and chance shaped ten writing careers.
1868-penelope-s-postscripts:
Penelope, the American traveller of a generation earlier, writes again — later journeys, new friends, old places revisited, and the same bright, observant voice. The postscripts follow her later journeys, in the company of new friends, among old places revisited, and in the same bright, observant voice.

A passage on Peppina, who would have made an admirable Borgia had she been born in the right class and century, shows Wiggin's gift for comic portraiture. Beppo's stinging verse reproof to Peppina shows her ear for social comedy. The book is a fond farewell to a favorite heroine, written for readers who had grown up with Penelope and wanted one more letter from her.
18705-the-poor-plutocrats:
Maurus Jókai's Hungarian novel, translated by R. Nisbet Bain and published by Doubleday, Page in 1899, opens on an old gentleman in his eightieth year, rich in rings and wrapped in a flowered silk kaftan. Around him sit members of his household, including a card-playing young woman, a frail sixteen-year-old girl, and the spinster Clementina, whose yawn starts the scene.

Later chapters carry the household through duels, a bride brought home, a cavern, a maid-market, black jewelry, and a fight for gold. The title's joke runs through it all: wealth here brings boredom, quarrels, and worry rather than ease. Jókai tells the tale with broad comedy and a keen eye for vanity and family pride.
18766-early-reviews-of-english-poets:
John Louis Haney edited this 1904 volume of early reviews of English poets for the Egerton Press of Philadelphia. It reprints what the great periodicals said when new poems first appeared, from Gray's Odes in the Monthly Review to Browning's Men and Women in the Saturday Review.

Between them stand Goldsmith, Cowper, Burns, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Southey, Lamb, Landor, Scott, Byron, Shelley, Keats, and Tennyson, judged by the Critical Review, Edinburgh Review, Quarterly Review, Blackwood's, and others. Haney's introduction traces the literary journal from London's Civil War Mercurii to the Journal des Sçavans of Paris in 1665. The book lets readers hear the first verdicts on poems now counted as classics.
18809-recollections-of-the-late-william-:
Charlotte Lansdown edited these recollections from letters her father wrote after meeting William Beckford, publishing them in 1893, fifty years after Beckford's death. Her father had meant to publish at once in 1844 but delayed, and his daughter brought the manuscript out to correct false notions of Beckford's character.

The letters describe a visit in August 1838 to Beckford's house in Lansdown Crescent, Bath, where a plain exterior hid a dazzling collection of paintings and works of art. They present Beckford as the author of Vathek, the builder of Fonthill, and a pupil of Mozart, a man of extraordinary memory and wide reading. The book offers a friendly, first-hand portrait of a figure many knew only by rumor.
18935-vanity-all-is-vanity-a-lecture-on-:
Elder J. J. Cranmer, editor of the Gospel Monitor in Hannibal, Missouri, issued this lecture against tobacco under the title Vanity, All Is Vanity. He frames the habit as a form of bondage, arguing that it taxes body, mind, and pocket daily and hourly. His text draws on ideas about nature's laws and the mind's control over the body in sickness and health.

Cranmer urges readers to break free from a habit he presents as costly, foolish, and harmful to health. The lecture mixes moral warning with plain talk about money spent and strength lost. Readers get a vivid sample of nineteenth-century temperance preaching, direct in tone and aimed at persuading ordinary smokers to quit.
19028-irish-plays-and-playwrights:
Cornelius Weygandt published this study in Boston and New York in 1913, with Houghton Mifflin. It treats the Celtic Renaissance in the Irish theatre, opening with the movement itself, then the players, their plays, their audience, and their art. Chapters follow the leading figures one by one, with an appendix of plays produced in Dublin.

William Butler Yeats, Edward Martyn, George Moore, George Russell under the name A. E., Lady Gregory, and John Millington Synge each receive a chapter. Younger dramatists, including Padraic Colum and Lennox Robinson, and William Sharp as Fiona Macleod, complete the survey. Readers get a contemporary guide to the Abbey Theatre generation, written while its triumphs were fresh.
19038-english-walnuts:
Walter Fox Allen compiled this 1912 guide to English walnuts, on planting, growing, and harvesting what he calls the most delicious of nuts. It gathers advice from growers and experiment stations, with notes on trees, soil, and seasons. The foreword sets out its practical aim.

A Michigan station writer weighs fall against spring planting, noting that fall trees root before winter but risk cold injury, while spring work is often rushed and careless. Thirty-year-old parent trees are shown as proof of long value. Growers get a short, useful handbook for a slow but rewarding crop.
19051-modern-religious-cults-and-movemen:
Gaius Glenn Atkins's 1923 study Modern Religious Cults and Movements examines the new religious movements that had come to prominence in the preceding decades. They include faith healing, Christian Science, New Thought, Theosophy, and Spiritualism. Atkins sets those movements against a wider account of Christianity, contrasting Catholic authority and Protestant faith with the newer groups' claims.

The book argues that many people withdrew from organized churches because they found conventional Christianity socially sterile. The new movements answered a restless craving for direct spiritual experience and practical results. Atkins surveys their teachings, their appeal, and their weaknesses with clarity and sympathy, while holding to classic Christian belief. The volume remains a useful early survey of American religious innovation, written when the movements it describes were still fresh.
19104-secret-societies-and-subversive-mo:
Nesta H. Webster wrote this study of secret societies and subversive movements, dividing past from present. It opens with Disraeli's 1856 speech in the Commons on a network of secret societies covering Italy, France, and much of Germany, bent on changing land tenure and ending church establishments. Webster treats such groups as a hidden power in history.

Later chapters turn to Cabala texts, the Sepher Yetzirah and the Zohar, tracing doctrines of emanations, numbers, and Hebrew letters through centuries of debate. Readers get a controversial, wide-ranging work on conspiracy and occult lore, best read as a document of its author's fears and theories.
1917-the-queen-of-hearts:
Wilkie Collins's Queen of Hearts gathers ten stories told over ten days by the brothers of a household. They are framed by a letter of dedication and chapters called Ourselves, Our Dilemma, Our Queen of Hearts, and Our Grand Project. Brother Owen's story of the siege of the Black Cottage opens the telling.

The tales that follow mix mystery, horror, and comedy, with a woman drawing a knife from her sleeve and watching a sleeper by his bed among the most vivid scenes. Collins writes the frame with warmth. The collection works as a showcase: ten short novels in miniature, each with its own turn, held together by a family telling stories to pass the time.
19179-kelly-miller-s-history-of-the-worl:
Kelly Miller, dean at Howard University, wrote this 1919 history of the World War for human rights, with contributions by General Pershing and others. It tells why America entered, what the Allies fought for, and the part taken by Black soldiers and sailors in defeating Germany. Official photographs illustrate new weapons and war methods.

Chapters cover nations at war, trench life with rats and disease, women in factories and ambulances, the terrible price in men and money, and world rulers from Wilson to the Kaiser. Readers get a powerful, proud account of Black service and the war for freedom, in the voice of its time.
19387-the-outcasts:
W. A. Fraser wrote this animal tale of the Canadian north, published in New York at the start of the nineteen hundreds with pictures by Arthur Heming. A'tim, a dog who speaks the talk of the Cree, is cast out among wolves and must learn their ways to live, while Shag the bear carries a dog-wolf on his back.

Scenes of hunger, theft from tents, and a slaughter pen at a Blood Indian corral give the story its hard edge. Told from the beasts' view, it is a northern adventure about belonging: what it costs to leave one's own kind and survive among strangers.
19458-the-loyalists:
Jane West wrote this historical novel in three volumes, published in London in the early eighteen hundreds. Its motto urges readers to hold loyalty and defend rights, and its story defends church and king against the spirit of revolt. The opening warns plainly that this is old English fare, not modern French cookery.

Through families, clergy, and debates on faith and rule, West argues that loyalty shapes sound minds as surely as good food builds strong bodies. The novel is a partisan work of its age, useful today for how conservatives of the time framed their case in fiction.
19484-editorial-wild-oats:
Mark Twain gathered these early pieces on editing and journalism, published in New York and London in the early nineteen hundreds. They cover his first literary venture, journalism in Tennessee, a printer named Nicodemus Dodge, and his famous stint editing an agricultural paper.

The humor comes from mismatch: a green editor solemnly advising farmers, and a local paper turning a Roman murder into hometown news. These wild oats show Twain learning his trade, and they remain among his funniest sketches of print life. Village jokers hide a skeleton in Nicodemus's bed, then watch him play Camptown Races on a paper-covered comb.
19605-a-book-of-quaker-saints:
L. V. Hodgkin wrote this book of Quaker saints, tales of early Friends told for younger readers, with pictures. Its heroes suffer prison, beatings, and threats with calm courage: one jailed Friend answers a jailer's wife who swore to have his blood by saying he would not have hers.

Letters from the time, such as James's note from the assizes, give the stories a documentary root. The book honors a tradition of patient witness, and it remains a warm introduction to Quaker history for children and newcomers alike. Later tales include the Angel of Beverley, the man in leather breeches, and the shepherd of Pendle Hill.
19724-home-pastimes-or-tableaux-vivants:
Tableaux vivants are living pictures: costumed people holding still as famous scenes. J. H. Head's Home Pastimes teaches families how to stage them at home. The book opens on the nature of a perfect picture. It claims such pictures are appreciated wherever they are shown. Poetic feeling, it argues, shows itself the same way everywhere.

Parlor entertainment mattered before radio filled the evenings. A good tableau needed costumes, poses, curtains, and nerve. Head gives home players the craft behind the trick. Readers learn how Victorian families amused their guests. The book also preserves period taste in scenes and dress. It is a handbook from the age of the drawing-room stage.
19740-make-your-own-hats:
Gene Allen Martin wrote this practical guide to making your own hats, published in the early nineteen twenties with pictures. It teaches home millinery step by step, for readers who want smart hats without shop prices.

The book belongs to a wave of do-it-yourself manuals for women after the Great War, when thrift and style met. Its plain directions and patterns made hat making a parlour craft, and it still charms as a record of home fashion. Martin taught millinery at a city school, so her directions suit beginners well. For a brim, eight creases mark the place of eight wire spokes, a plain rule the guide spells out.
19860-the-arabian-nights-entertainments:
The Arabian Nights Entertainments gathers the tales of the Thousand and One Nights. This 1914 edition traces the collection's deep roots. Tenth-century Arabic writers already mention a Persian book called The Thousand Nights. In it, Scheherazade wins one more day of life with each tale. Many stories show Persian or Hindu origins beneath Arabic dress. Aladdin, Sindbad, and Ali Baba live in this tradition.

No single author made the Nights; centuries of tellers did. Frame story, genies, and Baghdad streets bind hundreds of tales. English readers met them through many translations and selections. The collection shaped Western dreams of the East profoundly. It also preserves folk tales of real antiquity. Every edition is a door into that shared story-hoard.
19870-illuminated-manuscripts:
Illuminated Manuscripts introduces the art of hand-decorated books. It begins from a broad claim: the desire for decoration is as old as the human race. Nature is the source of beauty, the author argues. Something in us reproduces felt beauty in material form. That reproduction may appeal to eye or ear. Medieval gold-leaf pages are the book's great exhibit.

John W. Bradley wrote standard handbooks on medieval art crafts. Illumination joined painting, calligraphy, and goldsmith work in one page. This guide explains styles, pigments, and famous examples. It served the Victorian revival of manuscript arts. Kelmscott Press designs drew on the same love. The book remains a friendly doorway into the scriptorium.
19978-35-sonnets:
Fernando Pessoa wrote his 35 Sonnets in English, publishing them in Lisbon in 1918. One sonnet here thinks on a long-dead beloved. The speaker could not think of her as mere rotted dust. She had been long dead, yet lived entire in his seeing thought. What she was in him had never fled, he insists. The argument turns grief into metaphysics in fourteen lines.

Pessoa, Portugal's great modernist, wrote under many invented authors, called heteronyms. The sonnets are signed with his own name yet feel Shakespeare-haunted. Their English is deliberately archaic and knotted. Readers watch a Portuguese genius wrestle English tradition itself. These thirty-five poems are small, dense, and strange. They reward the slowest possible reading.
2-the-united-states-bill-of-rights-the-t:
Ten short amendments set hard limits on federal power in the young United States. Passed by Congress in September 1789 and ratified in December 1791, they form the Bill of Rights. The first amendment guards speech, press, assembly, and petition.

Later amendments cover arms, quartering, searches, and criminal trials. They bar double jeopardy, forced self-incrimination, and taking property without due process. Unlisted rights stay with the people, and undelegated powers stay with the states. Together, the ten form the core charter of American liberty. The amendments still shape court cases on speech, guns, searches, and fair trials today.
20161-sophisms-of-the-protectionists:
Sophisms of the Protectionists attacks the case for tariffs that guard home trade. A sophism is a slick argument that sounds true but is not. Free traders offered this small book at the cost of printing. They urged each reader to hand a copy to protectionist friends.

That push shows how hot the tariff fight ran in its day. Cheap imports, jobs, and prices all hung on the debate then. The book answers guard-trade claims point by point in plain words. Readers get a neat fossil of a fight that still echoes in trade politics.
20176-the-drone-a-play-in-three-acts:
Rutherford Mayne wrote The Drone, a play in three acts, published in 1912. An elderly man with a gloomy face enters a kitchen slowly. Sly humor in his eyes relieves that gloom at once. He looks at Kate, then scans the dresser with a disgusted shake.

Mayne wrote Irish plays that mix rural talk with sharp character study. A drone, in hive terms, is one who lives off others' work. That charge hangs over the men in this kitchen drama. Readers get Ulster speech, family friction, and humor with a sting in it.
20177-john-bull-or-the-englishman-s-fire:
George Colman the Younger wrote John Bull, a comedy in five acts, for the English stage. Colman defends true comedy against the pull of broad farce. Farce, he argues, has trained crowds to love hearty laughter alone. Smiles, by contrast, are now scorned as weak and insipid fare.
