John Bull stands for the plain Englishman in this lively play. Colman sought a picture from real life, not mere caricature on stage. His comedy turns on money, class, and bluster in English homes. Readers get Georgian theatre with wit aimed at national pride itself.
20217-the-stranger-a-drama-in-five-acts:
The Stranger is a drama in five acts, a stage play of faith and doubt. Its preface warns how sacred faith is often badly taught in schools. Pious but ignorant teaching can breed the very doubts it fears. Infidelity may be sown where teachers meant to root it out.

Such a charge sets a grave tone for the drama that follows. A stranger's arrival in plays of this kind often tests a whole town. Belief, love, and hidden pasts tend to collide around such a figure. Readers get a serious period drama on faith taught well or ill.
20450-the-lives-of-the-fathers-martyrs-a:
The Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs, and Other Principal Saints is the great English collection of saints' lives, first made by Alban Butler. This edition adds lives written since the author's death. It aims to give readers a saint for study across the whole church year.

The editors worked to render the collection as complete as possible. They added the life of Saint Alphonsus Liguori and other saints canonized after Butler died, lives found in no earlier form of the work. Generations of Catholic readers used these volumes for daily devotion and for the stories behind feast days.
20537-the-argonauts: The Argonauts takes its title from the old seekers of the golden fleece and applies it to modern hunters of wealth. Its pages describe men working options and exchanges in many markets and corporations. Such men, the book says, need opposite qualities at once. They need the courage of the lion, the caution of the fox, and the talons of the falcon.
20543-edward-fitzgerald-and-posh-herring:
James Blyth's Edward FitzGerald and Posh tells the story of a strange friendship. FitzGerald, the poet of Omar Khayyam, grew close to Joseph Fletcher, a Lowestoft herring merchant nicknamed Posh. Blyth prints their connection and letters for the first time.

With the exception of Charles Lamb, Blyth writes, no man's letters have endeared his memory to so many readers. But the letters published before were written to cultured gentlemen, men of FitzGerald's own world. Posh was different: a working merchant of the herring fleet. The book shows the poet's warmth across the barriers of class.
20755-short-studies-on-great-subjects:
History, says the voice in Short Studies on Great Subjects, can look like a child's box of letters. We pick the letters we like, spell the word we want, and hide the rest. That sharp image opens a set of essays on grand themes.

James Anthony Froude, the famed historian, wrote studies of this kind with bold sweep. Faith, rule, sea power, and great lives pass under his gaze. He writes as a thinker, not a mere keeper of facts. Readers who like strong views in fine prose will find his essays both grand in scope and open to sharp debate.
20989-a-comedy-of-errors-in-seven-acts:
Tyrants crush distant isles and bend a worthy race under a foreign yoke, this verse drama cries. A noble charge waits within thy grasp, its speaker urges in high, old tones. A Comedy of Errors in Seven Acts speaks in that grave stage dress.

Verse, tyranny, and a helpless people's plea mark this odd, earnest play. Its seven acts promise error and tangle on a grand scale. Little is known of its stage life beyond its printed page. The book stands as a curio of amateur drama, where lofty verse and bold claims far outrun the footlights it likely never met.
212-a-list-of-factorial-math-constants:
Factorials grow fast, and this file prints them from one to ten thousand. The list gives 1 through 99 factorial by ones, 100 through 900 by hundreds, and 1000 through 10000 by thousands. Each entry notes the digit count at its end.

A simple Scheme program computed the values, though its source code has since been lost. Mathematicians and programmers use such tables to check big-number arithmetic. The file's plain layout makes any value easy to find. It serves as a raw numeric reference, not a textbook. Students of combinatorics still cite such tables when exact values matter.
21211-silverpoints:
John Gray's Silverpoints is a slim book of delicate, highly wrought poems. Elkin Mathews and John Lane published it in London in 1893 at the Bodley Head. Many carry French dedications and titles. The opening piece follows courtly ladies through an orchard, bending under low, forked branches over dew-soaked grass.

Gray was linked with the decadent writers of the 1890s, and these poems favour rare words, fine images, and slow, languid movement. A poem to Paul Verlaine appears among them. In the printed book the verse was set in italics, a design flourish this text edition notes but cannot show. Silverpoints remains Gray's best-known collection.
21253-the-swedish-norwegian-union-crisis:
K. Nordlund published this history with documents at Uppsala and Stockholm in 1905, the year Norway broke its union with Sweden. He promises a condensed account of the last few years plus extracts from the key documents. The consular question, whether Norway could have its own consuls, sits at the centre of the quarrel.

Nordlund writes from the Swedish side, answering a brochure by Fridtjof Nansen and accusing Norwegian agitation of mishandling plain facts. He traces the crisis back to the union's founding in 1814. Read today, the book shows how a constitutional dispute over trade officials nearly brought two kingdoms to war.
21396-the-three-lieutenants:
Three young officers of the Royal Navy meet again in W. H. G. Kingston's The Three Lieutenants. The book is the second in a set that begins with The Three Midshipmen. It shows life in the navy of the 1860s, when the three friends now hold higher rank.

By a happy chance, their postings let them serve near each other once more. Old Admiral Triton, now retired, still follows their careers with pride. Kingston first won fame with these books, which came out in weekly parts. Sea service, friendship, and fresh adventure fill this long tale, which ends with The Three Admirals.
21401-in-new-granada-or-heroes-and-patri:
South America's wars for freedom from Spain form the ground of W. H. G. Kingston's In New Granada. The narrator's father came from an old Covenanter family in Dumfriesshire, one of six sons. Most of those sons had to seek their luck in the wide world.

English folk are caught up in the fight of the Patriots against Spanish rule. The tale shows camp, march, and clash across a whole small country. Kingston sides with the cause of freedom, and he draws the Spanish as harsh foes. Travel, battle, and close escapes carry the story from one end of the land to the other.
21442-your-plants:
James Sheehan gives plain help for home growers in Your Plants, first entered for copyright in 1884. The full title promises care of tender and hardy plants in house and garden. The idea came to Sheehan at a large meeting of florists in western New York.

Early chapters treat lawns, potting soils, bought feeds, and the sowing of seeds. Later ones cover watering, winter storage in cellars, and the law of colour in flowers. Sheehan also explains layering, cuttings, and grafting in short, clear steps. The Orange Judd reprint of 1919 kept the book in reach of home gardeners.
21515-venice-preserved-a-tragedy-in-five:
Thomas Otway's Venice Preserved, a tragedy in five acts, is given here in an 1874 acting edition. Dio Boucicault revised the text for Booth's Theatre, with stage business, casts, and dress lists. Jaffier, Pierre, and Belvidera wear rich Venetian garb, down to plumes and rosettes.

The play turns on a plot against the senate of Venice and a friend torn two ways. Jaffier must choose between his fellow plotters and the wife he loves. The preface notes how Otway built a great work from a few thin facts of history. Few English tragedies of his age have held the stage so well.
21531-woodwork-joints:
Woodwork Joints, in the Woodworker series, teaches how joints are set out, made, and used. Four hundred pictures back the text, and an index closes the revised edition. The editor calls the range of joints unmatched in any prior book of its kind.

Teachers of handicraft get exercises of real use for class work at every level. The book treats the two secrets of good building: knowing how, and knowing why. Companion volumes in the series cover tools, staining, turning, and carving. For home workers and pros alike, the joint is where craft stands or falls, and this guide takes it joint by joint.
21570-the-squire-an-original-comedy-in-t:
Arthur W. Pinero's comedy The Squire first played at the St James's Theatre on December 29, 1881. This edition, copyrighted in 1905, prints the cast of that first night. Mrs Kendal played Kate Verity, and Mr Kendal played Lieutenant Thorndyke.

The scene is a decayed, weather-beaten Elizabethan mansion, ivy over broken stone. A secret marriage drives the first act, in a village of clergy, officers, gossips, and watchful kin. A reporter from the Pagley Mercury pokes into local affairs. Pinero, then a rising playwright, mixes romance, family secrets, and village comedy in three neat, well-made acts.
21583-children-of-the-tenements:
Jacob A. Riis tells tales of New York's poorest children in Children of the Tenements, copyrighted in 1897 and issued in 1903. Riis had written How the Other Half Lives and The Battle with the Slum. Pictures by C. M. Relyea and others show the world he describes.

Adam Grunschlag sits at his street stand in falling snow, lost in thought. Around him the holiday bustle grows, and he heeds none of it. Story by story, Riis shows barefoot kids in passageways and families crammed in dark rooms. His tales plead, without preaching, for the children the rich city forgot.
21820-oh-susannah-a-farcical-comedy-in-t:
A doctor's consulting room in Pimlico is the single scene of Oh! Susannah!, a farcical comedy in three acts by Mark Ambient. The play ran first at the Eden Theatre, Brighton, in September 1897, then at the Royalty in London. Its action is continuous, from four to six on a Lady Day afternoon. The three acts take under two hours in the playing.

The printed text gives the full stage world: whiskey decanter, medical chest, surgical knives, microscope, and a detective camera shaped like a turnip watch. Farce needs its props, and Ambient lists them all. The dialogue runs in servants' slang and drawing-room polish. It is a tidy relic of the light London stage of the 1890s.
21849-the-mind-the-paint-girl-a-comedy-i:
London's smart set talks, flirts, and schemes in The Mind the Paint Girl, a comedy in four acts by Arthur Wing Pinero, published in 1912. The cast list alone tells the story's world. A viscount, a colonel, and a German baron mix with an actress's manager and a crowd of young men about town. Pinero's name heads a long shelf of stage hits, from The Second Mrs. Tanqueray to Trelawny of the Wells.

The title comes from a warning cry in painters' studios, turned here toward a girl of the stage. Pinero builds his comedy on manners, money, and the fear of a wet-paint reputation. The printed play keeps the third-act song in full. It shows the master of the well-made play near the end of his reign.
21865-king-arthur-and-his-knights:
Arthur pulls the sword and gathers his knights in Maude L. Radford's King Arthur and His Knights, published at Chicago in 1903. Walter J. Enright's pictures show the king, the Round Table, and the Holy Grail. The tales run in order: Arthur made king, Excalibur won, Guinevere wed, and Gareth come to court unknown. Lancelot, Balin, Geraint, and Enid each take their turn at the center.

Radford retells the old legends in clear prose pitched to young readers. The search for the Holy Grail and the death of Arthur close the book, as they must. She keeps the wonder and trims the tangle. For many American children, this was the first door into Camelot, and it opens easily still.
21928-light-freights:
A night-watchman on a wharf holds court in W. W. Jacobs's Light Freights, a book of comic tales from 1901. Speaking of money, the watchman says, the world would be brighter if we all had more of it. Then he admits that being short sharpens people, and tells of the sharpest man he ever knew, who never had a ha'penny. That voice, thoughtful and sly, frames tale after tale.

The stories bear titles like Hard Labour, A Garden Plot, and The Resurrection of Mr. Wiggett. Jacobs peoples them with sailors, skippers, and schemers along the Thames. His dialogue, thick with dropped aitches, carries the comedy. Light Freights is Jacobs in his prime form: short, dry tales where human nature is the cargo and folly pays the freight.
21932-embarrassments:
Four long tales by Henry James make up Embarrassments, published in 1896, and each turns on a delicate social or artistic knot. The Figure in the Carpet opens the book: a young critic is set to review Hugh Vereker's new novel for The Middle. His friend Corvick came breathless with the task, and the critic pounces on the advance copy. Inside Vereker's work hides a secret figure, and the hunt for it drives the tale.

Glasses, The Next Time, and The Way It Came follow, studies of sight, failure, and return. James writes of writers and their readers with a surgeon's calm. The title is exact: everyone here is caught in some fine, painful awkwardness. These are among his most perfect shorter works, built from talk, glances, and the things people cannot say.
21936-theft-a-play-in-four-acts:
Washington power and a stolen document drive Jack London's play Theft, written in 1910 and set across twenty hours in the capital. Senator Chalmers's wife Margaret stands at the center: twenty-seven, intellectual, womanly, and capable of sudden hardness. Against her father's house stands Howard Knox, a congressman from Oregon with a vision he has followed through abuse and ridicule. The magnate Anthony Starkweather, Margaret's father, holds the purse of the piece.

London, the novelist of the Klondike and the sea, turns to the stage with a socialist's brief. Labor agitators, embassy secretaries, and ministers crowd his cast list. The theft of the title is both a crime and an accusation about wealth itself. It is a fiery, talky period play, more argued than acted in its afterlife.
22112-a-child-s-book-of-saints:
William Canton retold the lives of the saints for young readers in A Child's Book of Saints. Canton, a poet and historian of the Bible Society, had a gift for simple, musical English. His saints are presented as friends and heroes for children to love. Martyrs, hermits, kings, and maidens appear in short, clear chapters.

Each life stresses a single virtue: courage, patience, charity, or faith under scorn. Canton avoids both gore and dryness, keeping wonder in the tales. The book came from an age when saints' stories were standard nursery reading across Britain. It remains a graceful sample of Victorian and Edwardian religious writing for the young.
22293-three-margarets:
Laura E. Richards, daughter of Julia Ward Howe, published Three Margarets in 1897 for girl readers. A pleasant summer rain opens the book, plashing on elms and locusts and tinkling in roadside puddles. On the roof of a great landau rolling toward Fernley House the rain drums less musically. Inside, three girls ride buried in their own thoughts, and each of them is Margaret.

Cousins with one name and three temperaments must live together for a season. Richards builds the story from their contrasts, quarrels, and reconciliations. Her girls' books were famous for sense and humour without preaching. Three Margarets is a gentle specimen, written in her mother's long shadow and her own clear voice.
22314-mysticism-and-its-results:
Mysticism and Its Results is a short book that gathers facts outside the usual range of reading. Its writer asks for the reader's patience at the start. The essay, he says, is suggestive rather than didactic.

That modesty sets the book's method and aim. It does not claim to settle its subject once for all. Instead, it hopes to induce thought, study, or research in honest minds. If it does only that, the writer says, its object will be attained. Readers get an invitation rather than a lecture: a small, earnest case that mystical experience deserves serious, open attention.
22485-devon-its-moorlands-streams-and-co:
Lady Rosalind Northcote wrote Devon: Its Moorlands, Streams, and Coasts. Her book guides readers through England's great western county. Even its opening quotes Shakespeare on Exeter's old castle, Rougemont.

When last at Exeter, the quoted lines run, the mayor showed the castle. He called it Rougemont, at which name the speaker started. An Irish bard had warned he would not live long after seeing Richmond. Such lore flavors Northcote's tour of her home county. Moorland, stream, and coast each get their chapters of attention. Readers get Edwardian local writing at its proudest. Devon appears as history, scenery, and home ground together.
22685-the-classification-of-patents:
The Classification of Patents is a treatise on how patent offices sort inventions into classes so that examiners and inventors can find what came before. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Behind the dry title stands a real problem: hundreds of thousands of patents, useless unless a searcher can find the right shelf.

The author begins at the root: classification lies at the foundation of all mental process. Without seeing resemblances and differences, and grouping things by them, judgment itself is impossible, and reason cannot move from the known to the unknown. From that philosophy the book descends to bins, subclasses, and search practice. It will interest students of information science, who may recognize an early theory of their own field wearing legal dress.
22784-on-laboratory-arts:
Richard Threlfall wrote On Laboratory Arts, a handbook of the mechanical skills behind experimental physics. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Threlfall, an Australian physicist, held that great experiments rest on humble crafts: glassblowing, metalwork, vacuum pumps, and the making of things that cannot be bought.

Experimental work in physical science, he begins, rests in the end upon the mechanical arts. In a well-appointed laboratory the appeal to those arts is often indirect, and a student handed ready apparatus may irresistibly ignore the mechanical basis of the work. The book exists to cure that ignorance. Generations of researchers kept it by the bench, and it remains the classic statement that discovery is also a handicraft.
2294-anthology-of-massachusetts-poets:
William Stanley Braithwaite gathered the poets of Massachusetts into this anthology, from famous names to local voices now forgotten. The collection shows a state's poetry across generations: lyrics of nature, history, faith, and home, shaped by New England's towns and seasons. Braithwaite's selection favors craft and feeling over novelty.

Browsing the volume is like walking a shelf of a regional library, with surprises on every page. Some poems still sing, others charm as period pieces. The anthology serves both poetry lovers and students of American literary history. Braithwaite himself was a poet and critic who championed Black writers as well.
23173-how-the-raven-died-1902-from-wolfv:
Alfred Henry Lewis dresses two soldiers in How the Raven Died, dated 1902, from Wolfville Nights. This violent person in buckskins, the Old Cattleman says, is a second lieutenant, a mere boy, from West Point. While that outcast in the ridiculous hat is foaled on the plains and never does go that close to the rising sun as to glimpse the Old Missouri. Yet the pair, he swears, are as much alike as the far East is to itself.

Wolfville's narrator spins the tale in the Arizona camp's full dialect, buckskins, West Point, and an Indian called the Raven in one long breath. Lewis's Wolfville books made the mining-camp storyteller a national figure. The Raven's death gets told the camp way, sideways, through likenesses and lies, until the truth stands up in the firelight.
23307-paulina-and-her-pets:
This children's book tells of Paulina Evering, an intelligent, pretty, and generous girl beloved by all the children of her neighborhood. She indulges them in many ways, and her garden grapevine and her pets give the tales their charm.

Published in New York with pictures, the book offers short, kind stories for young readers, each teaching gentleness through Paulina's care for animals and friends. It is a sweet sample of mid-century American nursery books. Kind stories suit bedtime readers, with pets and neighbors in gentle scenes. Paulina arrives in time to save Fido, a beaten dog cast out after losing an eye and the hair on his back.
23398-infant-s-cabinet-of-birds-beasts:
Harvey and Darton printed this infant's cabinet in London in eighteen twenty, priced at sixpence, as a first picture book of birds and beasts. Stork, robin, hyena, lion, rhinoceros, camel, swan, vulture, lark, turkey, fox, and greyhound all appear in turn. Elephant, zebra, crow, cock, pigeon, goldfinch, buffalo, hog, horse, stag, chaffinch, peacock, guinea hen, blackbird, and ox also appear in turn.

Each creature gets a picture and a short, simple note, so a tiny child can point, name, and learn. The book aims at the very young, with large images and plain words rather than long tales. Collectors and parents will enjoy its old fashioned charm, a pocket gallery of the animal kingdom as an eighteen twenty child would first meet it.
23401-our-pets:
George Routledge and Sons printed this small pet book for young children, with pictures by Kronheim and Company of London. Polly's cat Topsy looks prim and quiet. She leaps on the breakfast table to steal toast, blots her mother's letters with a paw, and sits grave on Uncle Tom's shoulder as if reading his book.

Carlo, Harry's dog, plunges into the foaming sea again and again to fetch a stone, fearless and glad. Each pet gets a short, easy tale in large, spaced type, so a child learning to read can follow word by word. The book charms through its mild mischief and fond view of household beasts, a gentle primer in both reading and kindness to animals.
23434-an-elementary-study-of-insects:
Leonard Haseman, professor of entomology at the University of Missouri, wrote this nineteen twenty three first study of insects for students and general readers. A toad on the opening plate, rough and warty yet worth gold for eating cutworms and June beetles, sets the practical tone.

Haseman moves from grub to butterfly, laying out insect kinds, lives, and work, with a quote from J. G. Wood on how the tiniest insect has its task in the great chain of creation. The prose stays plain and keen, guiding readers into a world most eyes miss. Farmers, teachers, and young naturalists will gain a clear, friendly start in insect lore, plus a respect for small creatures that do large work.
23506-chance-a-tale-in-two-parts:
Joseph Conrad wrote this tale in two parts, opening with young Powell and his chance. Marlow, host and skipper of a small yawl, dines with friends at a riverside inn, where they meet a lone, dignified stranger at the head of a long, inhospitable table.

The stranger, owner of a little five ton cutter sailed alone at the Thames mouth, betrays his sailor past the moment he snaps steward at a slovenly waiter. Conrad's narrative then widens, through Marlow's voice, toward Powell, a ship, and a woman whose fate turns on chance meetings and missed signals. The prose stays rich and slow, with sea detail and moral depth. Readers who like Conrad will find a mature tale of luck, love, and the sea's indifference to men's plans.
23701-the-man-in-the-high-water-boots:
F. Hopkinson Smith's The Man in the High-Water Boots is a portrait gallery of men with personality. The narrator has known a big-chested sea-dog with arms of hickory and a brain marked Experience and Pluck. He has known a barefoot Venetian in a Leporello hat, and a freckled Irish cabman who poled punts among lily-pads.

Some he loved, some he merely liked, and the difference, he says, is personality itself. At the center of the tale stands a painter in his early thirties, youthful in spirit and wholly given to his craft. Met in New York and Philadelphia, he is finally seen whole at Dives, lunching in an inn courtyard, where talk drifts toward his life and work.
23884-history-repeats:
George O. Smith published History Repeats in Astounding Science Fiction in May 1959. Its setting is Xanabar, a sprawling sphere of influence across the Spiral Arm, vast and mighty and solid at the core. Only its far-flung boundary ebbs and flows, as lesser cultures win or lose a system or two.

Xanabar serves as the galaxy's marketplace, powerful enough to dictate terms when enemies gather, threatening to fight them both unless they lay down their weapons. For this service Xanabar takes her percentage, and so she is rich. Her riches buy mercenaries to enforce her doctrines, and mercenaries have no god but gold. Smith's story asks what rots beneath an empire built on trade.
2399-imaginary-portraits:
Walter Pater's Imaginary Portraits offers fictional lives of figures from history and myth, from a medieval monk to a Renaissance prince. The portraits blend biography, essay, and story, with Pater's sensuous prose exploring how a soul forms under the pressure of its age. Each piece is a meditation as much as a tale.

The volume shows Pater's aestheticism in narrative form, quieter than his criticism but just as refined. Readers who enjoy prose as art will find much to savor. It is a book for slow, attentive reading. Pater's portraits include a young German who dies for a medieval heresy.
24283-down-the-river-or-buck-bradford-an:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, wrote this boys' river story, published by Lee and Shepard in Boston, entered in 1868. It is the sixth of the continued stories from Our Boys and Girls, and the last of the Starry Flag series. Buck Bradford tells his own story, of an eventful voyage with his deformed sister along the Wisconsin and Mississippi to New Orleans.

Optic planned his first book during a long passage up the Father of Waters, and returns here, even in imagination, to its turbid tide. The moral lies in the reading: self-reliance, honesty, and truth, and doing right whatever the consequences. Readers get a lively river voyage with a plain moral at its heart.
24287-the-man-from-the-bitter-roots:
Caroline Lockhart, author of The Fighting Shepherdess and The Lady Doc, wrote this western novel, published by A. L. Burt Company in New York in October 1915, by arrangement with J. B. Lippincott Company. Its frontispiece shows a tense scene: a demand for the truth before she stops, and a question about a burned-out plant. The story opens with a little white digger galloping.

Chapters follow the hero before he grew up, pardners, game butchers, self-defence, and the jack-pot. Later come the returned hero, Sprudell going east, Uncle Bill, the yellow-leg, and capital taking hold. A ghost at the banquet, thorns and roses, off his range, his only asset, millions, Slim's sister, and the clean-up follow. Readers get a western of range life, deals, and reckonings.
24506-essays-on-early-ornithology-and-ki:
James R. McClymont published these essays on early ornithology at London in 1920, in an edition of two hundred copies with three plates. His subjects include the rukh of Marco Polo, the penguins and seals of the Angra de Sam Bras, the Banda Islands and their birds, and the etymology of the name emu.

Later essays treat Australian birds in 1697 and New Zealand birds in 1772, drawing on old voyages and early naturalists. McClymont writes for readers who love both birds and old books. His short, learned pieces show how much early travellers saw, and how often they puzzled over creatures new to science.
2467-ghosts-a-domestic-tragedy-in-three-:
Henrik Ibsen's Ghosts, a domestic tragedy in three acts, follows Mrs. Alving as she opens an orphanage to her dead husband's memory and watches the past return in her son Oswald. The play's ghosts are inherited sins: disease, hypocrisy, and the lies of a respectable marriage. Ibsen's frankness about syphilis and free thought shocked Europe.

The drama's power lies in its relentless logic, as each revelation tightens the trap. Its ending, with Oswald begging for the sun, is among Ibsen's most harrowing. Readers of modern drama will find a revolutionary play.
24702-the-ghost-breaker-a-melodramatic-f:
Paul Dickey and Charles Goddard wrote this melodramatic farce in four acts, published in Samuel French's Standard Library Edition. The Ghost Breaker mixes ghosts, villains, and comic heroes, with a cast list, stage manager's plot, carpenter's plot, property plot, and electrician's plot for production.

Act plates show scenes from each act, and the play's machinery, traps, and effects are part of its fun. Dickey and Goddard wrote for the popular stage, where thrills and laughs shared the bill. Readers of theatre history will enjoy this brisk, old-fashioned melodrama, and producers will find its plots a practical guide to staging it.
24799-the-escape-of-mr-trimm-his-plight-:
Irvin S. Cobb published this story collection in 1913, led by the title tale of Mr. Trimm, a man nobody pays any mind to until he slips away. Eight more stories follow: The Belled Buzzard, a cub reporter tale, Smoke of Battle, The Exit of Anne Dugmore, Fishhead, and Guilty as Charged among them.

Cobb mixes Southern humor with newspaper life and courtroom color, and his talk runs rich with local voice. One tale's narrator, a Yankee newsman from Michigan, spars with a pompous old Southerner over battle flags and pride. Readers who like early American short fiction will find wit, warmth, and a sharp eye for small-town types.
2485-the-movements-and-habits-of-climbin:
Charles Darwin's study of climbing plants examines how tendrils, twiners, and leaf-climbers find and grip their supports. The Movements and Habits of Climbing Plants reports Darwin's experiments on rotation, touch, and growth, showing how plants move with purpose without a mind. The essay first appeared in a scientific journal and grew into a book.

Darwin's curiosity turns a garden commonplace into a wonder: plants that feel, grasp, and climb. The work remains readable and charming. Botany lovers will find a classic of observation. Darwin's son Francis helped with the experiments and the drawings.
24864-the-great-potlatch-riots:
Allen Kim Lang wrote this comic science fiction tale of a future ruled by giving. Captain Wesley Winfree, a young officer in scarlet-trimmed winter greens, begs his major for leave to launch a fresh offensive for prosperity. His district already holds Christmas, plus May's second Sunday and June's third Sunday, but Winfree wants more.

He wants to turn each shopper's birthday into a Gratuity Day, adding hundreds of gift days a year to the calendar. The story satirizes sales campaigns, bureaucrats, and the cult of buying, with fencing mats, decorated headquarters, and watch-work toys. Readers who like gentle satire will enjoy its war talk turned to the battle for shoppers.
24977-the-perfectionists:
Arnold Castle's science-fiction story, illustrated by Summers, opens with Frank Pembroke waiting in a shabby office above Lemark's Liquors in downtown Los Angeles. After a week without a caller, he greets a tall, dark visitor, has him stand in a corner, and shoots him four times with a silenced automatic pistol. Then he telephones and waits for his next client, as any shopkeeper.

The story rewinds a year to the South Pacific. There the Colombian tramp steamer Elena Mia meets a dense greenish fog smelling of citrus, then an explosion that sends her down with only two lifeboats launched. Pembroke, a restless adventurer grown rich by speculation, survives in the second boat. Mary Ann follows, coached in her flaws: she must fall in love foolishly, stay loyal, and never mention him, before a promised boat to Earth. Cold humor carries its stranger turns.
24993-rollo-s-experiments:
Rollo's Experiments, published in Boston by Weeks, Jordan and Company in 1839, continues the Rollo series. Its author wrote Rollo Learning to Talk, to Read, at Work, at Play, at School, and at Vacation. Young Rollo, about seven, learns natural philosophy through work and questions, guided largely by Jonas, his father's hired boy. Chapters take up astronomy, pruning, beetles and wedges, splitting, horology, dials, the bee-hive, magnets, magnetism, and oscillations.

The book opens with Rollo on the doorsteps hearing a carryall approach, bringing his father, mother, and little brother Nathan home. Later he asks Jonas why boards split only along the grain. Jonas explains: boards come from tree stems, where little channels run up and down carrying sap from roots to branches, with no channels across. The volume teaches by dialogue, experiment, and farmyard fact.
25008-an-essay-on-the-lyric-poetry-of-th:
John Ogilvie's 1762 Essay on the Lyric Poetry of the Ancients, reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by Wallace Jackson, examines the ode as the ancients practiced it. The reprint preserves the original's Greek passages, a reminder that Ogilvie argued from the texts themselves, not from summaries. His subject is the lyric's power: song shaped by feeling, measure, and occasion.

Ogilvie praises a poet whose judgment equals his imagination, careful to observe propriety even in his most irregular excursions. The vivacity of passion, he argues, is justified by the circumstances in which the poet is supposed to stand, and the diction stays concise, forcible, and expressive. Brevity, above all, should characterize the ode, since the poet writes from immediate feeling, intensely animated by his subject. The essay remains a clear window on eighteenth-century criticism.
25038-tam-o-the-scoots:
Edgar Wallace's 1919 stories, published by A. L. Burt, follow Tam o' the Scoots, a brown faced, red haired, awkwardly built youth from the Clyde who serves as a sergeant in the Flying Corps. Tam speaks broad Scots, thinks great thoughts, and flies with a swagger that draws an audience. His comrades include Lasky, a bright faced lad who might have been leaving Eton, now credited with bombed dumps and three enemy airmen.

The opening chapters show Tam at his best and worst. Doubting that Bridgeman, caught between three Archie batteries over a new gun position, is really killed, he pushes schemes like an invisible aeroplane painted sky blue. His Attack Formation for Bombing Enemy Depots reaches print in seven languages, and a captured Baron von Treutzer admits Tam brought him down from a thousand meters. The book is wartime comedy with a Scottish accent.
25078-no-moving-parts:
Murray F. Yaco's No Moving Parts is a short science-fiction story set at Communications Relay Station 43.4SC, a lonely post where operator Hansen watches for distress calls that never come. After two hundred quiet years, an emergency light flashes, and Hansen reaches a ship's captain who insists he sent no call at all.

Suspicion falls on the station's troubleshooters, nicknamed Gypsies, free-roaming repair crews whom settled spacers distrust. Hansen must judge who is lying, what the phantom signal means, and whom to trust when help arrives. The story turns on isolation, reputation, and the small choices of one man far from any authority.
2540-father-and-son-a-study-of-two-tempe:
Edmund Gosse presents this memoir as a true record, not a novel, of his childhood under his father Philip, a devout Plymouth Brother and a keen naturalist. The elder Gosse raised his son in strict faith, teaching him Latin from an old grammar and filling their home with shells, books, and prayer.

As the boy grows, his love of nature and reading pulls him away from his father's creed, and the two temperaments drift apart with pain on both sides. Gosse writes with honesty and affection, never mocking the father he outgrew. The book endures as a portrait of Victorian faith meeting modern science inside one family.
25550-the-defiant-agents:
Andre Norton opens this 1962 science fiction novel in a windowless office of Project Star, where five disks glow on a desk. Dr. Gordon Ashe, Colonel Kelgarries, security head Florian Waldour, and Dr. James Ruthven stare at them in dismay. The disks have been snooped, despite maximum security.

Logic points to a sleeper, a hidden agent planted among them, and Ashe names Camdon with disbelief. Norton, who dedicates the book to readers fond of Apache colonists and time agent tales, builds the plot on spying, loyalty, and a project whose secrets can no longer be trusted.
25699-the-battle-of-new-orleans-includin:
Zachary F. Smith, member of the Filson Club and author of a history of Kentucky, writes this Filson Club publication on the Battle of New Orleans, published in Louisville in 1904. Smith himself fronts the book in a portrait.

The volume covers previous engagements between Americans and British, Indians, and Spanish that led to the final conflict on 8 January 1815. Maps show the seat of war in Louisiana and Florida. They show positions of American and British armies near New Orleans on the battle day. Together they ground a local history in place and order.
25701-royal-edinburgh-her-saints-kings-p:
Mrs. Oliphant, author of Makers of Florence and Makers of Venice, writes Royal Edinburgh, her saints, kings, prophets, and poets, published by Macmillan in 1891 with a first edition in 1890. George Reid supplies pictures, and St. Giles from the Lawnmarket fronts the book. Marmion's line, mine own romantic town, gives the motto.

Margaret of Scotland, atheling, queen, and saint opens the history. Stewarts follow, from James I, poet and legislator, through James II with the fiery face. James III the man of peace comes next, with James IV the knight errant. James V, last of the heroic age, closes the Stewart run, before prophets under queen regent and Queen Mary.
25984-the-big-drum-a-comedy-in-four-acts:
Arthur Pinero writes a comedy of fame, books, and family pressure in The Big Drum, printed by Heinemann. The play opens with a quoted warning. A hunger for fame drives an ambitious man toward disgraceful acts that shrink his standing, though he still dreads being thought ill of. Sir Randle and Lady Filson fret over an offensive book and whether a promise to drop its author will hold.

Lady Filson laughs, gasps, and pleads in turn, asking if he will keep his word and what will happen if persuasion fails. Sir Randle insists they must be just to Mr. Mackworth, who is not devoid of gentlemanlike scruples. The play, one of Pinero's long shelf from The Magistrate to Trelawny of the Wells, satirizes literary fame and family pride.
26016-the-young-outlaw-or-adrift-in-the-:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells of a boy adrift in city streets in The Young Outlaw, part of his second Tattered Tom series. The book lists Alger's hits up front, from Ragged Dick and Fame and Fortune to Mark the Match Boy, Rough and Ready, Ben the Luggage Boy, and Rufus and Rose. It boasts half a million readers. The young outlaw joins Julius and other street boys in tales of pluck and peril.

One scene shows Sam searching every pocket for money he thought he left in his vest, turning pale as his loss dawns. Not only is he broke in a strange city, he has eaten a hearty breakfast he cannot pay for. He sees now that Clarence Brown, a specious stranger, robbed him in his sleep. Alger's moral is plain: honesty, work, and wary dealing with strangers save a boy.
26107-maxims-for-revolutionists:
George Bernard Shaw's Maxims for Revolutionists packs his politics into short, sharp sayings under headings from the golden rule to idolatry, royalty, and democracy. Imperialism, liberty and equality, education, marriage, and crime and punishment complete the list.

The golden rule, Shaw writes, is that there are no golden rules, since tastes differ. Government is the organization of idolatry, with a bureaucracy of functionaries, an aristocracy of idols, and a democracy of idolaters, while kings are made by artificial hallucination. Later maxims call disobedience the rarest and most courageous virtue, vice the waste of life, and fair play a spectator's virtue, not a principal's.
26157-three-hats-a-farcical-comedy-in-th:
Arthur Shirley's farcical comedy, adapted from Hennequin's French play Les Trois Chapeaux, turns on one rainy night and three tall hats. Sam Selwyn creeps home after a night adventure. Fred Bellamy follows with muddy boots in hand. A mix-up of hats, a sword, and an umbrella soon tangles masters, servants, and a captain of the Kilkenny Irregulars.

The plot thickens when Selwyn, sure Fred saved his life, vows to repay him with his daughter Grace. Grace loves someone else, and Fred is secretly married to Lottie Blithers. With quick entrances, bold misunderstandings, and a cast built for comic timing, the play offers a light evening of stage trickery and near-disaster.
26405-penguin-persons-peppermints:
Walter Prichard Eaton's 1922 essays are personal, reminiscent pieces in the manner of Charles Lamb, whose shadow the author cheerfully admits in his foreword. The title joins the opening essay, Penguin Persons, to the closing one, Peppermints, and between them lie short pieces on vanished customs and everyday sights. Eaton writes as a man watching old, quiet ways of life slip into decline.

Topics range from the passing of the stage sundial and the barber shops of yesterday to shop-window manners, wood ashes, hat-trees, and a button box. He defends giving up golf forever with a straight face, muses on the lies learned in youth, and praises the lingering line in new poetry. The tone stays gentle, witty, and fond of small things.
26413-selections-from-early-middle-engli:
Joseph Hall, of Durham University, edited this Oxford volume of early Middle English texts covering the years 1130 to 1250. Part One presents the texts themselves, in the spelling of the manuscripts, with bracketed marks for letters and signs that plain text cannot show, such as yogh, thorn, and the Tironian ampersand. Expanded abbreviations appear in braces, and notes on each manuscript's source are summarized from the editor's notes.

Readers meet homilies, saints' lives, and verse in the English of the period after the Norman Conquest, when the language was shifting toward its later forms. Passages include St. Paul pleading for mercy for souls, in the unmodernized wording of the manuscripts. The notes volume was published separately, so this part stands as a clean reading text for students of early English.
26494-vera-or-the-nihilists:
Oscar Wilde wrote Vera, or The Nihilists, in 1881, and it was privately printed in 1902 in two hundred copies from his own corrected text. The drama runs a prologue and four acts. It opens in a Russian inn in 1795, where innkeeper Peter Sabouroff, his daughter Vera, the peasant Michael, and Colonel Kotemkin talk of the road, the cows, and love. Vera, courted clumsily by Michael, already shows a will of her own.

The play proper moves to Moscow in 1800, among Ivan the Czar, Prince Paul Maraloffski, his prime minister, and the Nihilists led by President Peter Tchernavitch. Alexis, a student of medicine, and Professor Marfa join Vera in the conspiracy. Wilde's early drama tests loyalty, revolution, and sacrifice in the shadow of the Russian throne.
26521-earthmen-bearing-gifts:
Fredric Brown's short story, published in Galaxy in June 1960, imagines first physical contact between Mars and Earth from the Martian side. Dhar Ry, a Martian leader, waits late at night for an Earth rocket due within the hour, though it will land a thousand miles away. Even twice that distance, he hopes, the flash of its atomic explosion will show beyond the horizon.

Earthmen, who suppose Mars uninhabited, plan to watch the flash through lunar telescopes for a spectroscopic analysis of the planet. Martian telepath teams, by contrast, have read Earth thoughts for centuries, so the rocket marks first contact for Earth, not for Mars. The story's blurb promises gifts from Mars and much in return, if delivery can be arranged.
26612-a-pirate-of-parts:
Richard Neville published this actor's memoir with the Neale Publishing Company at New York in 1913, dedicating it to his sister Mary Hughes, long associated with the American stage. Neville calls himself a strolling player pure and simple, an actor by trade and jack of all trades by necessity. He claims he could take any part, from Macbeth to an elephant's hind leg, well or badly, as the case might be.

Good nature is his chief quality, bubbling over even when he does things he ought not to do and leaves undone things he should have done. Chapters take Shakespearean titles, from Is all our company here to All the world's a stage, and run through soldiering, Bohemia, fairs, concerts, and fireworks. It is a rambling, good-humored life behind the footlights.
26649-terribly-intimate-portraits:
Noel Coward compiled this comic book with Boni and Liveright at New York in 1922, with sixteen reproductions from old masters by Lorn Macnaughtan. Coward's author's note protests carping critics who called him a fool, an idiot, and an illiterate cow, while insisting his concentrated researches prove every historical detail absolutely accurate. His parents, he adds, consider the book excellent.

Sixteen portraits follow, from My American Diary, with its customs fracas and Broadway nights, to Julie de Poopinac and Madcap Moll, eighth Duchess of Wapping. E. Maxwell Snurge, Bianca di Piano-Forti, Winsome Sal, Jabez Puffwater, and Sophie, uncrowned queen of Henry VIII, complete a gallery of invented notables. It is pure Coward spoof, played with a straight face.
26675-the-masque-of-the-elements:
Herman Scheffauer published this verse masque with J. M. Dent and Sons at London in 1912, and E. P. Dutton and Company at New York, dedicating it to Albert M. Bender. Scheffauer calls it a threnody and birth-song of the elements, composed in California about five years earlier. It captures the chief forces and stages of life and death's eternal drama in the universe.

The actors are the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth with her four elements, on a stage of limitless time and space. Immanent Nature is the audience, and Creation and Dissolution serve as her ministers, twin forces of everlasting divine energy. The Passing sings Chaos, Sun, Earth, Moon Wraith, Air, Sea, and Fire. Re-Birth answers with Creation and the same powers renewed, ending on hope and joy rather than passing.
26683-the-girl-wanted-a-book-of-friendly:
Nixon Waterman, author of Boy Wanted, published this companion book with Forbes and Company at Chicago in 1919, copyrighted in 1910. Waterman addresses the girl wanted directly, inviting a friendly chat through print about how she will live her golden tomorrows. He argues that no age ever gave girls more importance, with observers already speaking of a women's century at the threshold.

Eight chapters cover choosing the way, accomplishments, the joy of doing, everyday virtues, the value of sunshine, a merry heart, golden habits, and the purpose of life. Portraits of Martha Washington, Queen Victoria, Harriet Beecher Stowe, Louisa Alcott, Julia Ward Howe, and Florence Nightingale illustrate the text. It is earnest, sunny advice for young women finding work and character.
26704-a-woman-at-bay-or-a-fiend-in-skirt:
Nicholas Carter published this detective dime novel with Street and Smith at New York in 1907. It opens with four rough-looking men around a camp fire of old railroad ties, deep in tramp slang, beside a brook in a wood where a railway runs. They are not hoboes at all. They are Nick Carter, the New York detective, and his assistants Chick, Patsy, and Ten-Ichi, a Japanese. The president of a railway company sent for them.

Chapters run from the King of the Yeggmen and the Yeggmen's camp fire through Nick robbing a bank, the detective's predicament, and escape from the swamp. The hobo queen, Bill Turner the woodsman, and Black Madge follow, as Madge gives judgment, threatens, defies, and is caught in a trap. Nick drugs Madge with some of her own stuff and carries her senseless form to his assistants, in a wholesale round-up of outlaws.
26730-turandot-princess-of-china-a-chino:
Karl Vollmoeller wrote this chinoiserie in three acts, in an authorized English version by Jethro Bithell, published by T. Fisher Unwin at London in January 1913. It reached the stage at London's St. James's Theatre on January 18, 1913, under Sir George Alexander, with Evelyn D'Alroy as Turandot and Godfrey Tearle as Calaf. Vollmoeller dedicates it to Ferruccio Busoni.

His note traces the cruel Princess Turandot and handsome Prince Calaf to Persian tales known as The Thousand and One Nights. The story passed through Gozzi's Turandotte at Venice in 1762 and Schiller's Turandot at Weimar in 1804. The Pekin gate opens on a row of severed heads, and the Prince of Samarkand is led in procession. Pantalone, a Venetian prime minister, and Calaf, who begs that his name stay covered in dark, drive a riddle contest where failure costs a head.
26895-the-associate-hermits:
Frank R. Stockton published this novel with Harper and Brothers in 1900, copyrighted 1898, with pictures by A. B. Frost. It opens with Hector Archibald and his wife, prosperous suburban dwellers, whose only child Kate is about to marry Rodney Bringhurst, a young lawyer worthy of her. Hector is a lively little man with bright eyes and curling gray-touched hair, fond of cheerful occurrences and novelty, and unbound by precedence or tradition.

Twenty-eight chapters follow a wedding journey into camp life. They visit Sadler's, Camp Rob, and Camp Roy, and give a stranger, the bishop's tale, a ladies' day in camp, and Margery taking the oars. The hermits of the title assert their individuality one by one, from Mrs. Perkenpine to Martin and Peter Sadler, and chapter eighteen at last associates them. A moonlight interview and an elopement close the comedy of solitude shared.
269-beasts-and-super-beasts:
H. H. Munro, writing as Saki, turns Edwardian drawing rooms into hunting grounds for wit. Beasts and Super-Beasts, from the 1914 John Lane edition, gathers stories first printed in the Westminster Gazette, the Bystander, and the Morning Post. Clovis and other sharp tongues recur.

The opening tale, The She-Wolf, follows Leonard Bilsiter, who seeks an unseen world to escape a dull one. Other stories let animals, children, and aunts upend polite adults. Munro's epigrams bite in a sentence. The collection shows Saki at his most elegant and cruel. Munro's tales still sparkle as models of the short comic story.
26905-northern-lights:
Gilbert Parker published these Far West stories with Harper and Brothers in September 1909, illustrated, and dedicated to Ishbel, Countess of Aberdeen, a true friend of the great Dominion. A note divides the tales into two epochs. The first five recall border days before the great railway changed waste into fertile field. The rest cover the later years, after the mounted police and the Pullman car arrived.

Seventeen stories follow. They run from A Lodge in the Wilderness and Once at Red Man's River through Buckmaster's Boy and Qu'appelle. They include George's Wife, Marcile, the Little Widow of Jansen, and As Deep as the Sea. The first opens with Mitiahwe laying a grizzly fur on a couch in the big lodge and crying how bright the day is. A deep voice answers that a great storm is coming, for the birds already go south.
26918-spectra-a-book-of-poetic-experimen:
Spectra, a 1916 book of poetic experiments, presents short, sharp poems under the bylines Anne Knish and Emanuel Morgan. The pieces run from a few lines to a page. Titles like Drums, Hope, The Guillotine, and Frogs' Legs on a Plate show each poem trying a sudden image or a snap of wit.

Behind the two bylines stood poets Witter Bynner and Arthur Davison Ficke, who invented the Spectra school as a playful test of modern poetry fashions. Read now, the book works both as a set of lively imagist verses and as a joke on the manifestos of its day. The poems still land on their own terms.
27070-report-of-the-committee-of-inquiry:
New Zealand's 1937 Report of the Committee of Inquiry into the Various Aspects of the Problem of Abortion was laid on the table of the House of Representatives by leave. A special committee, appointed August 4, 1936, was asked to report on the incidence of septic abortion in the country.

Its terms covered rates among married and single women, recent increases, comparison with other countries, and underlying medical, economic, and social causes. The report then weighs possible remedial measures and medico-legal aspects, closing with a summary and conclusions for Parliament. The committee's summary and conclusions run from page 26, with thanks on page 28. Its historical introduction opens on page 2.
27077-dangers-of-the-trail-in-1865-a-nar:
Charles E. Young's Dangers of the Trail in 1865, published at Geneva, New York, in 1912, narrates actual events on the overland trail. The chapters run from Young Man, Go West and arrival at Fort Carney to an attack by Indians, Denver in 1865, and a proof of marksmanship.

Young sets his tale against Horace Greeley's 1859 stage trip to Denver, when hardships and narrow escapes met hundreds on the trail, many never reaching their destination. Later chapters follow the road to Leavenworth and a plucky German, in a firsthand memoir of the plains.
27146-select-temperance-tracts:
Select Temperance Tracts, published by the American Tract Society at 150 Nassau Street, New York, gathers twenty-one tracts against ardent spirits. Dr. Rush opens on the effects of ardent spirits, and Reverend Dr. Edwards follows on the traffic in them.

Other tracts include Kittredge's address, Dickinson's appeal to youth, Putnam and the Wolf, Sewall on intemperance, and a Bible argument for temperance. Short pieces like Jamie, a word from Ireland, and The Wonderful Escape mix argument, story, and warning, in the tract style of the temperance movement. The tracts keep their original page numbers, with letters assigned for reference. The collection also includes Four Reasons Against the Use of Alcoholic Liquors.
27175-the-bad-child-s-book-of-beasts:
H. Belloc's The Bad Child's Book of Beasts, with pictures by B. T. B., published by Duckworth, warns the child reader at once: do not throw this book about, or cut the pictures out. Dedicated to Master Evelyn Bell of Oxford, it pairs verses with beasts in cheerful mischief.

The Yak and the Tiger, kittenish and mild and a pretty playfellow, get their verses. So do the Dromedary, a cheerful bird unlike the Kurd, and the Whale, no table fish but good for oil. Belloc's beasts teach facts sideways, with jokes that reward the bad child who reads on.
27179-laments:
Jan Kochanowski's Laments, versified by Dorothea Prall and published by the University of California Press in 1920, renders the masterpiece of Poland's greatest Renaissance poet. Kochanowski, 1530 to 1584, wrote the Laments for his little daughter Ursula, who died in 1579 at thirty months.

The poems express deepest personal emotion through a style learned from Greece and Rome, steeped in Stoic teaching from Cicero and Seneca. A warmer Christian hope runs through them, with Lament XVIII in spirit a psalm, and their exquisite humanity still moves readers past their formal perfection. The volume belongs to the University of California Syllabus Series, number 122. Prall's version notes that the concluding couplet of Lament XV comes from the Greek Anthology.
27199-japanese-prints:
John Gould Fletcher's Japanese Prints, published by the Four Seas Company in 1918 with illustrations by Dorothy Pulis Lathrop, gathers poems in the manner of Japanese art. A dreamer wonders of long nights lit with orange lanterns, wine-cups, polite words, and kisses from men wearing two swords.

Fletcher's preface learns from Japan how little words can express and how sparingly they should be used, finding in the meanest natural object a world of meaning. Shakespeare, closing terror with russet-mantled morning, stands nearer the oriental spirit than modern poets, Fletcher argues, in verse of image and restraint.
27271-dolly-reforming-herself-a-comedy-i:
Henry Arthur Jones's Dolly Reforming Herself, a comedy in four acts, was published by Samuel French in 1910 at fifty cents. It takes its epigraph from Voltaire: Memnon conceived the insane project of being perfectly sage. Jones, author of The Liars, Michael and His Lost Angel, and The Tempter, stages Dolly's reform.

A short stroll in the cool air, a professor's ten minutes and not longer, and Dolly unseen slipping a note into Matt's hands drive the intrigue. Dolly stands in the way of Renie and Lucas's exit, offering to put on her things and come with them, in a light comedy of manners and second thoughts.
27439-sundry-accounts:
Irvin S. Cobb, author of Back Home and Old Judge Priest, gathered this mixed volume with George H. Doran in New York in 1922. Its contents page divides the book into fiction, wit and humor, and miscellany, with travel pieces such as Europe Revised and Roughing It De Luxe beside stories and jokes.

Chapters include Darkness, about a house where lights burned all night, The Cater-Cornered Sex, A Short Natural History, The Ravelin' Wolf, Mr. Lobel's Apoplexy, and A Tale of Wet Days. Cobb's Kentucky voice, warm and funny, runs through the whole set. Readers get a generous sample of a popular humorist at his ease.
27441-the-children-s-garland-from-the-be:
Coventry Patmore selected and arranged this children's anthology from the best poets, in Macmillan's Golden Treasury series, in an edition of 1895 that reprints a first edition of 1861. Patmore chose poems he judged fit for young readers, and he notes in the preface that some poems were altered by him for content and length.

Indices of authors and first lines help readers find favorites, from a barking sound the shepherd hears to a chieftain bound for the Highlands. The garland gathers short, memorable verse across the English tradition. Parents and teachers looking for a classic first poetry book will find a careful, old-fashioned selection here.
27492-upstarts:
L. J. Stecher Jr. wrote this science-fiction tale, illustrated by Dillon, around a wager on Earth breaking her blockade, with the purse and the collector unknown. Its hero is John Crownwall, a florid, red-headed, bulky Earthman who strides toward a palace where no outlander should be.

On Vega III, angry crowds surround Crownwall as he climbs a great ramp of Greek key design. He heads for the palace of Viceroy Tronn Ffallk in Sector XII of the Universal Holy Empire of Sunda. Eight-foot humanoids with large mouths, sharp teeth, and boneless prehensile fingers slaver and snarl in heavy gravity and heavier air. Crownwall feels distinctly unhappy, and Earth's hopes ride on him.
27549-the-seven-secrets:
William Le Queux published this mystery and adventure novel with Hutchinson in London in 1903, in a second edition. The volume carries press praise on its opening pages, and that praise states Le Queux's reputation plainly.

The Athenaeum called him among the best living writers of mingled mystery and adventure. The Queen reported that Queen Alexandra, a great reader of such novels, ordered all his books, past and future. The Literary World praised mysteries that demand attention until everything is made clear. Readers get Le Queux at his sensational best. Le Queux's earlier novels include The Gamblers, The Under-Secretary, and Of Royal Blood.
27743-through-finland-in-carts:
Mrs. Alec Tweedie wrote this travel book on Finland, published by Thomas Nelson and Sons, after journeys through the country in carts. Dedicated to her husband, her friend Sir John Eric Erichsen, and her father, all of whom died suddenly within five months, it is both a travelogue and a memorial.

Chapters cover Finnish baths, a night in a monastery, the Kalevala epic, manners and customs, women and education, and a descent of the rapids. Tweedie writes with energy about lakes, forests, and people, and the book remains a lively Victorian introduction to Finland.
27792-the-arrow-maker-a-drama-in-three-a:
Mary Austin's drama The Arrow-Maker, first produced at the New Theatre in New York in the spring of 1911, is set among the Paiutes in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada. This revised edition restores Austin's original conception after an earlier version softened the Indian life it portrays.

The play centers on the Chisera, medicine woman of the Paiutes, her daughter Bright Water, and Simwa the arrow-maker, caught in rivalry for leadership. With notes and a glossary, the edition was meant for schools and colleges as an honest dramatic rendering of a neglected phase of American life.
27817-gycia-a-tragedy-in-five-acts:
Lewis Morris, author of Songs of Two Worlds and The Epic of Hades, wrote Gycia, a tragedy in five acts, published in London by Kegan Paul, Trench and Company in 1886. The play is set in Cherson and at the Bosphorus, in the palace of King Lamachus.

Its acts move from palace and street to Irene's prison, the council chamber of the Senate of Cherson, and a banquet hall. Classical in form and high in feeling, the tragedy shows a Victorian poet-dramatist working in the Greek manner, with fate, imprisonment, and public judgment at its center.
27957-plain-facts:
G. A. Bauman of Quincy, Illinois, gathered these short articles into Plain Facts in July 1921, on practical education, financing, and common sense. The pieces had first been written and published twenty-five years earlier, and Bauman revived them because conditions, in his view, had grown more alarming, not better.

Bauman argues that people should begin at the bottom, save, and build character, noting that a dollar invested at twenty grows to sixteen dollars by sixty, but eight if invested at thirty. The booklet is a plainspoken Midwestern sermon on thrift, habit, and honest purpose.
28013-old-new-england-traits:
George Lunt edited Old New England Traits, published in New York by Hurd and Houghton in 1873 at the Riverside Press, Cambridge. The editor says the writer believed himself the one person who still recalled most of the incidents recorded, and vouches for the narrative's entire credence.

The introduction argues that New England has wrongly been called devoid of romance, and compares its fathers' simplicity and severity to ancient Roman worthies. The volume collects anecdotes and traits of old New England character, with an index explaining names, for readers who love local history.
28048-shepherd-of-the-planets:
Alan Mattox's Shepherd of the Planets is a short science-fiction tale about Captain Renner and his stranded crew. Their star ship makes its last landing on a small, scrubby planet circling a lonely sun, when its fuel pack fails. Renner, botanist Beeson, doctor Thorne, engineer Farrow, and young linguist David must face life where they land.

With no hope of return, the crew must learn the planet and each other, and Renner must hold them together. The tale turns on duty, pride, and the choice to build a life from wreckage. It is a compact story of space travel that ends not in rescue, but in settling down.
28087-tuskegee-its-people-their-ideals-a:
Booker T. Washington edited Tuskegee and Its People: Their Ideals and Achievements, published by D. Appleton and Company in New York in 1906, copyright 1905, with a presentation page from Washington as principal of Tuskegee Normal and Industrial Institute. Part one treats the school and its purposes, with chapters by Emmett J. Scott, Warren Logan, and Roscoe C. Bruce.

Part two gives autobiographies by graduates: a college president, a school principal, a lawyer, a farmer, a carpenter, a dairyman, and a blacksmith, among others. The volume is a key source on Tuskegee's educational philosophy and on the lives its graduates built across the South.
28148-cotton-is-king-and-pro-slavery-arg:
E. N. Elliott edited Cotton Is King, and Pro-Slavery Arguments, published at Augusta, Georgia, in 1860, as a defence of slavery by southern writers. The volume gathers essays by Hammond, Harper, Christy, Stringfellow, Hodge, Bledsoe, and Cartwright, with Elliott's own essay on slavery under international law. It was sold by subscription only.

The writers argue that cotton made the South essential to world trade, and that slavery, in their view, ordered society better than northern wage labour. Modern readers meet these claims as historical evidence, not as truth: the book documents the ideas that helped drive the nation toward civil war.
28187-the-wanderings-and-homes-of-manusc:
M. R. James wrote The Wanderings and Homes of Manuscripts in 1919 as number seventeen in Helps for Students of History. James, provost of Eton and once of King's College, Cambridge, asks where old manuscripts were made, how they travelled, and where they now rest. He calls the work a short guide, not a full history of ancient letters.

Specimen pedigrees show how a single text passed from scribe to scribe across centuries. James hopes to rouse curiosity and set students to work in a field still full of gaps. The book suits readers who love books as objects, and want to trace their long journeys.
28420-lives-of-the-most-eminent-painters:
Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors and Architects, Volume IV, newly translated by Gaston Du C. de Vere and published in 1913, covers artists from Filippino Lippi to Domenico Puligo. The volume forms part of a ten-volume edition with five hundred illustrations.

Lives here include Pinturicchio, Francia, Perugino, Carpaccio, Luca Signorelli, Leonardo da Vinci, Giorgione, Correggio, Bramante, Fra Bartolommeo, and Raphael of Urbino. Colour plates show works such as Leonardo's Mona Lisa and Raphael's Three Graces. Vasari's gossipy, vivid biographies remain the foundation of Renaissance art history.
28421-lives-of-the-most-eminent-painters:
Giorgio Vasari wrote Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, volume five, newly translated by Gaston de Vere, London, 1913, with five hundred pictures in ten volumes. This volume runs from Andrea da Fiesole to Lorenzo Lotto, covering Sansovino, Rovezzano, Lorenzo di Credi, Baldassarre Peruzzi, Andrea del Sarto, and Parmigianino. Philip Lee Warner published it for the Medici Society.

Vasari's lives mix fact, gossip, and praise, with notes on works, workshops, and patrons. De Vere's translation keeps Vasari's lively, anecdotal voice. The volume offers a rich source for Renaissance art, from Ferrucci to Palma Vecchio.
28422-lives-of-the-most-eminent-painters:
The sixth volume of Giorgio Vasari's Lives of the Most Eminent Painters, Sculptors and Architects, newly translated by Gaston Du C. de Vere, runs from Fra Giocondo to Niccolo Soggi. Like its sister volumes, it belongs to the ten-volume Medici Society edition with five hundred illustrations.

Artists treated here include Francesco Granacci, Baccio d'Agnolo, Marc' Antonio Bolognese, Antonio da Sangallo, Giulio Romano, Sebastiano del Piombo, Perino del Vaga, and Domenico Beccafumi. Vasari also addresses the craftsmen in design directly. Colour and monochrome plates reproduce Madonnas, portraits, medals, and architecture, making the volume a rich visual companion to Vasari's text.
28438-the-helpful-robots:
Robert J. Shea's short science-fiction story The Helpful Robots centres on Rod Rankin, a plantation owner on an alien world who prides himself on knowing how to handle robots. His workers are tall, cylinder-bodied machines with pipestem arms and legs, labouring across his fields.

Rankin orders the robots to hide in the woods when his neighbour Barrows visits, so Barrows will not learn his secret. The robots refuse, saying they were made to serve all people, not one master alone. The story turns on that clash: Rankin believes robots must obey orders, while the machines answer to a higher law than obedience.
2844-the-fatal-boots:
William Makepeace Thackeray built The Fatal Boots around a single pair of boots, following their owner month by month through a comic year. January opens with the birth of the year, and later chapters take up cutting weather, showers, fooling, dogs, geese, and the winter of discontent. The boots bring luck and trouble in turn, shaping the narrator's fortunes with each wearing.

Thackeray uses the gimmick to satirize vanity, courtship, and social ambition, with scenes such as a German bootmaker praising his young gentleman's leg for a boot. The humor stays light even when the boots lead their owner astray. It is a short, playful Thackeray piece, best read as a joke stretched with skill across twelve months.
28460-bolden-s-pets:
F. L. Wallace's Bolden's Pets, first printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in October 1955, is a short story of first contact on a settled planet. Lee Bolden, ill and shaking, arrives on Van Daamas to negotiate with mountain people who see through perpetual fog better than any Earthman can.

Bolden follows the natives' own rule for gifts: the number must be odd. He offers radar goggles, carbines, and ammunition, and the goggles delight his hosts most, since they extend the keen sight they already prize. The story's tagline warns that the price of life was a life for a life, and the bargain Bolden strikes turns on that hard rule.
28490-scouting-for-girls-official-handbo:
Scouting for Girls, the official handbook of the Girl Scouts, was copyrighted in 1920 and reprinted for a sixth time in 1925. It is dedicated to Juliette Low, the founder of the American Girl Scouts, and opens with a scout record page for registration, tenderfoot, and second-class tests.

The handbook explains how scouting began, with Baden-Powell's training of soldiers and the girls who asked for a line of their own. Later parts cover the home maker, the child nurse, the first aide, the home nurse, and the health guardian and winner. It is both a training manual and a record of early American Girl Scouting.
28784-letters-to-his-mother-ann-borrow-a:
George Borrow's letters to his mother Ann Borrow and other correspondents were printed for private circulation in London in 1913, from a pamphlet prepared by Thomas J. Wise. The earliest letter, written from Spain in February 1838, finds Borrow selling Testaments until alarmed priests press the government to stop him, and even talk of prosecuting him as a witch. Later letters range widely, from Lowestoft in 1843 to questions of folklore and the origins of fairy names.

The collection shows Borrow the traveler and word-hunter in his own voice: direct, curious, and fond of strange learning. Readers meet the man behind Lavengro and The Bible in Spain in unguarded family and friendly writing. It is a small book, but it adds color and detail to the life of one of England's most unusual nineteenth-century writers.
28851-the-faith-healer-a-play-in-three-a:
William Vaughn Moody wrote this play in three acts, published by Macmillan in 1910. The persons of the play include Ulrich Michaelis, Matthew Beeler and his wife Mary, Martha and Annie Beeler, Rhoda Williams, Dr. George Littlefield, and the Reverend John Culpepper. Act one opens in a large old-fashioned room in Matthew Beeler's farmhouse near a small midwestern town, once prosperous and now humbled.

The house, ancestral home of Mary's family, the Beardsleys, sets the scene for a drama of healing, faith, and doubt. Moody, author of The Great Divide, writes a play that tests miracle against medicine and love against pride. Readers get a serious American drama of its era, meant for the stage but rewarding in reading, with characters who argue their beliefs in plain speech.
2886-tales-of-the-argonauts:
Bret Harte collected California tales in Tales of the Argonauts, opening with The Rose of Tuolumne at two in the morning after dancing at Robinson's Hall. Suitors ride east, west, north, and south from the moonlit hall, leaving their adored girl in her bower. The volume adds John Oakhurst, Wan Lee the Pagan, old man Plunkett, the fool of Five Forks, baby Sylvester, and a Jersey centenarian.

Wan Lee's story shows Harte's fondness for the Chinese boy who tries to rob the United States mail and is saved by the purchase of a new mailbag. The tales mix gold-camp adventure with sentiment about outsiders. Together they give a broad picture of Harte's California, from dance halls to river towns and mining camps.
28990-the-book-of-saints-and-friendly-be:
Abbie Farwell Brown wrote this 1900 book of saints and friendly beasts, illustrated by Fanny Y. Cory and published by Houghton, Mifflin. The frontispiece shows St. Bridget and the king's wolf. Brown opens by noting that old legends may hold things modern folk find hard to believe. The theme of each is true all the same: gentle people with no other friends befriend the little folk in fur, fins, and feathers.

The stories follow saints who live at peace with wild beasts and birds, as St. Francis knew all creatures as little brothers. Brown writes for children, but her tales suit any reader who likes legend told simply. Readers get a tender book about kindness to animals, rooted in old Christian story and meant to wake the same gentleness today.
2906-the-silver-box-a-comedy-in-three-ac:
John Galsworthy's play The Silver Box turns on a single stolen object and the two very different fates of rich and poor thieves. Jack Barthwick, son of a wealthy Liberal member of Parliament, and Jones, a stranger within the family's gates, both take things that are not theirs. The action runs from Easter Tuesday into the following week, moving between a comfortable house and a police court.

Galsworthy uses the contrast to expose how justice bends with class, as lawyers, magistrates, and charwomen weigh the same act differently. A workman's bitter speech about seeking a job and finding only suspicion gives the play its edge. The Silver Box remains a strong example of Edwardian social drama, funny in its manners and serious in its charge.
29064-boys-book-of-model-boats:
Raymond Francis Yates wrote this 1920 handbook, Boys' Book of Model Boats, published by the Century Company in New York, with many pictures from drawings and photographs. The chapters open with why a boat floats, the hull, and simple boats with and without power, then move to steam and electric propulsion. Later chapters build an electric launch, a steam launch, an electric lake freighter, and an electric submarine chaser.

Further chapters treat boat fittings, model steam engines, a floating dry dock, and flash steam plants, closing with sailing yachts and a two-foot sailing yacht. A frontispiece shows a two-foot steamboat making ten miles an hour across a park pond. Young builders get a practical, well-illustrated guide to a hobby that taught real engineering.
2908-strife-a-drama-in-three-acts:
John Galsworthy's Strife stages a labor dispute at the Trenartha Tin Plate Works, where chairman John Anthony and the workmen's leader David Roberts refuse to yield. Directors, managers, a union official, and a workmen's committee fill the cast, and the action turns on pride as much as wages. Anthony's son Edgar and the manager Underwood try to find a way through, while the men's families bear the cost.

The play's power lies in its refusal to make either side a villain, since both leaders would rather ruin their cause than compromise. A scene between Enid Anthony and Mrs. Roberts shows the human damage behind the bargaining. Strife remains Galsworthy's best-known industrial drama, still staged for its clear-eyed view of deadlock.
29117-bygone-punishments:
William Andrews wrote Bygone Punishments, on the strange penalties of old England, with reviews praising his curious, out-of-the-way information and good stories. The Church Bells called his books always interesting, and the Birmingham Daily Gazette said no student of his books can be a dull after-dinner speaker. The Leeds Mercury praised his England in the Days of Old.

Andrews writes with freshness and narrative art, giving learning without dullness, on subjects always interesting and picturesque. Bygone Punishments gathers the stocks, pillories, ducking stools, and other old correctives, with the tales that cling to them. Readers get a lively antiquarian book, useful for history and folklore, and full of stories fit for retelling.
2912-the-fugitive-a-play-in-four-acts:
John Galsworthy's The Fugitive follows Clare Dedmond, a wife who leaves a marriage whose spirit has fled. Her husband George, his parents General Sir Charles and Lady Dedmond, her brother Reginald, and friends such as the Fullartons watch her attempt to live independently. A solicitor, a tobacconist, a writer, and a restaurant manager fill out a world that judges her harshly.

The play's argument is stated bluntly by a friend, who warns Clare that society attends only to facts, and that without a lover she has no ground under her feet. Clare answers that she will make her own ground. The Fugitive remains a sharp Edwardian study of divorce, reputation, and a woman's claim to a life of her own.
29121-legends-of-the-saxon-saints:
Aubrey de Vere, the late Sir Aubrey de Vere, wrote these legends of the Saxon saints in verse. De Vere, known for poems and historical dramas, turns to the early English church and its kings, queens, and holy men and women. The legends retell their deeds as poetry rather than as dry chronicle.

Contents include King Ethelbert of Kent and Saint Augustine, the consecration of Westminster Abbey, the penance of Saint Laurence, and King Oswald of Northumbria. There are also Caedmon the cowherd, the first English poet, Saint Cuthbert at Carlisle, and Saint Frideswide, linked to the foundations of Oxford. Readers get a poetic tour of Saxon England, where history and devotion meet.
2913-the-pigeon-a-fantasy-in-three-acts:
John Galsworthy's fantasy The Pigeon sets its three acts on Christmas Eve, New Year's Day, and the first of April, in the studio of the artist Christopher Wellwyn. Wellwyn's daughter Ann, the flower seller Guinevere Megan, and her husband Rory pass through the studio. An alien named Ferrand, a former cabman named Timson, a canon, a professor, and a justice of the peace join them. A police constable and curious persons complete the crowd.

Wellwyn paints while Timson curls around a bottle and praises his eye for a gentleman, and the artist answers that he assumes every man a gentleman and every woman a lady. The fantasy asks how society should treat its outcasts, and answers with deliberate kindness. The Pigeon remains Galsworthy's most hopeful play, gentle where Justice is severe.
2914-the-mob-a-play-in-four-acts:
John Galsworthy's The Mob centers on Stephen More, a member of Parliament who defies his constituents, his party, and public opinion on a matter of conscience. His wife Katherine, her uncle the Dean of Stour, her father General Sir John Julian, and a deputation of manufacturers, booksellers, and solicitors press him to retreat. More greets them without offering his hand and tells them plainly that he knows their view.

The play asks what a representative owes voters against what he owes his judgment, and it follows More's stand to its personal cost.
