A Book of Ghosts, by S Baring-Gould, with eight illustrations by D Murray Smith, was first published by Methuen and Company at London in October 1904. It reached a second edition that December. The stories include Jean Bouchon, Pomps and Vanities, The Leaden Ring, The Mother of Pansies, and Glámr.

Colonel Halifax's Ghost Story, The Bold Venture, A Dead Finger, and The 9.30 Up-Train fill out the contents. The first tale opens at Orléans, where the narrator had gone to gather local colour for a life of Joan of Arc and found the town dull and modern.
36651-the-castle-of-andalusia-a-comic-op:
John O'Keeffe's comic opera The Castle of Andalusia, in three acts, was performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden. This edition was printed in London for Longman and his partners from the prompt book, under the managers' authority. Remarks by Mrs Inchbald open the volume, praising O'Keeffe as the originator of a drama made of whim and frolic.

Inchbald notes that since the Beggar's Opera the town has asked operas for music and broad humour. She singles out the songs' comic effect and the mistakes bred by the impositions of Spado. The cast begins with Don Fernando, and an engraved frontispiece shows Pedrillo in the second act.
36825-tablets:
Tablets is a book of short reflective pieces by Bronson Alcott, published at Boston in eighteen sixty eight. Roberts Brothers issued it, with a motto from Fuller on curious method. Two books divide the work, the first called Practical and the second Speculative. Short numbered essays are grouped under heads such as the garden and friendship.

Book one treats gardens, rest, fellowship, friendship, culture, books, and counsels in turn. The garden opens with Cowley's wish for a small house and ample ground. Virgil's wishes, to be wise and a good husbandman, are quoted with praise. Book two turns to tendencies, method, mind, ideas, and the soul's gifts. Genesis, sleep, memory, and deathlessness close the thinking man's table book. Alcott writes as a sage in brief, oracular paragraphs for slow reading.
36915-his-lady-of-the-sonnets:
Robert Norwood wrote poems printed at Boston in 1915. The book is given to his wife, with lines of Browning at the front. I shall never, in the years remaining, paint you pictures, no, nor carve you statues, Browning is quoted. Verse and nothing else have I to give you, the quote closes. The title piece, His Lady of the Sonnets, leads the volume.

Antony to Cleopatra after Actium, Paul to Timothy, and Dives in torment follow. A set of sonnets and songs comes next: Fellow Craftsmen, Posca, Reincarnation, Jacob's Dream, Keats, and A Poet's Prayer. What Is Religion, A Song of Spring, A Fallen Angel, A Litany, and The Great Comrade fill the shelf. My soul awoke from slumber, the title piece begins. Norwood sings wife, faith, and poets in a high old style.
36917-the-story-of-fifty-seven-cents:
Robert Shackleton wrote The Story of Fifty-Seven Cents, published by Harper and Brothers in 1915 as part of a National Extension University set. Despite the title, the book is a life of Russell Conwell, the preacher and lecturer famous for the talk called Acres of Diamonds. Shackleton calls him a man of power, initiative, and persistence.

Conwell rose from farmer's boy to teacher, war correspondent, soldier, and lawyer. He then left the law for the ministry and built a great church from nothing. He founded hospitals and lectured to thousands each year. Sections treat his power as a preacher and his gift for inspiring others. The famous title story belongs to his legend of small gifts put to great use.
36979-finger-prints:
Francis Galton's study of finger prints, published by Macmillan in London and New York in 1892, opens with the finger prints of the author himself as its frontispiece. The first chapter sets creases apart from ridges and tells how the inquiry began.

Earlier chapters trace old uses of prints: hand-prints and seals, Chinese finger marks, the tipsahi of Bengal, and nail-marks on Assyrian bricks and Chinese coins. Official use by Herschel in India is noted. Methods of printing fill the next chapter, from inked slabs and rollers to smoke prints, casts in sealing-wax and gutta-percha, and photographs. Later chapters study the ridges and their uses, then the patterns, their outlines and cores, and the hard work of sorting prints into classes.
37169-ariadne-in-mantua-a-romance-in-fiv:
Ariadne in Mantua is a romance in five acts by Vernon Lee, printed at Portland, Maine, in 1912. Mosher issued it. Lee dedicates the play to Ethel Smyth, thanking and begging her for music. A line from Twelfth Night stands at its head, where Viola offers to serve the Duke with many sorts of music.

The cast names Ferdinand, Duke of Mantua, his uncle the Cardinal, and Hippolyta, Princess of Mirandola. Magdalen appears disguised as Diego. The action fills the palace of Mantua across a year, shortly before Othello's expedition to Cyprus. Act one opens in the Cardinal's study, where a volume of Machiavelli lies open with a manuscript of Catullus inside it.
37195-the-beaux-stratagem-a-comedy-in-fi:
The Beaux Stratagem is a comedy in five acts by George Farquhar, printed from the prompt book of the Theatres Royal with remarks by Mrs Inchbald. Farquhar's last play sends two fortune-hunting beaux, Archer and Aimwell, into the country to pose as master and servant and catch heiresses. Its heroine, Mrs Sullen, is trapped in a hateful marriage.

Inchbald's remarks make an early case against the play she introduces. The comedy is seldom performed now, she says. Its wit is a poor atonement for its contempt of principle. She also tells the famous story of its writing: Farquhar, dying at twenty-nine, finished it in six weeks, and died within days of its triumph. The volume preserves both the masterpiece and the age that had begun to blush at it.
37219-little-susy-s-little-servants:
Little Susy's Little Servants is a book for small children by Mrs Prentiss, first copyrighted in 1856 and again in 1883 by Anson D F Randolph and Company. The book's puzzle is that Susy, who has a kind mamma to care for her, was given many servants of her own.

The servants are the parts of her body. Two black twins she keeps shut up most of the time are her eyes, which soon learn to show her the fire. Another pair of twins slap and scratch her face until they learn better: these are her hands. Restless fat twins that kick holes in socks are her feet. Another pair lets her hear her mamma sing and the cat say mew. One hidden servant helps her take her breakfasts, dinners, and suppers. The lessons teach children what each gift is for.
37416-the-princess-of-bagdad-a-play-in-t:
Alexandre Dumas the younger wrote a play in three acts, translated from the French and printed in London in 1881 under his sanction. The scene is Paris, in the elegant drawing room of John de Hun and his wife Lionnette. A lawyer named Richard comes by night with bad news, and asks John to muster all his courage.

They are ruined, Richard tells him. Lionnette was reared in luxury and without order, and John never knew how to refuse her anything. Worse, he gave her power of attorney over his property as well as her own. The debt stands at one million, a hundred and seven thousand, one hundred and twenty-seven francs, fifty-two centimes.
37420-paint-technology-and-tests:
Paint Technology and Tests is a trade science book by Henry Gardner, printed in nineteen eleven. Gardner led a test shop for the paint trade group of the United States. The McGraw Hill house of New York brought the book out that year. Its first part treats paint oils and thin fluids and how they dry. Counts and traits of each oil are set side by side for the trade.

A part on driers tracks how each kind speeds or harms the dry. Paint earth hues and their traits fill the next long part. Lab tests of made paint get a full part of hands on trials. Field test fences and what watch of them shows close the book. The whole aims to put paint make on a proof base.
37543-watt-s-songs-against-faults:
Watt's Songs against Faults is a children's verse booklet from Isaac Watts's Divine and Moral Songs, issued in New York by McLoughlin Brothers. The first song is against lying, and it opens with praise for youth who walk in wisdom's way. To fear a lie and speak the truth is its first lesson, so that all may trust what children say.

Liars can never be trusted, even when they happen to speak the truth, the song warns. One fault hidden by a lie makes two faults, it counts. Ananias, struck dead for lying in the Bible, is held up as the dread example. Watts's songs taught morals in rhyme to generations of children, here in a cheap picture edition.
37546-the-female-wits:
The Female Wits, an anonymous play of 1704, appears here as publication number 124 of the Augustan Reprint Society, printed at Los Angeles in 1967. Lucyle Hook supplies the introduction. The full title adds: or, the triumvirate of poets at rehearsal. The original title page credits an unnamed author, and the play was staged at the Theatre Royal in Drury Lane around October 1696.

Hook's introduction calls the piece a devastating satire in the manner of Buckingham's Rehearsal. It attacks all plays by women playwrights. Its chief target is Mary Manley's blood and thunder tragedy The Royal Mischief of 1696. The reprint preserves a sharp piece of theatrical warfare: a rehearsal play in which three women poets watch their own works mocked on stage.
3768-the-lamp-and-the-bell-a-drama-in-fi:
Edna Saint Vincent Millay wrote this verse drama for the fiftieth anniversary of the Vassar College Alumnae Association, and it was played by alumnae themselves. The action moves in an Italian Renaissance world of kings and dukes, where Lorenzo rules Fiori and Mario rules Lagoverde. At its heart stand two young women, Beatrice, called Rose-Red, and Bianca, called Snow-White, whose friendship outlasts courts, marriages, and wars.

The lamp and the bell of the title name what each means to the other. One is a flame the wind cannot blow out, and the other is a bell that tells a traveler she is near home. Millay writes in lyric verse that stays clear even in passion. Readers who like poetic drama will find a play about love between friends, rare on stage then and now, and tender without sentiment.
37685-the-brass-bottle-a-farcical-fantas:
The Brass Bottle, a farcical fantastic play in four acts by Anstey, was first performed at the Vaudeville Theatre in London on September 16, 1909, and printed by Heinemann in 1911. The first-night program names Laurence Grossmith as Horace Ventimore, a young architect, and Holman Clark as Fakrash-el-Aamash, the spirit bound in the bottle. Professor Futvoye, his wife, and Sylvia fill the mortal cast.

Acts one and two play in Ventimore's rooms; later scenes move to a suburban house and a police court. The plot turns on a freed efreet bound to serve his rescuer, whose gifts bring chaos instead of ease. Anstey, famed for Vice Versa, builds farce on the old genie tale: wishes granted by the letter, masters undone by their own luck.
37808-carlyon-sahib-a-drama-in-four-acts:
Gilbert Murray wrote a play in four acts, issued in London in 1900 by William Heinemann. Murray wrote the play at Viareggio in 1893, and it reached the stage six years later, on June 19, 1899. Campbell played it at the Princess of Wales' Theatre at Kennington and helped him reshape it.

Sir David Carlyon, once a chief officer in India, lives in a country house in England for three acts. His girl Vera studies medicine at Zurich, and a past servant named Selim returns. The last act moves to a bungalow in the Ghautgherry Hills in India. Murray denies any aim at the Indian Civil Service.
37827-the-open-question-a-tale-of-two-te:
The Open Question, by Elizabeth Robins, was published in 1899. Harper issued the tale in New York and London. Copyright of 1898 stands on the title page. Robins wrote it under the name Raimond. Its subtitle calls it a tale of two temperaments. George Mandeville's Husband stands among her earlier books. Chapter one traces an American family, the Ganos. Clergymen, West India merchants, and southern planters fill their hundred years. Before the Civil War their line is clear; further back, darkness. The name is accented on its final syllable. To be born a Gano was itself a shining achievement, the family held. Neighbours shared the faith, the narrator notes dryly.

A Gano's agreement settled any vexed question in company. The family founded a religious paper and a seminary. The faith those gifts served, they themselves soon abandoned.
37965-c-sar-s-wife-a-comedy-in-three-act:
W S Maugham wrote Caesar's Wife, a comedy in three acts. William Heinemann issued it at London in 1922. The Royalty Theatre staged it on March 27, 1919. C Aubrey Smith played Sir Arthur Little in that cast. Fay Compton played Violet in the same run. George Relph took the part of Ronald Parry.

Sir Arthur's wife Violet stands at the tale's heart. Henry Pritchard, the Applebys, and Osman Pasha fill the cast. A butler, native servants, and an Arab gardener serve. The scene is laid in Cairo, the cast list begins. Stage rights stay guarded by the author's agent. Golding Bright of Green Street handled all such asks. A sleek drawing-room comedy of marriage and rumor, the play shows Maugham's cool hand with talk that cuts.
38021-the-baculum-in-microtine-rodents:
Sydney Anderson published a zoological study in the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History. It is volume twelve, number three, pages 181 to 216, with forty nine figures. The paper is dated February 19, 1960. Editors E Raymond Hall, Henry S Fitch, and Robert W Wilson supervised the series. A methods section opens the paper: bacula were obtained from specimens, it begins. The baculum is a bone found in many male mammals.

Anderson compares its form across voles, lemmings, and their kin, the microtine rodents. Such small bones carry taxonomic signal for separating species. The state printing plant at Topeka printed the paper. Museum monographs like this one underpin mammal classification.
38068-essays-on-modern-novelists:
William Lyon Phelps wrote Essays on Modern Novelists, issued by The Macmillan Company in New York in nineteen ten. Phelps had taught English at Harvard and then held a chair of English at Yale. Twelve essays fill the book. Three short parts at the end treat novels as a study at a university and the stance of a teacher toward new books.

Essays treat William De Morgan, Thomas Hardy, and William Dean Howells at length. Later essays treat Mark Twain, Henryk Sienkiewicz, and Robert Louis Stevenson. Rudyard Kipling and Mrs Humphry Ward also get full essays. A last essay treats the novel Lorna Doone on its own. Phelps writes as a keen, warm guide for readers who want to judge new fiction with care. His book shows what skilled readers prized in that age.
381-memories-and-portraits:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathers personal essays in this volume, meant to be read straight through like a life in pieces. Childhood, college days, an old Scots gardener, the manse, and talks with friends fill the pages. Portraits of his father and grandfather sit beside musings on dogs, talk, and romance.

Stevenson says the thread that binds them is his own young face, glimpsed as if in a well. The tone is fond, frank, and at times sad for friends now gone. The book gives a rare self-portrait by indirection, through places and people who made the writer he became.
38145-human-all-too-human-a-book-for-fre:
Friedrich Nietzsche wrote this book for free spirits, and Alexander Harvey translated it for Kerr in Chicago in 1908. The contents name its parts: of the first and last things, the history of moral feelings, and the religious life. A preface by Nietzsche opens the volume in numbered sections.

Readers had told him, Nietzsche says, that all his books share something ordinary and unusual. From 'The Birth of Tragedy' to his latest work, they hold snares and nets for short-sighted birds, in his image. They press, quietly and steadily, toward an overturning of habitual opinions and approved customs in their readers.
38182-curious-church-customs-and-cognate:
Curious Church Customs and Cognate Subjects is a volume of essays edited by William Andrews, published at Hull and in London in 1895. Andrews had already written Curiosities of the Church and Old Church Lore. His contributors were known authorities on church history and custom.

J Charles Cox opens with sports once held in churches. Other essays treat holy day customs and church bells: when they were rung and what their inscriptions say. Laws of the belfry and ringers' jugs follow. Baptism, marriage, and burial customs each get a study. The churchyard, altars, the rood loft, and armour hung in churches are covered. Beating the bounds, the story of the crosier, bishops in battle, and the cloister round out the volume. Such books fed a wide Victorian taste for the odd corners of parish life.
38207-on-the-origin-and-metamorphoses-of:
John Lubbock wrote this study of insect origin and change of form. Macmillan issued the new edition in London and New York in 1890. The book first came out in 1873 and was reprinted in 1874. Lubbock had spent years on insect build, growth, and habits.

His preface says spare hours went to the Annulosa, chiefly insects. Prints throughout show forms and stages of growth for the reader. The work stands in the Nature Series for general science readers. Lubbock writes as a keen observer with a clear, calm style. His study follows insects from egg to adult form.
38246-heroes-of-science-chemists:
Pattison Muir wrote this volume on chemists for the Heroes of Science set, printed in London in 1883. Muir was a fellow and teacher of chemistry at Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge issued the book. A line from Buckle heads the front matter, calling the truths of great men immortal.

In his preface Muir states the charge laid on him by the Society's committee. He was to show, by chosen lives, the progress of chemistry from the start of the inductive method to the present time. That progress forms the central theme of the book. Around it he groups short accounts of the lives of those who most helped the science forward.
38314-storm-bound-or-a-vacation-among-th:
Storm-Bound, or A Vacation Among the Snow Drifts, is a boys’ novel by Captain Alan Douglas. Douglas wrote as a scout leader for young readers. The tale forms one part of the Hickory Ridge Boy Scouts series. The New York Book Company sold each cloth volume in the series for forty cents.

Series notes printed at the front sum up the plot in brief. The boys start out on the wrong track. Deep snow turns a planned break into a hard test. Their scout training then helps them set things right. The same front matter lists sister tales about camp life and woodcraft. Each book in the line adds facts on wild animals, trees, and birds.
38354-the-history-of-the-inquisition-of-:
The History of the Inquisition of Spain is Llorente's great work, abridged and translated, in a second edition printed at London in 1827. Juan Antonio Llorente had served as secretary of the Inquisition itself. He became chancellor of the University of Toledo and a knight of the Order of Charles the Third. His history was composed from original documents of the Supreme Council's archives.

The chapters start with the church before Constantine. They move through the old Spanish Inquisition to the modern Holy Office. Llorente traces the Grand Inquisitor, the royal council, and the lesser tribunals. The expulsion of the Jews follows in the contents. An insider's papers give the book its weight.
38564-happy-hearts:
Happy Hearts, by June Isle, is a set of tales for little readers. Poe and Hitchcock of Cincinnati issued it in the Maple Grove Stories. Rights were entered in eighteen sixty four for the small volume. Four chapters carry the book, from Whom Have We Always to the close.

Chapter one sets Mr and Mrs Payson and their three small children. Payson tells the children he has bought a country home for them. The little ones talk from morning to night of that new home. In the country they watch birds build nests and teach young to fly. Fritz Dead Yet Lives and What the Stars Saw stand among later tales.
38583-heroes-of-science-physicists:
Heroes of Science: Physicists, by William Garnett, gives the lives of great British workers in physical science for young readers. The Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge published the volume in London under its committee for general literature and education.

Garnett claims no originality for the book. His aim is to bring within reach of every boy and girl matter found only in big libraries. Schools, he complains, teach the rules of the science but neglect the history of how those rules were won. The volume therefore deals with the lives of a few noted men, all British by birth, with only passing words on the living. Even so, the founding of the Royal Society, the American Philosophical Society, and the Royal Institution all fall within its scope.
38653-such-things-are-a-play-in-five-act:
Mrs Inchbald's Such Things Are, a play in five acts as performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, is kept in its second edition, printed in London, 1788, for the Robinsons. A prologue by Thomas Vaughan, spoken by Mr Holman, opens the performance in the book.

Inchbald's advertisement tells where the piece came from. The travels of an Englishman through Europe and parts of Asia, softening the sorrows of prisoners wherever he went, gave her the subject. The play earned far more from the theatre, she notes, than a successful comedy usually brings. Not knowing where in the East her hero was then at work, she fixed the scene on the island of Sumatra, whose English settlement and manners, she argues, make the incidents probable.
38678-green-stockings-a-comedy-in-three-:
Green Stockings is a comedy in three acts by A E W Mason, first copyrighted in 1910. The hosted text is the Samuel French acting edition, printed in New York and London for stage use. A caution page warns that both amateur and professional rights are protected and require permission.

Acting editions like this one were working tools for theatre companies, with the publisher handling amateur rights from New York and professional rights through an agent on Broadway. Readers can study how a popular stage comedy of the period was packaged for production. The edition preserves the full play text along with the business terms that governed its performance.
38685-the-truants:
The Truants is a novel by A E W Mason, printed in London by Smith, Elder and Company in 1904. Mason had written the Four Feathers, Clementina, Miranda of the Balcony, the Watchers, and the Courtship of Morrice Buckler. Twenty chapters trace two runaways from duty.

Chapters open with Pamela Mardale learns a very little history, Pamela looks on, and the Truants. Tony Stretton makes a proposal, and Pamela makes a promise, follow. News of Tony, the lady on the stairs, and Gideon fleece pace the mid tale. The new road, Mr Chase, and on the Dogger Bank raise the run. Tony inspiration, Tony returns to Stepney, and Mr Mudge comes to the rescue drive onward. The Foreign Legion, Callon leaves England, and south of Ouargla close the flight. Novel fans get Mason at adventure and conscience.
38759-next-door-neighbours-a-comedy-in-t:
Next Door Neighbours is a comedy in three acts by Mrs Inchbald. It was printed in London in 1791. The play was performed at the Theatre Royal, Haymarket. Inchbald drew it from two French dramas. Their titles are L'Indigent and Le Dissipateur. A prologue by Vaughan opens the printed text. It was spoken by Bannister the younger on stage.

The prologue jokes about puffing, or self-praise in print. Quacks of state and healers of vapours puff alike, it says. The bard is called a harmless female scribbler. She claims no more than a translator's due. The cause is left to the audience as a jury. Inchbald was an actress turned playwright and novelist. Her comedies held the London stage for years. This piece shows her light hand at adaptation.
38909-andromache-a-play-in-three-acts:
Gilbert Murray wrote Andromache, a play in three acts, printed in London in 1900. All acting rights in English are reserved on the title page. A prefatory letter to his friend Archer tells how the play began. On an April day in 1896 the two dragged bicycles up hills round Rievaulx Abbey in blinding rain.

Their talk ran on whether all sincere comedies must be cynical, and on the lost plays of the Greek tragedians. They agreed that a plain historical play in the Greek Heroic Age might prove a good trial. Archer wanted verse and the Greece of the English poets. Murray wanted the real Greece of history, and even of the study of early peoples.
38916-the-trial-of-oscar-wilde-from-the-:
Shorthand reports of the trial of Oscar Wilde fill a volume privately printed at Paris in 1906. The issue was limited to fifty copies on Japanese vellum and five hundred on handmade paper. The hosted copy is number one hundred and eighty-four of that printing.

A long preface quotes De Profundis at length, where Wilde tells a friend he meant to eat of the fruit of every tree in the world's garden. The preface weighs his claim that he had shunned the garden's shadow side, only to taste sorrow, disgrace, and remorse in turn. It doubts that claim and sets the confession beside the fall. Readers get the court record of a famed trial, framed by a grave study of Wilde's own last account of himself.
39011-disease-in-plants:
Disease in Plants, published in 1901, is Marshall Ward's guide to the sicknesses of crops and garden plants. Ward taught botany at Cambridge and led the British Mycological Society. He wrote the book for growers: planters, foresters, farmers and gardeners. Such readers, he says, want to know what is wrong and what to do, not the whole life story of a fungus.

Ward meets them halfway, giving the cause of each malady in plain terms. He still insists that real cure needs some grasp of how disease works. Wheat rust, phylloxera and soil bacteria appear as cases, not as lectures. The book stands as an early bridge between the lab and the field.
39013-north-pole-voyages-embracing-sketc:
North Pole Voyages, by the Reverend Z A Mudge, was printed in New York by Nelson and Phillips, with a Cincinnati house, in 1875. Mudge wrote Views from Plymouth Rock, Witch Hill, and Arctic Heroes. Five plates fill the book, one showing Captain C F Hall. The book came out for the Sunday school trade.

Mudge sketches the chief facts and events in the latest American efforts to reach the North Pole. The run goes from the second Grinnell expedition to that of the Polaris. In his preface he says that for more than three hundred years a strong desire has moved explorers to bare the secrets of the pole. Learned geographers, skilled sailors, and men of science have joined the quest with warm interest. Young readers got the ice tale as a lesson in brave endurance.
39268-the-eliminator-or-skeleton-keys-to:
Westbrook wrote a freethinker's attack on priestcraft, dated 1894. The Eliminator calls itself a set of skeleton keys to sacerdotal secrets. Its index starts with pagan mythologies. Westbrook nails his theses to the church doors of Catholics and Protestants alike, he says, and stands his ground.

Almost all in the Christian faith, he argues, came as an afterthought. It is the least original, he says, of the ten great faiths of the world. The great error was to read as fact what wise men of old meant as figures. Custom, not proof, is the base of the scheme. The creed sung each Sunday, he adds, was framed long after the last apostle died. He sums up that the Christ of the New Testament is a myth.
39275-directions-for-collecting-and-pres:
Riley's Directions for Collecting and Preserving Insects was issued by the Smithsonian Institution in 1892. It forms part F of Bulletin 39 of the United States National Museum. Riley, honorary curator of insects at the museum, wrote it for collectors in the field. An introduction treats the characteristics of insects, the scope of entomology, and the classification of the hexapods order by order. Collecting follows: general rules, then the apparatus in detail.

The sweeping net, water net, umbrella, beating cloth, sieve, chisel, fumigator, and haversack each get their section. Orders are then taken one by one, with seasons: winter, spring, summer, and fall collecting for beetles alone. Attracting by lights, traps, freshets, and night work are all covered. Killing and preserving close the manual, with alcohol, chloroform, and cyanide of potassium among the agents. Special directions serve each order. The bulletin is the federal museum's field handbook for amateur collectors.
39357-texas-honey-plants:
Texas Honey Plants is a state farm test sheet, out in January of nineteen eight. Two bug and bee men of the state wrote it. The sheet is the work of the bug branch of the state farm school. A shot of a bee on a mint bloom heads the work.

The front note calls it a first sketch of the theme. Work for it ran past the terms of four heads of that branch in a row. Each let the mass of bloom facts and notes grow. A bee man of a town in the state gave much of its store. The state sends such sheets free to all who ask the head of the school, a fact the sheet states in plain words.
39380-famous-european-artists:
Famous European Artists is a set of artist biographies by Sarah Bolton, printed at New York by Thomas Crowell with copyright of 1890. Bolton had already written Poor Boys Who Became Famous, Girls Who Became Famous and Famous Men of Science. Her motto is Marcus Aurelius: do not act as if you had ten thousand years to throw away; death stands at your elbow. The book is dedicated to Elizabeth Bullard.

Ten lives fill the volume. Michael Angelo opens it, then Leonardo da Vinci and Raphael of Urbino. Titian and Murillo follow, then Rubens and Rembrandt. Sir Joshua Reynolds, Sir Edwin Landseer and Turner close the roll. By reading of these great men, some may be led to think and act like them. The lives are improving biography for young readers, art history taught as character.
39662-the-magic-nuts:
The Magic Nuts, a fairy story by Mrs Molesworth, was issued at London and New York by Macmillan in 1898. Pictures by Rosie Pitman go with the tale. A front plate shows an unselfish mermaid in her sea world. Molesworth dedicates the little story to her granddaughter, Violet Sara Molesworth.

A verse by Cardinal Newman on childhood heads the dedication page. Night and Morning is the title of the first chapter. Apples and nuts open the list of the chapters that follow. Molesworth was the queen of the nursery tale in her age. Her magic here stays gentle, moral, and close to home. Children cross into wonder by small doors in her books. This tale of nuts with a spell on them is pure Molesworth.
39833-the-old-pincushion-or-aunt-clotild:
The Old Pincushion, or Aunt Clotilda Guests, by Mrs Molesworth, was published in London, with pictures by Mrs Adrian Hope. Molesworth had also written Carrots and The Palace in the Garden. She gives the book to three dear though unknown little friends, Bertha, Hilda, and Lesley.

Chapter one is a letter with bad news. Philippa has an idea, and Aunt Clotilda replies. The children reach Ty-Gwyn, fall into a grave predicament, and at last reach the white house. Breakfast in bed, news from Philippa, and a cottage near the creek follow. A plague of feathers, a pincushion manufactory, and a found chapter close the list. Full page pictures show after dinner play time, a cart ride, and a figure in a doorway. Readers get a gentle childrens tale of a visit and a kind aunt.
40060-the-christian-faith-under-modern-s:
William Hallock Johnson wrote The Christian Faith Under Modern Searchlights. Fleming H Revell Company issued it in 1916. The talks form the L P Stone Lectures at Princeton. Johnson taught Greek and New Testament at Lincoln University. Francis Landey Patton wrote the intro. He had led Princeton Seminary as president.

Chapter One asks what the Christian faith is. A clear statement of terms comes first there. The New Testament writers stress the Passion, it says. The Resurrection shares that stress in their pages. Christ's person draws their stress as well. Primitive faith and Paul's faith stand compared next. Was Paul the founder of the faith, it asks. A scholar's defense, the book tests old belief under the hard lights of new doubt and print.
4029-true-stories-about-dogs-and-cats:
A book of true animal stories gathers plain tales of dogs and cats and the people who kept them. In one sampled tale, a pet cat who had lost all her kittens but one takes in strange young orphans. She carries them one by one to her nest and nurses them as her own.

Soon the old cat and her roguish adopted children range through every room of the house. Such stories favor kindness, pluck, and the odd wisdom of animals over fine writing. The book suits young readers and animal lovers, offering short, true anecdotes that can be read one at a time at bedtime or in class.
4038-imaginary-portraits:
Walter Horatio Pater's imaginary portraits sketch invented figures who feel truer than real people, set within a tree architecture of moss-grown balusters, statues, and fountains. The portraits group themselves with a fittingness no real life quite shows, lit by a light sought in vain on anything actual.

Windless afternoons hang over the scenes, and the narrator always expects rain by evening, as storms gather beyond the garden calm. Pater uses these figures to test ideas about art, faith, and character. Readers who enjoy prose portraits and quiet speculation will find a book of strange, polished beauty.
40587-yellowstone-nights:
Yellowstone Nights is a novel by Herbert Quick, author of Aladdin and Company. Bobbs-Merrill held the rights in 1911, and Grosset and Dunlap issued the book at New York. The scene is the gateway town at the park's north entrance in Montana. The tale opens on the third of August.

A stalwart young fellow and a girl in lace float through the little park by the station. They seem to hover inches above the earth as lovers do. A bald stranger with a magnifying glass studies the flower beds nearby. He notes the paving, the soil, and the far peaks in a huge pocket book. His gaze creeps ever closer to the bench where the lovers sit. Quick mixes courtship with a comic portrait of the born observer.
40700-dandy-dick-a-play-in-three-acts:
Dandy Dick is a farce in three acts by Arthur Pinero, printed at Boston in 1893. Pinero also wrote Sweet Lavender and The Cabinet Minister. The play was the third of his farces for the old Court Theatre in London. An introductory note gives its history.

Those Court farces gave playgoers a fresh source of laughter and the English stage a new order of comic play. They also brought rich profit to managers Arthur Cecil and John Clayton. A melancholy interest clings to this one, though. Dandy Dick was the swan-song of the old theatre and of the partnership. Clayton was acting in this very piece when death overtook him. The text that follows is a model of the well-made farce, built on a dean, a racehorse, and a parish in trouble.
40736-the-second-mrs-tanqueray-a-play-in:
The Second Mrs Tanqueray is a play in four acts by Arthur Pinero. Heinemann published it at London; impressions ran in 1895, 1898, and 1900. The play was produced at a London theatre on May 27, 1893. A list of Pinero's plays fronts the text. The Magistrate, Sweet Lavender, and The Notorious Mrs Ebbsmith stand there.

Aubrey Tanqueray heads the persons of the play. Paula, the second wife, stands next on the list. Ellean, Cayley Drummle, and a captain named Ardale follow. A lawyer and a doctor complete the chief company. The first act is set in Tanqueray's rooms at the Albany in November. The later acts move to his house, Highercoombe, in the country. Pinero's drama of a woman with a past was his great serious success. Its four acts test whether society will let Paula begin again.
40839-the-new-woman-an-original-comedy-i:
Sydney Grundy wrote The New Woman, an original comedy in four acts, printed in London in 1894. The title names the burning figure of that decade: the educated, independent woman. Grundy puts a woman doctor, Mary Bevan, in his cast.

The people gather around Gerald Cazenove. His uncle the Colonel and Captain Sylvester open the cast. The women are Margery, Lady Wargrave, Enid Bethune, Victoria Vivash, and the doctor. Acts one and two play in Gerald's chambers, a sitting room decorated like a boudoir, all antimacassars and flowers. The Colonel enters, sniffs at the stench of flowers, and throws a bunch of lilies out of the window. Act three moves to Lady Wargrave's drawing room, act four to an orchard at Mapledurham. Theatre readers get the 1890s debating the New Woman in comedy form.
40898-the-friendly-club-and-other-portra:
Francis Parsons wrote a set of essays dated 1922, most first run in the Hartford Courant with no name shown. Three pieces are new here, on the Friendly Club, a tavern tale, and a poet of battle song. Front thanks cite a fresh book on the Elizabeth Whitman tale as a key help for one essay.

Club life, a bell tavern in Danvers, and the poet known as Peter Parley fill the early essays. A friend of Lincoln, a shrine of the muses, and a quiet life close out the set. Prints show Joel Barlow, the Sigourney house, and a fine town library of the place and time.
41033-the-silver-shield-an-original-come:
Sydney Grundy wrote The Silver Shield, an original comedy in three acts, first played at the Strand Theatre in London in May 1885. A New York cast list for June 1885 stands beside the London one. Sir Humphrey Chetwynd heads the cast, with his son Ned and the painter Tom Potter. Alma Blake, Lucy Preston, and a clergyman named Dozey fill out the company.

Act One opens in a hall with a stained glass window on a lawn. Tom works at an easel while Ned opens and destroys his letters at a table. Lucy teases out that most of the letters come from creditors and lawyers. The bright talk about art and realism sets the comic tone at once.
41034-a-philadelphia-lawyer-in-the-londo:
A Philadelphia Lawyer in the London Courts, by Thomas Leaming with his own drawings, reached a second, revised edition in New York in 1912, from a 1911 copyright. Early chapters give first impressions of the Law Courts on the Strand: a court room, the players in a trial, wigs and gowns, easy talk, and agreeable voices.

Later chapters explain the making of lawyers, the Inns of Court, and a barrister's chambers and call to the bar. Leaming splits the bar into common law and chancery parts, then treats solicitors, fees, and dress, down to bags in blue and red. An American eye finds much alike and much strange, in a clear, genial guide to English legal life.
41232-hungry-hearts:
Hungry Hearts is a book of stories by Anzia Yezierska, printed at Boston and New York in 1920. Yezierska gives the book to Mrs Henry Ollesheimer. Ten tales fill it, from Wings and Hunger to My Own People and How I Found America.

The first tale opens on a bright Sunday in May, in a dim basement room. Shenah Pessah wails that her heart chokes in her like in a prison, and that she dies for a little love with nobody to give it. A voice rebukes her tears and asks who will listen or care. Yezierska writes of poor immigrant women in New York, their want, work, and dreams. Readers get raw, warm tales told in the speech of the streets.
41304-the-mother-of-parliaments:
Harry Graham, who wrote A Group of Scottish Women, made this bright handbook on the British Parliament. Little, Brown printed The Mother of Parliaments at Boston in 1911, with twenty plates. Graham gave the book to his wife.

Party and Parliament open the tour, then the Lords and the Commons in turn. The Palace of Westminster, the king's servants, the Lord Chancellor, and the Speaker each take a chapter. How Parliament opens, how debate is ruled, and what members may and may not do fill the middle. Dress, speech, work, strangers, and the men who report it all close the book. Views of both houses in 1742 face early pages.
41688-keats:
Keats, a critical life by Sidney Colvin, belongs to the English Men of Letters series edited by John Morley. Macmillan of London first published it in 1887 and reprinted it many times, this copy in 1909. Colvin was a critic and a keeper of prints at the British Museum. The series set brief scholarly lives of the great writers side by side.

The preface pays a debt. With the name of Keats, Colvin says, that of his first biographer, Lord Houghton, must always remain joined. But Houghton's record no longer suffices: since 1867 much new matter has come to light, and some old matter has been proved mistaken. No life of Keats matching the present state of knowledge existed, and Colvin was asked to supply one. His authorities list runs from Leigh Hunt and Medwin's Shelley to Haydon's life and Keats's own letters.
41750-the-magistrate-a-farce-in-three-ac:
Arthur Pinero wrote a farce in three acts, first printed in 1892 and reprinted many times up to 1914. A note at the front calls it, after Sweet Lavender, the most liked of Pineros plays. The note says Pinero found his own clear voice in this farce for the first time.

That voice, the note adds, made a new and fresh kind of English comic play on the stage. Later farces in the same Court set include The Schoolmistress, Dandy Dick, and The Cabinet Minister. A list of Pineros plays at the front runs from The Times and The Profligate to later works such as Iris and Letty.
41775-cornish-characters-and-strange-eve:
Baring-Gould gathered these Cornish lives and odd tales in a book published in London and New York in 1909. Sixty-two full-page plates, copied from old prints, support the text. A matching volume on Devonshire had gone before, and the Cornish set follows the same plan of short lives mixed with strange events.

The contents open with William Pengelly, a geologist, then move to a knight, a regicide and a wrestler. Henry Trengrouse the inventor, the Botathan Ghost and John Couch Adams the astronomer all appear. Pirates, murders and local wonders keep the county's past vivid, one figure and one story at a time.
41828-general-bounce-or-the-lady-and-the:
Whyte-Melville wrote this novel, drawn by Frances Ewan for Ward, Lock. The London house issued the tale of General Bounce in full. Contents open with My Cousin, The Abigail, and a handsome governess. A race horse name, Libitina, and Uncle Baldwin follow in the list.

Later chapters move from a ball to want, plenty, and campaigning abroad. Forgery, club law, dispatches, and a hospital scene raise the stakes. The Widow, King Crack, and Flood and Field close the long tale. Melville blends sport, society, and army life in his known style.
41949-cyrano-de-bergerac-an-heroic-comed:
Cyrano de Bergerac, an heroic comedy in five acts, is a play by Edmond Rostand, translated from the French by Charles Renauld. Frederick A Stokes printed it at New York in 1898 and 1899, with an introduction by Adolphe Cohn of Columbia University. A photograph of Mansfield as Cyrano fronts the volume.

Cohn calls the play's success one of the most important literary events of the last quarter century. It placed Rostand, a young man of twenty-eight, at the head of French dramatic writers at a stroke. The verdict of the French public in December 1897 has since been approved in nearly every country of Western civilization. Cohn asks whether an American or Englishman can find in Cyrano all that the French find. Such works, he answers, join what is purely human with what belongs to their time and place.
42009-glimpses-of-three-coasts:
Glimpses of Three Coasts is a travel book by Helen Jackson, who wrote as H H, printed at Boston in 1886. Jackson was the author of Ramona and A Century of Dishonor. The contents divide into California and Oregon, Scotland and England, and Norway, Denmark, and Germany. The first essay treats outdoor industries in southern California.

Climate, she opens, is to a country what temperament is to a man: fate. The word climate is primarily a statement of bounds set by the slant of the sun. The tropics are tropic because the sun shines down too straight, vegetation leaps into luxuriance, and human activities languish. Other essays treat Father Junipero and his work, and the present condition of the Mission Indians. A Burns pilgrimage, glints in Edinburgh, and Chester streets make the British part. Bergen days and the Passion Play at Oberammergau close the book.
42041-studies-of-contemporary-poets:
Mary Sturgeon wrote these studies of the poets of her day, published by Dodd, Mead in New York in 1916. She had written 'Women of the Classics' before this volume of criticism. Thanks go to Masefield, Presland and others for leave to quote their poems, her acknowledgment notes at the front.

Lane gave poems by Abercrombie and Woods for her pages, the acknowledgment adds. Sidgwick and Jackson gave Macaulay's work for quotation in the studies. Sturgeon reads the living poets closely, with long extracts set in her chapters, and ranks their music and thought for readers meeting Georgian verse while it was still new.
42060-the-town-its-memorable-characters-:
The Town, by Leigh Hunt, appeared in a new edition in eighteen eighty-nine from Smith, Elder, and Company of London. Forty-five illustrations accompany the text. Hunt's subject is London, treated partly as topography and history. Mostly, though, he recalls the remarkable characters and events tied to its streets.

His London is the stretch between St Paul's and St James's. That district was what people meant by the Town in the word's fashionable sense. The advertisement promises the entire contents unabridged in this edition. Hunt walks street by street, hanging anecdotes of poets, wits, and scandals on each corner. The result is a literary man's memory map of the old city, written with his usual genial ease.
42068-the-tyranny-of-tears-a-comedy-in-f:
The Tyranny of Tears, a comedy in four acts by Haddon Chambers, was copyrighted in Boston in 1902. Long legal notices guard the acting rights and warn that staging the play without leave brings fines or jail. Chambers dedicates the play to his mother. Rights queries go to Charles Frohman at the Empire Theatre in New York.

The persons concerned are Parbury and his wife, her father Colonel Armitage, a Miss Hyacinth Woodward, a butler named Evans, and a maid named Caroline. The title hints at the plot's engine: a wife's tears used as a tool of rule in a smart household. Chambers, a famed stage writer of his day, builds a light, keen comedy of marriage and pride.
42152-the-mormon-battalion-its-history-a:
B H Roberts wrote this history of the Mormon Battalion, published by the Deseret News at Salt Lake City in 1919. The contents begin by comparing the battalion's march with the retreat of the Ten Thousand and Doniphan's expedition.

Roberts calls it the world's record for a march of infantry. Chapters follow the call: the Mormon appeal to the government, consultations with the President, and Brigham Young's work raising the men. Then come the marches, Leavenworth to Santa Fe, Santa Fe to the Gila, and on to the Pacific, with a fight with wild bulls and opposition at Tucson. Later chapters cover service in California and the homeward road. A famous episode of the Mexican War gets its church history.
4216-touch-and-go-a-play-in-three-acts:
D. H. Lawrence's play Touch and Go, in three acts, follows Oliver, Anabel, and Gerald through a friendship turned to bitterness. Oliver speaks bitterly of Gerald's sneering attitude in the deepest things, and of a passion that has cooled to something almost casual.

Anabel answers that she was awfully fond of Oliver, trusted him, and trusts him still, knowing how fond Gerald was of him. Lawrence writes the triangle in plain, charged speech, where love, work, and class collide. Readers who like modern drama of feeling will find a short, intense play.
42248-your-national-parks-with-detailed-:
Your National Parks is a guide book by Enos Mills, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1917. Mills wrote the park tales and essays. The detailed information for tourists was supplied by Laurence Schmeckebier. Maps and illustrations go with the text. The book opens with Yellowstone, the first of the parks. John Colter, its discoverer, stands in a front plate. Yosemite and its history follow. The Sequoia and General Grant parks, with their big trees, come next.

Mount Rainier, Crater Lake, and Glacier park take the tour north and west. Mesa Verde, the Rocky Mountain park, and the Grand Canyon fill its heart. Lassen Volcanic and Hawaii close the main list. Three national monuments and a run of small parks end the book. Mills was the great voice for the parks of his age. His guide joins love of the wild to road facts.
42371-dissertation-on-the-progress-of-th:
The Augustan Reprint Society brought back a study by John Robert Scott on the growth of the fine arts, at Los Angeles in 1954. Roy Harvey Pearce wrote the opening notes. The Clark Memorial Library at the University of California put out the book as number 45 in its set.

Pearce sets Scott in a wide field of thought from the age of print's youth in the arts. He lists works on Homer, Ossian, song, and early genius by Blackwell, Hurd, Blair, Duff, and Wood. His point is that views on art and on rude peoples form one large claim about how culture grows. Scott's own text then takes up that growth.
42378-chats-to-cello-students:
Chats to Cello Students, by Arthur Broadley, is number 7 of The Strad Library, published in London in 1899. A portrait of Broadley fronts the book. First chapters weigh how hard the cello is to master. They take up the choice of a teacher, and of an instrument and bow. Holding the instrument and the use of a sliding pin come next.

Later chats cover notation and the tenor clef, which Broadley calls a must for the cellist. Fingering, bowing in its many forms, staccato and spiccato, and the positions follow. A late chat weighs the differing needs of orchestral players and soloists. The tone is that of a working teacher talking shop: plain, strict, and full of small points that save years of bad habit.
42391-our-national-forests:
Richard Boerker, an arboriculturist who served with the United States Forest Service from 1910 to 1917, wrote this short popular account of the service's work, published by Macmillan in 1918. Its first photograph shows a fire lookout's observation point.

Vigilance is the watchword, the caption says: in 1916 forest officers extinguished 5,655 forest fires. The opening essay argues that the forest problem is a governmental one, since wood is indispensable and forests regulate stream flow. America's yearly take is reckoned in billions: firewood, lumber, railroad ties, barrel staves, pulp wood, and mine timbers. Boerker writes science plainly, as his motto demands. Citizens get the young Forest Service explained by one of its own.
42395-the-circle-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
The Circle is a comedy in three acts by W Somerset Maugham, published in New York with copyright in nineteen twenty one. Lists of Maugham's plays and novels front the volume, including Of Human Bondage and The Moon and Sixpence. A note directs all questions on performance rights to a New York play agency. The persons of the play are listed before the action starts.

Clive Champion Cheney heads that list of characters. Maugham's circle turns on marriage, desertion, and the same choice faced by two generations in one house. A wife who ran off with a lover returns, and the young face her path again. Wit carries a bitter pattern of repetition.
4243-sir-thomas-more-or-colloquies-on-th:
Robert Southey first published these dialogues in 1824. Their full title was Sir Thomas More, or Colloquies on the Progress and Prospects of Society. The present volume reprints a selection from an 1887 Cassell edition. In them Southey talks with the ghost of Thomas More. Their subject is how society changes and where it may be heading.

The chosen colloquies treat the chief rules of social life. They show Southey as he saw those principles late in life. One pleasant piece portrays the author himself among his books. Some topical pieces were left out, but the dialogues keep their mix of hope and doubt.
42446-many-fronts:
Many Fronts is a book of war sketches by Lewis Freeman, published in London by John Murray in 1918. Freeman was a traveller and war correspondent. The sketches first appeared in magazines on both sides of the Atlantic, among them the Atlantic Monthly, the Cornhill, and the World's Work.

The contents cross the whole map of the First World War. The fight for the Garden of Eden opens the book, on the river front in Mesopotamia. Air corps pieces follow: the sharks of the air and the passing of a Zeppelin. A tribute to British merchant captains stands beside fighting for Serbia. The blowing up of the Castelletto and the wonders of the mountain cableways take the reader to the Italian front. Freeman's gift was to be everywhere at once, and the book is a correspondent's album of a war fought on many fronts at once.
42581-the-deacon-an-original-comedy-dram:
The Deacon is a play in five acts by Horace Dale. Its full title calls the work an original comedy drama in plain words. This print gives cast, garb, sets, and stage moves in full for troupes. Rights date the work to the year eighteen ninety two.

Stage plots name doors left and right and the place of each man in a scene. Cast lists cite a first run at a grand house in Reading town in the state east. Home troupes may play the work free by the note at its front. Town types and church pride form the stock fare of the light play. The print serves as both book and guide for the stage crew.
42672-the-wanderings-and-fortunes-of-som:
The Wanderings and Fortunes of Some German Emigrants is a tale of emigration by Frederick Gerstæcker. David Black turned it into English, and it was printed at London in 1848. A long notice from the Athenaeum stands at the front in place of a preface. The notice holds that the book is in substance no fiction.

The tale follows a company of German adventurers bound for the land of promise. Their design is to form a colony there. The reviewer argues that the story is too close in detail to be made up. Its writer, he says, plainly saw and suffered what he tells. To English readers the interest is fresh. Much was known of British emigrants. Little was known of how Germans fared in the New World.
42696-field-and-woodland-plants:
Field and Woodland Plants, by Furneaux, belongs to the Outdoor World series from Longmans of London. The series was made for young collectors of nature lore. This volume carries eight coloured plates and a great many drawings in the text.

Some drawings are by Patten Wilson, and others come from photographs. The first plate shows spring flowers of the woods, with the green hellebore at their head. Sister books in the series treat butterflies and moths, life in ponds and streams, and the sea shore. Each sold at six shillings net with gilt edges. Furneaux wrote most of the set himself. The plant book teaches a rambler to name what he finds in field and wood, season by season.
42718-field-mice-as-farm-and-orchard-pes:
Field Mice as Farm and Orchard Pests is Farmers Bulletin 670 of the United States Department of Agriculture, set out at Washington on June 3, 1915. Its author, D E Lantz of the Bureau of Biological Survey, opens with the loss: short-tailed field mice gnaw crops, bark young trees, and thin the woods. Two tribes do the harm. Meadow mice run on the top ground and nest high and low; pine mice live like moles in deep runs.

More than fifty kinds of the clan range the land, and litters of six to ten come again and again in a year. In fat years they swarm like a plague of old tale. The bulletin maps their range, tells their ways, and gives the means to kill them. It also pleads for their foes: hawks, owls, and snakes earn the farmer's thanks.
42720-speciation-in-the-brazilian-spiny-:
Speciation in the Brazilian Spiny Rats is a study of rats of the genus Proechimys by João Moojen. The University of Kansas issued it in 1948 as part of its museum series. The work runs to more than a hundred pages with many figures.

Moojen sets out his methods, then turns to fossils and to how new forms arise. He weighs size, coat, skull and teeth as marks that set one form apart. Long sections name and describe each species and race in turn. A key helps readers sort the groups, and tables of measures close the study. The list of works cited at the end runs to several pages of sources.
43108-white-turrets:
Mrs Molesworth wrote a tale for young readers called White Turrets. W and R Chambers issued the book in London and Edinburgh in an 1895 form. Pictures by W Rainey stand through the text. The tale opens at a charity concert on a dull November day in London.

Two sisters, guests of Mrs Balderson, sit in front and drink in the music. Celia and her elder sister are on their first real visit to London. Fog dims the hall, yet the girls glow with interest in all they hear. Young readers gain a gentle tale of town, kindness, and growing up.
43185-by-force-of-impulse-a-drama-in-fiv:
By Force of Impulse is a play in five acts by Harry V Vogt, sold in New York for fifteen cents. The front pages list the full cast and their dress act by act. Morris Maitland is a stern father whose word is law. His son Reginald stands against him.

The five acts move from love to split, then to duty, then to peace, and at last to a higher call. Henry Lowville, Ralph Murdell, and Colonel Morrell fill out the male cast. Adrienne Lowville and Hilda Wallace carry the love plot. Sammy Dewdrop and his chum add light scenes. Costume notes help small groups stage the play.
43211-english-economic-history-select-do:
Three editors, A E Bland, P A Brown, and R H Tawney, compiled these select documents of English economic history, first published in 1914 and here in a seventeenth impression. Part one covers the years 1000 to 1485.

The contents begin with the early English manor and borough: the rights and duties of all persons, the Domesday inquest of 1086, and the customs of Dover, Norwich, and Wallingford. A second section lays out the feudal structure in records of knight service, serjeanty, wardship, and marriage fines. A third treats the Jews under charters and ordinances. Students get the evidence itself, document by document, rather than a narrative.
43259-pittsburgh-in-1816-compiled-by-the:
The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh put together a portrait of the city in the year of its charter, issued in 1916 for the one hundredth year mark. Staff drew the facts from the papers and records of 1816 itself. A sketch of the town in 1817 by a bride on her wedding tour fronts the book.

Short parts cover the new city vote, early guests' views, the census, trade and mills, and trips east. Taverns, steamboats, ferries, bridges, churches, schools, banks, and the post all get their own brief notes. The book also treats the Fourth of July, the police, the water supply, slavery, and ads from the papers of the day. It is a neat civic time capsule.
43492-the-five-knots:
The Five Knots is a mystery novel by Fred White. Little, Brown published the book at Boston in 1908, from rights dated the year before. White had written The Slave of Silence among other tales. The contents run to forty six chapters of pursuit and hidden treasure.

The first chapter opens at Maldon Grange, home of a rich ship owner. On a December afternoon, before the lamps are lit, a shadow flickers across the dim hall. The watcher cannot tell whether the visitor was real or a trick of the mind. Chapter titles promise a bit of string, a registered letter, and a shadow on the wall. A yellow hand, a diamond moth, and a tangled clue mark the middle. The tale ends among vaults, a sinking ship, and a cave of treasure.
43502-votes-for-women-a-play-in-three-ac:
Votes for Women is a play in three acts by Elizabeth Robins, published at London in nineteen oh nine. The hosted copy prints the bill of its Court Theatre staging. The bill names the full cast, with parts for lords, ladies, a working woman, and a young campaigner named Vida Levering.

The acts are set at a country house in Hertfordshire, in Trafalgar Square, and in Eaton Square. All the action takes place between Sunday noon and six in the evening of the same day. A note in the cast list records two changes of character names in the text. The play opens at twelve on a Sunday in late June. A butler crosses to answer the door as Lady John Wynnstay enters briskly from the garden.
43518-old-picture-books-with-other-essay:
Alfred W Pollard gathered his essays in Old Picture Books, with Other Essays on Bookish Subjects, for Methuen at London in 1902. He dedicated the volume to John Macfarlane, librarian of the Imperial Library at Calcutta. The two men had shared bookish studies during Macfarlane's seventeen years at the British Museum.

Most essays first ran in journals such as Bibliographica, The Library, and Longman's Magazine. One piece, England and the Bookish Arts, served as an opening essay to The English Bookman's Library. Pollard hopes the essays will keep his friend's love of old books alive in India. Early printing, picture books, and the trade in rare volumes fill the pages.
43533-a-brief-bible-history-a-survey-of-:
James Oscar Boyd and John Gresham Machen wrote a brief survey of both testaments, printed at Philadelphia in 1922 for a church press. Lessons are grouped in two main parts, the growth of the church in old testament times and the life of Christ with the early church. Each lesson ties to a named stretch of scripture.

Old testament lessons run from the days before Abraham through exile and return to the hope of a coming one. New testament lessons follow the baptism, the work in Galilee, the cross, and the rising again. Paul takes the last lessons, with his trips, his letters, his jail time, and the close of his age.
43545-detection-of-the-common-food-adult:
Detection of the Common Food Adulterants is a laboratory manual by Edwin Bruce, an instructor in chemistry at the Indiana State Normal School. It was printed in London in 1907. The contents read as a tour of the kitchen and the market, article by article, with the tests a chemist can run at the bench.

Dairy products come first. Milk is coloured with annatto, caramel, and coal-tar dyes, and preserved with formaldehyde, boric acid, and salicylic acid. Butter hides saffron and turmeric, or turns out to be oleomargarine and cottonseed oil. Meats and eggs follow, with diseased meats and horse-flesh in sausages named plainly. Cereal products close the early set. The book arms the food inspector and the student with named frauds and named tests.
43601-freaks-of-fanaticism-and-other-str:
Freaks of Fanaticism and Other Strange Events is a book of historical essays by Sabine Baring-Gould, published in London by Methuen in 1891. Baring-Gould wrote novels, lives of saints, and books of oddities. This volume first appeared as a second series of his Historic Oddities and Strange Events, and the new title names its true subject.

The preface explains the choice. Several essays treat the history of mysticism, the outbreak in man of a spiritual element that cannot be ignored or wholly suppressed. Rightly directed, Baring-Gould calls it man's noblest element. Unregulated, it turns mischievous. Other essays take up political and racial fanaticism, including the charges laid against the Jews in an age of expulsions from Russia. The book is a clergyman's tour through the strange fevers of belief, half warning and half wonder.
43643-foods-and-culinary-utensils-of-the:
Charles Martyn compiled this survey of ancient food from standard historical works, published by the Caterer Publishing Company at New York. He opens with Feuerbach's pun, man is what he eats, and argues that tracing the history of foods and utensils is tracing the history of the world. Primeval man, ill-fitted by teeth and gut for most natural foods, lived on fruits and soft-shelled nuts until cooking made nearly everything edible to him.

The chapters then visit the tables of the ancient world: Assyria, Egypt and its vegetable kingdom, Greece before the age of luxury, and Rome in the days of her greatest prosperity. The ancient Jews and the Chinese close the tour. It is a caterer's history, written for readers of the trade.
43834-comic-insects:
Comic Insects is a picture book of verses for children by Reid. Warne published it in London. Berry drew the illustrations. The Dalziel brothers engraved them. Coloured plates came from another firm. Six creatures speak in their own voices.

A preface in verse wonders at the contents. Can insects talk, and do they have brains? The caterpillar speaks first. He enters his chrysalis rather unwillingly. In spring he will rise as a fascinating moth. The moth, the snail, and the bee follow in turn. A black-beetle and a spider close the set. Each rhyme teaches a small natural lesson. The pictures show the creatures at their work and play.
43887-sleep-and-its-derangements:
Sleep and Its Derangements is a medical book by William Hammond, issued by Lippincott in 1869. Hammond taught diseases of the mind and the nervous system at Bellevue in New York. He had served as surgeon general of the United States Army before this work. A preface traces the book to his 1865 journal paper on insomnia in patients.

Wakefulness, with a chapter on the physiology of sleep, was its earlier separate form. Warm reception drew out this enlarged volume on sleep gone wrong in health. Dreams, somnambulism, and sleeplessness fall under his clinical survey of the night. Neurology in America claims Hammond as a founder, and this is his popular text.
44118-zones-of-the-spirit-a-book-of-thou:
August Strindberg wrote Zones of the Spirit, a book of thoughts translated by Claud Field and published by Putnam of New York and London in 1913. Arthur Babillotte supplies the introduction. Strindberg's Inferno and The Son of a Servant stand under his name. The pieces come from his Blue Book, the strange notebook of his last years.

A history of the Blue Book opens the contents. Then the thoughts scatter across every field: the thirteenth axiom, bad digestion, the song of the sawyers, a nightingale in a vineyard, and the miracle of the corn-crakes. Electricity meets theology in The Electric Battery and the Earth Circuit. Swedenborg's hell, the conversion of the cheerful pagan Horace, and the lice-king follow. Somnambulism in everyday life, stars seen by daylight, and the right to remorse close the run in view. Readers get Strindberg thinking aloud, aphorism by aphorism, between science and faith.
44206-old-time-nautical-instruments:
Old-Time Nautical Instruments, by John Robinson, curator of the Marine Room at the Peabody Museum in Salem, was printed at Boston in 1921 in one hundred copies. The piece is reprinted from Old-Time New England for April 1921, with an illustration of the ship Grand Turk of 1786.

Robinson asks what instruments colonial ship-masters carried, what the Mayflower had, and what Columbus used. The ship-master of today, he says, uses instruments so different that he knows nothing of the earlier ones. A skilful navigator of Salem's last square-rigger, the ship Mindoro, held a Davis quadrant and confessed he had no idea how to use it. The Peabody collection holds two such quadrants, dated 1768 and 1773, and an older undated one.
44231-the-miraculous-medal-its-origin-hi:
Aladel traces a devotion in The Miraculous Medal, its origin, history, circulation, and results, printed at Philadelphia with copyright in 1880. Kilner made the book, rendered from the French by a translator signing P S, a graduate of Saint Joseph's at Emmitsburg. A plate shows Sister Catherine Laboure, the Daughter of Charity favored with the vision of the medal in 1830. She died on the last day of 1876.

The book is given to the Virgin Mary, conceived without sin. An author's declaration follows the old decree of Pope Urban: the terms miracle, revelation, and apparition, as here employed, have no other than a historical value. The whole contents are submitted to the judgment of the church's see. An American preface then opens the case for the medal. Since the hour when the beloved disciple took the Virgin to his own, it begins, her Son's followers have cherished her.
44245-historic-oddities-and-strange-even:
Historic Oddities and Strange Events, first series, gathers curious lives and mysteries by S Baring Gould. Methuen and Company published the book in London in 1889. Gould explains in his preface that general histories pass such matter by. Eccentric persons and odd events, he says, always awakened his interest. He collected their details wherever he found them.

The opening narrative treats the disappearance of Benjamin Bathurst. Bathurst vanished on November 25, 1809. English opinion blamed a secret murder ordered by Napoleon. The Times asserted the charge in January 1810, and the Moniteur repudiated it. Other chapters cover the Duchess of Kingston and General Mallet. The locksmith Gamain, the snail telegraph, and the wonder-working Prince Hohenlohe appear. Two pieces, Gould admits, dress their facts slightly into stories. He dates the preface from Lew Trenchard in Devon, July 1889.
44396-child-labor-in-city-streets:
Child Labor in City Streets is a reform study by Edward Clopper. Macmillan published it in New York in 1913. Clopper served the National Child Labor Committee. His district was the Mississippi Valley. A bibliography and appendices support the argument. The book runs to nearly three hundred pages.

The first chapter names the neglected problem. Reformers had fought for factory and mine children. Street-working children waited unprotected. Later chapters count them in America and Europe. Newspaper sellers earn a chapter of their own. Bootblacks, peddlers, and messengers follow. The effects of street work on children are weighed. Its link to delinquency gets a chapter. The struggle for regulation in two continents closes the case.
44520-pamphlets-and-parodies-on-politica:
Pamphlets and Parodies on Political Subjects gathers the squibs of William Hone, with many wood cuts by Cruikshank. The lead piece is The Political House That Jack Built, here in its fifty-first edition, printed by and for Hone at London in 1821 and priced at one shilling. A straw thrown up to show which way the wind blows, says its motto.

Hone gives the piece to Doctor Slop, his political godchild, and to the nursery of children six feet high, his readers. The verse builds its house piece by piece, in the manner of the nursery rhyme, laying the wealth of the nation inside it. Hone's cheap, cutting pamphlets were among the sharpest weapons of the radical press of his day.
447-maggie-a-girl-of-the-streets:
Stephen Crane tells of Maggie Johnson, a girl raised in the slums of New York, in this stark early novel. Rum Alley fights, a drunken mother, and a brutal brother shape her youth. When a bartender named Pete courts her with fine clothes and music halls, Maggie dreams of escape from the tenement.

Crane writes in short, hard scenes, with dialect speech and a cold eye for poverty's traps. Hope curdles fast, and the streets claim Maggie in the end. The novel shocked readers of its day and now stands as a landmark of American realism, unsparing yet full of pity for its heroine.
44849-colouration-in-animals-and-plants:
Alfred Tylor left Colouration in Animals and Plants, edited by Sydney B J Skertchly and printed at London in 1886. Tylor did not live to see the full text done. Skertchly was late of the Geological Survey. The book is given to George Young in memory of a long friendship.

The front note sums up Tylor's main thought. Dress in beasts rests on build, he held. In clear, low beasts hue sits on the organs at once. In thick beasts the same plan holds on the skin. Where work shifts, the mark shifts. Like parts bear like marks, and marks repeat. Tylor came to hold that low life holds a kind of mind and passed on memory.
44855-elizabethan-jacobean-pamphlets:
George Saintsbury edited Elizabethan and Jacobean Pamphlets for the Pocket Library of English Literature. Percival and Company issued the volume at London in 1892, as the sixth of the series. The series mixed extracts from long books with short pieces of one class. Saintsbury's contents open with Thomas Lodge's Reply to Gosson. John Lyly's Pap with a Hatchet follows, then Nicholas Breton's Pretty and Witty Discourse.

Robert Greene's Groat's Worth of Wit stands fourth, and Gabriel Harvey's Precursor to Pierce's Supererogation fifth. Thomas Nash's Prognostication and Thomas Dekker's Gull's Hornbook close the set, with notes behind. Saintsbury's introduction treats Gosson's Schoole of Abuse, the attack that drew answers from Lodge and from Sidney. The pamphlet wars of the 1590s were print's first rough literary criticism in England. Saintsbury made them pocket reading again three centuries on.
44922-the-last-of-the-flatboats-a-story-:
George Cary Eggleston, author of The Big Brother and other boys' books, tells here of a flatboat voyage down the Mississippi. Lothrop published the story at Boston in 1900. Eggleston dedicated it to his last-born boy Cary, a brave, manly fellow who could swim, catch fish, handle his boat, shoot straight, and tell the truth. The crew is of his kind: Ed Lowry, the wise and kindly leader, speaks first, calling tired boys out of the water where they have been diving after something lost.

Captain Phil takes the boat past Louisville and Memphis, through the home of the earthquakes, the chute, the fog, and the crevasse. There are castaways to rescue, a wrestle with the river, and red-letter days in New Orleans at the end. It is a river boy's epic from the flatboats' last days.
4497-the-sentimentalists:
George Meredith left this comedy unfinished, under the title The Sentimentalists. Its persons include Homeware, Professor Spiral, Arden in love with Astraea, Swithin the sympathetic, Osier, Dame Dresden sister to Homeware, Astraea her niece, Lyra a wife, Lady Oldlace, Virginia, and Winifred. The scene is a Surrey garden in early summer.

It is set outdoors in Surrey, in early summer, among tall boxwood hedges, a stage for talk, sentiment, and comedy of manners. Meredith's unfinished play shows his late interest in sentiment itself: how feeling is performed, praised, and mocked. Readers get a fragment, charming in itself, and a glimpse of a comedy its author did not live to finish.
45084-notes-on-collecting-and-preserving:
J E Taylor edited this handbook on gathering and keeping natural history objects, in a new edition printed by W H Allen of London in 1883. The essays first ran in Science-Gossip. Taylor and a dozen fellow workers each took a field. E F Elwin took bones, Thomas Southwell birds' eggs, and Doctor Knaggs butterflies and moths. Others took beetles and stones.

The preface says young naturalists kept asking how to do the work well. The book saves them time by lending the skill of older hands. Chapters run from rocks and bones to eggs, insects, and plants. A closing word warns that reading should breed love of the things themselves, not mere hunger to collect.
4514-tales-of-men-and-ghosts:
Edith Wharton published Tales of Men and Ghosts in London in 1910, gathering ten stories that mix the supernatural with social life. The contents run from The Bolted Door and His Father's Son through The Daunt Diana, The Debt, and Full Circle, to The Legend, The Eyes, The Blond Beast, Afterward, and The Letters. Each tale sets a polished, well-mannered world against something uncanny or unresolved.

Wharton's ghosts are often less frightening than the guilt, greed, or pride of the living people who meet them. A murder concealed, a debt unpaid, or a letter kept too long can haunt a character more surely than any spirit. Readers get finely written ghost stories for adults, where manners hide sharp moral choices, and where the past refuses to stay buried.
45228-such-is-life-a-play-in-five-acts:
Frank Wedekind's Such Is Life, a play in five acts, appears here in Francis Ziegler's English version, published by Brown Brothers at Philadelphia in 1912. Wedekind also wrote The Awakening of Spring. The scene is Perugia: Nicola, king of Umbria, is taken prisoner, and armed workmen crowd his throne room. Pietro Folchi, master butcher, calls the citizens to give the state a constitution before they bury their dead. Andrea Valori asks whether they shall proclaim the Umbrian Republic, as Florence, Parma, and Siena have done.

The crowd cries for freedom and moves to elect a podesta on the spot. The cast runs to tailors, journeymen, judges, a jailer, a circus rider, an actor, and two theatre managers, beside Princess Alma. Wedekind's play turns a revolution into a fable of power: the butcher-king makers of one act become the next act's rulers and prisoners.
45536-little-fishers-and-their-nets:
Little Fishers and Their Nets is a novel by Pansy, the pen name on a long shelf of household stories. Lothrop of Boston copyrighted it in 1887 and sold it at a dollar fifty in cloth. The front pages list dozens of Pansy books, from Ester Ried to Four Girls at Chautauqua. An early picture shows a handsome boy named Norman in his married days.

The chapters open at the Deckers' home. A girl begins her life, the truth is told, and new friends appear. A great undertaking is launched, and the tale watches how it succeeds. A Sabbath to remember, a bargain and a promise, and pleasure mixed with disappointment follow. The little picture makers and a concert lead toward a complete success.
45571-the-convolvulus-a-comedy-in-three-:
The Convolvulus is a jest play in three acts by Allen Norton, out in nineteen fourteen. A Claire Marie house of New York holds that right claim in full. Norton gives the play to Carl Van Vechten in its front leaves. Its folk are Jane Gibbs, her sis Gloria, Kathryn, and Dill the man. Jack and Peter Hargrave and a rank man Crapsey fill that cast list.

Act one plays in Jane house on Gramercy Park in one day span. Dill sets tea in silk knee pants while Jack, age twenty, steps in. Tea at this hour is the last thing, all home folk do it, Dill says. It keeps pace with London time, where tea hour stands now, he adds. Jack then drops grave news: Dill is the twin face of his sire.
45677-popular-amusements:
Popular Amusements is a book by the Reverend J T Crane, a Methodist minister of the Newark Conference, printed in 1869. Bishop E S Janes wrote its introduction. Crane takes up a grave question for church folk: how Christians may play. His first chapter argues that recreation is a good thing, and that laughter can be as pious as tears.

Crane then lays down rules that govern true recreation. Pastimes must not be immoral, must not harm a Christian's good name, and must not clash with duty. They must not injure health, waste money, or waste time. They ought to improve the mind and the heart and to impart pleasure. The contents go on to plays, dancing, and other common amusements of the day. The book shows a church wrestling with a world that wants to play, and setting the terms on which play is allowed.
45806-faust-a-lyric-drama-in-five-acts:
