A word book of Gounod's Faust gives the opera in French and English side by side, with the music of the chief airs. It belongs to a Boston set of grand opera word books. The set lists Aïda, Carmen and Samson and Delilah at set prices in paper covers. Light operas stand in a second list below.

Faust runs in five acts, as the price list notes. Such word books let hearers follow a sung tale in a tongue not their own. The French text stands first in the book, and the English follows it. Buyers could keep the book as a record of the night and as a way to learn the airs at home on the piano.
46018-loyola-and-the-educational-system-:
Thomas Hughes, a Jesuit, wrote this account of Loyola and the educational system of his order for the Great Educators series, edited by Nicholas Murray Butler. Scribner published it at New York in 1892. Hughes promises a critical statement of the principles and method adopted in the Society of Jesus. The first part is therefore biographical and historical, with the founder for its chief subject: how Ignatius Loyola's own schooling and conversion shaped the schools he founded.

The second part analyses the Ratio Studiorum, the order's official plan of studies. Hughes quotes the documents accurately and fully, drawing on the great Monumenta Germaniae Paedagogica, where rare sources had lately been made accessible. Custom, he adds, is the best interpreter of law, and he tests the rules against the practice of Jesuit schools. The book remains an insider's account of the most influential school system of the Catholic world.
46091-the-octoroon-or-life-in-louisiana-:
The Octoroon, or Life in Louisiana, a play in five acts by Dion Boucicault, was printed, not published, with the casts of the Boston Museum and the Howard Athenaeum of 1861. Boucicault also wrote The Colleen Bawn. The stage is Terrebonne, a great farm on a branch of the Mississippi, with a low, broad house and a wide porch. Cast lists name George Peyton, Salem Scudder, and the rogue Jacob McClosky. Zoe, the girl of the title, stands in white muslin.

Wahnotee the Indian, old Pete, and the boy Paul fill the roll of the place. Dress notes fix each part: planter's nankeen, steamer chief's black, and the kerchiefs of the house slaves. The first act opens at the breakfast table in noise and sport. Stage fans get the famed plea of blood and bondage in full.
46198-conquest-or-a-piece-of-jade-a-new-:
Marie Stopes offers a play in Conquest, or A Piece of Jade, a new play in three acts, printed in New York and London in 1917. Samuel French publishes it, with copyright by the author the same year. A comic letter to a manager fronts the text, in place of a preface.

Dear Mr Delightfulest Manager in the World, the letter begins, from Leatherhead in Surrey. She is sending the play printed instead of type written, she explains, because it is much easier to slip into a pocket and read. She does not know his address. Printed books have a way of finding people without being addressed, she holds. Do not judge the length by the pages, she warns. It is a full length play. The printer is war economising, and has printed it on fewer pages than in the days of paper, peace, and plenty.
46221-items-on-the-priesthood-presented-:
John Taylor, president of the Latter-day Saints church, issued this ruling on priesthood order at Salt Lake City in 1899. Items on the Priesthood speaks to bishops and to all who held the Aaronic or Levitical priesthood. Doubt had grown, Taylor says, and he writes to end it.

More or less uncertainty stands in the minds of many bishops and others, he begins. It touches the true status and authority of the bishopric. So he lays a general word before the brethren. The Aaronic priesthood's ranks, the bishop's court, and who may act in what name fill the short text. Taylor was the third president of his church, and this is doctrine in the form of a memo: brief and binding.
46226-niobe-all-smiles-a-farcical-comedy:
Harry and Edward Paulton wrote Niobe, All Smiles, a farcical comedy in three acts published by Samuel French in London and New York. French's list sold acting editions to amateur companies, and the notice at the front is all business. The amateur fee for each representation is three guineas, payable in advance. Every performance of a copyright play, the publishers warn, is liable to fees, and agents across the kingdom are authorised to collect them and exact penalties.

The play itself is a famous farce of the eighteen nineties. Its device is a statue of Niobe brought to life in a modern household, where the weeping mother of Greek myth meets suburban manners. The Paultons' comedy ran in London and New York and lived for decades in amateur hands.
46240-chains-a-play-in-four-acts:
Elizabeth Baker wrote a play in four acts on the chains of plain life. The book came out in London in 1911. Act one is set in a sit room at 55 Acacia Avenue. A core table is laid for a meal for three at its heart. Fold doors at the back lead to the front room of the house.

Wicker and bent wood chairs mix round a fire on the right. A sideboard stands there, and a French pane leads to the yard. Kin photos and a cricket group hang on the walls. A brass clock ticks over the small, neat room. In that plain room, lives chafe at their tight bounds. Stage fans get a keen, true slice of home life.
46298-mary-broome-a-comedy-in-four-acts:
Allan Monkhouse wrote Mary Broome, a comedy in four acts first produced at the Gaiety Theatre in Manchester in October 1911. Horniman's company played it, with Irene Rooke in the title part. This text is the second impression, published in 1913. The scene opens in the drawing room of a biggish suburban villa, its furniture in middling taste. Edgar Timbrell sprawls on the sofa while his sisters open a parcel of wedding presents.

The cast names the comedy's design. Mary Broome, the family's servant, becomes Mary Timbrell by marriage to Leonard, the younger son. Her parents, plain Broome folk, face the Timbrells across the class line. Monkhouse, a Manchester critic and novelist, wrote the play that made his name. It is a comedy of manners in which a servant girl marries into the family she serves, and both households must adjust their pride.
46420-married-life-a-comedy-in-three-act:
Married Life is a stage comedy in three acts by John Baldwin Buckstone. The play was performed at the Theatre Royal, Haymarket, in London. Strange published the text at London in 1834. Buckstone dedicates the comedy to the actor William Farren in warm terms.

In a front note Buckstone claims the play is wholly original. He grants that some couples in it, above all the Coddles and the Doves, were sketched from life. The cast list pairs husbands and wives for the comic action. Farren played Samuel Coddle, and Buckstone himself took a husband's part. The dedication letter praises Farren's range across fifty roles. It thanks him for care given to the author's earlier plays. The comedy turns on the frictions and affections of wedded pairs.
46605-thomas-otway-the-best-plays-of-the:
Thomas Otway, in the Mermaid Series of the best plays of the old dramatists, was issued in London in 1888 in an uncut edition edited by Havelock Ellis. Roden Noel wrote the opening essay and notes. The series set out to give cheap, sound texts of early English plays, with volumes on Jonson, Dryden, Chapman, and others in plan.

Otway was a leading stage writer of the late 1600s, known for sad, high-flown tragedies of love and fate. A portrait after Riley fronts the book. Readers get the plays with help on the author's life and times, in a form made for study as much as for the shelf. The volume helped keep old drama in print for new readers.
46623-at-war-with-society-or-tales-of-th:
James M'Levy, of the Edinburgh police detective staff, wrote At War with Society for Cameron and Ferguson. His earlier Romances of Crime heads the title page with pride. Twenty-one tales fill the contents, from The Ingenuity of Thieves to The Mustard-Blister. Orange blossoms, blue bells, whiskers, and a white coffin title the early cases.

The opening essay boasts that prison reports show jail numbers falling since 1849. M'Levy credits early rescue of the young more than late punishment for that gain. He scolds masters who trap servants with laid coins, then cast them out to steal elsewhere. Each tale then works a theft, fraud, or murder out to its end. A working detective sells hard wisdom with his cases.
46705-in-the-land-of-mosques-minarets:
In the Land of Mosques and Minarets is a North African travel book by Francis Miltoun. L C Page and Company published it in Boston in 1908. The publisher's list prices it at $3.00. Blanche McManus made the illustrations from drawings and paintings. Her portrait of the Caid of the Msaaba fronts the book. Miltoun had already written rambles in Normandy, Brittany, and the Riviera.

The chapters cross Algeria and Tunisia. Going and coming opens the journey, and the real North Africa follows. The regence of Tunisia, the religion of the Mussulman, and mosque architecture get chapters. Poetry, music, and dancing stand beside Arabs, Turks, and Jews. The camel appears as the ship of the desert on his ocean of sand. Algiers, the great white city, fills two chapters. Biskra, Constantine, Tunis and its souks, and the glory that once was Carthage close the route.
46753-chats-on-japanese-prints:
Chats on Japanese Prints is a prize guide by Arthur Davison Ficke for the Chats set. Fifty six cuts and a hue front plate dress the book in full. A Fisher Unwin house of London first brought it out in nineteen fifteen. Print runs of the book came in sixteen, seventeen, and twenty two. The front plate shows Hiroshige bow moon print, wide and low in shape.

The book sits in a long line of chats on china, lace, and coins. Ficke gives the book to two mates named as guards and fans of fair form. Verse at the give leaf calls them pour men of a rare host line. Print craft, schools, and great hands of Japan fill such chat books. Price, marks, and shape lore guide the prize hunt in its pages.
46760-hints-to-servants:
An Upper Servant versified Hints to Servants from Swift's Directions. Effingham Wilson issued it at London in 1843. Kenny Meadows drew its twelve designs. John Jackson engraved those plates. Dean Swift's famed ironic directions form its base. Sharp passages unfit for kitchen reading stand cut. Something is added to the Dean's text as well.

A preface speaks to all fellow servants in verse. The Dean was keen as a hawk on faults, it says. Swift to blame and slow to please, it adds. His dogged humor won all men's wonder, it claims. Rhyme relieves where irony would tingle most, it hopes. Had Swift held his dish up, a bishopric was his, it jokes. Pope's line on ridicule heads the title page. A cleaned, rhymed Swift for below-stairs readers turns a master's satire into servants' own sly handbook.
46809-six-major-prophets:
Edwin E Slosson profiles the thinkers of an age in Six Major Prophets, from Little, Brown of Boston in 1917. Slosson was literary editor of The Independent and author of Major Prophets of To-Day. A Mohammedan proverb heads the book: whoever dies without recognizing the prophet of his time dies the death of a pagan.

The six are George Bernard Shaw, H G Wells, G K Chesterton, F C S Schiller, John Dewey, and Rudolf Eucken, each with a portrait. The Shaw chapter opens by declaring that August 4, 1914, cuts time in two like a knife. Postwar stock-taking drives the book.
46918-single-life-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
John Baldwin Buckstone wrote this comedy in three acts, first played at the Theatre Royal, Haymarket, on Tuesday, July 23, 1839. The printed text follows the prompter's copy, with the cast, dress, stage plan, and the sides for each entrance and exit. An etching by Pierce Egan the younger, drawn during a show, faces the text. Chapman and Hall of the Strand sold the London edition.

The cast is built of bachelors: John Niggle, who shifts; David Damper, who hates women; Peter Pinkey, who is shy; and Narcissus Boss, who loves himself. Buckstone made it a mate piece to his Married Life, but here all the men are lovers, and the fun lies in courtship and its quirks.
47195-a-nest-of-linnets:
Nest of Linnets is a novel by Frank Frankfort Moore, issued at London in nineteen oh one with sixteen pictures. Moore is billed as author of I Forbid the Banns and The Jessamy Bride. The scene of the opening is Bath in the age of Handel. Chapter one begins in a music lesson that goes wrong.

Mr Linley scolds his daughter Betsy for a half hearted phrase in her singing. Sir Joshua calls her Saint Cecilia, he says, but the name is wrong if she sings so. No angel would stir a wing for a girl who implored aid in so faint a way, he cries. He bids her sing as if she meant to storm the ears of heaven. He leaps from the harpsichord to drive the point home.
47331-michael-and-his-lost-angel-a-play-:
Henry Arthur Jones wrote a five-act play about a clergyman torn by love and faith, first staged in London in 1896. The play ran at the Lyceum Theatre from January 15 to January 25 of that year. In a note Jones gives the nightly takings to rebut the claim that the short run meant a great failure.

The cast centers on the Reverend Michael Feversham, his kin, and Audrie Lesden, the woman at the heart of the story. Scenes move from a vicarage parlour at Cleveheddon to a shrine on an island, then to the minster church. The last act shifts to a monastery in Italy. Readers get a serious stage drama of duty, passion, and loss, printed with the author's own defense of its first run.
47379-a-bold-stroke-for-a-husband-a-come:
A Bold Stroke for a Husband is a comedy in five acts by Hannah Cowley, set in Spain. Clayton's edition of eighteen thirty one prints it from the prompt book. It had been played at Covent Garden and at the Park Theatre, New York. Remarks by Mrs Inchbald open the volume with a judge's view of the play.

Don Caesar, Don Julio, and Don Carlos head the list of male parts. Donna Olivia, Donna Victoria, and Donna Laura carry the female side of the plot. Inchbald notes that Victoria, a wife, passes herself off as a man. That bold stroke, to keep her husband, makes the more affecting plot. Olivia's own stroke, to gain a husband, gives the play its title. The remarks praise the piece for joining fun with clean moral teaching.
47386-yorkshire-oddities-incidents-and-s:
Yorkshire Oddities: Incidents and Strange Events is a book of county characters and strange happenings by Baring-Gould, issued in a fifth edition by Methuen of London in 1900. Its epigraph quotes the Abbot of York writing to Cromwell in 1556 that Yorkshire held more wilful gentlemen than all England besides.

Baring-Gould explains that years of residence in the county made him an inveterate collector of odd information about its eccentric children. He left Yorkshire in 1872 with a large store of material gathered. A friend's remark that every other Yorkshireman is a character frames his claim that no county breeds so much originality, or carries it so far into eccentricity. A later preface notes the book preserved strong characters then passing away, some recorded only in chapbooks already scarce, and that the new edition was thoroughly revised.
47559-the-prude-s-progress-a-comedy-in-t:
The Prude's Progress is a comedy in three acts by Jerome and Eden Phillpotts, printed in London in 1895. Act one opens in a poor but neat room high up in a Bloomsbury lodging house. Nelly Morris sits at a table with a pile of medical books and talks to a skull.

Nelly and her brother Ted have three sausages between them for dinner. She longs for roast beef and fears Ted will fail his exam for want of food. The landlady figure, Wheedles, comes in and adds warmth and fuss. Cast lists name Jack Medbury, Adam Cherry, and Primrose Deane among the rest. The play mixes want and cheer in the lives of two young people who laugh at their own hard luck.
47560-the-schoolmistress-a-farce-in-thre:
Arthur Pinero wrote a farce in three acts that was first played at the Court Theatre on March 27, 1886. An introductory note tells how the success of The Magistrate had set that house on a policy of comic plays. The Schoolmistress ran there until January 22, 1887, for a total of 290 performances.

The scene is Volumnia College, a school for the daughters of gentlemen, whose principal is a Miss Dyott. The cast adds an admiral and his wife, a young lieutenant, and a popular composer named Otto Bernstein. Acts are titled The Mystery, The Party, and Nightmare. A touring company then carried the play through the provinces with great success.
47561-trelawny-of-the-wells-a-comedietta:
Arthur Pinero wrote a comedietta in four acts, produced at the Court Theatre, London, on Thursday, January 29th, 1898, and printed in 1899 with the original casts of London and New York. Its folk divide on the page into theatrical and non-theatrical, and the period is somewhere in the early sixties.

Tom Wrench, James Telfer, and Rose Trelawny belong to the Bagnigge-Wells theatre, familiarly the Wells; Sir William Gower, a vice-chancellor, and his sister belong to Cavendish Square. The acts move between the Telfers' Clerkenwell lodgings and the Gower house, and end on the stage of the Pantheon Theatre a few days after Christmas. A note warns that costumes must keep the crinoline and horsehair of the sixties unmodernised. Theatre nostalgia, wrought as farce, is the play.
4764-a-family-man-in-three-acts:
John Galsworthy wrote A Family Man as a play in three acts, in the fifth series of his plays. Its characters include John Builder, of Builder and Builder, his wife Julia, and daughters Athene and Maud. Ralph Builder, John's brother and partner, Guy Herringhame, a flying man, and Annie, a young person in blue, also appear, with Camille, Mrs. Builder's French maid, and Topping, Builder's manservant.

The mayor of Breconridge, his secretary Harris, and Francis Chantrey, a justice, round out the cast. Moon, a constable, Martin, a police sergeant, a journalist from The Comet, a poacher's figure, and voices of small boys complete it. Action passes in Breconridge, in the Midlands, from Builder's study after breakfast to a studio, then to Builder's study at lunchtime, and to the mayor's study the following day. Readers get a Galsworthy domestic drama about a strong-willed family man and those who resist him.
47721-southern-hearts:
Florence Hull Winterburn's Southern Hearts was published in New York in 1900 by the Lupton company. Winterburn, who had written Nursery Ethics, gives the volume to her Virginia friends. Most of the tales had run in magazines such as Romance, Godey's, and The Independent; three are new.

Nine stories fill the book, from When Love Enslaves to Apple Blossoms, with The Wife of Lothario and The Laziest Girl in Virginia between. The first opens on an October morning in the mountain region of Virginia, at the old Fitzhugh homestead. An Englishman who wed the family's only daughter has bought the place back from creditors with British gold, and Aunt Rose rules the kitchen.
47830-the-burgomaster-of-stilemonde-a-pl:
Maeterlinck's play in three acts, translated by Teixeira de Mattos and published by Dodd, Mead in 1918, is set at Stilemonde in Belgian Flanders at the end of August 1914. All three acts pass on a single day.

Cyrille Van Belle, the burgomaster, is sixty; his son-in-law Hilmer is a German lieutenant, and Major Baron von Rochow commands the occupying force. The first act opens in the burgomaster's study, part office and part garden laboratory, full of orchids, peaches, and grapes. Jean Gilson enters in peasant clothes, his arm in a sling from a bullet taken outside Aerschot. The whole action runs from ten in the morning to seven at night.
47911-dactylography-or-the-study-of-fing:
Henry Faulds published Dactylography, or the Study of Finger-Prints, with Milner and Company at Halifax. A frontispiece shows greasy, accidental, and negative thumb prints side by side. Chapter one reviews early hints and recent progress in print study. Later chapters take up sweat pores, ridges, and furrows in close detail.

Pattern types, life science questions, and print technique fill the middle of the book. Faulds then argues the persistence of prints and sets out a syllabic classification scheme. Practical results and future prospects close the text, with a glossary, bibliography, and index. Police forms, curve rules, and a Kew micrometer appear among the pictures. Readers get a founder's case for prints as proof of identity.
48008-inorganic-plant-poisons-and-stimul:
Inorganic Plant Poisons and Stimulants, by Winifred E Brenchley, reports research on how small doses of mineral substances harm or help growing plants. Brenchley worked at the Rothamsted Experimental Station and was a fellow of University College, London. The book is a Cambridge Agricultural Monograph, published by the Cambridge University Press in 1914.

Early chapters set out the methods of work: water cultures, sand cultures, pot cultures in soil, and field trials. The first full study treats copper compounds. Brenchley asks whether copper is found in plants, how it poisons growth and seed sprouting, and how other substances mask its action. Sprays and solutions on leaves get their own tests. Later chapters take up other elements in the same way. The work helped found the study of the trace elements plants need.
48067-sonnets-and-canzonets:
Bronson Alcott's Sonnets and Canzonets was published by Roberts Brothers of Boston in 1882, under the author's copyright. A Schiller line stands as motto: love can sun the realms of light. The contents open with introduction pieces: a letter to Alcott by Sanborn, on reading his octogenarian poems, and an essay on the sonnet, with sonnets of illustration.

Sanborn's letter places the aged poet among his masters. A scholar of eighty-two belongs, he writes, to the epoch of his own golden youth, his companions the books and friends of his heart. Landor, Sanborn notes, returned in the white winter of his age to the epigram and the idyl. The poems proper divide in two parts: domestic sonnets and canzonets first, then sonnets of character, and a prophetic ode to close. Among the illustrative sonnets stand Love in Spring, The Nightingale, The Fair Saint, and The Poet's Immortality.
48195-a-report-upon-the-mollusk-fisherie:
The Commonwealth of Massachusetts put out this report on its trade in soft-shell fish in 1909. It was made by the men in charge of the trade in fish and game of the state. G. W. Field, their chair, sent it to the two houses of the state in January of that year. The report was made by the word of four acts of the state of 1905. Each act dealt with one kind of fish.

Those kinds are the scallop, the oyster, the quahaug, and the clam. The plan of the work was laid out by the chair of the board. He gave care to such points as the check of facts of science, and the shape and the truth of the end work.
48219-red-belts:
Hugh Pendexter wrote Red Belts, for Doubleday in 1920. From Over the Mountains opens the contents of the romance. The Dead are Dangerous follows. A Jug of Whisky prices the third. For Watauga and America names the fourth in the contents.

The Ancient Law fills the middle. An emperor of the Creeks stands later. A little ruse crowds the list. Sevier offers the red ax in one late chapter's head. A sentence of the wilderness closes the contents in judgment. On the ground lay a girl, hurled there by a bandit. A huge brute of a man bent over her in the plate. Along three rivers the western country was held by red men. Wild beasts and white renegades shared that holding, it says. Pendexter gives the Watauga frontier its red belts of war.
48394-an-account-of-the-insects-noxious-:
Maskell's account of the scale insects of New Zealand was printed at Wellington in 1887 by George Didsbury, government printer. Maskell, registrar of the University of New Zealand, wrote for the State Forests and Agricultural Department. A glossary opens the volume, followed by chapters on the characters, life history, and changes of form of the family. Further chapters treat their products, honeydew and black fungus among them, the parasites that check their increase, and the remedies used against them.

The bulk of the book is a catalogue of the insects with a diagnosis of each species. The groups run from the Diaspidinae through the Lecanidinae and Hemicoccidinae to the Coccidinae. The preface explains that scattered papers in journals were hard for gardeners and tree growers to reach. A second volume on the other plant pests of the colony was planned but left for a future time.
48474-scorn-of-women-a-play-in-three-act:
Jack London wrote a play in three acts, published in 1906, set at Dawson in the Northwest Territory in 1897. Its three scenes are the Alaska Commercial Company's store, the anteroom of Pioneer Hall, and a woman's cabin, and the whole action takes thirteen hours. The cast list reads like a census of the Klondike.

Freda Moloof is a Greek dancer whose furs are the finest in the Yukon and whose name is common on men's lips. Floyd Vanderlip, an Eldorado king worth a couple of millions, is simple and childish in emotion for all his strength. A Hungarian adventuress, a government captain and his cold wife, and an Indian dog-driver complete the triangle's world. Gold-rush manners are the subject.
48507-devonshire-characters-and-strange-:
Devonshire Characters and Strange Events, by Baring Gould, was printed by John Lane in London and New York in 1908. Fifty five full page illustrations, reproduced from old prints, accompany the sketches. A frontispiece shows the actress Maria Foote on stage as Maria Darlington in 1824.

The contents list runs to some sixty pieces. Hugh Stafford and the Alphington ponies open it; then come the impostor Caraboo, wife sales, white witches, the demon of Spreyton, and the Bideford witches. Jack Rattenbury the smuggler, Richard Parker the mutineer, Joanna Southcott, and the pirate captain Avery all appear. Inventors Savery and Newcomen, the singer Edward Capern, and two hunting parsons show the range: Devon oddity in every walk of life.
48538-comrades-a-drama-in-three-acts:
George Baker wrote Comrades, a drama in three acts, in 1877. The play was printed, not published, at Boston that year. It is protected by law, the title page warns the reader. Performance needs special arrangement with the author, it states. Costumes for every part are set out in the front matter.

Royal, aged thirty-five, wears a velvet breakfast jacket in act one. Light pants, a dark vest, and gray-sprinkled hair dress him there. Matt, aged forty-five, wears a ragged suit and an army cap. A full gray ragged beard and a red nose mark the drunkard. In act two the same man stands neat, clean shaved, and florid. Marcus at twenty-four wears a genteel riding suit with whip. Simon at twenty-five is dressed fashionably in the same act. Baker gives the amateur stage its wardrobe in full.
48693-notes-on-railroad-accidents:
Charles Francis Adams wrote Notes on Railroad Accidents, published at New York with copyright in 1879. Adams also wrote Railroads: Their Origin and Problems. Seventeen chapters open with the death of Mr Huskisson, run down at the opening of the Liverpool and Manchester line.

The Angola and Shipton wrecks and the Wollaston wreck follow, with a chapter on wrecks and old habits. Telescoping and the Miller platform, the Versailles wreck, wire-sent trains crashing, and oil-tank fires come next. Draw-bridge disasters, Norwalk and Revere, bridge safety, car-couplings, and rear-end crashes fill the list. New devices and the block system close it. Readers get America's first great railway regulator learning safety from wreckage.
48911-a-mine-of-faults:
A Mine of Faults, translated from the original manuscript by Bain, was published by Putnam in New York and London in 1910. Three tales fill the contents: An Instrument of Policy, A Diplomatic Interview, and A Cordial Understanding.

The first tale opens in the Himalaya. The God of gods plays in the evening on the edge of a precipice with his wife, the Daughter of the Snow. She falls into a brown study and will not own her thought. He reads it anyway: she was comparing her own eyes with a blue chasm in the ice, and finding the eyes superior. She blushes and asks why he called her a mine of faults. Every woman is one, he answers, and she is Woman incarnate. If women had no faults, half their charm would disappear.
48920-the-present-state-of-hayti-saint-d:
The Present State of Hayti, by James Franklin and published in London in 1828, surveys the island once split between French Saint Domingo and the Spanish side. The title promises remarks on its farming, trade, laws, religion, finances, and people.

The opening chapters look back to the colony before the French Revolution and trace the revolt of the enslaved in 1791. Franklin follows the decree of 1792, the freedom declared to the enslaved, and the coming of British forces. Later chapters cover the British withdrawal, the rule and fall of Toussaint, and the French army under Le Clerc. The book then turns to the island as Franklin found it, judging its fields, markets, courts, church, money, and population after freedom.
49181-the-fool-a-play-in-four-acts:
Channing Pollock wrote The Fool, a play in four acts, published by Brentano's in New York in 1922. The book went through three printings in three months. A photograph of Act Three from the Selwyn production stands at the front, and the full original cast is printed with the text.

The play opened at the Times Square Theatre on October 23, 1922, produced by Frank Reicher. James Kirkwood played Daniel Gilchrist, the fool of the title, a man mocked in the public squares as one who wears a crown of thorns. Lowell Sherman played Jerry Goodkind. The verse on the title page gives the theme: a man who lives by the Sermon on the Mount in a world of money and force. Theatre readers get a hit play of the 1920s, cast list and all.
49198-past-redemption-a-drama-in-four-ac:
George M Baker wrote Past Redemption, a drama in four acts of fall and hope. His own house in Boston issued the play in eighteen hundred seventy five. Law guards the piece: no stage may use it save by his leave. Full dress lists for each act fill its opening pages.

John Maynard wears a bald grey wig and striped shirt in act one. His son Harry starts neat, with game bag and leggings, in act one. By act three Harry stands unshorn, in rust rags, with hollow eyes. Robert Thornton falls from silk and jewels to torn, soiled rags. Those shifts of dress trace two plunges from grace to the gutter. Charity, Jessie, and Kitty wear muslin, then grey travel cloaks. Captain Bragg struts in brass buttons and a tall felt hat. Baker’s stage was the parlour and hall, not the great playhouse.
49407-nevada-or-the-lost-mine-a-drama-in:
Nevada, or The Lost Mine, a drama in three acts, was copyrighted in 1876 by George Baker and published in Boston by his firm. The playlet appears under the Globe Drama banner, all the world's a stage. Around it, the publisher's leaves advertise Baker's new plays at twenty-five cents and Spencer's Universal Stage set at fifteen cents each, with full stage business for public or private performance.

The title sets the scene: Nevada mining country, and a mine lost and sought. Plays of this line were built for amateur and small-town companies, with clear types, strong situations, and business that a hall stage could carry. Baker's firm supplied much of America's home theatricals in the decades after the Civil War. Nevada belongs to that trade: a western melodrama of mines, claims, and fortune, in three short acts.
49494-latter-day-sweethearts:
Burton Harrison wrote this novel, copyrighted in 1906 and issued in a special edition in 1907. Merrill illustrated it with water-colors, and a plate shows a flower shot down amid a crowd. French lines at the front call love the scourge of the world, and the doctor in the quote answers that love alone cures our ills.

Chapter one goes aboard the Baltic on an exceptionally fine October morning. An ocean crossing opens a tale of modern courtship among wealthy travellers. Harrison had written 'A Bachelor Maid,' 'The Carlyles' and 'The Anglomaniacs' before this story of latter-day sweethearts and their tangled affections.
49602-the-lame-lover-a-comedy-in-three-a:
Samuel Foote wrote this comedy in three acts, The Lame Lover. Vaillant printed it in London in 1770 for the Hay-Market stage. Foote gives the play to the Earl of Hertford with thanks. A prologue, spoken by Mr Gentleman, opens the printed text here.

The prologue mocks flattery cards and pleas for tender care alike. Reason and nature are the judges here, it tells the house. If the drawn figures keep just light and shade, applause follows. Gross disproportion in the group would earn the crowd scorn instead. The play was performed at the Theatre Royal in the Hay Market, its title page states.
49604-the-lives-of-the-fathers-martyrs-a:
Alban Butler compiled The Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs, and Other Principal Saints from old records and sound sources. The set is Volume VII, issued in New York in 1908, and it covers the month of July. Each day lists the saints kept on that date, with a life for each. July 1 opens with St Rumold, bishop and martyr, and Julius and Aaron, martyrs.

Later days treat the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin, St Ulric, and St Peter. Irish saints such as St Modwena and St Edana appear, as does St Palladius, called Apostle of the Scots. The set claims to be the only full and plain edition, with a long index at the end. It serves as a daily guide to the church year.
49693-the-machine-that-floats:
The Machine That Floats is a science fiction story by Joe Gibson, illustrated by McCauley, from the March 1953 issue of Other Worlds. Its blurb poses the dilemma: a man who invents a space ship and refuses to give it to the world may be hunted down as a criminal.

The story opens in a cellar, where Bill Morrow stares at his invention, a chunk of glittering grids, coils, and metal loops that floats in mid-air. Four dry-cell flashlight batteries in clamps feed the device. A thumb on its switch lights a pilot lamp, and the machine rises from the bench, drifting away from the oil furnace and the wall. It dislikes surfaces, Morrow finds, yet he can trap and hold it, since its magneto-gravitic coils need no high voltage and run at their lowest setting.
49771-the-unknown-a-play-in-three-acts:
The Unknown is a play in three acts by Maugham, published by Heinemann of London in 1920. It was first produced at the Aldwych Theatre on August 9, 1920. Maugham dedicates it to Viola Tree.

The cast put Charles France as Colonel Wharton beside Basil Rathbone as his son John. Lady Tree played the colonel's wife, and Hignett the Reverend Norman Poole. The scene is the Manor House at Stour, in Kent. Maugham's preface disclaims any new light on the questions the play discusses. He offers no solution to problems he calls insoluble. His aim, he says, was dramatic form for thoughts that had agitated many, using ordinary characters of his circle.
49778-the-profligate-a-play-in-four-acts:
Arthur W Pinero wrote The Profligate, a play in four acts on a stained past. William Heinemann issued the play in London, first printed in eighteen hundred ninety one. A saw on curds and stolen honey fronts the printed text. The play was writ in eighteen hundred eighty seven by its note.

No Ibsen bolt had yet struck the English stage in that year. Pinero still held a bright faith in his craft and his age. He built the play to fit no one troupe or house, the note says. Free growth of thought, not stage needs, shaped its scenes. True life in its own loose beat is his aim in the work. High marks of conduct stand in its close drawn folk. New prints came in nineteen hundred two, nine, and fourteen. French’s firm in the Strand takes all stage rights calls for it.
49852-the-life-of-man-a-play-in-five-act:
The Life of Man is a play in five acts by Leonidas Andreyev. Hogarth translated it from the Russian for this edition. Allen and Unwin published it in London in 1915. Macmillan issued it in New York the same year. The persons of the play are listed before a prologue. A Being in Grey heads that list of figures. The Man, his father, and his wife follow in the list. Doctors, an old serving woman, and semi supernatural old women attend. Friends, enemies, relations, and ball guests fill the crowd.

The prologue opens in a large square empty room. It has neither doors nor windows in the stage directions. All is uniformly grey and misty within it. A dim unflickering light flows from a hidden source. The Being in Grey detaches himself from the wall to speak. Andreyev stages a whole human life as an allegory.
49916-the-tenth-man-a-tragic-comedy-in-t:
Maugham wrote a tragic comedy in three acts, printed at Chicago. His plays Jack Straw, Penelope, Mrs Dot, The Explorer, A Man of Honour, Lady Frederick, Smith, and Landed Gentry stand in uniform editions. The play was produced on February 24, 1910. Arthur Bourchier played George Winter, Edmund Maurice Lord Francis Etchingham, and Godfrey Tearle Robert Colby.

Kate Sergeantson played Lady Francis, Francis Dillon Catherine Winter, and Daisy Markham Anne. George Winter, a member of Parliament, heads the characters, with Lord Francis, Robert Colby, Mr Perigal, James Ford, Colonel Boyce, and a clergyman. The scene opens in a drawing room with an archway at the back and a large bow window on the left. A rich man counts his friends and finds the tenth man who will stand by him.
49918-the-land-of-promise-a-comedy-in-fo:
The Land of Promise, a comedy in four acts by Maugham, was published at London in 1922. Heinemann issued the play in print after its stage run in town. It was produced on February 26, 1914, at the Duke of York Theatre. Irene Vanbrugh played Norah Marsh in that first cast, the list shows.

Godfrey Tearle played Frank Taylor and Athol Stewart played James Wickham in it. Maugham other plays fill a list at the front of the volume. The Circle, The Unknown, Lady Frederick, and Mrs Dot stand in that roll. An English girl seeks a new life in Canada in this comedy of emigration. Stage success of 1914 gave the printed play its first readers.
50097-lady-huntworth-s-experiment-an-ori:
Carton wrote this original comedy in three acts for the London stage. It was first played at the Criterion Theatre on April 26, 1900. Samuel French printed the play in 1904 in New York and London. A full cast list and stage plans open the book.

Acts are set in a vicarage garden, kitchen, and library in turn. The cast holds two clergy, their kin, and the house servants. Caroline Rayward, the vicarage cook, stands at the heart of the cast list. Notes on the breakfast table show the care stage crews must take.
50099-mollentrave-on-women-a-comedy-in-t:
Alfred Sutro wrote a comedy in three acts held under a 1905 right, first played that year at a London stage house. A cast list from the first night bill shows Eric Lewis in the lead role of Mollentrave. His book on women, with a fond word for women as sweet souls, starts the talk of the play.

Acts move from a study in the house of Balsted to rooms and a garden at the home of Mollentrave in Swanage. A faded companion gushes over photos on a mantel in the first scene, to dry scorn. Wit on sex, rank, and sense in the draw room mode drives the light, neat play.
50156-anecdotes-about-authors-and-artist:
Anecdotes About Authors and Artists is a gathering by John Timbs of London. Diprose and Bateman of Lincoln Inn Fields printed the little book. Part one treats books and authors, with curious facts and character sketches. Timbs says no claim of completeness is made for his gleanings here.

The field is so wide and fertile that many volumes could not hold it. He offers the facts and incidents that struck him in wide reading. Passages he admired, jests that amused him, and fond memories fill the pages. Small claim to new matter is made for most of the contents within. He trusts the taste and truth of his choice to please readers.
50180-penelope-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Penelope, a comedy in three acts by Maugham, was published by William Heinemann in London in 1912. The play was first called Man and Wife. It was produced at the Comedy Theatre on 9 January 1909, with Marie Tempest in the title part.

The scene is the house of a young doctor in John Street, Mayfair; the time is the present day. Penelope, Professor Golightly and his wife, Davenport Barlow, and a parlour maid named Peyton fill the chief parts. The first act opens between six and seven in the evening. Peyton shows Barlow into the pretty drawing room and tells him her mistress is not at home. Yet she has orders: he is to sit down, make himself comfortable, and be given the Morning Post. Barlow is pompous with surprise. His hostess telegraphed that afternoon, asking him to come at once.
50331-the-honeymoon-a-comedy-in-three-ac:
The Honeymoon is a stage jest in three acts by Arnold Bennett. A Methuen house of London first brought it out in October of nineteen eleven. It first played at the Royalty stage house that same month and year. Marie Tempest took the lead role of Flora Lloyd, a young widow. Flora charm, grace, and looks turn the whole play, the notes say.

A book wife and her man, with two sons, fill the house cast. The elder son is a famed sky man of still tongue and craft mind. A bishop, a Swiss waiter, and a butler round out the nine roles. Dion Boucicault led the first stage run of the play in London. Third print of the book came in nineteen fourteen from the same house.
50385-jack-straw-a-farce-in-three-acts:
Jack Straw is a farce in three acts by W S Maugham. The play was first staged at the Vaudeville Theatre on March 26, 1908. Charles Hawtrey played the lead part of Jack Straw.

The first act sits in the lounge of the Grand Babylon Hotel. The last two acts move to the Parker-Jennings place in Cheshire. Lords, a count and a cleric crowd the cast list with the host's family. Maugham sets up a game of false rank and sly manners. The fun turns on who Jack Straw truly is. Light talk and sharp class jokes carry the piece. The cast list names lords, a count and a parson in the fun.
50552-acids-alkalis-and-salts:
Acids, Alkalis and Salts, by Adlam, belongs to Pitman's Common Commodities and Industries series, short cloth volumes that explained the trades behind everyday goods. Adlam, editor of the School Science Review, wrote for readers who wanted to know how basic chemicals are made and used. The preface argues that useful knowledge trains the mind as surely as abstract study.

The book surveys the great chemical industries: how acids, alkalis, and salts are produced, refined, and turned into soap, glass, fertilizer, and a hundred other products. Illustrations and charts support the text. Volumes like this one carried industrial chemistry to clerks, teachers, and students, and they record the state of British chemical manufacture in the early twentieth century.
50601-landed-gentry-a-comedy-in-four-act:
W S Maugham wrote this comedy in four acts, produced at the Duke of York's Theatre on October 15, 1910 under the title Grace. The printed cast names Dennis Eadie as Claude Insoley and Irene Vanbrugh as his wife Grace.

The action sits at Kenyon-Fulton, Claude's place in Somersetshire, in a drawing-room whose solid, unfashionable comfort stands for the family rather than any one taste. The first act opens at night, with Moore the butler showing in Gann, the gamekeeper, who has been sent for after dinner and will not say why. Edmund Gwenn played Gann. Readers get early Maugham: country-house manners with a secret waiting in the hall.
50712-will-shakespeare-an-invention-in-f:
Will Shakespeare is a play in four acts by Clemence Dane, subtitled an invention. It was first acted at the Shaftesbury Theatre, London, on November seventeenth 1921. Basil Dean produced the play, with music by Wood and designs by Harris. Philip Merivale played Will, with Claude Rains as Kit Marlowe in the cast.

Act one sets a cottage in Stratford, and act two jumps ten years on. The palace, then the first night of Romeo and Juliet, frame the rise to fame. Anne, her mother, Henslowe, Queen Elizabeth, and Mary Fitton people the invention. Dane imagines the poet loves and losses behind the plays he wrote.
50772-famous-givers-and-their-gifts:
Sarah Knowles Bolton wrote lives of famed givers and their gifts for young readers. Thomas Y Crowell and Company held the rights in 1896 in New York and Boston. Bolton had written Poor Boys Who Became Famous and Girls Who Became Famous. A portrait of Stephen Girard fronts the book.

Bolton holds that how wealth is used beats how it was made. Sketches treat John Lowell and his free talks, Girard and his school for orphans, and Carnegie and his gifts. The book hopes to stir readers to give in their own lives. Teachers and parents of the time used such lives as guides to kind, wise giving.
51021-the-geological-history-of-plants:
The Geological History of Plants forms volume sixty one of the International Scientific Series. Each book of that series stood complete in one cloth volume. Forms of Water by Tyndall opens the list at the front pages. Physics and Politics by Bagehot stands second in the series.

Foods and Mind and Body fill the next places of the catalogue. The series carried science to general readers at a dollar and a half a volume. A history of plants in the rocks fits that plan of popular learning. Coal forests, ferns, and the slow rise of flowering kinds fill such a work. Fossil leaves in stone tell the story it pursues. The volume is a doorway into deep time for the lay reader.
51080-among-the-burmans-a-record-of-fift:
Among the Burmans is Henry Park Cochrane's record of fifteen years of missionary work in Burma and its fruitage. Revell published it in New York in 1904, with many illustrations. A picture of a typical Shan fronts the book. First chapters tell of the author's first experiences and of living like the natives.

Later chapters describe the customs of the Burmese and the chief races of Burma. Buddhism as it is, Burma's outcasts, and a nation in transition get chapters of their own. Pictures show Kachins, dancing girls, tattooing, and Buddhist shrines. The book closes with obstacles and with the summing question, what hath God wrought. It is a missionary's full report from the field.
51102-the-sentimentalists:
Murray Leinster wrote The Sentimentalists, a science fiction tale printed in the April 1953 issue of Galaxy Science Fiction, with pictures by Hunter. Its heroes are Rhadampsicus and Nodalictha, a wed pair on honeymoon, wed only seventy-five years before. No human would call them tender. They bear sixteen eyes on stalks and move by blasts from beneath their mantles. Their kiss is a twining of eye stalks, gazing with all eyes at once.

On their tour they pass the sun men call Cetis Gamma, and Rhadampsicus notes a strange thing soon to be seen there. His bride, full of a new wife's pride in his wisdom, begs that they stop and watch. The tale plays its joke with a straight face: the most alien pair turns out to be soft at heart, and their softness may steer what comes next.
51200-passamaquoddy-texts:
Passamaquoddy Texts is a volume of native texts edited in the publications of the American Ethnological Society. Franz Boas edited the series, and this is its tenth volume, issued in 1921. John Dyneley Prince gathered and translated the Passamaquoddy texts of the volume. Stechert in New York and a Berlin house share the imprint of the book.

Contents open with a preface and a first series holding the Wampum Records of the people. A second series gives the tales of Kuloskap, the culture hero of the Wabanaki in their tradition. Kuloskap and Pukjinskwes, Kuloskap and the Loon, and Kuloskap and the Whale stand in the list. Prince prints the tales in the Passamaquoddy language with his translations for the scholar. Such text volumes, made under Boas rule of exact record, are the bedrock on which the study of the native languages of Maine still stands today.
51219-princess-badoura-a-tale-from-the-a:
Laurence Housman told this tale from the Arabian Nights once more, with cuts by Edmund Dulac. The list of cuts maps the tale. Two fiends of the air, Dahnash and Meymooneh, open the roll: as a shape rises through clouds, one knows Dahnash by his tail. The King of China and the maid Badoura come next. The King came in haste, and found that which he had but feigned of his child come true in seem.

Then comes Prince Camaralzaman in the guise of a man of the stars. He cures Badoura, and she runs forth and throws her arms round him. The Prince finds a charm: a great stone tied in the folds of a sash.
51240-the-addicts:
The Addicts, a short tale by William Morrison with drawings by Ed Alexander, first ran in Galaxy Science Fiction in January nineteen fifty two. The head note says the tale came from that magazine. Palmer and his wife live on a lone rock outpost in space. She sits by a false fireplace and reads, as calm as if she were home on Mars. Palmer loves her and hatches a kind plan for her own good.

Palmer tells himself his scheme is pure care, though it stills qualms in his mind. His wife has borne the lone post well, from thin air stores to odd shifts in false gravity. One thing she has not borne well is her husband and his bad habit. The blurb hints that wives try to cure husbands of bad habits, even on lone rocks. A dark joke drives the tale.
51284-the-ways-of-the-planets:
Martha Evans Martin wrote The Ways of the Planets, issued at New York and London in 1912 by Harper and Brothers. Martin had writ The Friendly Stars. A front print shows a whirling spiral nebula. Such a cloud is the likely birth place of the sun and planets, the caption says. That nebula lies under the handle of the Big Dipper.

Chapter One is named On Making Acquaintance with the Planets. Our relation to the plane of the system comes next. Martin writes for plain readers who watch the night sky. Photos from Mount Wilson Observatory aid the text. One moon sign cannot be shown in digital form and is left as an open circle, a note warns. The dense centre of the cloud becomes the sun and small knots become planets, in the view set out.
51493-kreativity-for-kats:
Fritz Leiber wrote this tale of a cat, first printed in a journal of the worlds of space in April 1961. Dick Francis drew its cuts. A note at its head calls the cats the aliens among us: their ways and their works are more strange than those of men from the stars. The tale opens with Gummitch, a young cat, at his bowl of water on the floor by the glass of the cook room.

Gummitch stares at the bright face of the sun in the bowl. He knows from past days that the stare will make dark ghost suns swim in front of his eyes for a while. That is of mild pull to him. Then he leans out over the bowl, with care not to break its face with his breath. Down in the water stares the cat of the glass, his twin.
51678-unique-ghost-towns-and-mountain-sp:
Unique Ghost Towns and Mountain Spots is a Colorado history booklet by Caroline Bancroft. The copy is copyrighted nineteen sixty one, in a seventh edition of nineteen seventy three. Bancroft was a third generation Coloradan, the author note says. She began writing history for a Denver newspaper in nineteen twenty eight. Her grandfather founded the Colorado Historical Society and was its first president, the note adds.

A list of her other booklets stands in the note. They treat Baby Doe Tabor, Aspen, Central City, and Leadville. Denver's lively past and Colorado's lost gold mines also appear. Her full size book on Central City is called the definitive history of that town. The text shown treats a building on a mining lode, bought in eighteen ninety seven. A date still stood on its wall, it says.
51751-oh-rats:
Miriam Allen DeFord wrote Oh, Rats, a short science fiction tale in Galaxy Magazine in December nineteen hundred sixty one. Wood drew the pictures. SK540 is the twenty seventh son of two plain white lab rats. Drugs fed his growth in a glass womb made him a super rat.

Three drugs spurred his brain as it formed in the lab. One side of his brain grew far past the other by plan. Most of his kin died or came out warped and were killed. He lived, with a mind past any rat and past men in some ways. Health, food, mates, and power form his rat dreams. Once he learns his cage latch, he picks meek mates to free. A rat realm waits past the lab door.
51847-birds-and-beasts:
Birds and Beasts is a beast tale set by Camille Lemonnier, turned by Allinson. Detmold drew the cuts for this London print of nineteen eleven. Jack and Murph, two tried mates, head the tale scheme at start. Jack came straight from the woods of Africa to a show man cage. Six years of mate ship bind the pair ere the tale voice starts.

He learned drill, slack rope, and spring board tricks in quick time there. Sad at heart, he shunned the nut games and scuffles of his cage mates. A caged goldfinch, a small white hare, and Friquet fill mid tales. A lost dog and an owl woes close the six tale scheme. Pity for caged and tame beasts runs through each tale in the set.
52039-the-jesuits:
Edward Hoare, a clergyman at Ramsgate, wrote a lecture on the Jesuits for the Islington Protestant Institute. The pamphlet reached a second edition in London in 1852, with much added matter. Hoare writes as a Protestant critic who grants the order great skill while questioning its aims.

Hoare calls the Society of Jesus perhaps the most remarkable human union ever formed. He praises how well its parts fit its end and how deftly it bends to meet all kinds of people. He then argues that such a machine counts as curse or blessing by its object and its guiding rules. Chapters treat the general object and organization of the order, backed by quoted sources. Readers get a sharp period attack, written for wide sale at reduced prices to Protestant groups.
52088-te-te-d-or-a-play-in-three-acts:
Paul Claudel wrote Tete-d'Or, a play in three acts, here in English by John Strong Newberry. Yale University Press issued the translation at New Haven in 1919, with Humphrey Milford at London. A dedication poem in verse stands before the play. The speaker tells of walking, laughing, where the riotous garden spread its honeyed share. He tells of feeling on his hair the holy blessing of things most excellent, with seeds and shreds of down mingled there.

The poem hails Vesper, the evening star, as first-born of the dawning future and only child of the King. Claudel's play, written when he was a young man, tells of a golden-headed hero who seeks power and the sea. Newberry's version brought one of the most famed and difficult of modern French plays to English readers in the years after the Great War.
52122-hospital-transports:
Hospital Transports recalls the embarkation of sick and wounded men from the Peninsula of Virginia in the summer of 1862. Ticknor and Fields issued the memoir at Boston in 1863. The Sanitary Commission asked for the work to be compiled and published.

A long dedication names men and women who died in the Commission's service. Surgeon J M Grymes of the transport Daniel Webster heads the list. Others fell at Fredericksburg or died after the battles of South Mountain and Antietam. Fanny Swan Warriner is praised for bearing a woman's part in war to the end. The memoir honours care work as a form of war service.
52600-bird-portraits:
Ernest Seton-Thompson drew bird portraits for a book issued in Boston in 1901, with descriptive text by Ralph Hoffmann. The song sparrow comes first, then the flicker and the brown thrasher. The barn swallow, chimney swift, and kingbird follow in short order. Each bird gets a plate and a brief account.

Later entries cover the Baltimore oriole, the wood thrush, and the scarlet tanager. The rose breasted grosbeak, redstart, and ruby throated humming bird appear. Bob white, the goldfinch, the blue jay, and the brown creeper round out the list shown. The book pairs close pictures with plain notes for bird lovers.
52784-heavenly-gifts:
Aaron Kolom wrote this science fiction story for Worlds of Tomorrow in April 1963. Its tag line warns that heartfelt prayers deserve an answer, but the answer may come in a peculiar way. At home with her knitting, Frisbee sees an electric blanket appear on her kitchen table. It lies neatly folded in the middle of the tiny room.

She thanks heaven in prayer and plans a further request at midnight, a bicycle for the paper boy. At work she mops a lab where Doctor Morrow sits at a control panel. A huge antenna outside aims at the stars. Alone at midnight, she notes his dial settings and turns to a keyboard with practiced fingers.
52993-a-collection-of-chirurgical-tracts:
William Beckett wrote the Collection of Chirurgical Tracts, printed for Curll at London. Beckett was a surgeon and a fellow of the Royal Society. The book has two lists of contents that do not quite match. A preface stands midway through the volume, the notes warn. Spelling and punctuation are archaic and unsettled throughout the text.

Five tracts make the set, as the title page lays them out. Wounds of the head and brain come first in the list. New discoveries relating to the cure of cancers follow. Chirurgical remarks on several curious cases take the third place. The history and antiquity of the venereal disease stands fourth. A new method of curing consumptions by specific medicines closes the set. Beckett gives early surgery in its own rough dress.
53083-the-antiquities-of-constantinople-:
The Antiquities of Constantinople, written originally in Latin by Petrus Gyllius, was translated into English and enlarged by John Ball, formerly of Corpus Christi College, Oxford. It was printed at London in 1729 for the benefit of the translator. Four books describe the city's situation, the conveniencies of its port, and its public buildings.

Statuary, sculpture, architecture, and other curiosities follow, with cuts explaining the chief of them. Ball adds an ancient description of the wards of the city as they stood under Arcadius and Honorius, with Pancirolus's notes and a large explanatory index.
53334-the-art-of-being-bored-a-comedy-in:
The Art of Being Bored is a comedy in three acts by Edouard Pailleron, translated by Barrett Clark and published by Samuel French of New York and London. The acting edition sold for thirty-five cents. French's list, printed around the play, is called the world's best plays.

The list describes companion French pieces. Labiche's Grammar and his Two Cowards appear, with casts and prices. Master Patelin, a famous early farce about a clever lawyer, is offered in three acts. Le Sage and Marivaux supply the older classics on the page. Pailleron's comedy of manners belonged to the Paris stage's polished line. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
53425-the-dearest-things-in-boots:
Edna Mac Kenzie wrote The Dearest Thing in Boots, a play for Paine. The Paine company at Dayton, Ohio, sold it for twenty-five cents. No plays were exchanged by that house, its rule states. Song specialties fill its front advertising pages. Susan Gets Ready for Church was her earlier piece.

The scene, by the stage directions, is Wilson's store for fitting shoes. A long table piled with boxes stands down stage in the plan. A small table holds a cash box and books for the trade. Teachers want songs that are real novelties, the ads urge. The words must be clever, the music rich in melody. Welcome songs and closing songs fill the lists for school programs. The play gives a shoe-shop comedy for amateur stages. Mac Kenzie writes for school and church entertainments of her day.
53432-flowers-of-the-southwest-deserts:
Flowers of the Southwest Deserts, by Natt Dodge with drawings by Jeanne Janish, is number four in the Popular Series of the Southwestern Monuments Association. The National Park Service backed the booklet, first printed in 1951 and revised in 1954. A map marks the parks and monuments of the desert west, from Big Bend to White Sands.

The booklet treats the common plants of three deserts: the Chihuahua, the Sonoran, and the Mojave. Companion volumes cover the higher mesas and the mountain zones above them. For park visitors and home readers alike, it names and pictures the blooms a traveler meets on desert ground, in plain and accurate terms.
53491-famous-fights-of-indian-native-reg:
Reginald Hodder wrote this war book for the Daily Telegraph's series, printed by Hodder and Stoughton of London, New York, and Toronto in 1914. Hodder had written British Regiments at the Front. A plate shows Indian troops with the expeditionary force of 1914. The book opens with the Padisha's words to his Indian soldiers, bidding them uphold the honour of the British Raj.

A general account of the Indian Army comes first. Then come the peoples: Sikhs, Rajputs, Mahrattas, Gurkhas, Dogras, and Baluchis. Famous fights follow, from the Golden Dagon Pagoda and Bhurtpore to the first Sikh war, Aliwal, and Sobraon. The book tells British readers who their new comrades in the great war were.
53516-this-misery-of-boots:
Wells wrote a tart tract on boots as a key to how the poor live. The tract came out in Boston in 1908. Wells wrote Socialism and the Family and A Modern Utopia. It does not do to think about boots, a friend warns him first. The World as Boots and Superstructure heads his first part.

He has long had a bent to look at boots, he grants in turn. Most great asks can be put in terms of foot gear, he holds. Shoe men are prone to deep thought for that cause, he jokes. Chance gave him the faith that boots tell the whole tale. Bad boots stand for bad pay and a bad world in sum.
5352-marjorie-s-three-gifts:
Louisa M. Alcott's Marjorie's Three Gifts opens with Marjorie shelling peas on a doorstep, roses peeping through the porch lattice, and wind playing in her curly hair. Sunshine turns her faded gingham to a golden gown. Old Rover lies at her feet, a white kitten purrs on her shoulder, and robins hop about chirping a happy birthday.

Alcott, author of Little Women, writes a short birthday story of a girl, her pets, and three gifts that teach kindness and gratitude. The book offers young readers a warm, old-fashioned tale, published in Boston in 1899, in the manner of Alcott's best stories for children.
53816-a-book-of-christian-sonnets:
William Allen wrote A Book of Christian Sonnets, issued at Northampton in 1860 by Bridgman and Childs. Allen was late president of Bowdoin College. He had writ the American Biographical Dictionary and a poem named Wunnissoo. A long front note treats the sonnet form and its past.

Allen calls the sonnet the best form for one short, whole thought on faith. The poems were mostly writ in a recent period, he says. Notes at the back give past facts and clear up brief lines. Allen marvels that so few American poets have writ sonnets in books. He claims the volume may be the first book of American sonnets. An old man in a sick room for a year, he wrote from a life of verse study.
53817-the-goddess-of-reason-a-drama-in-f:
Mary Johnston wrote The Goddess of Reason, a drama in five acts, issued in Boston and New York by Houghton, Mifflin and Company in MDCCCCVII. Johnston inscribed the drama to the household at Woodley. The time of the action is seventeen ninety one to seventeen ninety four. Act one sits at the Château of Morbec in Brittany. Act two moves to the garden of the Convent of the Visitation in Nantes.

René Amaury de Vardes, Baron of Morbec, heads it. Rémond Lalain, deputy from Vannes, and the Abbé Jean de Barbisan follow. Count Louis de Château Gui and Captain Fauquemont de Buc stand in the list. Yvette, the Marquise de Blanchefôret, and three sisters of the convent appear. The mob at Nantes fills the crowd scenes. Drama readers get a French Revolution tragedy in verse and prose.
53924-abroad-and-at-home-practical-hints: Abroad and at Home, practical hints for tourists, opens in this copy with pages of notices for the traveller. The Inman Line lists its mail steamers sailing between New York, Queenstown, and Liverpool, first cabin passage from sixty dollars upward. A London house, Simpson's in the Strand, bills itself as the place for the best English dinner at a fair price. Railway pages for the London and North Western line follow, with baggage checked through from New York to London.
54650-suffrage-snapshots:
Suffrage Snapshots is a set of humorous paragraphs by Ida Husted Harper, issued at Washington in 1915. Its motto is have a smile with me, printed under her name on the title page. A note says the paragraphs had appeared in Judge magazine before this book. They express the lighter side of the so called woman question, the note says.

That question centres in the suffrage movement, but a woman quest of the vote is not a joke, Harper writes. It means hard work, anxious hours, and keen disappointments for those in the fight.  Harper, a leader of the suffrage cause and its historian, gathered these squibs in the last years of the long campaign. They show the movement laughing at itself on the road to the vote it would win five years later.
54698-woodbarrow-farm-play-in-three-acts:
Woodbarrow Farm is a play in three acts by Jerome K Jerome, printed by Samuel French at London in 1904. A cast list opens the text: Allen, Rollitt, Luke Cranbourne, Mike Stratton, Purtwee, the Honourable Tom Gusset, a baron, and Clara Dexter among them. The scene plan is given act by act.

Act One plays in the kitchen at Woodbarrow Farm on Exmoor. Act Two moves to a flat in Saint James's Mansions, London. Act Three divides between the library there and the farm again. The opening kitchen is an ideal old farmhouse room. From smoke-blackened beams hang huge sides of bacon, strings of onions, herbs, and poultry. Guns stand over the great fireplace. Jerome, of Three Men in a Boat fame, works his gentle comedy between moor and town.
54705-the-sorceress-a-drama-in-five-acts:
Victorien Sardou wrote The Sorceress, a drama in five acts, in an authorized translation from the French by Charles Weissert, copyrighted in 1917. A long introduction, Sardou and His Work, opens the volume. Sardou was born in Paris on September 7, 1831.

His father, from the country near Cannes, came to Paris in 1819 and followed scholastic pursuits; his mother came from ancient Troyes. The father edited textbooks, taught, and won many friends, yet fell so deep in debt that he gave up Paris for his southern olive groves. The play itself belongs to Sardou's Spanish manner, a drama of the Inquisition's age. Readers get the master of the well-made play in a costume tragedy, with his life attached.
54772-the-turning-of-the-tide-or-radclif:
Elijah Kellogg wrote The Turning of the Tide, or Radcliffe Rich and His Patients. The book belongs to his Whispering Pine series of tales for boys. Lee and Shepard issued the Boston edition in 1892.

Kellogg opens with a preface on sloth and the spur of hard times. A college teacher, he says, told each new class that all men are as lazy as they dare be. Kellogg holds that more folk fail from sloth than from lack of skill. Hard luck, by contrast, tests and tempers a stout heart. His tale of a young doctor puts that creed to work. The series took its name from Kellogg's pine woods tales.
55255-anecdotes-of-big-cats-and-other-be:
Anecdotes of Big Cats and Other Beasts, by David Wilson, was first printed in London by Methuen in 1910. A verse at the front holds that good and true stories lighten our ills. A second motto says the better we see through men, the gladder we look at beasts again.

Chapters open with Three Men Together and the wonderful escape of Tiger Hill. Sherlock Holmes in a Wood and Where Tigers Flourish follow. The Girl and the Tigress, the Old Men and the Tiger, and Recovering the Corpse pace the tiger part. A lesson from the water buffalo, the buffalo and the crocodile, and a nest of crocodiles fill the mid book. Useful snakes, the leopard as a killer of men, and mother love among the monkeys stand late. Beast fans get India hunting tales told round true events.
55269-a-description-of-the-famous-kingdo:
A Description of the Famous Kingdome of Macaria was printed in London for Francis Constable in 1641. The tract shows Macaria's government, where the inhabitants live in prosperity, health, and happiness. The king is obeyed, the nobles honoured, vice punished, and virtue rewarded: an example to other nations. It is cast as a dialogue between a scholar and a traveller.

An epistle to the High and Honourable Court of Parliament, dated October 25, 1641, offers the book as a widow's mite. The writer delivers his conceptions in fiction, taking for patterns Sir Thomas More and Sir Francis Bacon. Parliament may use what serves, and laugh at the rest. In the dialogue, the traveller meets the scholar near the Exchange and lures him to the fields. The traveller trades in knowledge, and has brought news over the sea without paying custom, worth all the merchandise in the kingdom.
55289-dealing-in-futures-a-play-in-three:
Dealing in Futures is a play in three acts by Harold Brighouse. It came out in New York in the year 1913 for the stage trade. The scene is a town on the edge of the shire of the red rose. The whole act of the play runs in the span of one day.

Jabez Thompson, a man who makes goods from chem stock, heads the cast. His girl Rosie stands by him at the meal board in the first act. A dye chief and his son bring the trade side to the plot in force. A young healer is the third man in the young set of the cast. The room is rich in a show way that marks the old man's pride. His girl's dress shuns that show, as the stage notes point out. Trade, pride, and love are the stakes of the day's work.
55291-graft-a-comedy-in-four-acts:
Harold Brighouse wrote a comedy in four acts published by Samuel French at London in 1913. Act one opens in a small first floor room, awkwardly crowded with a whole cottage's furniture. A pile of furniture under a sheet fills one corner. An iron bed stands right, a table center, and a fireplace left. It is seven on a September evening.

Jim Pilling, a gardener, has finished tea and sits in his shirt sleeves. Brighouse was a Lancashire playwright of the Manchester school. His comedies treat working class life with sympathy and bite. French published acting editions for amateur and professional stages. The crowded room states the play's theme of housing pressure at sight.
55377-pre-raphaelite-and-other-poets:
Pre Raphaelite and Other Poets collects lectures by Lafcadio Hearn, selected and edited with an introduction by John Erskine of Columbia University. Dodd, Mead printed it in New York in 1922. Nine chapters move from Rossetti through Swinburne and Browning to William Morris, the poetry of George Meredith, a note on Robert Buchanan, and Robert Bridges.

The first lecture ranks Dante Gabriel Rossetti as not inferior to Tennyson in workmanship, in the very first rank of nineteenth century poetry. Yet Rossetti, Hearn argues, had no sympathy with the ideas of his own century. He lived and thought in the Middle Ages, Italian by blood, religion, and feeling, a man of the thirteenth century reborn into the nineteenth. He was a great painter before becoming a great poet, and he detested modern science and philosophy. Hearn promises to study the poetry by groups, taking specimens from each.
55423-le-coq-d-or-the-golden-cock-an-ope:
Rimsky-Korsakov's opera Le Coq d'Or, The Golden Cock, fills this book in three acts, copyrighted in New York in 1918. The text appears in both French and English, act by act in turn. A summary of the plot at the front tells the tale before the singing starts.

King Dodon, a lazy and greedy ruler, frets over his warlike neighbours. His advisers fail him until an astrologer brings a wonder: a golden cock that foretells events from a spire. The bird cries peace and war by turns. After a war alarm, Dodon's army fares badly and retreats into a gorge heaped with the dead. Then a beautiful queen steps from the enemy tent, singing a bold hymn to the sun.
55447-the-younger-american-poets:
Jessie Rittenhouse wrote The Younger American Poets, printed at Boston in 1904. Portraits illustrate the studies, with Richard Hovey at the front. Rittenhouse gives the book to Louise Chandler Moulton, in warm affection.

Eighteen poets get chapters: Hovey, Lizette Woodworth Reese, Bliss Carman, and Louise Imogen Guiney lead. Santayana, Josephine Preston Peabody, and Madison Cawein follow. Later chapters treat Alice Brown, Clinton Scollard, and Gertrude Hall. Hovey, Rittenhouse writes, was a poet of convictions rather than fancies, standing for comradeship and a hearty surrender to life. The studies mix the facts of each life with close readings of the poems. A biographical index closes the volume.
55474-a-manual-of-shoemaking-and-leather:
A Manual of Shoemaking and Leather and Rubber Products, by William H Dooley, was published at Boston in nineteen twelve by Little, Brown, and Company. Dooley was principal of the Lowell Industrial School. The frontispiece shows an old-fashioned shoemaker at his bench. The manual was written for trade students learning a factory industry.

The chapters begin with fundamental shoe terms and hides and their treatment. Processes of tanning take a long chapter, with rotating drums illustrated. The anatomy of the foot, shoe styles, and the departments of a shoe factory follow. McKay and turned shoes, old-fashioned shoemaking and repairing, and leather products manufacture come next. Rubber shoe manufacture and a history of footwear close the book. Lowell was a mill and shoe town, and Dooley's manual taught its next workforce.
55492-behind-the-footlights:
Alec-Tweedie wrote a book about life on the stage in London. The book came out in New York in 1904. It has twenty pictures and a front view of an actress in Greek dress. Tweedie had wrote books on travel and on a London doctor before this one. Her aim here is to show what the stage is like off stage.

Chapters move from the lure of fame to pay, dress, and hard work. She talks with stars such as Mrs. Kendal and Ellen Terry. She notes long runs, weak speech, and loud bands. Readers get a close, plain view of stage folk at work.
55611-karma-a-re-incarnation-play-in-pro:
Karma is a play of reincarnation by Algernon Blackwood and Violet Pearn, published in New York by Dutton in 1918. Its frame is a prologue and epilogue set in the present day. Phillip Lattin, a British agent in Egypt, and his ill wife stand at its heart. The three acts then show their past lives together. The first act is set in Egypt in the year 2000 before Christ. The second moves to Greece in 325 before Christ. The third is set in fifteenth-century Italy.

The same two souls meet, love, and wound each other in each age. The debt of one life is paid in the next, as the title's law demands. The epilogue brings them back to the Egypt of the play's own day. Blackwood was a master of the strange tale. Here he gives his theme the full form of the stage.
55877-the-widowing-of-mrs-holroyd-a-dram:
The Widowing of Mrs Holroyd, a drama in three acts by Lawrence, was published in London in 1914. The persons are few: Mrs Holroyd, Holroyd, Blackmore, the children Jack and Minnie, a grandmother, Rigley, Clara, Laura, a manager, and two miners. Act one opens in the kitchen of a miner small cottage.

A deep, full red fire burns at the left. A white curtained window and an outer door stand at the back, with wooden stairs at the right. A sofa, a painted dresser, and a table with a red and blue check cloth furnish the room. It is dark twilight, full of warm fireglow. A tall woman enters from the outer door, carrying a basket. Outside, the colliery rail can be seen, and pit headstocks far back. Readers get Lawrence mining play of marriage, desire, and death, set in one cottage room.
55898-solitude-with-the-life-of-the-auth:
Zimmerman praises retreat in Solitude, with the life of the author, in two parts, printed at New York in 1840. Wells made the book. The life leads, then the treatise walks its ground in order: the influence of solitude upon the mind, and upon the heart.

General advantages of retirement, and the advantages of solitude in exile, in old age, and on the bed of death, close the first part. The second weighs motives to solitude, its disadvantages, and its influence on the imagination. Effects on a melancholy mind, influence on the passions, and the danger of idleness in solitude fill the run. His preface calms weak and delicate minds that the title may alarm. The author is no extravagant misanthrope, it says: he does not expect men to seek refuge in forests and lonely cells.
55927-derelicts:
William Locke wrote Derelicts, a novel put out by John Lane at London and New York in 1897. It opens on a warm Bank Holiday, the first Monday in August, in Holland Park. A policeman trades words with a man who sits bareheaded on steps, then walks on. The man gazes at a great house across the road, its blinds drawn in the noon sun. The house seems left to sun and quiet, like most great homes on that street.

Once the rooms of that house were as known to the man as his boyhood home. Its folk once flattered him, yet a cloud has since fallen on his life. Locke starts, then, with a man cast out of wealth and warmth. The tale that follows traces how far such a fall can go, and what can be saved.
56048-jewish-portraits:
Jewish Portraits, by Lady Magnus, appears here in a second revised and enlarged edition from David Nutt of London, dated 1897. Magnus had earlier written Outlines of Jewish History and About the Jews Since Bible Times. The first portrait treats Jehudah Halevi, physician and poet of the exile songs.

Other pieces plead for Heinrich Heine, weigh Daniel Deronda and his Jewish critics, and tell of Manasseh ben Israel and Moses Mendelssohn. Charity in Talmudic times and the story of a false prophet fill out the set. The national idea in Judaism stands among the essays. The dedication leaf reads simply: These, to his memory.
5605-the-power-of-movement-in-plants:
Charles Darwin, assisted by his son Francis Darwin, wrote The Power of Movement in Plants as a study of how plants move. The contents run from circumnutating movements of seedlings through sensitivity of the root tip to contact. They cover mature plants, climbing plants, sleep movements of leaves and cotyledons, and movements excited by light and gravitation, ending with concluding remarks.

Darwin shows seedlings bending, roots feeling their way, leaves folding at night, and stems climbing, all through small, steady motions. Readers get a classic of plant science, careful, experimental, and full of observation. It remains a landmark for anyone curious about how plants sense their world.
56129-the-book-of-the-fly-a-nature-study:
The Book of the Fly is a nature study of the house-fly and its kin by Hurlstone Hardy, published by Heinemann at London in 1915. Its subtitle adds The Fly Plague and a Cure. Halford Ross supplied the opening words. The publisher's notice at the front praises the age's zeal for making common things known in plain form.

The chapters call the fly a product of human filth, then teach the reader to know the common house-fly. Other flies and their ways follow, with a chapter on the flesh-burrowing kinds. The fly's life story, build, spread, and natural enemies are treated in turn. Later chapters weigh flies as carriers of disease and the means of fighting the plague.
