56414-a-candid-history-of-the-jesuits:
Joseph McCabe published A Candid History of the Jesuits in London in 1913. McCabe had already written The Decay of the Church of Rome, and his title promises plain dealing with the famous Catholic order. Sixteen chapters carry the story from the founding of the Society of Jesus to what he calls its last phase.

The first chapter opens in the early summer of 1521, months after Luther burned the Pope's bull at Wittenberg. A young Basque soldier, Inigo of Loyola, lies in his father's castle with a leg broken by a French ball at the siege of Pampeluna, his knightly ambitions wrecked with it. Later chapters follow the first Jesuits, their storms and missions, their expulsion from Portugal and Spain, and the suppression and restoration of the order. Readers get a full, critical survey of four centuries of Jesuit history.
56463-bacon-s-essays-and-wisdom-of-the-a:
Bacon's Essays and Wisdom of the Ancients, printed at Boston in 1884 by Little, Brown, pairs the Essays, or Counsels Civil and Moral, with Bacon's readings of old fables. A life of the author by Spiers opens the volume. The preface of Basil Montagu and the notes of earlier editors are folded in, with the Latin rendered for plain readers.

The advertisement says the notes come chiefly from a standard English edition, translations included. For the Wisdom, the editors chose a modern rendering over the version made in Bacon's own lifetime by a contemporary. The older one, they grant, keeps the style of the age. The volume was built as a full kit for study: text, life, notes, and tables in one binding.
56998-a-second-letter-to-the-rev-william:
A Second Letter to the Reverend William Maskell is a theological pamphlet by Mayow Wynell Mayow. Pickering issued it in London in 1850. Mayow was vicar of Market Lavington and a rural dean. His theme is the dogmatic teaching of the Church of England. A quote from Manning heads the letter. It asks if the English church stands cut off from the universal church.

In a short advertisement Mayow regrets the delay of the piece. Work on kindred subjects held him back, he says. In the meantime Maskell had taken a decisive step. That step made the letter seem useless for its first aim. Mayow still holds the subject worth a reply. The letter belongs to the Oxford Movement quarrels. Churchmen then fought over doctrine in print. Such pamphlets mark the road many took toward Rome.
57149-the-camp-fire-girls-at-driftwood-h:
Margaret Love Sanderson wrote a Camp Fire Girls novel copyrighted in 1918, drawn by Mildred Webster and issued at Chicago. A caption quotes Jane Pellew crying that something is the worst example of pure and unadulterated nerve she ever heard of. The series followed groups of Camp Fire Girls through camps, schools, and adventures.

Driftwood Heights gives this group its setting. The Camp Fire movement, founded a few years before, sold its ideals through such fiction. Girls in these books camp, work, and solve problems together. Sanderson's volume is one of many series entries that kept the organization's name before young readers during the first World War years.
57218-a-book-of-jewish-thoughts:
The Chief Rabbi, Dr J H Hertz, selected and arranged A Book of Jewish Thoughts, issued by Humphrey Milford and Oxford University Press in fifty six eighty, nineteen twenty. Hertz gave the book to the sacred memory of the sons of Israel who fell in the Great War, nineteen fourteen to nineteen eighteen. A prefatory note states the design. The first part, I am an Hebrew, covers the life and consciousness of the Jew.

The second part, The People of the Book, deals with Israel religious contribution to mankind, the note says. It touches on Jewish martyrdom and spiritual achievement through the ages, it adds. Sayings from Bible, rabbis, poets, and modern writers stand in short pieces. Themes run from God and Torah to suffering, hope, and the land of Israel. Jewish readers get a pocket treasury of their tradition, made in mourning and pride after the war.
5735-the-valley-of-the-giants:
Peter Kyne sets The Valley of the Giants in California in the summer of 1850, opening as a topsail schooner slips into a cove under Trinidad Head. A man lands with a long squirrel rifle, an axe, and a brown canvas pack of food and clothing, watches the small boat return, and steps into the redwood country. From that landing, the novel grows into a lumber saga of giant trees, claims, and rivalries.

You get a big, vigorous adventure of the early West, where forests are both wealth and wonder. Kyne writes with energy about work, risk, and the men who measured themselves against trees larger than houses. The book suits fans of western and lumber fiction, and readers who enjoy a story that opens quietly on a beach before widening into a fight for a valley.
57356-stella-australis-poems-verses-and-:
Stella Australis is a small book of poems, verses, and prose fragments by Coungeau, printed at Brisbane in 1914. The author traces its start to the death of King Edward the Seventh. She tried to mark that date with a few lines of verse, and from then on felt moved to keep writing. Many pieces first appeared in the Brisbane Courier, whose courtesy she thanks.

The contents are patriotic and local by turns. Poems treat the pioneers, Ibrahim Pasha at Scutari, and the loss of the Yongala. Others mark the loss of the Titanic, a song of Australia, and the Glasshouse Mountains in Queensland. There are pieces to a child, on a haunted chair, and on the seven ages of woman. The preface asks readers' leniency for the book's faults. Its aim, she says, is that Queenslanders and others may see beauty in everything God has made.
57451-woodcock-s-little-game-a-comedy-fa:
John Maddison Morton wrote some of the most popular farces of the Victorian stage, and Woodcock's Little Game is a comedy-farce in two acts. It was first played at the Royal St James Theatre on October 6, 1864, and runs about an hour in performance. The scene is the house of the widowed Colonel Carver at Stow-on-the-Wold, where Woodcock has just married her daughter Caroline, and the servant David opens the play writing home about the wedding.

Samuel French published the acting edition in London and New York. The cast is small: Woodcock and his wife, Christopher Larkings and his, the young Adolphus Swansdown, David, and the bride's mother. Morton's farces turn on mix-ups and mistaken aims, and this one keeps its little company tangled from the first entrance.
57897-the-story-of-the-highland-regiment:
Frederick Watson tells the story of Scotland's famed regiments in a history issued in wartime London in 1915. He dedicates the book to his brother, Captain Henry Trelss Watson of the 2nd Battalion.

The frontispiece shows the Camerons at Fuentes de Onoro. A verse by Lauchlan Maclean Watt gives the book its tone. Scotland is a grey, old mother throned amid northern waters. Her children scatter east and south, yet come back with brave hearts. Watson lists his earlier novels and boys' books on the same page. Macmillan houses in New York, Toronto, Melbourne, and India handled the work abroad. Written while Highland battalions fought in France, the history links old Peninsular glory to the new war's sacrifice.
57914-the-romance-of-wills-and-testament:
Edgar Vine Hall wrote The Romance of Wills and Testaments. T Fisher Unwin issued it at London in 1912. Hall had written Songs and Lyrical Poems in 1908. A book of spiritual testaments stood in prep. Francis Quarles heads the mottos in verse. My life's my dying day, Quarles wrote.

I still am making my will in it, he adds. Christina Rossetti's remember-me lines join the front. A Carthage stone verse of 1663 stands there too. Thomas Hughes cut that stone's words at Stepney. Time consumes all and spares none, it warns. Constable and Company lent an article for it. The Occult Review shares thanks in the front matter. Queer wills and last words make dry law glow in this gather of love, spite, and whimsy signed in death's shadow.
58007-hurrell-froude-memoranda-and-comme:
Hurrell Froude: Memoranda and Comments gathers what survives of a leader of the Oxford Movement. Louise Imogen Guiney compiled the book, published by Methuen at London in 1904. Seven plates include Froude as a child and his burial place at Dartington. Guiney was an American poet who settled in England.

The first part gives memoranda of Froude's life and ideals. The second reprints comments on him and his place in the Oxford Movement. Guiney opens with a claim about genius and interest. The persons who compel us, she writes, are rarely the coldly eminent. Vital spirits who make no pact with their age win the eye instead. Froude died young in 1836, leaving letters and a fierce name. His friend Newman kept his memory green for decades.
58009-russian-portraits:
Clare Sheridan, a sculptor, wrote an account of her stay in Moscow, issued in London in 1921. She says the book was not written for print, but came from her diary, and that she went to Moscow because portrait work was offered her there. Busts of Lenin and Trotsky were among her tasks.

Plates show her sitters and scenes: Krassin, Kameneff, Litvinoff with his son, and Trotsky at the front. She notes that some in England were angry at her for doing Lenin and Trotsky at all. Politics, she insists, are not her concern; humanity, with its force and weakness, is. Few English writers saw the new Russia so close.
5806-the-pot-boiler-a-comedy-in-four-act:
Upton Sinclair writes about writing itself in The Pot Boiler, a comedy in four acts edited by Haldeman Julius. Its real play characters include Will, the author, Peggy, joint author and critic, Bill, their eight-year-old son, and Dad, among others. The comedy turns on a household trying to produce a potboiler, a book written quickly to sell, while art, money, and family pride collide.

Readers and theatre groups will find Sinclair in a lighter mood, mocking literary commerce without losing sympathy for writers. The play-within-a-play structure lets arguments about art happen as jokes and quarrels. It suits those who enjoy Sinclair beyond his novels, and anyone who has wondered what happens when a writer must please both muse and market.
58230-shavings-scrapes-from-many-parts:
Shavings and Scrapes from Many Parts is a book by Jules Joubert. It came out in Dunedin, New Zealand, in 1890 from J. Wilkie and Company. The book is given to the members of the Savage Club of Dunedin, of the year 1889. A verse from Wordsworth on the sights of youth stands at its front, a lament that the things once seen are seen no more.

The contents open with a set of early scrapes, the first of them called A Stray Shot. The title of the book and its contents mark it as a gathering of tales and sketches from many lands and times of the author's life. The text was made from scans of works in the public stock held by the National Library of Australia, as the note at the head states.
58435-lollingdon-downs-and-other-poems-w:
John Masefield gathered poems and sonnets in a book issued in London in 1917 by William Heinemann. He gave the book to his wife. Other works of his, plays and verse alike, are listed at the front in the same dress.

The first poems ask what life is, in beads of bright days strung on the self. War, tears, work, and birth all pass through the lines. One sonnet shows the poet by the bedside of a dying Black man, where two souls feel made one. Beauty, faith, and man's search for one city by a vast count of ways run through the set.
58469-carpets:
Carpets is a trade survey by Brinton in Pitman Common Commodities and Industries series. Pitman and Sons published the book in London from Amen Corner for the series. A frontispiece shows a British fine Wilton carpet after the Ardebil carpet in the Victoria and Albert Museum. The preface faces the problem of writing on carpet manufacture for general readers.

Carpet making involves looms and other machinery of a complicated nature, the preface allows. The author had to decide how far it was necessary or desirable to explain such devices in the book. A certain standard of mechanical intelligence is assumed in the reader, the preface adds. The series taught the trades of Britain one commodity at a time. This volume treats wool, dyes, looms, and the great carpet towns for the clerk and the schoolboy who would never see a mill.
58471-partial-portraits:
Henry James wrote short lives and notes on fellow writers of his time. The book first came out in 1888 and was reprinted in 1894. Most parts first ran in well known monthlies in America. James knew some of his subjects in person.

He writes on Emerson, George Eliot, and Anthony Trollope at length. He also treats Stevenson, Daudet, Maupassant, and Turgenev with close care. The last part sets out his views on the art of prose tales. Readers find sharp, calm praise and blame from a great peer of theirs. Macmillan issued the book in London and New York alike.
58527-eric-s-book-of-beasts:
David Starr Jordan made Eric's Book of Beasts in water-colours with jingles, and Paul Elder issued the volume at San Francisco in 1912. Shimada Sekko redrew the colour cartoons in black and white, adding quaint touches of his own. Jordan, of Stanford University, dated his note January 19, 1912.

The cartoons were made one by one in leisure moments to please a small boy, and are now reprinted for other children. A front verse takes readers to a Hague hotel where all creation lives in peace. Eric's Planet opens the set, then a caravan, Jack the Rabbit, an elephant, and a hippopotamus. Crocodile, giraffe, goat, possum, pelican, lion, and horned toad follow in rhyme.
59243-the-pacifists:
The Pacifists is a science fiction story by Charles E Fritch, printed in Worlds of If in May 1955. A rocket lands a hundred yards from a silent village. The houses stand white and windowless, and no one comes out to look. Compton insists the people must have seen them land.

Parker amends that this may be a ghost city. Hinckley agrees that perhaps no one lives here, or anywhere on the planet. The editor's blurb gives Parker his character in advance. He was a troublemaker wherever they landed, always hunting the easy chance. Here is the ideal planet, and the chance he has awaited, easy as taking candy from a baby. Fritch builds the tale on that collision: a planet of peace and the one man who cannot leave peace alone.
59468-the-scottish-highlands-highland-cl:
This first volume of a two-volume history treats the Scottish Highlands, their clans, and their famed regiments. It was printed first as four small books, now bound as one. The second volume stands as its mate for those who read on.

Highland history runs from the old clan world to the regiments that carried its names round the world. The clans' lands, chiefs, feuds, and falls form the base of the tale. Then come the regiments raised from those same glens, in their tartans and with their pipes. Such a set served Scots at home and abroad who wished their past in full. Plates from the first printings stand through the text.
59469-the-scottish-highlands-highland-cl: Second of a two-volume set of the 1875 history of the Scottish Highlands, Highland clans, and Highland regiments, first issued as a subscription work in eight separate books. This volume joins books five through eight and runs past eight hundred pages. The publishers printed the front matter for the whole work in the final book. Gaelic passages appear with English translations set after them, and large tables of regimental names fill many of the closing pages.
59768-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of William Butler Yeats is a guide compiled by David Widger. It lists the Yeats books held by Project Gutenberg and gives the table of contents for each. Eight volumes of the Collected Works head the list, followed by single works in verse, prose, and drama.

Among the titles stand The Wind Among the Reeds, The Secret Rose, and Irish Fairy Tales. Plays appear as well, such as The Land of Heart's Desire and The Hour Glass. The index also flags books that have no linked contents, among them Four Years and Reveries over Childhood and Youth. It serves as one map to a large and varied body of work.
59782-london-in-the-time-of-the-stuarts:
Sir Walter Besant wrote on London in the time of the Stuarts. Adam and Charles Black issued the book in London in 1903. A portrait of Charles the First, from van Dyck, fronts the work. Chapters run by reign, from James the First to Queen Anne.

Parts treat church and trade, then the Great Plague and the Fire in depth. Food, dress, weddings, theaters, coaches, and crime fill the manners part. A key to Ogilby and Morgan's map of 1677 closes the survey. London lovers gain a fat, vivid portrait of the city across a stormy age.
5987-in-kedar-s-tents:
Henry Seton Merriman sets a tale of sowing and reaping that moves from Ronda and a Moorish garden to Madrid and Toledo. The chapters promise contraband, a love letter, a war of wit, a tangled web, and a cross-examination, with priestcraft, swordcraft, and womancraft weighed in turn.

One sows and another reaps, and the road runs through cities of discontent and strife toward midnight, dawn, and at last the dawn of peace. Merriman blends romance with intrigue across Spain. Concepción takes the road, Larralde names his price, and honor is tested before the end.
59883-how-to-collect-and-preserve-insect:
How to Collect and Preserve Insects, by HH Ross, is a practical circular from the Illinois Natural History Survey for beginners who want to build an insect collection. Circular number thirty-nine was printed at Urbana in November 1966, in its eighth printing.

Ross was assistant chief of the survey, whose chief was George Sprugel the younger. The pamphlet appears under the authority of the State of Illinois, in the Department of Registration and Education. Long lists at the front name the board and the scientific staff of the survey, most of them working in the study of insects that harm crops. The guide itself teaches the standard craft of the hobby: how to catch, kill, pin, label, and keep specimens so that they last for study.
5996-essays-on-russian-novelists:
William Lyon Phelps opens with Russia humbled by the Japanese war, her navy destroyed, armies beaten, treasury drained, and pride laid in dust. He argues that a nation's greatness lies not in battleships or wealth, but in intellectual splendor, in ideas given to the world, and in gifts to literature and art.

The essays that follow read Russian fiction as a window on national character. Phelps invites American readers, proud of industrial power, to weigh their own gifts against Russia's in literature and music. The book treats novels as evidence of a people's inner life, not mere entertainment.
60007-earthquakes-and-other-earth-moveme:
John Milne, professor of mining and geology in the Imperial College of Engineering at Tokio, wrote this volume of the International Scientific Series. Appleton published it at New York in 1886, with thirty-eight figures. Milne's object is a systematic account of earth movements of every scale. Earthquakes are the sudden violent movements of the ground. Tremors are minute movements that escape notice by their smallness. Pulsations hide by the length of their period, and oscillations matter to the geologist.

The scheme treats earthquakes at length: seismometry, earthquake motion, effects on land and in the ocean, and the determination of origins in space and time. Distribution and cause follow, and the book ends with prediction and warning. Milne worked where the ground itself was his laboratory, in Japan. He admits how little accurate knowledge existed, and how tangled cause and effect can be when a coast rises with a shock.
60025-miss-leslie-s-complete-cookery-dir:
Miss Leslie wrote full directions for cookery in all its branches. Henry Carey Baird issued the forty-ninth form at Philadelphia in 1853. The work first entered Congress records in 1837. A long, firm front note praises good food as a housewife's plain duty.

Leslie holds that no one should boast of not knowing good food from bad. A wife careless of the table will keep bad cooks, she warns. New receipts and fixes fill the revised form throughout. Home cooks gain a vast, trusted guide that made plain cooks of new brides.
60056-scrap-book-of-mormon-literature-vo:
Scrap Book of Mormon Literature, volume one, holds religious tracts of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, put out by Ben E Rich. A motto at the front says the gatherers took posies from other men flowers, and only the thread that binds them is theirs.

The index opens with the Articles of Faith by Joseph Smith. Notes to be referred to daily by missionaries, from President Francis M Lyman for the Council of Twelve Apostles, follow. The prophet Joseph Smith then tells his own story at length. It runs from the first vision and the angel Moroni visits to the plates and the founding of the church. The martyrdom of Joseph and Hyrum closes his tale. A What Mormons Believe part sums the doctrines, the apostasy, and the restoration. Church readers get a missionary handbook of texts.
60184-the-story-of-king-arthur-and-his-k:
The Story of King Arthur and His Knights was written and drawn by Howard Pyle. Charles Scribner's Sons published it in New York in November 1903. Pyle began the work in 1902, by his foreword. He calls Arthur the most honourable, gentle knight who ever lived. The knights of the Round Table took him as their mirror of chivalry. Pyle hopes to finish the tale in a later book.

The contents split into books and parts. The winning of kinghood comes first. Kay breaks his sword at a London tournament, and Arthur finds him a new one. Arthur draws the sword from the anvil where kings and dukes failed. A wounded knight then comes to court in the next part. Pyle's rich drawings match his high, old style prose for young readers.
60225-the-preparation-mounting-of-micros:
Thomas Davies wrote this handbook on making microscope slides, printed by Robert Hardwicke of Piccadilly in London. The title page gives no year, and the front pages carry the publisher's ads for kindred books. Among them sits Half-Hours with the Microscope by E Lankester, with drawings of 250 objects from nature by Tuffen West.

Davies says in his preface that he fills a want long felt. Facts on preparing and mounting objects lay scattered as side chapters in books about the microscope itself. A worker had to search many works for one method. Davies gathers the lore in one place, quotes rival methods where experts differ, and thanks the friends whose work he drew on. The book serves the amateur at the bench.
60263-verses-and-sonnets:
Verses and Sonnets, by Hilaire Belloc, is an early book of his poems. Ward and Downey issued it at London in 1896, rights reserved in full. Belloc dedicates it to John Swinnerton Phillimore on the title page here. The Night leads, a prayer for rest from the holy night keeper.

Homage and Cuckoo close the opening verses in short lyric form next. Sonnets follow: the harbour, her youth, love and honour, her music, her faith. Grotesques add Noël, the world end, and the moon funeral in odd tones. Epigrams sting an actor, a poet, a singer, a reviewer, and a don. Twelve sonnets of the months round out the slim volume.
60465-lady-patricia-a-comedy-in-three-ac:
Rudolf Besier, author of Don, wrote this comedy in three acts. Duffield and Company published it at New York in the series Plays of To-Day and To-Morrow. Its other volumes are praised in the front pages from the Saturday Review, the Times, and the Nation. The play is dedicated to Elizabeth Fagan.

A cast list gives the production at the Haymarket Theatre, London, on March 22, 1911, under Herbert Trench's management, with Campbell in the title part of Lady Patricia Cosway. Her husband is Michael Cosway, and the others are the Dean Lesley, his daughter Clare, and the Irish Bill O'Farrel with his mother. The first two acts play on a platform and summer-house built in an oak tree at Ultima Thule, Cosway's country seat at Norman Arches. Five weeks pass before the second act, and one night before the third, set in the Deanery garden.
60523-the-torch-bearers-a-satirical-come:
The Torch-Bearers is a satirical comedy in three acts by George Kelly, printed in New York in 1923, with a preface by Kenneth Macgowan. Stewart and French first staged it at the Savoy Theatre in Asbury Park in August 1922. The printed form matches the version played at the Vanderbilt Theatre in New York.

The scene moves from Frederick Ritter's drawing room to behind the scenes at Horticultural Hall, then back two hours later. Paula Ritter leads an amateur company, and a line given to the formidable Pampinelli heads the book: there will be actresses when husbands are a thing of the past. Kelly staged the play himself and kept control of all performance rights.
60537-scenes-and-portraits:
Scenes and Portraits is a book of imagined encounters by Frederic Manning, published in London in 1909. John Murray issued the volume from Albemarle Street in that year. Manning is named as author of The Vigil of Brunhild on the title page. A Latin dedication, to a dearest mother, stands at the front of the book.

Contents list five pieces for the volume in a row of scenes. The King of Uruk opens the book with the Babylon of Gilgamesh for its scene. At the House of Euripides and The Friend of Paul follow in the list of pieces. Manning method is the imaginary portrait: a moment in a great life, rendered as a scene with speech. He wrote with a scholar patience and a poet ear, and these early scenes began the reputation that his later work on the war would carry far beyond the study.
60726-summer-guests:
James H Schmitz wrote this short story, printed in Worlds of If Science Fiction in September 1959. Rain drums all Saturday night on Sweetwater Beach, with thunder, lightning, and the boom of the Pacific surf a block off. Mel Armstrong, snug in his duplex, sleeps through it in comfort. He wakes at nine to a Sunday of pure sun and no cloud.

The morning starts his two-week paid holiday from Marty's Fine Liquors, a wholesale house where he sells. He is twenty-eight and bored by the job, and the bright day makes him feel it afresh. The storm has strewn his courtyard with branches and a drowned Sunday paper, which his low rent obliges him to clear. The title promises guests out of season.
60795-arizona-argonauts:
Bedford-Jones wrote this Western tale, Arizona Argonauts, printed at Garden City in 1924. Thirteen chapters carry odd names: Two Palms, Shipwrecked Men, Bill Hobbs Arrives, Sandy Invests Twice, Deadoak Feels Remorse, Stung, and Doctor Scudder, ending with Untangled. A frontispiece shows a gunman and a horse.

Chapter one sits on a hotel porch. Piute Tompkins, owner of the Two Palms House, drops his chair feet with a bang and spits at a lizard in the sand of Main Street. A mystery has the town flabbergasted, he tells Deadoak Stevens. A Chinese prospector has come with an automobile and a pretty daughter. He asks the way to Morongo Valley, and heads out into the wastes like any other gold hunter.
60912-on-the-training-of-parents:
On the Training of Parents, by Ernest Hamlin Abbott, was published in nineteen o eight at Boston. Its title turns the usual aim of such books on its head at once. Six chapters treat spasm and habit, the will and the way, and rule of wit. Peace at a price, nature, and the beginning of wisdom close the set.

The first chapter opens with a sharp scene in long grass outdoors. A young mother with a switch orders her small daughter to fetch canned salmon. The frightened child wavers, whimpers, and at last runs crying down the road. Abbott calls that scene government by collision in family life. Its rule is to wait till the child does wrong, then collide with her. He grants that most parents collide in private, with finer phrases, not in public.
60950-footlights:
Footlights is a set of theatre tales by Rita Weiman of New York. Dodd, Mead and Company issued it in 1923, with rights from 1919 on. Weiman dedicates the book to her mother, on whose love the curtain never falls. Eight tales bear stage names: Footlights, Madame Peacock, Grease Paint, The Back Drop. Two Masters, Up Stage, and Curtain fill out the bill of fare.

A preface called The Curtain Rises paints the house before the show. Wide soft chairs face a curtain in long, mystic folds of cloth. The air holds a scent with no name in that hushed, waiting world. Behind the curtain lies the same world bound by brick walls. Scenery with act numbers scrawled in charcoal waits to be shoved in.
6117-success-with-small-fruits:
E. P. Roe dedicates Success with Small Fruits to Charles Downing, neighbor, friend, and horticulturist, from whom he hopes to keep learning. His preface says a book should be judged by what it attempts, and this volume aims to lure men and women back to their original calling, that of gardening.

Roe imagines Eve helping Adam, especially as the sun declined, with small fruits for breakfast, dinner, and supper, and perhaps between meals. Even mortals who have sinned more than once can fare as well, he says. The Adams and Eves of every generation can have an Eden if they wish, and Eve often creates it.
61260-it-s-fun-to-sew-aprons-and-skirts:
A 4-H club sewing book on aprons and skirts was issued by the cooperative extension service as series L-86, phase two. Theta Johnson, clothing specialist at Utah State University, prepared it. Read this book from cover to cover before you start your project, the first page bids.

Take care of your clothing, shine your shoes, and sew on buttons start the habits. Assemble your sewing tools, do your shopping, and learn to buy cotton fabric. Learn to use the sewing machine and to press cotton. Then sew and have fun: make a scarf, a sewing kit, and TV slippers. Make your apron or skirt last: a peasant apron with band or elastic top, or a gathered skirt. Girls learned dressmaking by doing.
61276-horse-secrets:
A S Alexander, professor of veterinary science at the University of Wisconsin, discloses trade tricks in Horse Secrets, published at Philadelphia in 1909 for twenty-five cents. Feeding secrets come first: hand raising a foal, feeding silage and molasses, fattening drafters. Secrets of vices follow, from halter pulling and stall kicking to handling a balky horse.

The heart of the book exposes horse-trading frauds: shutting a heaver, plugging a roarer, gingering a show horse, hiding a spavin, making an artificial star and bishoping a horse's teeth. Sections on stallion selling, veterinary secrets and auction rules teach buyers to protect themselves.
61281-heliogabalus-a-buffoonery-in-three:
H L Mencken and George Jean Nathan wrote this play, Heliogabalus, a buffoonery in three acts, printed in New York in 1920. A note warns that the play is for readers only, and that no stage show may be given without leave from the authors. The cast names Varius Avitus Bassianus Heliogabalus, Emperor of Rome, at its head.

Around the emperor stand his senior wife Paula and five junior wives. The cast adds a Christian maiden, a Christian clergyman, a fleet commander, two doctors, and a pickpocket. Act One sits in the palace atrium on the night before New Year's Day in the year 221. Later acts move to the bed-chamber and the banquet hall.
61293-gimp-braiding-projects:
Charles White wrote and illustrated Gimp Braiding Projects, covering lanyards, leashes, belts, and bracelets, copyrighted in 1940 by Fellowcrafters of Boston. A foreword explains the aim. For craftsmen's convenience, directions for many popular gimp projects are assembled in one booklet.

The directions are illustrated in colour, the publisher says, so every step can readily be understood, since braiding's true simplicity is often obscured by complicated instructions. The material is a special coated tape in many colours and shapes; standard gimp is flat and a hair under a tenth of an inch wide. General directions open the lessons: always start with the seam next to the core. Readers get a camp-craft classic in pamphlet form.
61598-london-sonnets:
Humbert Wolfe published London Sonnets at Oxford in 1920, in the Adventurers All series of young poets unknown to fame. The series motto comes from Tennyson's Ulysses: not too late to seek a newer world. Wolfe's dedication imagines the first anemones blossoming in a London street, blown from a valley in Lyonesse.

The first group, London Pseudo-Sonnets, works the streets in rough voices. The Old Clothes Dealer speaks in his own defense, counting the cost of holy days lost to trade and asking if his people have not paid their sins. Other pieces visit a bun-shop, a fried fish-shop, the streets behind Tottenham Court Road, and the suburbs. Later sections add sonnets of love and war verse, including The Moon in Flanders and The Soldier Speaks. Wolfe threads Kipling's Gods of the Copy-Book Headings into his own lines. Readers get a young poet's London, street by street.
61734-postscripts:
O Henry left short newspaper pieces that Harper and Brothers gathered as Postscripts at New York and London in 1923. Florence Stratton wrote the opening essay, and the pieces are dedicated to Mr Roy G Watson. The Houston Post held part of the copyright. A long contents list shows the scale: dozens of brief sketches.

Titles run from The Sensitive Colonel Jay and A Matter of Loyalty to Toddlekins and Buying a Piano. A green hand, a righteous outburst, a fatal error, and a telegram each get a page or two. Leap year advice, answers to inquiries, and city perils fill the middle. Bill Nye and a portrait draw tributes. The pieces show O Henry as a young Texas journalist, quick and comic.
61823-the-old-time-spelling-school-in-th:
John Ellenbecker wrote this old time spelling school in three parts. Brodrick printed it at Marysville, Kansas, in the year 1922. Part one is Golden Valley, part two The Contest, part three Musical. Ellenbecker gives the book to Marshall County schools and their pupils.

Verse opens the tale, calling friends to raise the past curtain. Parents and youth swung round the school house in those days. Young folks today would scarce guess the stress of stubborn words. Lines of spellers stood hours round the dingy school house wall. The country school was then a kind of home spun university, the verse recalls fondly.
62035-a-planet-for-your-thoughts:
A Planet for Your Thoughts is a science fiction story by James Norman. It appeared in the magazine Planet Stories in the winter of 1941. Its headnote sets a universe where mankind has given up thinking. The grape-headed Uvans do the brain work for everyone else.

Bill Petrie, a freebooter, has begun getting original ideas of his own. That small rebellion threatens a crisis for the whole cosmos. The story opens with Bill clamped in a pillory in a strange market-place. Aliens stream past below him, their eyes placed anywhere on their heads. Uva, the world he hangs above, is the brain-register of the universe. It is the most respected, yet least visited, body in the skies of 2451.
62325-menace-of-the-mists:
Richard Storey wrote Menace of the Mists, a science fiction tale printed in Planet Stories in May nineteen forty-three. The scene is Venus, a world of white fog and black seas. Four Earthmen face a horror rising from the sea floor.

MacAloon rides a saddle-lizard and peers through the mist with special glasses. Below him, a vast wave of foot-long beasts pours out of the water. The creatures, like huge centipedes with human-like fronts, form dense marching ranks. His Venusian guide begs to flee to the man city, saying more always come. A cold, soulless mind drives the horde.
62428-a-battle-for-right-or-a-clash-of-w:
A Battle for Right, or A Clash of Wits, is a Nick Carter detective story in the New Magnet Library. Those paper books sold at fifteen cents a copy. A page at the front boasts that Nick Carter stands for an interesting detective story. The books in the line are uniformly good, it claims, by one cause.

That cause is the work of a specialist in detective plots. The man who wrote these stories produced no other type of fiction. His mind was set on new plots where his hero wins through. Carter outwits crooks, cracks disguises, and springs traps in every number. A clash of wits is the promise of this title in full. Dime novel readers got a complete case for their fifteen cents.
62494-five-men-and-pompey-a-series-of-dr:
Five Men and Pompey is a set of dramatic portraits in verse by Benét. The Four Seas Company issued it at Boston in 1915. Elihu Vedder designed the cover. Six portraits make up the book. Sertorius speaks first, at his last banquet. Twelve years of striving weigh on his speech. Pompey lives, and Metellus presses him hard. His own camp mutters toward mutiny.

Lucullus dines in the second portrait. A forlorn campaign and letters to Atticus follow. The civil war and Pharsalia's aftermath close the set. Benét was young when he wrote these pieces. He later won fame for John Brown's Body. His Romans speak in taut, modern verse. Ambition and slow ruin are his theme throughout.
62687-the-arabian-nights-entertainments:
Arabian Nights Entertainments stands here in the old Grub Street line. Wardle printed this revised one volume edition at Philadelphia in 1835. The text descends from Galland French version through unknown English hands. Nearly one hundred engravings embellish the tales in this printing.

A frontispiece scene shows a lady waking two princes in a tree. Contents open with the genie and the lady in a glass box. Fables of the ass and ox and dog and cock follow. The merchant and the genie and three old men tales come next. The text rests on the old Grub Street English version.
62703-a-bill-of-divorcement-a-play-in-th:
Clemence Dane wrote a play in three acts, first put on at the St Martin's Theatre on Monday, March 14th, 1921. Heinemann of London issued the text that year. The cast list names Lilian Braithwaite as Margaret Fairfield and Meggie Albanesi as Sydney, her girl.

The scene is a small country house on Christmas Day, 1933, in a time when new divorce rules from a royal report have become law. Acts pass in the hall and the drawing room, from morning to late day. Hester Fairfield, a keen old lady in black who keeps a grievance as a pet, spars with Margaret at a table laid for three.
62762-american-beer-glimpses-of-its-hist:
The brewers' own trade body at New York put out a book on American beer in 1909. Its title joins peeks at the drink's past with an account of its making. The first part treats New England. Even there, the writer owns, the tale starts in haze.

Old peoples gave the drink's birth to kind gods, male or female. On New England soil, he argues, men of Europe drank beer long before the Pilgrims landed. The Vikings, he holds, brought their store on the Vineland trips. Gosnold in 1602 came with ale from Falmouth, he says, as every ship then did. The book then turns to how the brew is made in modern works.
62835-party-sweets:
Mary Blake wrote a candy booklet for the Carnation Company of Los Angeles in 1960. Its claim is plain: canned milk works like cream in candy, with half the fat. Good candy, it says, must be creamy smooth, never coarse or grainy. The proof of the candy is in its texture.

Peanut clusters come first, built on brown sugar, peanut butter and chopped nuts. Chocolate bon bons follow, rolled in nuts and chilled. Cream pralines make twenty or so patties from two sugars and milk. A hint urges the candy heat glass to take the guess work out of the pot. Such booklets sold the milk by teaching sweet making at home.
62842-in-fashions-for-him-for-her-in-kni:
Star Book Number 230 gives knit and crochet plans for men and women. American Thread issued the book from Stamford, with a price of thirty-five cents. Long V-neck vests, shown in color on the cover, lead the set. Sizes run small, medium, and large for both women and men.

Each plan lists yarn, needles, hook, and gauge in full. Rows spell out how to cast on, shape armholes, and join facings stitch by stitch. Counts for each size sit side by side so knitters can track their own. Home makers who knit by the book gain clear, checked steps to a neat vest.
62967-revolving-lights:
Revolving Lights is a novel by Dorothy M Richardson, first published in London by Duckworth and Company in 1923. It forms one volume of her long sequence about Miriam Henderson. The earlier volumes are listed in order: Pointed Roofs, Backwater, Honeycomb, The Tunnel, Interim, and Deadlock.

Reviewers quoted in the front matter grasp her new method. The Nation says the ordinary novelist stands on the bank of the river of life. Miriam pulls us with her into the yielding water. The Daily Telegraph praises the half subconscious revelation of personality. Richardson was building, book by book, one of the first great stream of consciousness works in English. Revolving Lights continues Miriam's London years in that inward manner. The novel is less a plot than a mind's weather, recorded hour by hour.
63073-limehouse-nights:
Thomas Burke wrote these tales of London's Chinatown and set them by night in Limehouse. McBride printed Limehouse Nights at New York in 1919, and the book ran to ten printings in two years. Burke gave it to Caradoc Evans, the Welsh writer.

The Chink and the Child leads the set, a famed and tender tale. The Father of Yoto, Gracie Goodnight, and The Paw follow. Beryl, the Croucher and the Rest of England takes a long place. The Sign of the Lamp, Tai Fu and Pansy Greers, and Gina of the Chinatown fill the list. A knight-errant, a gorilla and a girl, and Old Joe close a book of dockside love, crime, and dreams.
63198-lords-of-creation-woman-suffrage-d:
Lords of Creation is a woman suffrage drama in three acts by Ella Cheever Thayer, published in Boston in 1883 by Geo M Baker and Company. The play argues for women's rights through the talk of one household and its servants.

The cast lists Kate Grovenor, who has a mind of her own, and Jennie, a chambermaid who believes in woman's rights. Against them stand Mr Grovenor, head of his family, his idle son Eugene, and Harold Doughlass, who has more money than brains. Dr Endicott is marked as a true man, the ally the cause needs. Jennie opens the play hunting for Eugene's buttonhole bouquet and mocking men who expect to be waited on as lords of creation.
63281-the-glebe-1914-04-vol-2-no-1-colle:
One monthly number of The Glebe, volume two, number one, dated April 1914, is devoted to Collects by Horace Traubel, priced at fifty cents or three dollars yearly. The magazine declares absolute freedom of expression as its only editorial policy. Its range runs from radical to conservative, the only requisite being unmistakable merit. Each issue is devoted to one individual alone.

That bulk, the editors argue, lets readers grasp a personality as magazine scraps cannot. Twelve such books a year were promised. Traubel was Walt Whitman's friend and Boswell, editor of the Conservator. The Glebe was an early little magazine of the modernist ferment. Alfred Kreymborg stood behind the venture.
634-miscellaneous-mathematical-constants:
Simon Plouffe collects high-precision values of mathematical constants in this reference volume, drawn from a Simon Fraser University index. Artin's constant, the Backhouse constant, Catalan's constant, Champernowne's constant, and dozens more appear, many to thousands of digits. Cosine, cube roots, gamma values, and Feigenbaum numbers share the store.

The book serves workers who need true digits to test code or theory, not casual readers. Its tables, gathered with Plouffe's permission, keep a public record of numbers that recur across math and physics. For the curious it stands as a quiet monument to how much order hides in a few strange digits.
6347-hobson-s-choice-a-lancashire-comedy:
Harold Brighouse's Lancashire comedy in four acts was first produced in America, then in London at the Apollo Theatre on June 22, 1916. Henry Horatio Hobson, bootmaker, rules three daughters, Alice, Maggie, and Vickey, with a strap and a temper, while Will Mossop, his boot hand, loves Maggie and she does the taking up. Hobson lifts a trap, calls Will up, and declares he cannot leather a lass, being female and exempt, but he can leather him.

The cast list names Lydia Bilbrooke, Edyth Goodall, and Hilda Davies as the daughters, Norman McKinnel as Hobson, and Joe Nightingale as Mossop. Brighouse writes Lancashire speech with comic precision, as Maggie, the cleverest Hobson, turns her father's shop and his choice against him. The play is a battle of wills in a boot shop, where a daughter's choice proves the best business of all.
63737-egypt-and-its-monuments:
Robert Hichens tours the Nile monuments in Egypt and Its Monuments, copyrighted in 1908 and published at New York by the Century Company in 1923, with paintings by Jules Guérin and photographs. Eighteen chapters move from the Pyramids and the Sphinx through Sakkara and Abydos to Denderah, Karnak and Luxor. The Colossi of Memnon, the Ramesseum and the Tombs of the Kings follow.

Later chapters cover Edfu, Kom Ombos and Philae, ending at Pharaoh's Bed and Old Cairo. The illustration list pairs Guérin's paintings with photographs of the same sites, from the summit of the Great Pyramid to recent digging at Deir-el-Bahari.
63821-love-among-the-robots:
Love Among the Robots is a science fiction story by Emmett McDowell, printed in Planet Stories in the winter of 1946. It opens on an asteroid station with clear plastic walls. The scientist Henry Ohm watches a girl, Sofi Jokai, flee across the jagged ground with a robot close behind her, waving a wrench.

The joke of the tale is in its title. The robots on the station have begun to take ideas from the humans around them, and Ohm can not keep his mind on his work with Sofi near. McDowell plays the scene for comedy, with a chase, an airlock, and a flood of angry words lost inside a helmet. The story is a light pulp piece from the early years of the space age in print.
63893-gli-idioti-the-idiots:
Gli Idioti, The Idiots, is a tale by Joseph Conrad in a twin tongue form. The host text was first put out in nineteen twenty. It was made for the feast of a band of proof folk. Hilda Campioni made the tongue of Italy form. Mansion ran the set as its chief. The book stands in a set of such twin texts. Its two forms stand side by side on the page.

The first words of that set, in both tongues, hail a new age. Its chief mark, they say, will be a more great bond of kin past the lands. The need to know and grasp each land will be felt more and more. It holds that the study of the tongues of past lands is now of prime weight.
6399-the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-vol:
After twelve emperors, Suetonius adds lives of poets: Terence, Juvenal, Persius, Horace, Lucan, and Pliny. Terence, Publius Terentius Afer, a native of Carthage, was a slave at Rome of Senator Terentius Lucanus. Struck by his abilities and handsome person, the senator gave him a liberal education and freedom at maturity. Some call him a war captive, but Fenestella shows his birth and death fell between the second and third Punic wars, when no such capture could have happened.

Terence lived familiarly with men of high station, and his comedies won Roman favour. A later poet in the set dies soon after honourable banishment as prefect of a cohort on Egypt's far frontier. The punishment was chosen as severe enough for a venial, droll offence, and he was worn down by grief and weariness of life. Suetonius gives literary lives with the same anecdotal care as imperial ones, in Thomson's translation.
64074-g-f-watts:
Watts is a critical study of the painter George Frederick Watts by Chesterton. Duckworth published it in London in 1904, with reprints to 1914. A list of photogravures opens the volume. The Habit Does Not Make the Monk serves as frontispiece. Portraits of Leslie Stephen, Walter Crane, and Cardinal Manning are listed. Matthew Arnold, Mill, Browning, and Tennyson appear among the sitters. Watts painted the great Victorians as a national portraitist. His allegories fill the rest of the plate list.

Chaos, The Minotaur, and The Court of Death stand there. Hope, Mammon, Jonah, and Love and Death are also plated. Orpheus and Eurydice and Eve Repentant give the mythic side. Hollyer photographed the works for these permanent plates. Chesterton writes on a painter of ideas and famous men. The little book is an appreciation, not a catalogue.
64169-tom-newcombe-or-the-boy-of-bad-hab:
Harry Castlemon wrote a boys tale in his Go-Ahead set, of a lad named Tom Newcombe and his bad habits. Long lists in the front show the scale of Castlemons fame, set on set of sea, war, and woods tales. Tom learns to be a sailor in a front print, cap and rope in hand on deck.

Chapters send Tom to sea, home again, and then into trade, where he learns how a lad can thrive. Farm life, game birds, and a storm tale with a hid twist fill the mid span. A school for cadets, a wish to be colonel, and a plot close a tale of fault cured by work.
64235-the-tale-of-the-argonauts:
The Tale of the Argonauts is the Greek epic of Apollonius of Rhodes, turned into English verse by Arthur S Way and shaped by Israel Gollancz. Dent printed it in London in 1901. Four books carry Jason and his crew on the quest of the Golden Fleece.

Way opens with a call to Phoebus and the heroes of old who sped at King Pelias word. An oracle warned Pelias of a man who would come with one foot bare. Jason lost one sandal in the swollen Anaurus river mire and came so to the king feast. The song then names Orpheus first among the crew. Classic tale fans get the Argo voyage, its perils and loves, in rhymed English verse.
64303-the-radio-beasts:
Ralph Milne Farley wrote this tale, first put out as a serial in a weekly sheet in 1925. The first part bears the head From Another World. The man who tells it sits on the steps of his farm house on an isle off the coast of Massachusetts, one warm eve in July. His day's work is done. He skims the sheet of that dawn from Boston, and one small item catches his eye by chance.

The item tells of a mad man at Lynn. The man, clad in a night gown alone, broke in by night into the labs of the General Electric works. He scared the man on watch in the room of the great set that takes in waves from the air. The watch man took him for a ghost.
64764-flame-jewel-of-the-ancients:
Edwin Graber wrote a tale of space empire called Flame Jewel of the Ancients, first run in Planet Stories in the spring of 1950. Two Terran super ships glide side by side in deep space, so sure of their might that they keep their shields down. No war craft in the known galaxy, they hold, can match them.

A third pilot named Jukes, lounging at his screen, spots a strange sparkling mote move across the stars. He slaps the call to quarters and speaks fast into his throat set as the ship swings to meet its sister. The head note names the prize: a tiny gold sphere of vast power, held by an out space horde, and a captain of the Stellar Guardians who drops in to view it.
65018-a-fool-in-spots:
A Fool in Spots is a novel by Hallie Erminie Rives, entered for copyright in 1894. She dedicated it to her mother and father. The picture at the front shows a man crying out at a woman's beauty, keyed to page 77 of the story.

The chapters open with two artists, then pass through dreams and schemes and an honest man's honest love. A Kentucky stock farm, a birth mark, and hearts laid bare follow. Later chapter titles promise sunlight, a wedding, chloral, a bold intruder, and an errand of mystery. Talk in the book weighs marriage in hard, practical terms for two poor young artists.
65112-rachel-a-play-in-three-acts:
Angelina Grimke wrote Rachel, a play in three acts, for the Cornhill Company at Boston under copyright of 1920. The cast centers on the Loving family in a northern city. Widow Mary Loving keeps a small flat with her daughter Rachel and her son Thomas. John Strong, a family friend, and callers Lane and her daughter Ethel complete the list.

Act one falls on October 16, act two on the same date four years later, and act three a week after that. The living room stays the sole set, neat and plain, with piano, sewing machine, and potted plants. Grimke notes that all the characters are colored, a rare stage direction for its day. Grief and resolve grow inside one home.
65141-the-vicious-delinquents:
The Vicious Delinquents is a science fiction story by Mark Reinsberg, taken from Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy for October 1958. A blurb says they were kids with personality problems who joined tough gangs and lived only to fight and kill. Society had to find a way to correct them.

The narrator flies back to the hideout with a sloppy hand, losing Jupiter shadow again and again. A showdown with Naomi over who leads the Callisto gang means a degravity fight with python whips and steel claws. Yet the girls might read peace as cowardice. He also stole money from his parents the day before, two thousand solars, on a false tale of a Mars technical school. It bought a sweet used 2064 model Spacer coupe. Space tale fans get girl gang wars on a moon of Jupiter.
65153-within-the-precincts:
Within the Precincts, by Mrs Oliphant, is here in the Tauchnitz edition, volume 1823 of its collection of British authors, printed at Leipzig in 1879. Oliphant other works fill the front list. The Chronicles of Carlingford are named first, in their volumes.

Contents of volume one open with St Michael. The Chevaliers Lodges and the Abbey Precincts follow. Lady Caroline, at the Deanery, and a chapter headed Law come next. A new light, triumph and terror, and visitors fill the middle. The minor canon, another evening at the Deanery, and brother and sister follow. Captain Despard enters late in the head. The setting is a cathedral close: its church, lodges, deanery, and resident families. Readers get an Oliphant novel of cathedral society, in the portable Tauchnitz form made for travellers. Her Carlingford readers would know the clerical world at once.
65188-a-book-of-medical-discourses-in-tw:
A Book of Medical Discourses is a health manual by Rebecca Crumpler, a physician, printed at Boston in 1883. The book stands in two parts. The first treats the cause, prevention, and cure of infantile bowel complaints, from birth to the close of teething, or till after the fifth year. It is dedicated to mothers and nurses.

The second part gives information on the life and growth of beings and the beginning of womanhood. It takes up the cause, prevention, and cure of many distressing complaints of women, and of youth of both sexes. The chapters open with How to Marry, then the present modes of washing and dressing the new-born. Crumpler's discourses are plain, kindly, and meant for the home rather than the surgery.
65519-the-escape-or-a-leap-for-freedom-a:
William Wells Brown wrote a drama in five acts on slavery and flight. R F Wallcut issued The Escape at Boston in 1858. Brown had written Clotel and sketches of places and people abroad. A front note says he wrote the play for his own amusement first.

Friends heard it read in private and pressed him to print, Brown writes. The main features of the drama are true, he states plainly. Readings in many parts of the country spread its fame before print. Stage readers gain a landmark play by a man who had himself fled slavery.
65569-histology-of-medicinal-plants:
William Mansfield, professor of histology and pharmacognosy at the College of Pharmacy of the City of New York, published a textbook on the histology of medicinal plants in 1916. The total issue was four thousand copies. Part one teaches the tools: simple and compound microscopes, measurements, and the care of the instrument.

Mounting specimens, cutting sections, and reagents take their own chapters. Part two turns to the plant itself: the cell and its division, the skin and bark layers, and the strong tissues of bast and wood fibres. Root hairs and other absorbing parts follow. Pharmacy students learning to name a powdered drug by its cells were the book's class.
65665-my-household-of-pets:
My Household of Pets is a memoir of animal life by Théophile Gautier. Susan Coolidge turned the French text into English. The Boston edition came out in 1882, with pictures.

Gautier looks back first to old times, when cats climbed over his shoulders at home. He then tells of his white cats and his black cats in turn. Dogs get a full chapter of their own. Lizards, magpies and horses close the roll. The book is fond and witty, and it shows how pets can rule a house. Each beast has its own traits, habits and small dramas. Gautier writes as a poet who knew each animal by heart.
65709-the-house-of-the-secret-la-maison-:
Claude Farrère wrote The House of the Secret, in an authorized translation by Arthur Livingston. E P Dutton and Company in New York issued the book in nineteen twenty three, in an edition limited to fifteen hundred copies. Chapter one opens as a testament. This day, January twentieth, nineteen oh nine, I have decided to set my story down in writing, the teller begins.

Dangerous and terrifying the task, but I must perform it, he says. For day after tomorrow I shall be dead, and death from old age, of this I am as certain as a man can be, he adds. What then have I to lose by speaking, he asks. He bequeaths a secret, the Secret, to unsuspecting survivors in danger. He is old beyond human experience of age, he muses. A tale of a house of undying men follows.
65893-atoms-at-the-science-fair-exhibiti:
Robert LeCompte and Burrell Wood wrote this booklet for the Division of Technical Information of the United States Atomic Energy Commission. Its title is Atoms at the Science Fair, and its subject is exhibiting nuclear projects. A foreword notes that more students each year build science fair projects on some side of nuclear science or technology.

Contents move from choosing a topic to showing the finished work. Chapters treat where to get help, how to document the work, how exhibits are judged, and how to design the display, down to advice on colour. A chapter on competition describes the rewards at the National Science Fair, including ten special awards for the best nuclear exhibits. Appendices list project ideas and references.
65915-gladstonian-ghosts:
Gladstonian Ghosts, by Cecil Chesterton, is an essay in political criticism printed in London. The book is given to Edgar Jepson, whose judgment Chesterton praises. Chapter heads name liberalism and the spirit of the age. Free trade is called a fetish in one head. Other heads treat militarism, retrenchment, and social reconstruction.

In his opening letter Chesterton says social and economic questions matter most. He scorns talk of Home Rule and the Lords while slums stand. Three centuries of trade without order, he says, left want and disease. Party men, in his view, chase a parlour game at Westminster. The book presses Liberals to face the state of the poor or lose the future.
65926-madeleine-one-of-love-s-jansenists:
Madeleine: One of Love's Jansenists is a novel by Hope Mirrlees, published in London by Collins in 1919. Two impressions came out in its first month. The tale is set in the Paris of the sixteen hundreds, among salon folk and church parties. Its chapters bear grand, odd names: The Symmetry of the Comic Muse, The Christian Venus, The Body of the Dragon. One chapter spends an evening at Mademoiselle de Scudéry's Saturday, the famed salon of the age.

The title's church word names the strict Jansenist strain in French faith. Mirrlees sets love and faith at odds in that world of wit and rule. Berthe's story is told inside the frame. A dinner at Madame Pilou's opens the book. An epilogue bears the strange name The Rape to the Love of Invisible Things. The novel is a rich, learned piece of its post-war moment.
65947-the-color-of-his-boots:
W C Tuttle wrote this western story, narrated by Ike Harper about his partner Magpie Simpkins. Magpie, he says, is too finicky, and a finicky man ought not to pack a gun just after acquiring fine new haberdashery.

Magpie paid twenty dollars for yellow boots, glowing like a sunset in Indian summer. Coming home from the Totem stampede, where the pair learned that honesty is a poor poker policy, a Pullman porter blackened them with polish. Magpie folds the ruined boots in a rainbow Indian blanket and rings for the porter. His third shot breaks the glass by the man's head, and the conductor tackles him in the aisle. Tuttle tells it in dry cowboy vernacular. Readers get a tall tale of vanity.
66038-wee-wee-songs-for-our-little-pets:
Leila Lee wrote wee songs in verse for the most small children. Her book came out in New York in 1859. Its rights were filed in 1858 by Henry Degen. A front note deals with Mother Goose and her old rhymes. Sue, a child in the first song, calls those rhymes bad and vain.

Willie's mother wishes those who love Christ read his words more. Feed my lambs is the charge that drives Lee's book. Her songs seek to swap vain rhymes for sweet, true words. Each piece is short, with a tune's lilt in its lines. Church homes of that age used such books at the knee. Soft faith in small words is the aim.
66094-dreams-and-images-an-anthology-of-:
Joyce Kilmer, the poet of Trees, gathered this anthology of Catholic poets in 1917. Boni and Liveright printed Dreams and Images in the United States, and Musson sold it at Toronto. Kilmer gives the book to Father Daly, a Jesuit of his circle.

Hilaire Belloc leads the roll with Our Lord and Lady. The South Country and Noel stand among his eight pieces. Robert Hugh Benson gives two quiet poems of retreat. Padraic Colum writes of Christ the Comrade and an old woman of the roads. Ethna Carbery sings of Tir-na'n-Og, the land of youth. Irish, English, and American voices share the pages: faith as song, in the last year of Kilmer's life.
66101-ploughshare-and-pruning-hook-ten-l:
Laurence Housman gave ten lectures on social subjects, first printed in September 1919. Titles include Great Possessions, Crime and Punishment, and Christianity a Danger to the State. Others treat the rights of majorities, what is womanly, and art and citizenship.

The first lecture, from 1913, opens with Thomas Traherne's saying that you never know yourself till you know more than your own body. Housman adds that you shall never know delight till you delight in more than your own body. Man, on Traherne's view, was sent into the world to enjoy himself and take great possessions. Housman builds his social thought on that paradox of holy greed.
66260-londinium-architecture-and-the-cra:
Londinium: Architecture and the Crafts is a study of Roman London by W R Lethaby, first published by Duckworth and Company of London in 1923. Chapters of it had appeared in The Builder during 1921. The book carries 175 figures and treats London as a Roman city built by working craftsmen.

Opening chapters deal with materials and methods, then with buildings, streets, walls, gates, and the bridge. Later chapters cover cemeteries and tombs, monuments, sculpture, and mosaics. Wall paintings, lettering, and the crafts get their own studies. The book closes with early Christian London and the origin of the city itself. Lethaby writes as an architect, so the evidence is read through making: how things were built, decorated, and used. The volume suits readers of Roman Britain and of design history alike.
66294-the-seven-lively-arts:
The Seven Lively Arts, by Gilbert Seldes, was printed by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1924. A line from Walter Pater fronts it, in praise of artists whose charm needs a fond voice to make its case. Seldes is that voice for the arts the grave world scorned. His first piece hails the Keystone screen clowns, with a front plate by Ralph Barton. Then Charlie Chaplin gets a full, warm study.

Jazz and ragtime take the next run: Berlin, Gershwin, and the Darktown Strutters on Broadway. Florenz Ziegfeld earns a tribute, and George M Cohan and Eddie Cantor walk the plates. Krazy Kat leads the comic strip's praise, and vaudeville, dance, and burlesque close the set. Arts fans get the first proud brief for the shows of the street.
66571-moonlight-and-robots:
Jerry Dunham wrote Moonlight and Robots, a tale from Imagination in May 1955. A front note says Thad hated the silly custom demanding a robot romance. If a man was not careful such a thing could linger on after the wedding, it warns. Thad Morgan looks round his little room at the start.

Two deactivated robots and a frame that holds a limp suit crowd the room. Thad feels mild disgust at the whole convention of engagements. Myrna, his bride to be, was filled with excitement at the final plans, he notes. A book of rules tells him to inspect the facsimile and see it is well groomed. He must get into the harness suit, activate his twin, and set the controls. Each move he makes will be duplicated by the robot. Each thing the robot feels will be transmitted to him as his own experience.
6680-the-bores-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Molière's The Bores, first played in August 1661, is a character comedy where the pests are not one or two leads, but a parade of figures. Each bore enters, performs a brief role, and leaves, strung on a weak thread of talk by an unwilling listener. The note that opens the text calls the method less artful, yet natural, a set of tableaux more than a plot.

Monologues, not situations, carry the fun, as each new bore shows a fresh folly. Molière's verse keeps the parade brisk. The Bores is a lively, if loose, early comedy, best enjoyed as a gallery of human pests, one after another.
67000-fabre-s-book-of-insects:
Fabre's Book of Insects retells the insect studies of Jean-Henri Fabre for younger or general readers. It is drawn from Teixeira de Mattos's translation of Fabre's Souvenirs Entomologiques, and retold by Mrs Rodolph Stawell. Dodd, Mead issued it in New York in 1921, with illustrations by Detmold. The first chapter introduces Fabre's work and his workshop.

The chapters then take up one creature at a time. The sacred beetle comes first, then the cicada and the praying mantis. The glow-worm, a mason-wasp, and the psyches follow. Later chapters treat the self-denial of the Spanish copris, two strange grasshoppers, and common wasps. The cricket, the sisyphus beetle, the capricorn, locusts, and the anthrax fly round out the cast. Each chapter keeps Fabre's close watching of insect habits, in plainer form for new readers.
67003-wanderings-in-three-continents:
Wilkins edited Wanderings in Three Continents from the papers of Captain Sir Richard Burton for Hutchinson in 1901. A photogravure portrait fronts the volume, with drawings by McCormick inside. Contents gather Burton's boldest journeys in one handy book. El Medinah and Meccah open the set, drawn from his pilgrimage of 1853.

A ride to Harar, a push to the lake regions of Africa, and the city of the Mormons follow. A mission to Dahomey, a trip up the Congo, Brazil, and Syria to Palmyra close the tour. Burton explains how years in Scinde among Muslims taught him to pass unseen. Languages, disguise, and sheer nerve carry every chapter of his wanderings. Three continents bend to one restless observer.
6706-the-emancipation-of-massachusetts:
Brooks Adams traces Massachusetts from a theocratic commonwealth toward emancipation, in dream and in reality. His prefatory note thanks Mellen Chamberlain, Charles Deane, and Frank Cushing, whose unpublished Zuñi research aided the work, along with William James and others. Faults, Adams says, are his own; any merit belongs to his helpers.

Chapters on the commonwealth, the Antinomians, and the Cambridge Platform lead into a long struggle for religious and political freedom. Adams writes as a bold, opinionated historian, keen on the clash of ideas. The Emancipation of Massachusetts is a sharp, classic study of New England's break with old rule.
67061-lives-of-two-cats:
Pierre Loti wrote Lives of Two Cats, here in Richards's English translation, published at Boston in 1900 with pictures by Allen. Loti opens by saying he has often met the soul of an animal in its eyes, seeking his own with tenderness or terror, and felt deep pity for such speechless souls. His two subjects are cats he kept and loved.

Both cats answer to Pussy, by their real household names. Pussy White is an Angora whose visiting card styles her Madame Moumoutte Blanche, first cat at Loti's house. Pussy Gray is often called Pussy Chinese. Pussy White arrived one winter evening on his return from an eastern campaign, bounding like a panther onto the hearth rug. The pictures trace their days, down to life in company with an everlasting tortoise. Readers get a tender, close study of two pets, told by a writer who took animal feeling in earnest.
67134-dairy-disagreeables-busy-the-bacte:
Four station men reported on dairy troubles that keep bacteriologists busy. F H Hall, H A Harding, L A Rogers, and G A Smith wrote the bulletin. The New York Agricultural Experiment Station issued it at Geneva in December 1900. It stands as Bulletin Number 183 in a popular form.

Governor Theodore Roosevelt heads the board of control list at the front. Whitman H Jordan directed the station staff named in the pages. Off flavors and faults in milk and butter drive the science here. Dairymen gain state-backed findings on the unseen foes of clean dairy work.
67174-samantha-on-children-s-rights:
Samantha on Children's Rights is a droll book with a grave heart. Marietta Holley wrote it as the wife of Josiah Allen in her books. It came out in New York in the year 1909 with plates. Samantha was a famed voice of plain sense in her day's print.

The front plate shows a boy shut in his room on bread and water. The caps of the plates tell of whips laid on in the name of faith. Samantha speaks for the young in the face of their dames and sires. She tells her tales in the broad speech of her own home town. A mare run wild and a boy at his prayers stand in the plate list. The wit is the wrap; the rights of the child are the goods inside.
67258-a-selection-of-cases-on-the-law-of:
James Barr Ames and Jeremiah Smith compiled a selection of cases on the law of torts, copyrighted in 1893, here in Roscoe Pound's new edition from Harvard University Press in 1919. Pound was Carter professor of jurisprudence at Harvard. The edition first appeared in four parts across 1916 and 1917, totaling over a thousand pages. A 1917 note by Pound prefaces the reprint.

The earlier printing was not stereotyped and soon exhausted, Pound explains. A few recent decisions are added in the reprint. Casebooks like this one taught law through appellate opinions, the Langdell method. Ames had been dean of Harvard Law School. The volume trained generations of American lawyers in tort doctrine.
67435-the-honey-bee-its-nature-homes-and:
Harris wrote this handbook of the honey-bee for the Religious Tract Society at London, from Paternoster Row and Piccadilly. A comb showing the different kinds of cells fronts the title. The introduction promises the bee whole: its nature, its homes, and its products. A historic sketch opens the work, from the Scriptures and the Vedas through Aristotle, Pliny, and Vergil to Shakespeare and the moderns.

Natural history follows: egg, larva, pupa, and the perfect insect, then the three classes of the hive. The queen gets her chapter, with the attentions paid her and the effects of her loss. Drones and workers follow, with Lubbock's experiments on their senses. Honey, mead, wax, pollen, and propolis are treated as products in turn, down to Queen Elizabeth's recipe for mead. The tract society published sound knowledge as improvement, and the hive, orderly and industrious, was its favorite sermon in fur and wings.
67493-tales-of-the-air-mail-pilots:
Burt McConnell told tales of the men who flew the mail in all weathers. No land matched the States in air mail grit, he holds. Great trials came to Uncle Sam's air post men since the truce. He flew as a guest from New York to Chicago with two such men. Slim Lewis and Wesley Smith held the sticks on that long hop.

Eight drab hours passed, then dark hid the field from view. They set down on the prairie west of town that night. Such a hitch is naught, he says, next to the true tales. Day on day in storm and fog is where the thrills lie. He then rode the whole route to San Francisco for more. Air past fans get their lore.
67612-love-in-excess-or-the-fatal-enquir:
Mrs Haywood wrote Love in Excess, or The Fatal Enquiry, a novel in three parts. D Browne printed the fourth edition, corrected, at London in 1722, at the Black Swan without Temple Bar. A verse motto heads the title: in vain from fate we fly, for first or last we all must love. E Kirkall cut the front plate. Verses to Mrs Haywood stand before the tale, signed by Richard Savage.

Savage praises her prose as sweeter in harmony than numbers through the muse's lines. When her Count pleads, he asks, what fair can fly his suit. An unknown hand adds a second poem, from a stranger muse who had not believed women's souls knew such strength. The fourth edition within a few years of the first shows the novel's hold on the town.
67806-mary-magdalene-a-play-in-three-act:
Mary Magdalene is a play in three acts by Maurice Maeterlinck, translated by Teixeira de Mattos and published by Dodd, Mead in 1910. An author's note explains the play's delicate origin. Maeterlinck borrowed from Paul Heyse's drama Maria von Magdala the idea of two situations. At the end of the first act, Christ intervenes to stop the crowd raging against Mary Magdalene. His words come from behind the scenes: he that is without sin, let him cast the first stone.

The second borrowed situation comes in the third act. The great sinner faces a dilemma: she can save or destroy the Son of God, according as she consents or refuses to give herself to a Roman. Maeterlinck had asked Heyse's permission beforehand and offered to recognize his rights as he wished. The answer was a refusal, none too courteous and almost threatening.
67988-the-vortex-a-play-in-three-acts:
Noel Coward's The Vortex, a play in three acts, was copyrighted in 1924 and published by Harper and Brothers in New York and London. The cast names Florence Lancaster, her son Nicky, David Lancaster, Helen Saville, Pauncefort Quentin, Tom Veryan, and Bunty Mainwaring.

Act one opens in the drawing room of Florence's London flat, its furniture simple but distinctly expensive. Helen and Pawnie, as Quentin is called, are shown in by the servant Preston and settle to talk of the room itself. Pawnie calls the coloring oppressive and typical of Florence in every way, while Helen defends her friend against his catty praise.
68088-glad-ghosts:
Lawrence wrote Glad Ghosts, a tale put out by Ernest Benn at London. The tale opens with the narrator's memory of Carlotta Fell, from days before the war. They met at the Thwaite art school. Carlotta took the still-life prizes there each time, calm as a victor. The rest of the students felt sore, and called it favor, since she was of a titled house.

Her father was a well-known peer, and she came into five hundred a year of her own at eighteen. That sum seemed vast to poor art students of the day. She posed in the smart papers with pearls, wistful and slant-eyed. Yet her yearning for something else, the narrator says, was quite real. Lawrence sets up a proud, rich girl whose ghostly tale gives the book its name.
68194-love-and-tea-a-comedy-drama-of-col:
Anna Phillips See, author of When Women Vote, wrote Love and Tea, a comedy-drama of colonial times in two acts. Walter Baker and Company of Boston issued the play. She wrote it at the instance of the D A R. The professional and picture rights are strictly reserved. Amateurs may stage the play without payment of royalty, so long as the author's name stands on all programs and notices.

The play stands in Baker's acting list, sold by mail from Boston. Its title joins love to tea, the taxed leaf that stood at the heart of the colonial quarrel with Britain. Two acts keep the piece within the reach of school and societies. Such patriotic plays were a staple of amateur stages in America, and the terms for amateurs show whom See hoped would act it.
68210-portuguese-portraits:
Portuguese Portraits, by Aubrey Bell, was printed at Oxford in 1917. Bell had written on Spain and Portugal before, and turned here to the great men of Portugal's past. The book is given to the countless lost heroes whose bones, he says, built their land.

The opening pages range over the kings of the House of Avis, from João the First to João the Third. Prince Henry the Navigator and his brothers stand out, as do Gama and Albuquerque in India. Cabral, who found Brazil, and Magalhães, slain at the height of his voyage, are named too. Bell notes that Portugal then held perhaps a million and a half souls, yet its men fought Moors and Turks across three seas.
68237-unravelled-knots:
Unravelled Knots is Baroness Orczy's set of thirteen detective tales, told by the Old Man in the Corner. Doran published the set at New York, with copyrights running from 1923 to 1926. The narrator stumbles on the old man again in a blameless teashop, after twenty years away. He sits unchanged by the fire, fidgeting with a piece of string tied into endless knots.

He points at a newspaper headline and begins. The cases run from the mystery of the khaki tunic to an Ingres masterpiece, a pearl necklace and a Russian prince. A tragedy in Bishop's Road, the miser of Maida Vale and a moorland tragedy follow. Each knot is untied by talk alone, in the corner, over tea.
68239-personality-of-plants:
Personality of Plants is a popular nature book by Royal Dixon and Franklyn E. Fitch, printed at New York in 1923. A fuchsia fronts it, praised for its distinct and aesthetic manner. The authors dedicate the book to Edwin Markham and his wife, who live their poetry.

The chapters give plants a full inner life. They trace the origin of plants, the life of a plant, and plant migrations. They treat plant comrades and allies, marriage customs, and art, music, science, and religion in the plant world. Plant mythology, mysticism, and intelligence follow, ending with plants and men. The introduction opens on the young earth, when its crust had scarcely hardened and an age of water reigned. The book courts wonder: every plant, it holds, has a character of its own.
68379-under-blanco-s-eye-or-hal-maynard-:
Under Blancos Eye, or Hal Maynard Among the Cuban Insurgents, is a war tale in a cheap weekly of the flag, first of its run. It came out at New York in the spring of the war with Spain, at five cents. Thrill tales of our win host, its head crows.

Its rights were set in law that year by its house. Its first part opens with a cry of stop. A boy of some eighteen or nine years stands at its heart. He is, as its first part name tells, the sole man of his land in the cap of the isle. The tale sends him through the war of the isle folk for their free days, under the eye of the stern chief of Spain.
68416-birds-and-their-nests:
Birds and Their Nests is a natural history book by Mary Howitt. Routledge published it at New York, with Partridge at London. Harrison Weir supplied twenty three full page illustrations. A robin and its nest make the frontispiece. Twenty two chapters follow an introductory chapter. Each chapter takes one bird and its nest in turn. The wren opens the procession, then the goldfinch.
