Song thrush, blackbird, dipper, and nightingale follow in order. Skylark, linnet, and peewit carry the middle of the book. House martins and chiff chaffs are called nest builders in their titles. Golden crested wrens, wagtails, and jackdaws come next. The introductory chapter marvels at nests found in every bush. All serve one purpose, Howitt writes, yet no two families build alike. Her book teaches young readers to know birds by their building.
68457-right-and-wrong-in-massachusetts:
Right and Wrong in Massachusetts is an abolitionist tract by Maria Weston Chapman. Dow and Jackson's Anti-Slavery Press in Boston issued it in 1839. A motto from Shakespeare on reading the nature of times fronts it. Chapter one, Retrospection, opens before the characters take the stage. Thierry's rule for drama guides her plan, she tells the reader.

She has made readers acquainted with the ground of the scenes first. The position of New England in 1829 was cheerless for freedom, she says. All the great interests of the country touched slaveholding near or far. Through all their ramifications, wealth and church stood bound to slavery. Chapman indicts her own state in the Garrisonian cause of abolition.
68506-the-forest-pilot-a-story-for-boy-s:
The Forest Pilot, by Edward Huntington, was published in 1915. Hearst's International Library issued it at New York. The subtitle calls it a story for boy scouts. Twelve chapters make the tale. A front plate shows a boy crying out to shoot. Chapter one is The Storm. A November sun, red and threatening, sinks behind cloud. Wind veers from south to northeast in a furious blast. Indian summer turns to winter gale in a moment. A little schooner yacht dances like a cork in the bay. Her captain, a weatherbeaten Yankee of forty years at sea, scans the shore with his glass.

Beside the forward mast sit a tall old man and a boy. Contents promise the home on the rocks and lessons in piloting. A blizzard, timber wolves, and a wounded moose wait in the woods.
6861-vautrin-a-drama-in-five-acts:
Honoré de Balzac's Vautrin was first played at the Porte-Saint-Martin in Paris in March 1840. It opens with an author's preface. Balzac writes on the difficulty of writing about his own play five days after its first night. Every spectator, Balzac says, has written his own preface, and his single voice will seem inferior to so many divergent ones. A cannon's report, he jokes, is never so effective as fireworks.

Must he explain his work, complain of the ban that delayed it, or name its only true commentator, the actor Lemaitre? Balzac leaves the play to speak. Vautrin is a bold, historic drama of a master criminal, written by a novelist at his peak.
68674-blood-on-my-jets:
Algis Budrys wrote a space story for Rocket Stories of July 1953, illustrated by Ebel. Its headnote calls its men the hired gun-rabble of the System, in the dirtiest, most thankless racket in all the worlds. Ash Holcomb was doing all right, it promises, until a girl walked out of his past with murder in her eyes.

Rocket Row, the joy street of three planets, runs by Flushing Spaceport, all neon, dives, and cheap hotels. In the New Shanghai bar, Ash drinks a Stinger and talks Venus fog with Ming the bartender, one of the few who admit knowing he is a detached operative. Too much blood has soaked into hot mud by his guns. Hardboiled pulp, translated to the spaceways, is the manner.
68767-rosaleen-among-the-artists:
Rosaleen Among the Artists is a novel by Elisabeth Sanxay Holding, printed in New York by George H Doran. Holding had also written Invincible Minnie. The book falls into four parts, from The Betrayal to The Honourable Lovers.

Rosaleen comes home in tears, climbs four flights of dark stairs, and falls on her cot in a bare, cold room. She clutches a card a man gave her, as if it could rebuild a lost enchanted hour. A quote at the front notes her view that scorned soft feeling often drives noble acts. Later parts take her among artists and leave her forlorn before the close. Readers meet a young woman ground by hope, love, and the art world of her day.
68918-assignats:
Assignats is a sea adventure novel by Henry Leverage, author of The Iron Dollar. It opens on a beach at Novgorod, on the Japan Sea, with castaways. Ivan, a bearded Russian with a long surname, finds three men in rags there. They are Micky McMasters, a skipper from Great Grimsby, and his two mates.

The three have no papers, a price on their heads, and a leaking past behind them. Ivan offers them the Shongpong, loading tea between there and Vladivostok for America. Her flag is Chinese, her crew loyal Russians, her cargo caravan tea. The run is east across the Pacific to Victoria, on Vancouver Island. McMasters, thirty years at sea, takes the bargain on the spot. One question hangs over it: is Ivan loyal Russian or Bolshevik.
69010-lafitte-a-play-in-prologue-and-fou:
Lucile Rutland and Rhoda Cameron write Lafitte, a play in a first part and four acts, with copyright in 1899. The cast is large and mixed. Jean Durand, afterwards Jean Lafitte, heads the list of parts.

Round him stand the D'Acosta clan, a marquis of the court of Ferdinand the Seventh and his son and niece. Beluche serves in the army of Napoleon, and Leon Duval is a rich Louisianian. Dominique You, Governor Claiborne, and Captain Lockyer of the British navy all appear. The first part is set at Bayonne in France. Act one moves to a hotel in New Orleans, then to a ship bound for France.
69063-to-the-lights:
To the Lights, by Roy Norton, is billed as a story of gallant men and angry seas. Norton also wrote The Unknown Kent and Captains Three. The tale opens with a sharp letter in a newspaper from the head of a large Billingsgate fish firm, who disputes a writer on fish prices.

The dealer claims that fishermen do get a fair share of the price paid for fish, and that tales of trawlermen's hardship are much overdone. He says the men are well fed, share in auction prices, and can run to shelter in storms. Norton sets that smooth claim against the real risks of trawler life at sea, letting the men's work test the words of the men of business.
69413-pamela-pounce-a-tale-of-tempestuou:
Agnes and Egerton Castle wrote Pamela Pounce, a tale of high life and a milliner’s girl. Hodder and Stoughton issued the book in London, Toronto, and New York. Pamela trims hats for fine ladies as the tale starts. Her aunt Lydia serves as own woman to Lady Kilcroney.

No man is hero to his valet, the prologue starts. Yet each woman is a heroine to her lady’s maid, it claims. Lydia, tart and cross by wont, still beams at her lady. Pamela’s Italian hat brings her into royal service in chapter one. Soon the hat girl weighs life and death in high rooms. A bandbox spills luck for a friend in mid tale. Pink flounces spark a vast scandal near the close.
69453-welcome-to-the-ransomed-or-duties-:
Daniel Payne, a bishop, preached a sermon at a church in Georgetown on April 13, 1862, and it was printed at Baltimore that year. The day had been set apart by Black churches in Georgetown and Washington for thanks and prayer. The cause was freedom for enslaved folk in the District of Columbia, granted that spring.

Leaders of the church wrote to Payne on April 14 to ask leave to print the sermon for all Black folk of the District. Payne sent the text on April 18, with a few thoughts grown fuller and three or four notes added. His text from Saint Paul charges the freed folk with duties in their new state.
69690-look-out-for-paint-a-farce-comedy-:
Cornelius Shea wrote a farce comedy in three acts, published at Boston in 1912 as an acting play. It was first produced at Tottenville, New York, on June 9, 1911. The cast list names Hiram Rodney, owner of High Up Farm, and his wife Susan and daughter Helen.

Percy Heartache, an artist, loves Helen. Hickory Homespun is a bashful farmer, well to do, and Trotwell Roamer is a tramp who is a painter by trade. A stenographer from the city, past thirty and anxious to wed, and a widow in love complete the set. The title warns where the paint is wet, and amateur companies were the play's market.
69756-the-child-s-curiosity-book-embelli:
Sold in London for one penny, a small book for young readers pairs short pieces with woodcut pictures called cuts. A verse on the first page promises good fare for children who are keen to be good and wise and who take care of their book. The pieces mix nature notes, home scenes, and short moral tales.

Contents open with a robin red-breast that comes into houses to pick up crumbs, then a scene in a nursery. Sally Sulkey shows what comes of a child who cries for all she wants and gets it. Later pieces cover a feast for good children, careless children, fireworks and crackers, and the sports of Harlequin.
69786-dreams-and-delights:
Adams Beck wrote Dreams and Delights, a book of tales from Dodd, Mead at New York in 1926. Beck had won note with The Key of Dreams and The Ninth Vibration, among other novels. The contents list ten tales with an Eastern cast. The Sea of Lilies, The Bride of a God, and The Beloved of the Gods lead the set. The Hidden One and The Marriage of the Princess come next.

Later tales treat the wisdom of the Orient, an island of pearls, and a pilgrimage to Amarnath. The Man Without a Sword closes the book. The first tale turns on a woman writer, proud of her new story, The Ninefold Flower. She had spent days on the pen name that must hide who she was.
69806-the-circe-of-the-deserts:
Paule Henry Bordeaux follows an exile in The Circe of the Deserts, printed in London. Hurst and Blackett made the book, with a frontispiece of Lady Hester Stanhope. The life is told as a voyage east, in ten chapters.

Farewell to England leads, then Mediterranean yachting and an oriental initiation. An excursion in the Holy Land and travel in the country of Djezzar Pacha and the Emir Bechir follow. Lady Hester and Lascaris, and the queen of Palmyra, name the mid arc. From the temple of Baalbeck to the ruins of Ascalon, and in the mountains of the Assassins, close the tour. Chapter one opens on February 10, 1810. The frigate Jason left Portsmouth, bound for Gibraltar. In the stern, a group of four watched the misty coast recede: three men, and a woman of gigantic stature.
69818-an-essay-towards-a-natural-history:
Charles Owen's Essay Towards a Natural History of Serpents, printed at London in 1742 and sold by John Gray near Cheapside, is in two parts, with a third added. The first treats serpents in general: their kinds, bulk, food, motion, breeding, colors, and their poison, with its cure in various nations, and notes serpents used as food and physic. The second describes the serpents known in the several parts of the world, with copper plates.

The third part turns to Scripture and worship. It takes up the primeval serpent in Paradise, the fiery serpents in the camp of Israel, and the brazen serpent of Moses. It ends with the divine worship paid to serpents and beasts by the nations. Owen dedicates the book to Sir Hans Sloane, whose collection of rarities held serpents of its own. Divinity and natural history sit side by side throughout.
69888-the-instinct-of-workmanship-and-th:
Thorstein Veblen's The Instinct of Workmanship and the State of the Industrial Arts, published by Macmillan at New York in 1914, follows his Theory of the Leisure Class. The argument starts from instinct: the life of the species, Veblen says, is conditioned by its inborn proclivities, and nothing counts as worth doing except what answers to them.

The chapters trace the instinct through the ages of technology. First come the contamination of instincts in primitive technology and the savage state of the industrial arts. Then the predatory culture and its technology, ownership and the competitive system, the era of handicraft, and at last the machine industry. Veblen notes at the start that biologists were already dropping the word instinct as too loose for science, and uses it anyway, in his own sense. The book is economics written as natural history.
6992-belinda-an-april-folly-in-three-act:
A A Milne's Belinda, an April folly in three acts, was produced by Dion Boucicault at the New Theatre in London on April 8, 1918. The cast lists Irene Vanbrugh as Belinda Tremayne, Isabel Elsom as her daughter Delia, Boucicault as Harold Baxter, and Dennis Neilson Terry as Claude Devenish. John Tremayne and Betty complete the household, and the action sits in Belinda's country house in Devonshire at the end of April.

The first act plays in the garden, the second and last in the hall, on a lovely April afternoon that foretastes summer. Betty, a middle aged servant, fastens a hammock to a tree as the play opens, with a garden table and chairs set for talk. Milne writes a light comedy of love, pride, and spring folly in three brisk acts.
70039-first-harvests:
F J Stimson, writing as J S of Dale, wrote First Harvests, an episode in the life of Mrs Levison Gower. Charles Scribner's Sons published it at New York in 1888. He calls the book a satire without a moral. His note to the reader says he sought an overtone of hope and faith within the satire. The early writers of America could all be optimists, he writes, for they wrote of virgin soil. The country's first-fruits are garnered now.

The contents open with the Silas Starbuck Oil Company. Flossie Starbuck aspires, and Flossie Starbuck attains. Arthur Holyoke's dreams and Gracie Holyoke's heart follow. The judge sums up his case midway. Arthur sees the world, and more of the world, and gets on in it. The diversions of fine ladies fill the later chapters.
70098-handbook-of-old-burial-hill-plymou:
Handbook of Old Burial Hill, Plymouth, Massachusetts is a guide by Frank Perkins. Burbank published it at the Pilgrim Bookstore in Plymouth in 1902. Its subtitle promises the hill's history, its famous dead, and its quaint epitaphs. An index of names runs to many pages of the small book.

The index alone reads like a roll of the colony's first families. Governor William Bradford holds the longest run of page references. Governor Carver, Elder Brewster, and Robert Cushman stand in the same list. The site of the old fort earns an entry among the graves. Verses printed in the book picture the Pilgrim Fathers at rest on the hill. The first ray of morning and the last of evening fall on that spot, they say. A visitor with this handbook can walk from stone to stone with the stories attached.
70394-travels-in-the-upper-egyptian-dese:
Travels in the Upper Egyptian Deserts is a travel book by Arthur E P Weigall, inspector-general of Upper Egypt in the Department of Antiquities. Blackwood printed the second impression at Edinburgh and London in 1913. Some chapters first appeared as articles in Blackwood's Magazine.

The journeys recorded were made in the ordinary course of Weigall's work of inspection and were reported in the usual official manner. These less technical accounts were written in his leisure hours. The illustrations are chosen from a large set of photographs taken on the trips. Weigall was also the author of a life and times of Akhnaton and a treasury of ancient Egypt. The book takes the reader into the wadis and desert stations east of the Nile. It joins an official's duty with a traveller's eye for ruins and desert life.
70497-the-oxford-methodists:
The Rev L Tyerman gathers the lesser lights of a revival in The Oxford Methodists, from Harper and Brothers of New York in 1873. The book holds memoirs of the Rev Messrs Clayton, Ingham, Gambold, Hervey, and Broughton, with biographical notices of others. A group plate shows the five men.

Tyerman calls the book a companion to his Life and Times of John Wesley, built from material that work had no room for. The Wesleys and Whitefield are deliberately left out, since full memoirs of them already exist. He owns that word on some of the brotherhood is meagre, resting on scraps and a few letters, but offers it gladly.
70515-yuletide-entertainments:
Ellen M Willard gathered Yuletide Entertainments for T S Denison at Chicago in 1910, with a copyright that year. The subtitle promises Christmas recitations, monologues, drills, tableaux, motion songs, exercises, dialogues, and plays suitable for all ages. Willard also wrote The Favorite Book of Drills and Fun for Little Folks.

Part one holds the Bell Song, a Cranberry March, and drills for holly, mistletoe, and sleighbells. Fred's Christmas shopping and Old Aunt Dinah's Christmas add recitation pieces. Part two holds dialogues and plays: Santa Claus in Many Lands, Santa Claus' Garden, and The Spirit of Christmas. Songs go to old familiar airs. The aim is a school or church programme ready to stage.
70528-english-printers-ornaments:
English Printers' Ornaments is a study by Henry R Plomer, author of a short history of English printing. The edition was limited to five hundred copies. It was issued at London in nineteen twenty four. Thanks at the front name librarians, scholars, and presses who lent blocks and leave to copy their work.

Among those thanked are the Cambridge and Oxford presses and the Kelmscott Press trustees. Type founders and modern presses lent samples for the chapter on modern work. A passage quoted from G Redgrave treats books printed at Venice in fourteen seventy six and seventy seven. Such books are rich in initial letters, sometimes printed in red ink, it says. Their title borders are called gracefully designed.
70654-submerged-forests:
Submerged Forests is a short work of geology by Clement Reid. Cambridge University Press published it in 1913. It belongs to the Cambridge Manuals of Science and Literature. A buried forest at low water on the Cheshire coast forms the frontispiece.

The chapters tour the drowned woodlands of Britain coast by coast. The Thames valley opens the survey, and the east coast follows. The Dogger Bank, that great shoal in the North Sea, earns a chapter. The Irish Sea and the Bristol Channel are treated together next. The English Channel and the Cornish coast complete the circuit of beaches. Fishermen at seaside resorts tell of black peaty earth between the tides. Hazel-nuts and tree-stumps, still rooted in the soil, appear in that layer. Reid reads those remains as forests that grew on dry land.
70670-overtones-a-book-of-temperaments:
Overtones, a Book of Temperaments, by James Huneker, was published in New York in 1904. Scribner issued the volume, with a portrait of Richard Strauss. The title page names its subjects in a row: Strauss, Parsifal, Verdi, Balzac, Flaubert, Nietzsche, and Turgenieff. A line from Whitman stands as motto: Do I contradict myself? Huneker gives the sheaf of studies to Strauss. He calls the composer a supreme master of the orchestra and an anarch of art.

Nine chapters make the book. Strauss leads, and Parsifal follows as a mystic melodrama. Nietzsche appears as a rhapsodist. One chapter treats literary men who loved music, Turgenieff and Balzac among them. Flaubert is named the Beethoven of French prose. Verdi and Boito, the eternal feminine, and the question after Wagner close the set.
70701-fine-prints:
Frederick Wedmore, a fellow of the Royal Society of Painter-Etchers, wrote this guide to print collecting. John Grant printed Fine Prints at Edinburgh in 1905, in a new and larger edition with fifteen plates. The book stands in a Collector Series beside works on coins, stamps, and porcelain.

Wedmore says in his note that the book has played some part in spreading the taste for prints in England. His changes for 1905 are chiefly in words, not in plan. He kept the unity of the first draft, faults and all. A few gains, forced on him by the years more than by choice, join the text. Collectors new and old get a sound, fond guide to the print room.
70748-the-speaker-s-ideal-entertainments:
The Speaker Ideal Entertainments gathers pieces for home, church, and school performance. George Vickers wrote and edited it; Bell issued it at Philadelphia and Chicago. Rights date to 1892, with gesture notes by Frances Peirce of Philadelphia. Peirce headed the Mount Vernon Institute of Elocution and Languages there then.

Recitals, dialogues, and dramas fill the book, picked for elocutionary merit in full. Many pieces appear in print for the first time from manuscript here. Gesture annotations guide even the raw novice through each recitation act. Half tone plates from life show poses at large expense, it boasts. No other speaker book, the publishers claim, matches its completeness.
70828-the-early-plantagenets:
The Early Plantagenets, a history by William Stubbs, belongs to the Epochs of Modern History series, edited by Edward E Morris and others. Stubbs was Regius Professor of Modern History at Oxford and the great constitutional historian of his age. The series aimed at short, sound manuals by scholars for schools and general readers. Two maps go with this volume.

The book tells the reigns of the first Plantagenet kings of England, from Henry the Second onward. Church and crown, barons and towns, law and administration are its matter. Stubbs built his history from the chronicles and records themselves, not from later summaries. The front matter lists the whole series, from the Greeks and Romans to the age of Frederick the Great, so the volume sits in a full survey of European history.
7084-a-girl-among-the-anarchists:
Isabel Meredith writes A Girl Among the Anarchists with a preface owning the courage needed to write on anarchism even with clinical sympathy or scientific detachment. Anarchists, she argues, are curiously interesting and much in need of observation, since leading article quacks show no insight into them as phenomenon, portent, or disease. Read with understanding, the book will show how anarchism grows endemic in Western civilizations as cholera is endemic in India.

Meredith, once a humble member of a newspaper staff, writes from inside knowledge of the movement's circles. The girl of the title moves among exiles, plotters, and idealists, learning their hopes and their follies. The book is a novel of political passion, told by one who watched it close at hand.
70923-an-experiment-in-gyro-hats:
An Experiment in Gyro-Hats is a humorous tale by Ellis Parker Butler, printed at New York and Chicago in a special edition. Butler also wrote Pigs Is Pigs. Albert Levering drew the pictures. The narrator is a practical hat dealer with a grievance against waste.

A top hat, he argues, is never full of head, and never can be until heads turn cylindrical. A shoe is full of foot and a glove full of hand, but the tall hat holds a large vacant space. His patents for using it ran from a small filing cabinet to an accordion hat rack. The public received the ideas coldly. His daughter Anne's uneasiness turns him toward the gyro-hat at last.
71002-debits-and-credits:
Rudyard Kipling gathered late tales and poems in Debits and Credits. Doubleday, Page and Company issued the book at Garden City, New York, in 1926. Tales and verses trade places through the contents in Kipling's late manner. The Janeites, The Wish House, and On the Gate lead the prose.

War tales of 1915 and 1916 stand beside tales of peace and faith. Poems drawn from Horace's fifth book of odes thread the set. A Madonna of the Trenches and The Eye of Allah close the main run. Kipling readers gain the grave, crafted work of his final decade.
71004-between-the-twilights:
Between the Twilights offers studies of Indian women by one of themselves. Cornelia Sorabji wrote the book. Harper published it in London and New York in 1908. Lockwood Kipling designed the cover. A glossary explains the Indian terms used.

The contents mix story and portrait. Early chapters bear titles like The Story of Wisdom. One chapter studies caste through a comic test. Another treats the mothers of fighters. Portraits of some Indian women form a long chapter. That piece was reprinted from a review. The first story opens with a spring guest. Women hasten from the bathing ghat with full water-pots. Only water from the Ganges serves that day.
71362-counter-currents:
Counter-Currents is a book of essays by Agnes Repplier. Houghton Mifflin published the work at Boston and New York in 1916. A note states that the nine essays first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly over three years. The book reached a third printing by August of its first year.

The essays treat the temper of the age, from the cost of modern feeling to Americanism. War, women, schooling, and the immigrant all receive a chapter. The opening essay pictures the age riding high on a wave of feeling. Repplier contrasts this flood with the thin, firm feeling of the mid Victorian years. She mourns the loss of taste as a guiding force. Duty, she writes with a borrowed phrase, is praised behind her back but rarely faced. The essays argue against the drift of the day with wit and polish.
71408-common-names-of-a-selected-list-of:
Kling L Anderson and Clenton E Owensby wrote Common Names of a Selected List of Plants, issued as Technical Bulletin One Hundred and Seventeen. Kansas State University issued the revised list in August nineteen sixty-nine. The list grew from an earlier Kansas list of grasses and legumes.

Common names, the authors warn, shift widely from place to place. One name may serve for several plants, which breeds mix-ups in talk and print. Fixed common names, paired with Latin names, are their cure. Sections cover grasses, sedges, ferns, legumes, and woody plants. A closing part gives the meanings of common species names.
71523-history-of-my-pets:
Grace Greenwood wrote this book of pet stories, in a new edition revised and enlarged at Boston in 1871, with engravings from designs by Billings. The first pet in the book is Keturah the cat, who came to the writer when she was about nine years old. Greenwood remembers the day plainly: she was trudging home from school, sad over a bad mark in geography.

The contents name the rest of the household. Sam the cockerel, Toby the hawk, Milly the pony, Carlo the dog, Cora the spaniel, and Jack the drake each get a chapter. A greyhound, a robin, and a cosset lamb get chapters too. Extra stories at the end add more cats, parrots, and bantams.
71537-historical-difficulties-and-contes:
Octave Delepierre wrote a book that tests famed tales of the past. The book came out in London in 1868. Delepierre was a clerk to the King of the Belgians at his court in London. French lines at the front call past lore a pact tale oft made up late. Truth shifts as light grows, Pascal is quoted to say.

The Colossus of Rhodes leads his list of hard asks. Belisarius, the Alexandrian book hoard, and Pope Joan come next. Abelard and Eloisa, William Tell, and Petrarch fill the mid parts. Joan of Arc stands in the list as well. Each tale is weighed for what can still be proved.
71639-wild-beasts:
Porter wrote this nature book, Wild Beasts, printed at New York in 1894. Its full title calls it a study of the characters and habits of nine great animals: the elephant, lion, leopard, panther, jaguar, tiger, puma, wolf, and grizzly bear. A photograph of the elephant forms the frontispiece, and Porter dedicates the book to a captain friend of his student days.

Eight chapters give the beasts in order, the leopard and panther sharing one. The elephant opens the book as My Lord the Elephant, first among four-footed creatures by age of line and by strength. Porter notes the elephant-headed god of wisdom in India, and the worship the animal won from China to the Indian highlands, and turns to the old writers on its nature.
71761-aunt-patty-s-paying-guests:
Eglanton Thorne wrote a tale printed at London by a tract society, with five drawings by Rainey. Her Own Way and other tales of hers are named on the title page. The front picture shows Paulina on her knees beside the teller. Twenty four chapters carry the story.

An unwelcome decree opens it: a doctor bans the teller, Nan, from books for twelve months at least. Her overworked brain needs rest, he rules. Study had been her whole hope, aimed at honours in her exams. Plans for paying guests follow, with ads, first comers, and a party of Americans. A princely gift, a hid name, and a flight fill the middle. Wedding bells close the heads the copy shows.
71768-old-english-colour-prints:
Malcolm C Salaman writes the text for a portfolio of old English color prints issued in London in 1909. Charles Holme edited the volume for The Studio, and collectors lent prints for copying. Salaman had already written on the old engravers of England.

The plates open with stipple work after Sir Joshua Reynolds, including Jane, Countess of Harrington and a child portrait called Robinetta. A mezzotint after Reynolds shows the Duchess of Devonshire with her daughter. Later plates turn to George Morland, with doors of squires and farmers, a boarding school visit, and park scenes. Works after Romney, Gainsborough, Hoppner, and Cosway fill out the set. Readers get fine copies of prized prints with notes that name each engraver and painter.
71887-advice-to-a-wife-and-mother-in-two:
Pye Henry Chavasse, a surgeon of Birmingham, wrote health advice for wives and mothers, here in a seventeenth edition printed at Philadelphia in 1881. Part one guides a wife on the care of her own health in pregnancy, labour, and nursing. A first chapter speaks straight to a young wife on hard truths.

Chavasse gives the book to his Birmingham patients, some of whom he served for more than thirty years. He notes sales in the tens of thousands and last editions of five and seven thousand copies. Part two, named at the front, turns to a mothers care of her children, the theme of his earlier book.
71924-the-secrets-of-black-arts:
The Secrets of Black Arts is a cheap popular handbook of the occult, put together by its publisher as a key note to witchcraft. Its title page promises divination, omens, warnings, visions, sorcery, demon lore, dreams, and pacts with the Devil, plus a history of the Salem witchcraft trials. The book opens with a long piece called the Devil's Legacy to Earth Mortals.

That opening argues over whether the Devil is one being or a crowd, citing scripture and old Scots speech. The tone mixes real fear with sales talk, the mark of the penny dreadful trade. It shows how widely magic beliefs still sold in the age of print.
72017-hervey-willetts:
Hervey Willetts, by Percy Keese Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade and Roy Blakeley books, was copyrighted by Grosset and Dunlap in 1927. It was published with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America and illustrated by Hastings. Opening verses present Hervey: reckless, happy go lucky, crazy, and fond of dares, yet liked by all.

Chapter one, Happy Go Lucky, concedes the case against him. Hervey lacked many qualities a scout ought to have, but he had nerve: always brave, often reckless, sometimes blithely heroic, and always wrong. His courage never paid because it was mixed with disobedience. Once he saved a boy from drowning in the wee hours, a gold medal deed, except that he had no right to be out swimming at night. His spectacular deeds were always byproducts of escapades. Thirty six chapters promise stunts, sentences, traps, the jaws of death, and a final question: reached?
72143-the-manufacture-of-mineral-and-lak:
Josef Bersch wrote a trade text book on how paint colors are made, turned into English by Arthur Wright and issued in London in 1901. The full title promises ways to make all made up colors for artists and painters, plus enamel colors, soot, and metal based colors. Forty three art cuts help show the steps and gear.

Bersch gives the chemic traits of raw stuffs first, since no one can make colors well with no grasp of that science. He keeps only methods he had tried and found sound, and he skips old rule of thumb mixes. Parts on tests teach dealers and users how to spot fake or cut goods fast.
72227-divots:
Wodehouse gathered golf tales in a book printed in New York with pieces dated from 1923 to 1927. A list at the front names Carry On, Jeeves and Leave It to Psmith. Wodehouse gives the book to his daughter Leonora, without whose sympathy it would have been finished in half the time, he jokes. The Sixth Bunker at Addington dates his note.

The Heart of a Goof opens the set. It was a morning when all nature shouted fore, and the breeze spoke of chip shots holed and brassies landing on the meat. A careworn man waggles his driver over a new ball. High stakes, magic plus fours, and Rodney failing to qualify fill the nine comic tales of links life.
72271-the-russian-novelists:
The Russian Novelists is a study of Russian tales in English dress. It came from a French work by de Vogue, a famed critic of the age. The English form was made by Jane Loring Edmands. It was put out at Boston in the late eighteen hundreds. A note from the hand that made the English text opens the book.

That note owns the hard task of Russian names in English letters. No fixed rule yet held at the time. It says the guide used was a set form drawn by a guild of book men. The true Russian form could not at all times be traced. It owns as well that the French work was cut down in parts to fit set bounds. A short word to the reader then frames the rise of taste for Russian letters.
72324-lectures-on-english-poets:
Lectures on English Poets is a course of lectures by James Russell Lowell, printed at Cleveland by the Rowfant Club in 1897 in an edition of two hundred and twenty-four copies. Lowell had delivered the lectures in 1855. A portrait head, and a motto from Chaucer about the half-told story of Cambuscan, face the title page.

Twelve lectures fill the book. Definitions open the course. Then come Piers Ploughman's Vision, the metrical romances, and the ballads. Chaucer, Spenser, Milton, Butler, and Pope have lectures of their own. Poetic diction and Wordsworth follow, and the function of the poet closes the course. In the first lecture Lowell owns his sense of the task's weight. Few men, he says, have twelve hours of talk worth hearing on any subject. The Rowfant printing preserved a famous American critic's early lectures for collectors.
72335-the-old-english-dramatists:
James Russell Lowell lectures on the early English stage in talks first read at the Lowell Institute in the spring of 1887. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued them at Boston in 1893. Charles Eliot Norton holds the copyright of 1892.

A prefatory note warns the reader honestly. Much was said off the cuff in delivery, prompted by passages read aloud from the plays. Those passages left no mark in the manuscript. Lowell never revised the lectures for print. The book thus keeps the shape of the spoken word. His subjects are the great makers of the English drama before and around Shakespeare. Lowell, poet, editor, and ambassador, brought a critic's love to the old plays. The lectures show his talk at full ease.
7239-men-women-and-boats:
Stephen Crane's Men, Women, and Boats gathers tales and sketches from out-of-print volumes and old magazine files, edited with an introduction by Vincent Starrett. Some pieces appear here for the first time between covers, and some for the first time in this country, rescued from scattered print. The Open Boat, one of Crane's finest stories, anchors the book by permission of its holders.

Starrett notes with regret that The Blue Hotel had to be left out for copyright reasons, a gap the editor marks rather than hides. The stories that remain show Crane's sharp eye for people under pressure, at sea and on land. This collection gives a fuller, fairer view of a short, brilliant career.
72545-on-books-and-arts:
Frederick Wedmore gathered On Books and Arts from his critical writings. Hodder and Stoughton published the volume at London in 1899. His note owns the pieces are contributions to reviews and to one great daily paper, the Standard. He has not brought them up to date. A suppression here and a changed phrase there are all he allowed himself. The essays remain frankly contributions, he says. The contents open with The Short Story.

My Rare Book and pieces on Balzac and George Eliot follow. My Few Things, Anne Oldfield, and Siddons and Rachel come next. Joseph Jefferson, Zola's Therese Raquin, and Macbeth with Irving treat the stage. Rembrandt opens the art run, with Dutch drawings, Velasquez, and French eighteenth-century painting behind him. Chardin, Moreau, Gainsborough, and Cotman fill the middle. Lord Leighton, Millais, and Burne-Jones close the painters.
72555-reign-of-the-telepuppets:
A science fiction story by Daniel F Galouye. It first appeared in the magazine Amazing Stories in August 1963. A Bureau of Interstellar Exploration team prepares for a trouble-shooting mission. The opening pages introduce Director Gabe Randall. His assistant Dave Stewart stands by him. Carol Cummings completes the group. She is a young specialist in direct radio empathy. Only young women can develop that rare gift.

A second thread runs behind the briefing-room talk. Bigboss believes nothing in creation stands above him. Yet he half remembers creatures who once challenged his rule. A starship crew, office banter, and a distant threatened ruler set up the tale. Hidden masters steer minds across space, and the mission heads straight toward them.
7258-dreams-waking-thoughts-and-incident:
William Beckford's Dreams, Waking Thoughts, and Incidents travels Europe in a series of letters. It opens on June 19, 1780, with a rare confession: shall he tell his correspondent his dreams, since giving an account of his time is little better?? A frequent mist hovers before his eyes, he writes, so that colours and forms delude him through a hazy medium.

Beckford owns himself a more ideal being than most travellers, and his letters mix dream, waking fancy, and incident without apology. The wise may scoff at such a guide, he admits, yet his correspondents reap vivid pictures of outlandish countries all the same. The book reads as a young man's grand tour through a mind half in dream.
72659-tom-swift-and-his-chest-of-secrets:
Tom Swift and His Chest of Secrets is a boys tale by Victor Appleton. Its next name calls it a trace of the stole craft finds in full. A Grosset and Dunlap house of New York holds its nineteen twenty five right. Ned Newton looks up from his desk at Tom bent on blue prints at start. Part names open with a roof crash, big bids, and foul work.

Free bonds, Ivan Barsky, and fire fill the next part ranks in scheme. Fast quit, a hid ear, and Mary word stand mid part names there. Twin risk, a ring of fire, and just in time crowd the scheme. Trap, bound in dark, and out of the pit mark the low point. Koku found and a blue craft close the chase scheme of parts.
72921-terence-s-andrian-a-comedy-in-five:
Terence Andrian is an English prose translation of the Roman comedy Andria, printed in 1820. Goodluck the younger translated the five act play and added critical notes. Longman and partners of Paternoster Row published the school and parlour edition. A Spectator motto praises the moral regard of Athenian and Roman plays alike.

The preface says verse was dropped for prose so all readers could follow. Learned and unlearned alike should relish the beauties of the great poet in English. Terence love tangle of fathers, sons, and a girl from Andros drives the plot. Students of Latin drama gain an early plain English door into Terence.
72957-the-aristocrats:
The Aristocrats, a novel by Gertrude Atherton, was published in London and New York in 1901. It takes the form of letters from the Lady Helen Pole to her friend the Countess of Edge and Ross. Helen writes from Boulder Lake in the Great North Woods of Hamilton County, New York. The book is dedicated to all lovers of the Adirondack peaks, forests, and lakes.

Helen and her friend Agatha climb a rough corduroy road of logs to reach their lake camp. She writes with wonder at the primeval forest, where pines and hemlocks had great grandfathers. At twenty six she finds herself keen for every new phase of this extraordinary country. Atherton sets an English lady's sharp eye on American wilderness and the rich campers who summer there. The letters mix scenery, society talk, and a stranger's delight in a young nation.
7310-mr-pim-passes-by-a-comedy-in-three-:
A. A. Milne's Mr Pim Passes By is a comedy in three acts, set in the morning-room at Marden House, Buckinghamshire, on a day in July. George Marden, justice of the peace, his wife Olivia, his niece Dinah, his aunt Lady Marden, Brian Strange, and the visitor Carraway Pim make up the cast, with Anne in service. The play lists its original casts at Manchester's Gaiety and London's New Theatre.

Milne builds farce from a chance caller whose talk threatens a settled marriage, letting wit and misunderstanding do the work of plot. The comedy stays light, civilised, and brisk, with each act tightening the knot before it slips loose. Readers get a stage piece that plays as well on the page.
73433-the-untouchable-adolescents:
Ellis Hart sets a hard case in The Untouchable Adolescents, from Super-Science Fiction in February 1957, with drawings by Kelly Freas. The blurb gives the hook: the aliens will not accept help though their world is about to explode. They are adolescents, and adolescence is the time when you are not smart enough to ask for help.

Captain Luther Shreve of the Wallower waits in dread for the survey plates of the planet Diamore. His psych officer Teller brings the verdict: less than five months before the Big Push, when eruptions will wipe out nine-tenths of the towns.
73462-the-tenderfoots:
Francis Lynde wrote this western novel of two tenderfoots on the plains. Scribner printed The Tenderfoots in New York in 1926. It first ran as The Prisoner and the Play-Boy in 1925. Lynde gives it to his wife, linked in memory with these pages.

Philip Trask sits in a crowded day coach crossing eastern Colorado. Prairie towns shrink as the train flies west toward the frontier. Sod houses of pioneer homesteaders thin out behind the coach too. Soon nothing but treeless, limitless plain rolls past the window glass. A prairie dog town or a flying bird breaks the plain now and then there.
73801-my-pets:
Marshall Saunders, author of Beautiful Joe, published My Pets in Philadelphia in 1908, subtitled Real Happenings in My Aviary. The book is illustrated from photographs and opens with lines from Emily Dickinson about saving one heart from breaking. Saunders dedicates it to boys and girls who want stories that are entirely true.

She says the account of her aviary comes straight from her diaries, and many of the birds were still living when she wrote. Early chapters tell the story of two owls and the owls starting on their travels. Readers get true pet stories from a writer famous for speaking up for animals, told without invention.
73991-the-orchestra-and-its-instruments:
The Orchestra and Its Instruments introduces every section of the modern orchestra. Esther Singleton wrote the survey. The Symphony Society of New York published it in 1917. A prelude opens the volume. Ten chapters follow the instruments family by family. Many photographs show famous makers' work.

The violin takes the longest chapter by far. The viola and violoncello come next. The double-bass closes the strings. Woodwind and brasswind families follow in turn. Percussion instruments earn their own chapter. A long chapter on the orchestra as a whole succeeds. The conductor gets a short one. The harp and the pianoforte close the book. A Hellier Stradivari of 1679 appears among the plates. Paganini's own Guarneri is pictured too.
74181-millions-of-cats:
Wanda Gág made Millions of Cats in 1928, a picture tale for children. Once upon a time there was a very old man and a very old woman. They lived in a nice clean house with flowers all around it. But they could not be happy, because they were so very lonely.

If we only had a cat, sighed the old woman: a sweet little fluffy cat. I will get you a cat, my dear, said the very old man. He set out over the hills, climbed the sunny hills, trudged the cool valleys, and at last came to a hill quite covered with cats. Cats here, cats there, cats and kittens everywhere: hundreds, thousands, millions and billions and trillions of cats. He chose the prettiest, a white one. Then he saw a black and white one, just as pretty, and took it too.
74182-the-triumph-of-the-innocents:
The Triumph of the Innocents is a devotional work printed at London in 1885, built around a picture of the Flight into Egypt. Its epitome sets the flight about sixteen months after the birth of Jesus, in the second April of his life. The holy travellers cross the Philistine plain on the road to Gaza, some thirty miles from their start.

By the last light of the moon, the spirits of the slain Innocents move in procession near the Virgin. Joseph watches signal fires on the slope for signs of soldiers on the road. Mary, glad for her saved son, feels pity for the childless mothers left behind. The text reads the picture part by part, in a mood of tender grief.
74232-special-talents-and-defects:
Special Talents and Defects, and their significance for education, is Leta S Hollingworth's study of uneven minds. The Macmillan Company of New York published it in 1923, in the Experimental Education Series. Hollingworth was associate professor of education at Teachers College, Columbia University.

The book asks whether intellect is one thing or many. Early chapters weigh the relationships among capacities: coefficients of correlation, general intelligence against special aptitudes, and whether an intellect can be trained as a unit. The measurement of the IQ and the psychographic picture of individuality follow, with the neural basis of it all examined and found unproven. Then the single gifts and gaps: reading, with word blindness and a four-year study of a non-reader; spelling, and whether reading teaches it; arithmetic, and the psychology of calculation. Cases throughout show children brilliant in one line and helpless in another.
7432-on-nothing-kindred-subjects:
Hilaire Belloc dedicated these essays to Maurice Baring, and their subject is announced in the title: nothing, and kindred subjects. The contents wander as Belloc's mind wandered. He writes on taking up one's pen, and on getting respected in inns and hotels. He writes on ignorance, on advertisement, and on a house. He writes on a dog and a man, and also on tea. Railways, conversations in trains, and the return of the dead all get their turn.

Later essays grow sharper, touching national debts, lords, and jingoes in the shape of a warning. But the tone stays that of a man talking after dinner, serious about small things and playful about great ones. Readers who know The Path to Rome will recognize the same voice here, looser and more mischievous, enjoying the freedom of having nothing in particular to prove.
74422-friends-in-strange-garments:
Friends in Strange Garments, by Anna Milo Upjohn, is a story set for children. Houghton Mifflin issued it at Boston and New York in 1927 in full. Rights rested with the American National Red Cross for the book then. Upjohn drew the pictures herself, some in colour, of children abroad.

An intro by Arthur Dunn of the Junior Red Cross sets the frame. In the Wilderness opens in Palestine, where Rahmeh feeds her camel Nib. Turkey, Greece, Macedonia, Albania, Montenegro, Bulgaria, and Serbia follow in tales. Kossovo Day, the fairy ring of Roumania, and the great amber road continue. Poland, Italy, and France close the tour of young friends.
75092-fix-bayonets:
Thomason, a captain in the United States Marine Corps, wrote these sketches of the Great War for Scribner's Sons, who published them in 1926 with his own illustrations as Fix Bayonets! He dedicates the book to the men of the First Battalion, Fifth Regiment, of the Marines in 1918.

The opening sketch, The Leathernecks, is set in June 1918 in a French field hospital behind the Marne salient, where the Second American Division fought around the Bois de Belleau. A wounded man on a pillow corrects a visiting lady: he is not an American, he is a Marine. Thomason then describes the big war companies, 250 strong, filled with lumber-camp men, university men, farmers, and old hands from navy ports. His sketches keep the speech and pride of the ranks.
75096-boots:
Boots opens as a jungle tale told around a man named Juan and three worn white men in a canoe. Juan lives by a small stream in Peru, where he farms and fishes. The head gives no title page, so the tale starts at once with his thoughts. One of the new men wears the boots of the title.

The prose lingers on heat, green growth, and the strange force of the three guests. Juan feels fear and doubt as he weighs what the men want from him. Love for a woman whose name is lost may drive what he does next. The scene sets up a tense tale of risk in a remote place.
753-arizona-nights:
Stewart Edward White wrote these tales of Arizona nights, when cowboys, miners, and travellers gather round fires and swap stories. The desert by night is the real hero: cool air, bright stars, and the long quiet after a day's hard riding. Each tale grows from a campfire yarn, told in the drawl of men who lived the life.

White knew the Southwest at first hand, and his prose carries its dust, heat, and humour. The stories praise courage and good fellowship without hiding the risks of frontier life. The book helped fix the image of Arizona in the American mind, and it still reads as a warm, authentic set of western tales.
75415-spectacle-secrets:
Spectacle Secrets, by George Cox, reached a second edition published by the author at 128 Holborn Hill, London, in 1844, and sold by opticians and booksellers. Numbered illustrations show spectacle frames, including the anti pressure, solid, and blue steel patterns.

Cox's preface warns that the public needs guarding against implicit belief in every promised remedy. A man who states plainly what benefit spectacles can fairly give, he says, is often met with contempt or suspicion. Readers then fall, he complains, as passive victims to pompous and plausible charlatans who make the largest promises.
75474-three-little-trippertrots:
Three Little Trippertrots, how they ran away and how they got back again, by Howard R Garis, was printed in New York by Graham and Matlack under a 1912 copyright. Garis wrote Uncle Wiggily Adventures and the Bedtime Stories. The book sold at sixty cents.

A publisher note says the Trippertrot stories, though never before in print, had been told to thousands of children in a new way. They were read over the telephone, nightly, to thousands of little folks, by the system of the New Jersey Telephone Herald Company. The tales so delighted the children that the author yielded to requests to put them in book form. Two little boys and a little girl lived with their papa and mamma in a house in a big city. Young readers get runaway fun by a phone story pioneer.
75545-the-romance-of-comets:
Mary Proctor, daughter of the astronomer Richard Proctor, wrote The Romance of Comets for Harper and Brothers, who published it in New York and London in 1926. She dedicated it to the memory of Professor Barnard, whose portrait serves as frontispiece. Her earlier books, like Evenings with the Stars, are listed on the title page.

Nine chapters tell the comet story. The first treats comets as portents, the signs that once scared kings. Then come comet hunting as a hobby, the story of Donati's comet, and comets in distress. A chapter shows what the camera did for comet study. The return of Halley's comet in 1910 gets a full chapter. The book ends with meteor streams and a bold question: did life first come to Earth in a meteor? Sky watchers get lore and science in one volume.
75552-wild-oats:
James Oppenheim wrote Wild Oats, with a foreword by Edward Bok, issued in New York by B W Huebsch in nineteen ten. Eighteen chapters fill the novel. Chapter one is Spring on East Broadway. The Mother and The First Night follow. Bok foreword urges the tale on thousands of readers. The truth behind the story cannot much longer stay in the background, he says.

The old saying that truth is stranger than fiction is peculiarly true of this story, Bok holds. Somewhere in the social body there is a festering sore that needs the surgery of public discussion, he argues. It is not meeting the question to call it not a nice subject, he adds. Tuberculosis and poverty in the tenements drive the plot. Spring Music and Mr Grupp Interrupts fill the middle. Reform readers get a Lower East Side novel with a cause.
75577-footprints:
Footprints is a novel by Kay Cleaver Strahan, published by Doubleday, Doran in 1929. Copyright entries reach back to 1928, in a magazine publisher's name. The story opens in the rosy lobby of a fashionable hotel. A revolving door lets the November mist, and a striking woman, into the room.

The entrant is wrapped in sealskin and a bright red hat. Two matrons watch her cross the carpet to the desk. One informs the other, in a whisper, who she is. She is one of the Quilters, among Oregon's best-known families. Their ranch lies east of the mountains, in a county named for them. Half that country seems to bear the family name, the gossip adds. Everything the Quilters touch turns into money, it is said.
75630-flashlights:
Flashlights is a book of short poems by Mary Aldis from 1916. Her past work held a play of a prince and plays for small stages. The poems first stood in the verse press of Chicago and New York. The book is cut in three parts by the plan of its list.

Town sketches open the book, with a barber's shop and the Loop. Love in the town, a talk, and a wish at a pane fill that part. The next part turns to form, prayer, boats, and gates of flood. A tale in verse of a jailed man starts the third part of the book. Two girls, a park bench, and two sisters have tales of their own. Aldis writes in free lines, in the new mode of her day.
75671-essays-on-horse-subjects:
Grenside, a veterinarian, privately printed Essays on Horse Subjects at New York in 1907 after twenty-eight years as a practical horseman and veterinarian. His preface says the essays cover the borderland between the veterinarian's and the horseman's ground, which both trades have neglected. The contents take up quality in horses, hereditary unsoundness, hitching, horseshoeing and hoofs, and correct action. They go on to forging and over-reaching, interfering, the horse's mouth, turning horses out, bitting and conditioning, and exercise. The coat through the seasons, digestive disorders, and burrs on bits close the list.

The opening essay attacks the word quality itself: horsemen mean breeding, conformation, finish, class, symmetry, or magnetism by it, and no two agree. Grenside argues quality is a separate attribute, present in degrees, and not the same as breeding or shape. A horse may be cow-hocked and calf-kneed, he says, and still show quality.
75731-the-regimental-roll-of-honour-and-:
Howlett and Son of London published a third edition in 1922 of the war record of the Artists' Rifles. The book covers the three battalions of that corps in the London Regiment from August 4, 1914. A war memorial panel at the Duke's Road headquarters, wrought by Captain Alwyn Carr, forms the frontispiece.

The heart of the book is lists of names. A roll of honour comes first, then the holders of the great awards, in their ranks of honour. Foreign orders, mentions in dispatches, and men brought to notice follow. A roll of commissions runs to hundreds of pages, and rolls of other ranks and of past members close the set. Drawings and photographs by members of the corps fill the book. It is a book of record, made so that each man's service can be found.
75874-personal-rights:
Personal Rights is the printed text of a presidential address by Mona Caird. She delivered it to the forty-first annual meeting of the Personal Rights Association on the sixth of June 1913. The Association published the speech in London and sold it for one penny.

Caird begins with a confession. She used to feel impatience with public speakers who spent half a speech explaining how they came to make it. Those gentlemen now have her profoundest sympathy, she says. She never speaks in public, and taking the chair feels like a cold plunge in the Atlantic in early spring. She cannot shed her deficiencies by listing them, so she throws herself on her hearers' mercy. The address that follows takes up the rights of the person, in a period when the Association campaigned against state interference and for women's freedom.
75952-the-rival-bicyclists:
The Rival Bicyclists, or Fun and Adventure on the Wheel, is a boys' novel by Captain Ralph Bonehill, published in 1897. Bonehill had written Gun and Sled and The Young Oarsmen of Lakeview.

The hero is Joe Johnson of Lockport, not quite fifteen, who bought his bicycle with money earned at odd jobs after school. His friend Dick Burns, aged seventeen and son of the town's leading lawyer, rides with him. The book opens with the two planning a moonlight ride to Greenpoint over the valley road. Joe's one enemy, a tall slim boy named Lemuel Akers, scowls at them from behind a pile of boxes at the grocery. From that grudge the rivalry of the title grows, in the great age of the bicycle craze.
75965-carrots-mangold-wurtzels-and-sugar:
Gregory, known for books on onion and cabbage raising, wrote this farm guide, entered for copyright in 1900. He argues that root crops give far more feed per acre than hay, and that feeding roots on the farm builds manure and lifts later crops. Carrots, mangold wurtzels and sugar beets are his three subjects.

Each crop gets plain, step-by-step help. Gregory covers soil, manure, bed making, seed, planting time and the best kinds to grow, from Short Horn and Danvers carrots to long and round mangolds. He then explains care, harvest, storage, cost and feeding, with yields drawn from trial crops in Massachusetts.
76132-living-lights:
Charles Frederick Holder, a fellow of the New York Academy of Sciences, wrote Living Lights, a popular account of phosphorescent animals and vegetables. Sampson Low published it in London in 1887. Holder inscribes the volume to his father, in remembrance of days passed among the living lights of the outer reef.

The preface gives the design: to interest young people in natural history through one of its most marvellous phases. The subject is luminosity, in animals, plants, and even inorganic matter. Above all it is the creatures that light the ocean. Holder spent many years on southern shores among marine life. He remembers the splendours of the night festivals of these ocean forms as beyond any fairy tale. A plate shows a glowing pyrosoma beside a diver. Young naturalists get the fire of the sea explained.
76173-footprints:
Annette Lyster wrote Footprints, a story of the snow, published in London by the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge. Lyster also wrote The White Gipsy and Fan's Silken String. The tale opens early in Queen Victoria's reign near a large Devonshire town. Farmer Marlowe, a prosperous man with a thrifty wife and six children, owns a large farm there.

Snow seldom lies in mild, damp Devon. One year a storm heavy enough for Scotland struck, with hard frost behind it. The Marlowe children greet it with glee, and the chapters follow snow and snowmen, a girl named Katie, and old Rover the dog. A frontispiece shows a drawer pointed out while a man named Harper takes the gold, hinting at the wrongdoing the story will bring. Lyster's tale mixes winter fun with the moral trials the Society's books were written to teach.
76304-secrets-of-scene-painting-and-stag:
Secrets of Scene Painting and Stage Effects is a craft manual by Van Dyke Browne. Routledge issued the seventh edition in London. The book is fully illustrated in colour and black and white. A frontispiece shows the old Globe theatre on Bankside. Shakespeare meets the Burbages in that plate. The text opens with a claim about stage craft. Scenery, it says, makes the impression of reality.

Browne argues that big London shows rest on their effects. At Drury Lane a strong melodrama draws talk for one big effect. A race of aeroplanes or a fight of submarines is his example. At His Majesty's the talk is of scenic beauty. Critics and the public weigh sets beside acting, he says. The manual then teaches how such effects are made. Stage painters and machinists were its first readers.
76505-australian-insects:
Australian Insects is a textbook of entomology by Walter Froggatt. Brooks published it at Sydney where Froggatt was government entomologist. Thirty seven plates hold two hundred seventy figures in the book. One hundred eighty text blocks add further illustration. Froggatt belonged to entomological societies in America and France. A preface notes many enquiries from people across Australia. Visitors from other countries also asked for such a book. The time has come for a textbook of Australian entomology, he writes.

His difficulty was writing in a popular style without losing science. The general reader must be interested into further study, he says. The student must still find characteristics and classification defined. Since 1770, when Banks captured the first diamond beetle, he begins. That shore catch opens the island's insect history. Froggatt serves both the curious reader and the working naturalist.
76748-on-art-and-artists:
On Art and Artists is a book of keen notes on art by Max Nordau, the hand of a famed work on the fall of art. Harvey made the English form of the book. It was put out at London in the year nineteen hundred and seven. Its list of parts gives the span of its theme. The charge of art in the life of men heads the run.

Art of the crowd faith, with a great carve man of that faith, comes next. The doubt of style, the old French greats, and a whole age of French art fill the first run. The school of a famed year, the win of a revolt by the true to life school, and three men of that school stand past them.
76758-heroic-airmen-and-their-exploits:
Walters wrote Heroic Airmen and Their Exploits, first printed in London in 1917. Walters had written The Souls of the Brave and Heroines of the World War. The book is given to the memory of the heroic airmen who laid down their lives in the service of their country. A front picture shows Flight-Commander Robinson, holder of the Victoria Cross. An author's note says the pages are far from technical in nature.

The aim, Walters writes, is to wake the reader's interest and throw fresh light on heroic deeds. Contents open with the birth of the airship and the pioneer work of Santos Dumont. The birth and growth of the aeroplane and the Zeppelin follow. Chapters then honor airmen one by one: Robinson, Sowrey, Brandon, Tempest, and Warneford among them. Albert Ball, Guynemer, and the heroes of the Royal Naval Air Service fill the later heads.
76822-four-american-poets:
Four American Poets is a book for young Americans by Sherwin Cody, giving short lives of four poets. The poets are William Cullen Bryant, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, John Greenleaf Whittier, and Oliver Wendell Holmes. Cody's book stands fourth in a school series of lives of great Americans, sold at fifty cents a copy.

The Bryant life runs from his childhood love of nature to his years as editor of a great newspaper. Chapter heads mark Thanatopsis, his turn to law, and his work as speaker and prose writer. The series aimed to give children sound lives to admire, told in a way the youngest reader could hold.
76852-the-chocolate-plant-theobroma-caca:
The Chocolate Plant and Its Products is a trade book on cacao by a famed firm. The Baker house in Massachusetts put the small book out for its trade. Rights date the work to the year eighteen ninety. Prints show pods and blooms that spring from the old wood of the tree.

First parts trace the old tale of the plant and its first farm use. How the seed came to Europe as a drink fills an early part as well. Field range and trade ties of the plant earn their own part next. Ways to make, test, and cook the goods fill the bulk of the book. The work served grocers and cooks who sold or used the firms goods.
76945-scottish-toasts:
Ivor Ben McIvor gathered Scottish toasts and table talk in a book held under copyright in 1908 and printed at New York and Boston. Groups run from toasts of homeland pride to toasts to women, love, and friendship. Merry toasts, after dinner tales, and a mixed bag at the back fill the rest of the book.

A Scots night menu opens the fun, with lines from Burns and other Scots poets tied to each dish. Cockie leekie soup, cod with oyster sauce, haddies, haggis, and sheep head and trotters all appear. Drams and toddy get their own verses, and the spread ends with a good night wish to all.
76958-over-the-straits:
Ernest Haycox sets this sea story in the salmon country of Alaska in 1920, a poor fish season. The cannery tender Star lies at Ketchikan with fifteen thousand sockeye salmon in her hold, worth forty cents apiece. The fish must cross the straits to the cannery within ten hours or sour. A fifty-mile blow is coming up the straits, and the weather flag is flying, but skipper Bob puts the question to his crew of seven.

Hal, the narrator, tells the run down Revillagigedo Channel toward Prince of Wales Island, thirty-four miles across open water. Ed Fraser, Milt, Al the engineer, and the silent Charlie make up the crew. Haycox writes the kind of quiet, unshowy heroism his blurb promises: business against weather, and men who go anyway.
77434-the-anatomy-of-plants:
The Anatomy of Plants sets out a philosophical history of plants in four books, built from lectures and close looking, with the microscope used on bark, wood, and pith. Book one treats the seed in its state of vegetation, then the root, the trunk, the branch and leaf, the flower, the fruit, and the seed again in generation.

Later books dissect roots and trunks in detail, follow the motion and course of the sap and of air, and end with leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds. Added lectures treat mixture, salts, the colours of plants, and tastes in plants. Readers get a founding work of plant anatomy, mapping the inner structure of vegetation part by part.
77481-the-misbehaviorists:
Harvey Wickham wrote an attack on the new schools of mind that the Dial Press published in 1928. He gives the book to enquiring minds troubled by views that war with their dearest beliefs. Chapter one names the foe: the modern temper.

Wickham takes the schools in turn. Behaviorism is tried by its missing mind. McDougall and his X come next. A long chapter treats Freud as a slave to dreams and a maker of fictions. The family tree brings monkeys and the breeding of men. Dorsey, Browne, and Durant stand for the unbelieving world. The last chapter pleads for the ancient temper against the new.
77612-valuable-cooking-receipts:
Thomas Murrey wrote this cookery book, Valuable Cooking Receipts, printed at New York in 1880. Murrey had been caterer at the Astor House and the Rossmore Hotel in New York and at the Continental Hotel in Philadelphia. A cover picture shows a cook at her table, mixing, while a lady reads the receipt aloud beside her.

The preface speaks first for the publisher. Cookbooks flood the market, good and bad, but this one rests on a working caterer's twenty-five years in leading hotels and private service. Murrey was famed as a salad-maker, with hundreds of receipts in that line. Here he kept economy in view, fitted his dishes to families of moderate means, and tested every receipt himself; the book is arranged like a bill of fare.
77622-impressions-of-great-naturalists:
Henry Fairfield Osborn wrote Impressions of Great Naturalists, for Scribner in 1924. The book holds reminiscences of Darwin, Huxley, Balfour, Cope, and others. Osborn was research professor of zoology at Columbia and president of the American Museum of Natural History. He also served as a senior geologist in the national survey. His own books run from Men of the Old Stone Age to Evolution and Religion.

Portraits stand in the book, and its pieces hold rights from 1896 onward. Osborn gives it to the memory of the naturalists, explorers, and authors touched here. A verse from George Eliot praises the immortal dead who live again in better minds. His foreword holds that there is no joy like the joy of creative work. All great men are creative, he says, and the creative naturalists among the greatest of them.
77638-life-among-the-ants:
Life Among the Ants is a small handbook by Vance Randolph, issued as Little Blue Book number 833 by the Haldeman-Julius Company of Girard, Kansas, with copyright in 1925. Peter Quinn drew the pictures, and ten short chapters carry the whole subject, from the ant's body to its dairies and guests. The book was made for the serious but not too serious student of ant life.

Randolph opens with the books about ants, from Aesop and Pliny to Lubbock's Ants, Bees and Wasps of 1881, long the standard work. Later chapters treat the harvesting ants, the mushroom growers, the honey ants, and the legionary ants. The red slave makers and the Amazons with their slaves close the survey of ant societies.
7765-night-must-fall-a-play-in-three-act:
Emlyn Williams's Night Must Fall, a play in three acts, takes place in the sitting room of Forest Corner, Mrs. Bramson's Essex bungalow, in the present day. The cast lists the Lord Chief Justice, Mrs. Bramson, her niece Olivia Grayne, Hubert Laurie, Nurse Libby, cook Mrs. Terence, maid Dora, and Inspector Belsize.

Act One opens on an October morning, later scenes follow twelve days and two days on, ending at nightfall. Performing rights rest with the author's agent, Walter Peacock of Haymarket. The play builds dread in a quiet house, where charm may hide a killer.
77725-popular-lectures-on-scientific-sub:
Hermann von Helmholtz's Popular Lectures on Scientific Subjects, second series, were translated by E Atkinson and reprinted many times from 1893 to 1908. An autobiography of the author accompanies this series. A preface notes the favour with which the first series was received.

Helmholtz was the century's great physicist-physiologist, master of energy, sound, and sight. His popular lectures carried laboratory science to general audiences in plain language, on subjects from optics to the age of the earth. Atkinson, a Staff College professor of experimental science, made them English. Readers get Victorian science explained by one of its makers, lecture-hall clarity preserved in print.
77828-there-s-not-a-bathing-suit-in-russ:
Will Rogers wrote a comic book of travel in Russia, with pictures by Herb Roth. Boni of New York copyrighted it in 1927. A page at the front lists the fare on offer. Mary Garden, flying, vodka, propaganda of all sorts, free love, bombs, and grand dukes all stand on the bill, with many other wrong ways to run a country.

Rogers jokes that more has been said of Russia than of honesty in politics, and as little done about it. He held back his own book till the crowd should finish, he says, but they never finish. Any man who cannot get into print should write on Russia, he advises, and take a regular man's place for a day. The chapters that follow are numbered one to eight. The pictures carry jokes of their own, of spies, shaves, and bathing caps. The humor is dry and plain.
77897-bettina-s-best-desserts:
Bettina's Best Desserts is a cookbook by Louise Bennett Weaver and Helen Cowles LeCron. Burt Company of New York brought the book out in the year 1923. Elizabeth Colborne drew the pictures, baked apples with brown sugar among them. The authors had writ A Thousand Ways to Please a Husband before. Give your table the Bettina touch stands as the book's proud motto.

Twenty-five sections run from apple desserts to whips at the end. Apricot, banana, blueberry, and cherry each get a section of recipes. Cream puffs, eclairs, custards, and frozen desserts fill the rich middle. Gelatine, grape juice, peach, and pineapple sweets stand in the list. Pies take a long section, and puddings take the longest of all. Apple cobbler opens the recipes, a good old-fashioned family dish. Four portions, with cinnamon and brown sugar, start the sweet course.
77943-pennsylvania-wild-cats:
Pennsylvania Wild Cats is a short plea and hunt book by Henry Shoemaker, printed in nineteen sixteen. The Altoona Tribune house of Pennsylvania brought it out that year. Its front words ask a new chance for wild cats near wiped out. Bounty laws, the book says, rest on trumped up proof of harm. Charts name the wild cat kinds of the state one by one.

Parts treat the bob cat, the big grey cat, and the Blue Mountain cat in turn. Cross bred kinds and the hunt craft get parts of their own. Hunt men of past and now fill a part with named lives. Photos of famed cat men line the book front to back. The plea asks that this fine and good beast be kept for days to come.
77956-a-pixy-in-petticoats:
A Pixy in Petticoats, published in New York in 1909, is a novel of Dartmoor in the west of England. Its twenty-seven chapters all begin with the word How. The hero is John Burrough, a scholar who has claimed a hidden nook on the East Okement river as his private retreat.

The first chapter opens like Robinson Crusoe in reverse: Burrough crosses the bog and finds a crumpled newspaper on the turf, proof that someone else has found his secret place. The contents weave in Beatrice, who walks with him, tells the story of Tregeagle, and sits with him on the pixies' bowling-green. Together they visit Bedlam, boil a kettle in the Devil's Kitchen, shelter in Tom-Tit-Tot's palace, and search for white heather. Burrough longs to enter Lyonesse, the drowned land of legend. Readers get a whimsical moorland romance steeped in local folklore.
77976-the-valley-of-ghosts:
Edgar Wallace's detective novel, published at Boston by Small, Maynard in 1923, brings Andrew Macleod to the town of Beverley on the track of a safe-breaker. The man is Allison John Wicker, called Four-Eyed Scottie for his spectacles. He opened the Regent Diamond Syndicate's safe with an acetylene blower and took seven parcels of stones. Andy, in his easy-running Spanz car, is soon chatting with headquarters from the post office.

Stella Nelson and her ring, a death shot, an inquest, and a valley of ghosts fill out the contents. Wallace was then at the height of his fame for swift crime tales. This one keeps his pace: short chapters, plain talk, and a mystery that ends with the laying of ghosts. It is a fair sample of his detective work between the wars.
78221-civilization-and-its-discontents:
Sigmund Freud wrote this short, famous study, and Joan Riviere made the authorized English translation. Cape and Harrison Smith published it in New York in 1930, and a second printing followed that October. Riviere thanks Anna Freud, Ernest Jones and James Strachey for careful revision of her manuscript.

Freud begins with a feeling reported to him by a friend, a sense of something boundless and oceanic. He tests that feeling against what he knows of the mind and of faith. The book argues that civil life demands hard curbs on human drives, and that those curbs leave a deep, lasting discontent in their place.
78254-silent-guests:
Silent Guests, a novel by Forrest, was published at Chicago in 1927. An odd motto stands at its head: what lurks behind the curtain, wouldst thou learn;. The first chapter is a confession. A mysterious thing, the human mind, the narrator begins. Can it keep a secret for ever?

Here he finds himself writing down things he had sworn never to reveal, sacred things with roots in the soul. These pages, he says, shall never meet a merely curious eye. They will be hidden away as a true record of the genesis of this house, unless fate decrees otherwise. He believes in fate, and holds us all its playthings. It was fate, he writes, that called him from a distant American city to a little churchyard in the Canadian backwoods. There a strange epitaph on an unknown grave drew him into a hidden realm.
78483-the-young-immigrunts:
Ring Lardner the younger tells a trip in The Young Immigrunts, printed at Indianapolis with copyright in 1920. Bobbs Merrill made the book, with a preface by the father and portraits by Gaar Williams. The spelling is a child's own, kept on purpose from title to tail.

Eleven chapters map a family drive east. My Parents and Starting Gaily lead, then Erie Lake. Legs from Buffalo to Rochester and from Syracuse to Hudson carry comic distances in the contents. My Father's Idear gets a chapter of its own. The Bureau of Manhattan and a run to Grenitch close the road. Plates show grandmother at Goshen, uncle and aunt in Detroit, a policeman at Albany, and the landlady. Young readers get a road trip told at knee height.
78684-some-nigerian-fertility-cults:
Some Nigerian Fertility Cults, by Amaury Talbot, a resident official in Nigeria, was printed by the Oxford University Press in 1927. A frontispiece shows Omone, son of Chief Benebo of Buguma, in the costume of the Peri play. Forty seven illustrations crowd the list of plates, from drums and shrines to clay figures and wrestling scenes.

Nine chapters structure the survey. The Great Drum opens it, and three chapters then treat the Mbari houses and their clay figures. Sky God and Earth Goddess follows, then the cults named Ibudu and Eku, the yam cult, and a closing chapter on Ale and the ancestors. Plates show the earth goddess Ale represented by a shape draped with blood stained linen and ringed with skulls in her shrine.
78736-dethronements:
Dethronements, by Laurence Housman, presents imaginary portraits of political figures in the form of dialogues. Housman had written Angels and Ministers in the same vein. Jonathan Cape published the book in London in 1922, in an edition of seven hundred fifty numbered copies.

Three plays fill the volume. The King-Maker, set at Brighton in October 1891, shows Charles Stewart Parnell in his last days. A note first reminds readers how the divorce decree, Gladstone's letter, and the split of the Irish Party brought Parnell down. The Man of Business is set at Highbury in August 1913. The Instrument moves to Washington in March 1921. Each dialogue catches a leader at the moment when power slips away, and the talk does the portrait work.
78798-the-battle-of-harlem-heights:
Emmet's paper on the Battle of Harlem Heights was reprinted from The Magazine of History with Notes and Queries for September 1906. It answers a New York Evening Post article on the fight, and it backs the account of the ground given in Professor Johnston's monograph.

The new proof is a diary extract from Lieutenant Samuel Richards of a Connecticut regiment. Richards tells of the retreat from Long Island in August 1776. He then tells of throwing up works on Harlem Heights on the night of September 15. He puts the enemy in the plain below at a force said to exceed twenty thousand, and the party beaten back under Colonel Knowlton at about five thousand. The American loss, he says, was about thirty killed and sixty or seventy wounded.
78872-the-divine-and-moral-songs-of-isaa:
The Divine and Moral Songs of Isaac Watts is a bibliographical study by Wilbur Macey Stone. It was privately printed for The Triptych at New York in 1918. Stone's essay is followed by notes and lists of British and American editions. A portrait of Watts, engraved by Bartolozzi, fronts the book.

Stone says the work grew from his hobby of collecting old children's books. He had meant to publish in 1915, the two-hundredth anniversary of the Songs' first edition.
