War delayed the book until 1919 was at hand. He notes that the hundredth anniversary was marked by the battle of Waterloo. The two-hundredth found Europe in a conflict beside which Waterloo seemed boys' play. No newspaper paragraph, he complains, marked the anniversary in 1915.
79018-outline-of-mexican-popular-arts-an:
Katherine Anne Porter's Outline of Mexican Popular Arts and Crafts was published at Mexico City in May 1922. It accompanied the Traveling Mexican Popular Arts Exposition in the United States, held under Mexico's Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Labor, with Xavier Guerrero as art director. Photographs come from Roberto Turnbull's collection, and the cover design is Guerrero's. Part one treats the pre-Hispanic roots of the art.

Porter argues that Mexico's past is interwoven visibly with its present: the descendants of the early Mexicans survive, almost pure in strain, after centuries of alien rule. They conformed outwardly to an imposed religion while mingling ancient meanings with its rituals, and wrought in the strangers' designs while keeping their own racial soul. Foreign influences, she says, were always slowly transformed into something incorruptibly Mexican. The decorated jars of Tonala illustrate the text.
79038-fables-of-sop-and-other-eminent-my:
Fables of Aesop and Other Eminent Mythologists is Sir Roger L'Estrange's English version of the classic beast tales, with morals and reflections attached. The third edition, corrected and amended, was printed in London in 1669 for a consortium of booksellers. A later reprint by John Gray and Company keeps the spelling and grammar of 1669 unchanged.

An alphabetical table sends readers to each fable by number: the Ant and the Fly, the Ant and the Grasshopper, the Ape and the Fox. L'Estrange appends a moral and a reflection to every tale, turning Aesop into a teacher of conduct. The transcriber notes that some fables are missing from the index while others appear twice. The book served Restoration England as both story collection and conduct manual, in deliberately old dress.
79164-american-honey-plants:
Frank Pellett wrote American Honey Plants, published by the American Bee Journal at Hamilton, Illinois, in 1920. Pellett had already written books on queen rearing and on practical bee keeping. His subject here is the plants that bees work, both for nectar and for pollen, across America.

Pellett notes that Professor Cook put the number of such plants at nearly eighteen hundred species. Most yield too little, or grow too thinly, to matter to a working keeper. Real honey crops rest on a few rich and common plants. Pellett urges keepers to learn the plants near their apiaries, their bloom times, and how a move of a few miles can save a crop when the main source fails.
79213-the-natural-history-of-ants:
Huber of Geneva wrote a natural history of ants, Englished by Johnson with added notes and printed at London in 1820. Huber was a member of the physical and natural history society of Geneva and a fellow of kindred bodies. The translator gives the book to his father James Johnson in token of filial respect. Four kinds of ants stand in a front plate.

Since the pages went to press, the translator prints a letter from the author. Huber had often re witnessed what he describes, he says, and affirms he was led aside neither by a fertile fancy nor by a love of the marvellous. Some facts seem romantic, he owns. Ant wars, slaves, milk cows of aphids, and nests built with craft fill a classic of close watching.
79279-the-graveyard-rats:
Henry Kuttner writes a horror tale in The Graveyard Rats, from the March 1936 issue of Weird Tales. The head blurb warns of a gruesome fate for the old caretaker of the cemetery. It waits in the horrible burrows beneath the graves.

Old Masson keeps one of the oldest, most neglected cemeteries of Salem. He has a feud with the rats. They came from the wharves long ago and settled in the yard, a colony of huge rats. Traps, poison, and shot have all failed to shift them. Some are as large as good sized cats. Their tunnels are wide enough for a man to crawl in on hands and knees. The last caretaker vanished, and no one knows how.
79318-virginia-s-wild-oats:
F E Baily wrote Virginia's Wild Oats, a novel issued at Indianapolis by the Bobbs-Merrill Company, with copyright of 1923 and 1924. The tale opens in the drawing-room at Wynwood, where the Honorable Virginia Lauriston speaks in her clear voice to Sir Charles Gillespie. A girl, she tells him, is not of need a fool just because she is a girl. The room's furniture was looted at the sack of a palace, and Titian's Pink Lady hangs on its south wall.

Virginia, twenty and dressed in old-rose, perches on a carved and gilded chair and teases Charles about little Vingie. Sir Charles, near sixty, a bachelor formed by Eton, the Guards, and embassy after embassy, smiles a smile no one can copy. Baily writes a light society comedy of a bold young woman and the older world she runs against.
79475-blue-jackets:
Kingston wrote Blue Jackets, or Chips of the Old Block, printed in London in 1854. The subtitle calls it a narrative of the gallant exploits of British seamen and of the principal events in the naval service during the reign of Queen Victoria. Kingston had written Peter the Whaler, Mark Seaworth, and Manco, the Peruvian Chief. A preface explains that the pages give accounts of gallant actions by naval men since Victoria came to the throne, not a complete naval history.

His chief object, Kingston writes, was to show that the present Navy has in no respect fallen away from that of olden times. The Blue Jackets of today, officers and men, have been found ready to dare and to do as was dared and done of yore.
79579-ukraine-under-the-soviets:
Clarence Manning, associate professor of Slavic languages at Columbia University, wrote Ukraine Under the Soviets for Bookman Associates of New York in 1953. A company of Ukrainian scholars stands behind the volume, with named chapters on law, economics, agriculture, language, literature, medicine, and religion. Manning's own chapters carry the story in order.

They run from the background of the communist triumph through the founding of the Ukrainian Soviet Republic, militant communism, and the New Economic Policy. Ukrainization, the literary renaissance, and the scholar Khvylovy follow, then the Five Year Plan and two chapters on the famine. Trials, the German attack, and the war years close the account. Manning opens flatly: the destruction of the Ukrainian National Republic, which had declared independence on January 22, 1918, was never the choice of the Ukrainian people.
7999-the-bible-king-james-version-comple:
Despite its title, the text hosted here runs from Genesis through the early chapters of 2 Chronicles, in the King James Version. It opens with creation, follows the patriarchs, the Exodus, the wilderness years, and the conquest, then traces Israel's judges and kings from Saul and David through Solomon. The run ends in the reign of Rehoboam, with Shishak of Egypt carrying off the treasures of the temple and the king's house.

Read as a continuous narrative, the volume carries the Bible's first great arc: a people chosen, delivered, settled, and divided. Its verse-numbered text suits steady, consecutive reading from the beginning. Readers should note the scope as it stands, since later books of the Bible are not included in this file.
8044-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Acts, the second volume addressed to Theophilus, picks up where Luke's Gospel ends, with Jesus risen and speaking of the kingdom for forty days. From Pentecost in Jerusalem, the story spreads outward: Peter preaches, Stephen is stoned, Philip meets an Ethiopian official. Saul the persecutor becomes Paul the apostle, and Paul carries the message through Asia Minor and Greece to Rome itself.

Luke writes Acts as a travel story and a church history in one, full of speeches, shipwrecks, trials, and escapes. It explains how a small Jewish sect became a movement across the Roman world. In the King James Version, its pace and drama make it the most readable history in the New Testament, and the bridge between the Gospels and the letters.
8079-pamela-giraud-a-play-in-five-acts:
Honoré de Balzac's play Pamela Giraud was first performed in Paris at the Théâtre de la Gaîté on September 26, 1843. Its persons include General de Verby, Dupré the lawyer, the merchant Rousseau and his son Jules. The porter Giraud, and Pamela Giraud herself, an artificial flower-maker whose attic workshop opens the first act. The scene is Paris during the Napoleonic plots under Louis XVIII, between 1815 and 1824.

The play turns on love, family pride, and political conspiracy, with police, magistrates, and gendarmes moving through its intrigues. Balzac, better known as a novelist, shows here his stagecraft and his eye for Parisian social types. For readers of his fiction, the play is a fascinating side piece, and a chance to see his characters speak rather than narrate.
8125-impressions-and-comments:
Havelock Ellis gathered these impressions and comments from notes made on random leaves over many years, on things in life and thought that chanced to strike his attention. His preface compares the notes to autumn leaves: having served their use, they no longer need to cling to the tree, so let them be scattered to the winds. He warns that such leaves cannot be judged as though they formed a book, since they are fragments, not a system.

The pieces range across psychology, literature, sex, society, and morals, in the voice of a humane and curious observer. Ellis, best known for his studies of human sexuality, here shows his wider mind. The book rewards dipping in at random, and it gives a candid portrait of an Edwardian thinker thinking aloud.
8196-under-the-skylights:
Henry Blake Fuller collected three stories under the skylights, with a prefatory note explaining that the final section. On Dr Gowdy and the squash, is reprinted by permission from Harper's Magazine, while the rest appears for the first time. The contents are The Downfall of Abner Joyce, Little O'Grady versus the Grindstone, and Dr Gowdy and the Squash. The first story opens with Abner Joyce taking a place in literature at once, when his first book, This Weary World, made readers feel fiction richer by one vital book.

Fuller's stories examine literary ambition, Chicago life, and the comedy of artistic failure. His prose is polished and ironic, in the manner of the American realist novel. For readers of Fuller and of Chicago fiction, the collection offers three sharp, well-made tales, and a portrait of authorship itself.
8202-sermons-on-national-subjects:
Charles Kingsley published Sermons on National Subjects in a first edition of 1880, reprinted in 1886 and again in this Macmillan edition of 1890. Its sermons begin with The King of the Earth, Holy Scripture, and The Kingdom of God, continue through Christmas, true abstinence, Good Friday. Easter, the Comforter, Whit Sunday, and Ascension Day, and include The Fount of Science and three sermons on the cholera. The subjects are national because Kingsley preached them as a citizen as well as a clergyman.

Kingsley argues that faith should speak to public life: to science, to sickness, and to the nation's duties. His preaching is vigorous, direct, and socially engaged, in the manner of the Christian Socialist movement he helped lead. For readers of Victorian religion, the volume shows a famous preacher addressing his country's crises from the pulpit.
8271-the-world-english-bible-web-acts:
Acts continues Luke's story after Jesus' resurrection, following his followers from Jerusalem out across the Roman world. The Holy Spirit falls on the apostles at Pentecost, Peter preaches to crowds, and the church grows amid arrests and miracles. Stephen's death scatters believers, and the gospel reaches Samaritans, an Ethiopian official, and a Roman officer.

The second half belongs to Paul: his conversion on the road to Damascus, three missionary journeys, shipwreck, and a final appeal in Rome. Acts is the church's earliest history, written with a storyteller's pace. Readers get both a travel narrative and an account of how a small Jewish sect became a movement spanning an empire.
839-new-arabian-nights:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these tales of London adventure in the manner of the Arabian Nights, where chance meetings lead to danger and romance. The Suicide Club opens the set, with a young man drawn into a secret society, and the Rajah's Diamond follows, with a stolen gem passing from hand to hand.

Stevenson writes with dash and wit, turning foggy streets into a stage for princes, doctors, and rogues. The tales are short, brisk, and full of surprise, and they show the young author finding his voice. The book delights readers who enjoy romance with a modern, urban twist, told by a master storyteller.
8397-expositions-of-holy-scripture-the-a:
Alexander MacLaren, the great Baptist preacher of Manchester, wrote these expositions on the Acts of the Apostles, chapters 1 to 12, verse by verse. Contents move from the Ascension and the forty days to Pentecost, the apostolic witnesses, and the growth of the Jerusalem church, with each passage turned into a sermon-length meditation.

MacLaren's method is textual and pastoral: he opens a verse, draws out its meaning, and presses it home to daily conduct. Generations of preachers kept his expositions on their desks as a model of clear, warm preaching. Readers get not a commentary for scholars, but sermons for the pew, grounded in the text and aimed at the heart.
841-men-women-and-ghosts:
Amy Lowell wrote these poems on men, women, and ghosts, in the free, vivid style that made her a leader of Imagism. The poems take small scenes, a room, a garden, a face, and let them grow into portraits of longing, pride, and loss. Ghosts here are memories as much as spirits, haunting the living.

Lowell writes with a painter's eye for colour and a musician's ear for rhythm, breaking lines to suit the thought. The collection shows her range, from tender lyrics to sharp character sketches. It remains a key volume for readers of modern American poetry, and for those who like verse that sees clearly and feels deeply.
8432-black-rebellion-five-slave-revolts:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson gathers five slave revolts in Black Rebellion, drawn from his Travellers and Outlaws, with an appendix of authorities. A transcriber's note confirms the five chapters are commonly called by this title, and Higginson's author's note frames episodes in American history where enslaved people rose against their bondage.

Higginson, an abolitionist minister and colonel of a Black regiment in the Civil War, wrote with sympathy for the rebels and care for sources. Readers get five episodes of resistance, told as history rather than romance. The book remains an early, important attempt to center enslaved people's agency in American history, written by a man who had fought beside them.
8599-fairy-tales-from-the-arabian-nights:
E. Dixon edited this first series of tales from the Arabian Nights, using the 1821 Galland text, lightly shortened for young readers. The selection opens with Persian princes and princesses of the sea, then moves through princes Ahmed and Camaralzaman, the story of Zobeide, and the voyages of Sinbad the Sailor. Each tale is told plainly, with the marvels left intact and the framing kept short.

Sinbad's seven voyages, full of strange islands, giant birds, and narrow escapes, anchor the second half of the book. Around them sit love stories, lost talismans, and fairy helpers, all in the Nights' familiar mix of adventure and moral turn. The volume suits readers meeting these tales for the first time, and it shows how Victorian editors shaped an old story collection for the nursery and the schoolroom.
8606-the-blue-bird-a-fairy-play-in-six-a:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote this fairy play about two poor children, Tyltyl and Mytyl, sent to find the Blue Bird of happiness, in Alexander Teixeira de Mattos's translation. A fairy sets them travelling with Light as their guide, while the dog, cat, bread, sugar, fire, water, and milk all take human shape and talk. Dead grandparents, Night, Time, and the Luxuries join the huge cast.

Across six acts the children visit the Land of Memory, the Palace of Night, and the Kingdom of the Future, always missing the bird they seek. The play's point lands at home: happiness was near all along, in kindness and in seeing familiar things with fresh eyes. Staged worldwide since its first success, it remains a gentle, strange fable that works for children on stage and for adults reading it as poetry.
8732-through-the-fray-a-tale-of-the-ludd:
G. A. Henty sets this tale in Marsden, Yorkshire, in 1807, where boys stream out of Mr Hathorn's academy at one o'clock in knee breeches and stiff, flat-topped caps. The schoolroom scene fixes a vanished England before the story moves into the Luddite riots, when textile workers smashed the machines they blamed for their hunger. A fishing expedition opens the book, but the fray soon claims its hero.

Through the hero's eyes, readers meet mill owners, workers, soldiers, and secret oath-bound bands, and learn how fear and anger spread through mill towns. Henty, writing for boys, sides with order while showing the workers' grievances plainly enough to follow. The novel gives a vivid, if partisan, introduction to one of Britain's first industrial conflicts, and to the world of early factories that made it.
8733-the-hermits:
Charles Kingsley tells the lives of the early Christian hermits in this 1891 Macmillan volume, first printed in parts in 1868. An introduction leads into Saint Antony, Paul the first hermit, Hilarion, and Arsenius, then the hermits of Asia, Basil, and Simeon Stylites on his pillar. Hermits of Europe follow, with Severinus, apostle of Noricum, the Celtic hermits, and Saint Malo, among others, and a picture of Saint Brendan setting sail.

Kingsley, clergyman and novelist, treats solitude as both heroic and strange, admiring the hermits' discipline while noting its excesses. The lives mix legend, history, and moral reflection, drawn from ancient sources retold for Victorian readers. Students of early Christianity will find a readable introduction to desert and island asceticism. General readers a set of vivid, sometimes startling portraits of men and women who fled the world to find God.
8832-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Weymouth's Acts opens as a sequel: Luke's former narrative, addressed to Theophilus, dealt with all Jesus did and taught as a beginning. Down to the day he was taken up to Heaven after instructing his chosen apostles through the Holy Spirit. After suffering, Jesus showed himself alive with many sure proofs, appearing at intervals during forty days and speaking of the kingdom of God. He charged the apostles not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the Father's promised gift.

John baptized with water, Jesus says, but before many days pass they will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. The story that follows carries the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome. Weymouth's plain English keeps Acts' travel, speeches, and conflicts moving briskly. Readers get the early Church's story whole, from Pentecost to Paul's house arrest, in a translation built for clarity rather than grandeur.
9374-a-knight-of-the-nets:
Amelia Barr wrote this fishing-village novel in 1896, set in Pittendurie, a place in Fife few travelers ever find. Grey sky and brown waters open the tale, as the narrator's heart flies back to northern seas and the winter rose of northern skies. Christina and Andrew lead the story, through an ailing heart and the lash of the whip.

A lost bride, a question of money, and a great deliverance follow, with the little Sophy near the end. Barr writes of fisherfolk with sympathy and grit. The novel remains a sturdy, romantic tale of the Scottish coast, its work, faith, and love.
9466-the-quest-of-happy-hearts:
Kathleen Hay wrote The Quest of Happy Hearts, a girls' tale of a visit to a great old house at Land's End. Nora and her friends, sent off while their father is away on business, face the trip with gloom. Their great-aunt Janice Meredith waits at a house set on the edge of a forest. What starts as a dull duty soon turns into a quest, with a tower room at its heart.

Chapters follow plans, forest walks, a party, and the tale of the tower room itself, as the girls add to their quest day by day. Marty and Jerry join the fun, and old secrets lend the house charm. A reader gets a warm, old-style girls' adventure, full of friendship, mystery, and the joy of a strange house explored.
9825-a-calendar-of-sonnets:
Helen Jackson, an American poet, arranged these sonnets by the months of the year, opening with January in 1886. Each poem takes one month's weather and mood, from winter's frozen pulse to summer roses and autumn quiet.

The sonnets are short, formal, and musical, and they ask readers to notice small changes: ice on streams, first warmth, harvest light, and the year's slow turn. Jackson keeps her language plain and her images close to nature. The little book works as a year in verse, meant to be read one month at a time, slowly, through all four seasons.
9838-strong-hearts:
George W. Cable wrote Strong Hearts in 1899, a book of tales on one principle, told three or four times over. Contents list The Solitary, The Taxidermist, and The Entomologist, with The Solitary first printed as Gregory's Island. Cable likens his tripled tale to Pharaoh's doubled dream: a thing established. Each story sets heroic natures and poetic fates to one universal truth.

The tales follow strong hearts through solitude, craft, and science, with Cable's Louisiana warmth. His prose favors moral poetry over mere plot. A reader gets a thoughtful set of linked stories, where courage proves itself in varied lives.
a-book-of-quaker-saints: Lucy Violet Hodgkin tells the lives of Quaker saints for young readers. Her chapters include the shepherd of Pendle Hill, the angel of Beverley, and the man in leather breeches. Each life shows steadfast faith, plain speech, and courage under trial in story form. The book presents these figures as models of a simple and faithful life.
a-brief-bible-history-a-survey-of-the-ol:
A Brief Bible History, published in 1922 by James Oscar Boyd and J Gresham Machen, surveys the history of the Old and New Testaments. The book presents that history as the story of God's redeeming grace. Its chapters trace the stream of God's redeeming purposes flowing down through the older, Old Testament times.

The survey then follows the same purpose broadening and deepening in the New Testament, in Jesus Christ and his Church. Boyd and Machen wrote as Bible teachers, and the book reads as a clear, ordered introduction for students. It gives readers the whole arc of scripture in brief compass, from the first histories to the early church, in one connected account.
a-calendar-of-sonnets: Helen Hunt Jackson writes a calendar of sonnets that follows the months of the year. Each poem takes its season as a theme, from winter snow and patient roses to summer streams and autumn fires. The verses link nature with love, loss, and the inner life in measured sonnet form. The collection offers a poem for the turning year, month by month.
a-catechism-of-familiar-things-their-his: This anonymous catechism explains familiar things, their history, and how they were discovered. In question and answer form it treats dew, rain, wind, lightning, corn, tea, coffee, cotton, wool, and many other everyday subjects. A short account of natural phenomena accompanies the history of each thing. Enlarged for schools and families, the book turns common objects into lessons in science and history.
a-family-man-in-three-acts:
A Family Man is a play in three acts by John Galsworthy, published in 1922. Galsworthy was an English novelist and playwright, viewed as one of the first writers of the Edwardian era, who challenged the ideals of the society that Victorian literature before him had depicted. He later won the Nobel Prize for Literature, and his Forsyte Saga became his most famous work.

On stage, this play puts a family man at the center of domestic tension. Galsworthy's drama typically sets private comfort against public duty and respectability, and A Family Man works that ground in three acts. The printed play preserves a piece of his Edwardian theatre, from the years when his stage work stood beside his novels in reputation.
a-girl-among-the-anarchists:
Isabel Meredith wrote A Girl Among the Anarchists from inside the London anarchist world she describes, and a preface by Morley Roberts insists that nothing in it is invented. The narrator tells her own story in the first person, beginning with a strange childhood and her arrival among the exiles, printers, and speakers of the movement.

Chapters follow a police scare, a rescue, the office of the paper called the Tocsin, and the escape of a dynamitard. Portraits of anarchist personalities sit beside meetings, flights, and quarrels over what the cause demands. The closing chapters bring a crisis and the last toll of the Tocsin, leaving a rare insider picture of a feared and mostly peaceful circle.
a-knight-of-the-nets: Amelia Barr writes a knight of the nets in a story of northern seas and hearts. Chapters follow Christina and Andrew through an ailing heart, the lash of the whip, and a lost bride. Questions of money, deliverance, and the righting of a wrong drive the plot. Barr sets her tale against grey skies and brown waters.
a-librarian-s-open-shelf-essays-on-vario: Arthur Elmore Bostwick opens a librarian's shelf of essays on various subjects. His pieces ask whether readers read, what makes people read, and how book titles change. Selective education, the uses of fiction, and modern education follow. Bostwick writes for librarians and book lovers about reading and libraries. Book lovers will enjoy these short talks on reading and libraries.
a-list-of-factorial-math-constants: A bare reference table of factorials, computed once by a simple Scheme program whose source code has been lost, as the file's own note explains. It gives every factorial from 1! through 99!, then jumps by hundreds to 900! and by thousands to 10,000!, printing each full value with its digit count. There is no prose beyond the heading notes. The file serves as ready-made big-number data for checking arithmetic, testing software, or satisfying curiosity about how fast factorials grow.
a-philological-essay-concerning-the-pygm: Edward Tyson examines the pygmies of ancient legend in this philological essay, newly edited with an introduction by Bertram Windle. Drawing on De Quatrefage's monograph and on facts gathered from other published sources, he brings forward tales chosen to establish his points about these small peoples of myth. The essay makes no claim to exhaust its literature, offering selected evidence rather than a complete survey.
acetaria-a-discourse-of-sallets: John Evelyn writes Acetaria, a discourse of sallets, in this reprint of the first edition of 1699, issued by the Women's Auxiliary of the Brooklyn Botanic Garden in 1937. The edition corrects a few typographical errors and incorporates the author's errata. It keeps the old-style S of the original. The Latin and Greek sprinkled through the treatise mark its author as a man of letters, praising salads as the first subject of his second volume of a garden manual.
airship-wave-1896-1897-press-accounts:
Seventeen newspaper pieces from 1896 and 1897 make up The Great Airship Wave of 1896-1897, drawn from the Library of Congress's Chronicling America scans. Reports from Sacramento, Oakland, San Francisco, and San Jose open the scare in November 1896. By April 1897 the wave rolled over Kansas, Omaha, and Chicago, with inventors claiming the sky craft as their own.

Editors argued, witnesses swore, and hoaxers confessed in the columns reprinted here word for word. Nothing real was ever found, which makes the papers themselves the true record. The set preserves the primary evidence of America's first great mystery-airship panic, decades before flying saucers.
albertus-magnus-admirables-secrets:
Secrets ascribed to Albert the Great fill this French chapbook of natural magic, in a 1729 printing. Recipes, charms, and wonders of nature promise help with health, love, luck, and beasts. For two centuries it ranked among France's most popular books of hidden knowledge among common folk.

Herbs, stones, and household tricks mix with spells and signs in its pages. Scholars doubt the great Albert wrote a word of it himself. That hardly mattered to the buyers who treasured its lore. The book opens a window on popular belief, where folk magic and medieval science blend without a seam.
an-english-garner-critical-essays-litera: Edward Arber gathers an English garner of critical essays and literary fragments, with an introduction by J. Churton Collins. The volume collects short pieces of English criticism and letters that illumine authors and their times. Arber's garnering preserves scraps that would otherwise be lost to general readers. The fragments repay a slow, browsing read.
anthology-of-massachusetts-poets:
William Stanley Braithwaite gathers the poets of Massachusetts into one anthology, arranged by author. The contents open with Joseph Auslander's Home Bound and Katherine Lee Bates's America the Beautiful and Yellow Clover. Gamaliel Bradford, Alice Brown, Grace Hazard Conkling, and the child poet Hilda Conkling all appear in the early pages.

The poems run from formal odes and sonnets to short lyrics on war, faith, gardens, and Boston streets. Braithwaite, himself a poet and the era's best-known anthologist of new verse, aimed to represent his state's living poetry rather than its classics alone. The book works as a snapshot of New England verse at the moment he made it.
arizona-nights:
Stewart Edward White gathers Western tales told in the voice of men who worked cattle country in Arizona. The table of contents names stories about rustlers, drives, branding, Texas Rangers, buried treasure, and a two-gun man. A storm over the mesas opens the first tale, and the dry land shapes every scene that follows.

The tales move between camp talk and longer linked stories, ending with a long section called The Rawhide. White writes plain speech, hard riding, and desert weather with the ease of a man who knew ranch life. The book preserves the talk and habits of the old Southwest cattle frontier.
artist-and-public-and-other-essays-on-ar: Kenyon Cox writes essays on the artist and the public, on Millet, Raphael, and Saint Gaudens, and on the American school. He defends craft, design, and tradition against what he calls the illusion of progress, and he judges new painting by old standards of form. Illustrations of Millet works anchor the talk in pictures readers can study. Cox speaks as a painter critic, direct, firm, and sure of his taste.
balfour-taoist-texts:
Frederic Henry Balfour gathered his Taoist Texts in English in 1884. His anthology sorts the writings by morals, rule, and deep thought. Victorian readers met the philosophy of the Way through books like this.

Short pieces from the Taoist tradition speak in Balfour's clear English. They teach softness over force, quiet rule, and scorn for mere show. Laozi's heirs prize the still mind above wealth and loud fame. Balfour's picks favor calm wisdom over magic and cult practice here. The book stands as an early Western window into Taoist thought and ethics. Its quiet counsel still speaks past its Victorian frame to readers.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-03-ancie:
John Lord's third Beacon Lights volume surveys ancient achievements, beginning with governments and laws. Greek and Roman law gets a long, ordered account. Lycurgus and Solon come first, then the Athenian Ecclesia and Rome's struggle between patricians and plebeians. The Twelve Tables lead to the great jurists and Justinian's Code, Pandects, and Institutes. Marriage, paternal power, slavery, and personal rights are all weighed.

Arts and crafts fill the later lectures. Egyptian bronze vases show great skill in compounding metals, highly polished, with knives and daggers springing like steel. Wilkinson's surprise at porcelain vessels, rich in colour and beautiful in shape, is quoted with admiration, one bowl in the British Museum singled out. Lord builds a Victorian progress report on the ancient world: law first, then the arts that law protected.
beasts-and-super-beasts:
Saki, the pen name of H. H. Munro, gathered Beasts and Super-Beasts in 1914, a book of short stories famous for their polish and bite. Saki sets polite Edwardian drawing rooms against sudden wildness: a hyena loose at a garden party, a cat that may carry a boy's soul, a pig that settles a garden feud. His beasts are often animals, and his super-beasts are often well-dressed people.

The set opens with The Story-Teller, in which a bachelor wins a train carriage of children with a tale about a horribly good little girl who gets eaten by a wolf. The Open Window, with its invented tale of a hunting tragedy, is also here. Few writers pack so much mischief into so few pages.
beautiful-thoughts:
Elizabeth Cureton arranged this devotional daybook from the writings of Henry Drummond, published in 1892 and inscribed to her friend Helen M. Archibald. Drummond, the Scottish evangelist and scientist, wrote in an epigrammatic style that lends itself to quotation. Cureton's preface hopes a taste of the spring will bring travellers back to the fountain at leisure. Entries run day by day through the year.

January opens on Christianity's wants; a July entry quotes Natural Law in the Spiritual World on man's dependence. Who would stay self-luminous, Drummond asks, knowing the Lord God is a sun? Who would keep a shallow vessel when Christ's well of living water stands open? Many extracts come from The Greatest Thing in the World, his famous meditation on love, though the editorial note admits their pages went unrecorded.
belinda-an-april-folly-in-three-acts:
A. A. Milne's Belinda, subtitled An April Folly in Three Acts, is a light comedy produced at the New Theatre, London, in April 1918. Belinda Tremayne, her daughter Delia, Harold Baxter, Claude Devenish, John Tremayne and the servant Betty make up its small cast.

The play is set in Belinda's Devonshire country house in late April. The first act plays in the garden, where Betty fastens a hammock for the season, and the later acts move into the hall. Milne, later famous for Winnie-the-Pooh, writes here in the witty, polished manner of the West End stage. Readers who enjoy drawing-room comedy will find Belinda charming and deft.
black-rebellion-five-slave-revolts:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson collected these five accounts of slave revolts from his Travellers and Outlaws, with an appendix of authorities. The Maroons of Jamaica and of Surinam open the volume: the word Maroon was once a word of peril, and terror spread along the skirts of the plantations. Gabriel's defeat, Denmark Vesey, and Nat Turner's insurrection bring the story to American soil.

Vesey's Charleston plot gets the closest narrative. Plans were to be announced only after the evening prayer-meetings on the appointed Sunday. Each leader had his company enlisted and his work marked out. When the clock struck twelve, all were to move: Peter Poyas would seize the arsenal and guard-house opposite St. Michael's Church, and detach men to cut off the city's exits. Higginson, who had commanded a Black regiment, writes slave resistance as military history, with sources, in 1889.
bracebridge-hall-or-the-humorists:
Washington Irving issued Bracebridge Hall, or The Humorists, as a two-volume medley under his Geoffrey Crayon pen name. Irving returns to Squire Bracebridge's hall, where the busy man, the widow, and Master Simon hold court. The subtitle names the cast: humourists, each ruled by one fond trait.

Volume one adds wives, story-telling, a stout gentleman, and a student of Salamanca to the hall sketches. Saint Mark's Eve and the library deepen the country-house world. Volume two roams wider, to English country gentlemen, graveyards, gypsies, and May Day customs. Dolph Heyliger and a storm-ship bring in full tales. Annette Delarbre and the haunted house close the set before the author's farewell to England. Crayon's peace blessing ends the medley.
brandes-eminent-authors-of-the-nineteent:
Brandes set aside his grand survey to write vivid portraits of leading nineteenth-century authors, gathered here in English. Many of his subjects were people he had met or known well. Memory and judgment mix in each sketch.

A portrait by Brandes is no dry summary of dates and books. He seeks the ruling passion of a mind and shows it at work. Praise and blame both come sharp and clear from his pen. The book pairs well with Main Currents, giving readers the critic as portrait painter, working from life as much as from the page.
britannica-1911-abraum-salts: Abraum Salts is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the name, from German Abraum-salze, salts to be removed, to a mixed deposit of salts. Halite, carnallite, and kieserite stand among its named members, with others left under an et cetera. The deposit lies in association with rock-salt at Stassfurt in Prussia, the entry states. One tight notice thus fixes the mining term, its German sense, and its famous Prussian home for readers meeting it in salt literature.
britannica-1911-accountants:
Accountants treats the expert in the science of book-keeping, and insists the title means more than a clerk who keeps books. A true accountant can design and control the systems of accounts that record the rapid transactions of trade and finance. Accountancy, as the long 1911 entry defines it, records every dealing in money or money's worth, prepares statistics, and works out the cost of operations on correct bases.

History and duties fill most of the article. Auditors appear in statutes from the reign of Edward I, and the first English book on the science appeared in 1543. Practising accountants serve as trustees, liquidators, receivers, and arbitrators, prepare bankruptcy statements, and build accounts for fraud prosecutions.
britannica-1911-adiaphorists:
Adiaphorists were a party in a Lutheran quarrel over things called indifferent, points that Scripture does not command or ban. The 1911 Britannica article sets the scene in 1548. That year the emperor Charles the Fifth sanctioned a stop-gap plan of faith at Augsburg. It pleased neither Catholics nor Protestants. The elector Maurice then won Melanchthon and others to accept the plan as to such side points. That soft form was known as the Leipzig Interim.

Its backers took the name Adiaphorists as a term of scorn. A fierce foe, Flacius, held that no earthly power could judge such points. He charged that the plan was a trick to bring back Rome. He fled to Magdeburg and made it the seat of stiff Lutheran faith. The peace of Augsburg in 1555 closed the clash in fact. Bitter strife on the bare point ran on for years more.
britannica-1911-angel-lights: Angel-lights, in architecture, are the outer upper lights in a perpendicular window. They are the small panes next to the springing, where the arch begins to rise. The name is probably a corruption of angle-lights. These upper lights are nearly triangular in shape. That one point explains the term. It joins a window word to its likely origin. It also rests on the shape of the panes themselves. The note is the whole of this short entry.
britannica-1911-annalists:
Annalists were a class of Roman history writers. Their name comes from annus, a year. Annales means annual records. They were active from the Second Punic War. Their activity lasted until Sulla's time. Most wrote Rome's history from the beginning. They carried it down to their own days. Recent events received much fuller detail. State and family records supplied their material.

The annales maximi stood behind them all. Rome's chief priest kept that official chronicle. He recorded each year's notable occurrences. The Gallic burning of Rome destroyed them. Restorers reconstructed them as far as possible. Publication finally came in eighty books. Two generations of annalists are distinguished. The older wrote plainly before 150 B.C. Their style was bald and unattractive. Cicero still grants them a certain trustworthiness. The entry traces the younger generation too.
britannica-1911-anti-federalists:
Anti-Federalists is the name given in the history of the United States to those who fought the new federal Constitution of 1787. They opposed its passage by the people of the states. The group was never set up as a true party. It drew in men who prized the rights of the states, men who prized the single person, and men of a strong free bent. They feared that a strong central rule would harm the states.

Some feared for the trade or local gain of their own places. Some feared for the liberties of each man. Some saw in the plan a new crown in disguise, set to take the place of British rule. In each state the fight against the plan was strong.
britannica-1911-argonauts:
Argonauts were the heroes who sailed with Jason for the golden fleece. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica retells why that fleece hung in Colchis. Jason uncle had seized the throne that was his father right. That uncle set the quest as a task to be rid of him.

The fleece came from a ram that had saved two children. One child drowned in a strait still called by her name. The other reached Colchis and hung the fleece in a grove. A sleepless dragon guarded it there night and day. Jason called the noblest heroes of Greece to the voyage. Fifty oars matched the fifty crew of the ship Argo. Athena herself watched over the building of that ship. A talking oak beam from Dodona sat in its prow.
britannica-1911-arts-and-crafts:
Arts and crafts is a broad title for the arts of fine design and hand work. With the mother craft of building, they go to the making of the house fair. Full accounts of each craft are found under their own heads in the book. The words are also tied to a movement in England for the rise of fine art in goods. That movement began about 1875, as a revolt.

The title came into common use when the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society was set up. That body held its first show at the New Gallery in London in the autumn of 1888. Since then, such shows have been common all over Britain. The plan for a society grew out of a revolt against the Royal Academy shows. In those shows, oil paintings in gilt frames took near all the room.
britannica-1911-assets:
Assets, in English law, is defined in a law entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word comes from a French term that means enough. In strict use it means the property of a person in debt that can pay those who are owed. The fund left by a bankrupt man is the clearest case. All of his property counts, even goods he has not yet taken in hand.

The entry then sorts who gets paid first. A secured lender, such as a mortgage holder, is paid from his own security first. Any sum left over then goes to lenders with no security. Since an act of 1869, those unsecured lenders all rank the same. The text also splits assets into legal and equitable kinds. That split turns on which court a lender had to use to claim payment.
britannica-1911-assignats:
Assignats is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a paper money of France. Assignats were issued in France from 1789 to 1796. They took their name from land assigned to their holders. The financial strait of the French government in 1789 was extreme. Coin was scarce, and loans were not taken up. Taxes had ceased to be productive in that crisis. 

In that emergency assignats were issued as a substitute for coin. They were at first like mortgage bonds on national lands. Those lands were church property confiscated by the Assembly. Mirabeau had moved that confiscation in November 1789. Crown lands taken over by the nation also backed them. The assignats were first to be paid to state creditors. The entry opens the history of a famous war time currency. Its backing in seized land sets it apart from plain notes.
britannica-1911-athletic-sports:
Athletic sports were grown by Egyptians and by peoples of Asia many hundreds of years before the Christian era. The early Greeks took the roots of their training from them. Greek games reached their height in the Olympic games and like meetings. The first Celtic folk of Britain were a hardy, active race. Early Teutonic tales are full of feats of strength and skill.

After the Norman conquest of England, nobles gave their time to the chase and the joust. The common folk kept their ball games, races, wrestling, and bouts with club and buckler on green and river bank. Scribes of later ages say little of folk sports. They note archery, since it trained men for war. They dwell instead on the feats of kings and their courts. Henry V, for one, is said to have been a swift runner.
britannica-1911-augustinian-hermits:
Augustinian Hermits, or Friars, are a religious order in the Roman Catholic Church. Their order entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. In the early thirteenth century, small hermit groups lived in central Italy. Each group kept its own rule of life in those early years.

Popes in about twelve fifty urged those groups to join as one body. The new order lived by the Rule of Saint Augustine as its base. Leaders were chosen by chapter, with heads for each land under them. The friars soon left wild places and lived in towns as groups. The order spread fast to forty provinces and two thousand houses.
britannica-1911-baptists:
Baptists, a body of Christians, are the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Their name points to the view that sets them apart from other churches. All Baptists hold that baptism should be given to believers only. Among most modern Baptists the manner is also distinct: the person is dipped under the water. Some groups, such as the Mennonites, still pour or sprinkle.

The article is careful to add that dipping is not theirs alone. Churches that baptize infants have always allowed it as a lawful mode, and the Orthodox Eastern Church uses no other. The entry then divides its tale into two groups in Europe. One is the Anabaptists, by then all but gone. The other is the modern Baptists, whose churches stood in nearly every land in Europe and beyond.
britannica-1911-batement-lights: Batement lights are an architectural term defined in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In a perpendicular window, the tall late Gothic window divided by upright bars, the batement lights are the lights in the upper part of the window. A light here means one glass pane section of the window. These upper lights are abated, that is cut down, to only half the width of the lights set below them in the same window.
britannica-1911-bollandists:
The Bollandists are the Belgian Jesuits who publish the Acta Sanctorum, the vast ordered collection of saints' lives and legends. Heribert Rosweyde first planned the work and set out his scheme in 1607, meaning to print manuscript lives in eighteen volumes with sober notes. He died in 1629 with much gathered but nothing begun.

John Bolland took the work to Antwerp and widened it. The two January volumes came out in 1643, and month by month the series grew, with Henschenius and then Papebroch as partners. Papebroch's sharp criticism made enemies and needed defence. The work stopped when the Jesuits were suppressed, wandered to Brussels and Tongerloo, and was taken up again in 1837 with Belgian state support.
britannica-1911-bottle-brush-plants: Bottle-brush plants are Australian shrubs of the myrtle family, known to botanists as Callistemon. The short entry explains the common name at once. The head of flowers looks like a brush for cleaning bottles. Their beauty comes not from petals, which are small, but from the many long, thread-like stamens that stand far out from the flower. Gardeners knew them well as greenhouse shrubs in Britain. One kind is picked out for use, not looks: Callistemon salignus yields a valuable hard wood.
britannica-1911-burial-and-burial-acts:
Burial and the Burial Acts are set out as English law in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word burial comes from an Old English root meaning to protect or cover. The article states the main lines of the law shortly. Every person may be buried in the ground of the parish where he dies.

Executed felons form the one exception to that right of parish burial. At common law, the householder where a death occurs must see the body decently covered. Executors must bury the dead in a manner fit for his estate. They are not bound to follow the wishes he left behind him. The disposal must not risk the health of the living. Cremation, under proper limits, is held allowable in law. Burial costs are paid from the estate before all other debts. A run of statutes, the Burial Acts, followed from 1852 to 1900.
britannica-1911-buriats:
Buriats is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on a Mongolian people who live near Lake Baikal. Most dwell in the government of Irkutsk and in the Trans Baikal Territory. They are split into tribes or clans that most often take their names from the places they frequent. Those groups are split again by kinship.

The entry describes their build and dress in the manner of its day. Men shave their heads and wear a pigtail in the Chinese style. In summer they dress in silk and cotton gowns, and in winter in furs and sheepskins. Their chief work is the raising of cattle and horses. The Buriat horse is famed for its power to endure, and the bond between master and horse is very great, the article says.
britannica-1911-cagots:
The Cagots were a cast out people found in the Basque lands, Bearn, Gascony, and Brittany. The first note of them in record dates to the late twelve hundreds. They then bore a name that meant Christians. In later ages they had a host of names in French, Spanish, and Breton speech.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists the foul tales told of them in the middle ages. Folk held them to be weak in mind and sick with leprosy. Folk held them false in faith, and worse. Shunned and hated, they were set in split quarters in towns. In the fields they lived in poor huts apart from villages. Barred from all rights, they could enter a church only by a side door. They sat apart by a rail, and took the rite, if at all, on the end of a stick.
britannica-1911-castanets:
Castanets is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on instruments of percussion used to mark the rhythm in dancing. They came into Europe from the East through the Moors by way of Spain. Castanets are always used in pairs, one in each hand. Each pair consists of two pear or mussel shaped bowls of hard wood, hinged by a silk cord looped over the thumb and first finger.

The player strikes the two halves together with the other fingers in single, double, or triple beats, making hollow clicks of no fixed pitch. For orchestra use the pairs are mounted on a wooden stick about eight inches long. Military bands use a spring frame fixed to a side drum, worked with a drumstick. The entry cites their use in the Habanera in Carmen. It also notes a quaint account with a sketch in a British Museum manuscript by Randle Holme, dated before 1688.
britannica-1911-cauterets:
Cauterets is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a watering place in south western France, in the department of Hautes Pyrénées, 20 miles south by west of Lourdes by rail. Its population in 1906 was 1030. The town lies in the fine valley of the Gave de Cauterets. It is well known for its rich thermal springs, used against diseases of the breathing organs, rheumatism, and skin complaints, among many others.

The springs number twenty four, and nine bathing establishments serve them. Their waters carry sulphur and silicate of soda, and their heat runs from 75 to 137 degrees Fahrenheit. Cauterets also serves as a centre for mountain excursions. The Monné, the Cabaliros, the Pic de Chabarrou, and the Vignemale, at 10,820 feet, all stand in its neighbourhood. The short entry joins the spa's medical draw with the peaks that frame its valley.
britannica-1911-cinque-ports:
The Cinque Ports were an old league of ports on the south coast of England. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists the first five: Hastings, Romney, Hythe, Dover, and Sandwich. Two more towns, Winchelsea and Rye, later joined with the same rights. Many smaller places hung on each port as limbs or members. Some of those members lay far inland. The league's reach ran along the coast from Seaford to near Margate.

The league grew from a need for sea defence. In an age with no standing fleet, the crown leaned on these ports. They held special rights in trade for their service at sea. By 1911 the body kept its shape but with shrunk power. The entry works through long lists of member towns for each port. It shows how a port's limbs could sit under its courts. Free members ruled their own ground much like the ports themselves.
britannica-1911-clay-with-flints:
Clay-with-flints is a term in geology for a stiff clay of red, brown, or yellow hue. The name was given by W. Whitaker in 1861. The clay holds whole flints that show no wear, as well as sharp, shattered bits of flint. It also holds a mixed share of rounded flint, quartz, and other pebbles. The deposit is found in sheets or patches over a large part of the south of England.

That area runs from Hertfordshire in the north to Sussex in the south, and from Kent in the east to Devon in the west. The clay near always lies on the face of the Upper Chalk. In Dorset it spreads to the Middle and Lower Chalk. Many students of rocks have held that the clay is the dregs left by the slow melting away of the chalk.
britannica-1911-cutts-of-gowran-john-cut:
John Cutts, Baron Cutts of Gowran, is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a British soldier and author. He lived from 1661 to 1707. He came of an Essex family of some standing. He had a short career at Catherine Hall, Cambridge. But he showed a clear taste for court and camp. A double ambition drove his first work in print.

He wanted fame in both arms and in letters. His first book came out in 1685. It pled the cause of gentlemen who made poetry a pastime. Next year he served as a volunteer in Hungary. He served under Charles of Lorraine in that war. He is said to have planted the imperial standard first at Buda. Its walls were stormed in July 1686. In 1687 he published a book of verse. Next year he served as lieutenant colonel in Holland.
britannica-1911-cyprinodonts:
Cyprinodonts, a group of small fishes, are the subject of a nature article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In spite of their name, they are in no way kin to the carp family. They are near allies of the pike, marked by a flat head, a mouth that can push out, and large scales. About two hundred kinds are known. Most live in the fresh and brackish waters of America, and only about thirty in the old world.

The article notes that many kinds bear their young alive, a trait rare in fishes. Their small size and lively ways make them prized for the aquarium. In many kinds the male and female differ, the female being larger and duller, with smaller fins. One strange group from Central and South America has eyes that jut out and are split in two by a band across them.
britannica-1911-emblements:
Emblements, from the Old French for corn sprung above ground, is a term of English law for the corn and other crops raised each year by labour, not by nature alone. Such crops belong to the class called fructus industriales, or industrial growing crops. They include corn and grain of all kinds, and hemp, flax, hops, potatoes, and sown grasses like clover. Fruit growing on trees is left out, since it follows the rule that what is planted in the soil goes with the soil.

Where a holding of unsure length ends without warning, by the tenant's death or another event not of his making, the law gives his personal representative the crop's profit. The entry notes that the right lost its weight in England in 1851. The Landlord and Tenant Act of that year instead lets a rack-rent tenant hold the land until his tenancy year runs out.
britannica-1911-epsom-salts:
Epsom salts is a chemical salt made of magnesium and sulphur, with water bound in it. It occurs dissolved in sea water and in most mineral waters of note. The waters at Epsom, from which it takes its name, hold it in plenty. It also occurs in nature as a fibrous crust called epsomite or hair salt. Compact masses of it are found in the mines at Stassfurt in Germany.

The salt is also found with limestone, as in the Mammoth Caves of Kentucky. It grows in crystals of a set system, like the zinc and nickel salts. In the arts it is used to weight cotton cloth in making. In farming it serves as a top dressing for clover hay fields. In medicine it is often used as a strong purgative for patients. It is prized in fever cases and in the constipation of painters.
britannica-1911-fine-arts:
Fine Arts, in the 1911 Britannica, is a long essay that sets out what the term covers and where its edge lies. The group holds five greater arts: architecture, sculpture, painting, music, and poetry. Lesser arts such as dancing and the drama stand beside them. In old times they were not named or marked off as a class at all.

The usual account says these arts serve the love of beauty, not basic needs. The essay shows that this falls short. Caricature and the grotesque are fine art, yet no love of beauty explains them, and even the terrible can fall within fine art when handled with meaning. In their place the essay puts a wider account: these arts spring from a drive to make things for a pleasure apart from use.
britannica-1911-franklin-massachusetts:
Franklin is a township of Norfolk county, Massachusetts, covering 29 square miles of rolling ground. Its population was 5017 in 1900 and 5641 in the census of 1910. The main village, also called Franklin, lies about 27 miles south-west of Boston on the New York, New Haven and Hartford railway.

The town has a public library in the Ray memorial building, holding 7700 volumes in 1910, and is the seat of Dean Academy, founded in 1865. Local works turn out straw goods, felt, cotton and woollen goods, pianos, and printing presses. Franklin was set off from Wrentham and incorporated in 1778, the first of many American places named for Benjamin Franklin. Horace Mann was born here.
britannica-1911-free-baptists:
Free Baptists are an American denomination, once called Freewill Baptists, holding Baptist views against infant baptism and against Calvin teaching. Their creed is much that of the General Baptists of Britain, stressing general redemption for all. Many early churches in Rhode Island and the South held such views, and a conference of this branch met at Newport in 1729.

The organised body rose in 1779-1780, when Benjamin Randall led seceders in New Hampshire towns and was ordained in 1780. Growth came between 1820 and 1830 across New England and the Middle West, and other open-communion groups joined in 1841 and after. The denomination founded Hillsdale, Bates, Rio Grande, and Parker colleges. At the close of 1909 it counted 1303 churches and 73,536 members, and its Boston journal, the Morning Star, dated from 1826.
britannica-1911-ghats:
Ghats are two ranges of hills that run by the coasts of India in this 1911 Britannica land entry. The word first meant passes or shore steps, then came to name the hills. The Eastern Ghats run in broken spurs down the Madras coast. They stand well back from the sea in most parts. Great rivers such as the Godavari cut through their line.

The Western Ghats form a more firm wall by the west coast. Save for one gap at Palghat, the range runs unbroken to the south tip. That gap bears the main rail line of the south. West slopes rise steep from the sea, while east slopes fall in a soft grade. High tops in the north pass five thousand feet, and a hill town serves as a summer seat.
britannica-1911-girondists:
Girondists were a political party of the French Revolution, active in the Legislative Assembly and the National Convention from 1791 to 1793. The 1911 Britannica entry warns that they were less an organized party than a group holding opinions in common. Their name came from the brilliant deputies sent from the Gironde.

Twelve such deputies are counted, six of them named: the lawyers Vergniaud, Guadet, Gensonné, Grangeneuve and Jay, and the tradesman Ducos. Around them gathered allies from other parts of France, among them Condorcet, Brissot, Roland and Petion. Madame Roland's salon was their meeting place, and her influence on their spirit and policy is called powerful. The long article then follows their rise, their advanced but not yet republican views, and their course through the Revolution.
britannica-1911-gloucester-massachusetts:
Gloucester, a city and port in Essex county, Massachusetts, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands on Cape Ann with a fine rocky shore. Its people numbered 26,121 in 1900 and 24,398 in 1910. Many were foreign-born, led by English Canadians. The city covers about fifty-four square miles. Its rugged coast has made it a loved summer resort.

Several villages lie within the city borders. Annisquam, Bay View, and Magnolia are chief among them. Near Magnolia lies a deep, narrow chasm in the rocks. A wreck site nearby is famed through a Longfellow poem. Trade by sea is small beside the fishing. Fishing has been the city's main work since colonial days. Cod, mackerel, herring, and halibut fill the year. Gloucester is the top fishing port in the United States. The catch of 1905 was worth over three million dollars.
britannica-1911-haverhill-massachusetts:
Haverhill is a city of Essex county, Massachusetts. It stands on the Merrimac river at the head of navigation. Boston lies 33 miles to the south. The 1910 census counted 44,115 people. The city runs ten miles along the river. It rises picturesquely from the banks over round hills. Fifteen public parks lie within its limits. Winnikenni Park, at 214 acres, is the largest. Its public library held about 90,000 volumes in 1908.

Boots, shoes and slippers dominate the city's industry. Haverhill is one of the world's largest producers of finer footwear. Woollen mills grew from an 1835 foundation. Woollen hats have been made since the mid-18th century. Morocco factories and a two-century-old brickmaking trade also figure. Bradford Academy for girls dates from 1803. The town incorporated in 1645 and became a city in 1869. A commission charter was adopted in 1908.
britannica-1911-hesychasts:
The Hesychasts were a quietistic sect of the later Byzantine empire, formed among Greek church monks, above all at Mount Athos. Their name comes from a Greek word for quiet. Their method was stark. Alone in his cell, the monk sat with chin on breast and thought turned to the navel, seeking the place of the heart. Kept up day and night, the search was promised to end in joy and a mystic light.

About 1337 Barlaam, a Calabrian monk, attacked the claim made for that light. The Hesychasts held it was God's own essence, the light shown on Mount Tabor at the transfiguration. To Barlaam that meant two eternal substances, a visible and an invisible God. Gregory Palamas took up the defence, and for a few years the quarrel gave the sect great weight in church and state.
britannica-1911-ipswich-massachusetts:
Ipswich, a township in Essex county in Massachusetts, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on both banks of the Ipswich river, north-east of Boston. The census of 1910 counted five thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven people. Low hills, vales, meadows, sand dunes, and tidal marsh spread across its face.

The entry dwells on the old houses and famed names of the town. The John Whipple House, of the sixteen hundreds, holds a hoard of antiques. Mary Lyon taught at the girls' school that once stood there and planned her own school on the spot. The town was founded in 1633 by John Winthrop the younger and twelve more. Its aim was to keep the French from the north of Massachusetts. Nathaniel Ward, who drew the first code of laws for New England, had his home by the common.
britannica-1911-mechitharists:
Mechitharists is the subject of a church entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name covers a body of Armenian monks. Those monks stand in union with the Church of Rome. Their founder, Mechithar, was born in Armenia in 1676. He joined a monastery as a young man in faith. Western envoys stirred in him a bold new plan. He sought to spread Western thought in Armenia.

He also sought to join his church with the Latin Church. In 1701 he formed a firm body with sixteen companions. Foes at home forced the group to move more than once. They built a monastery in the Morea in 1706. War then drove them on to Venice in Italy. An island there became their base in 1717. Mechithar died there in 1749 with his work made firm. Their rule drew in time on the Benedictine rule.
britannica-1911-menai-straits:
Menai Straits is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a channel of the Irish Sea. It splits Anglesea from Carnarvonshire in north Wales. The channel runs fourteen miles from Beaumaris to Abermenai point. Its breadth shifts from two hundred yards to two miles.

Two great bridges that cross it give the strait its fame. The suspension bridge bears the Holyhead road from Bangor town. Telford drew its plans, and work began in the year 1819. The first chain went over in April 1825, the last in July. It opened to the public on the 30th of January 1826. The roadway hangs one hundred feet above high water mark.
britannica-1911-milford-massachusetts:
Milford is a township in Massachusetts, south east of Worcester. Its count of folk in nineteen ten was past thirteen thousand. A town of the same name stands on a stream in its bounds, served by three rail lines and by electric cars. A hall that holds the town book store and a good house for the sick are named.

The town ships farm and mill goods to a wide tract. Boots and shoes lead its trades, a craft set up in seventeen ninety-five. Scores of stone pits work a pink grey stone prized for builds. The tract was the east part of a town till seventeen eighty.
britannica-1911-mountjoy-barons-and-visc:
Mountjoy, Barons and Viscounts, is the line traced in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica from Sir Walter Blount. He died in fourteen seventy four and held land in Derbyshire. He took his father post at Calais in fourteen sixty. A year later he was made head of that town as a prize for help in a great battle.

The king gave him rich lands seized from a fallen earl. In fourteen sixty five he was raised to a baron. That grant is marked as an early case of a rank name not drawn from land. The name came from a match in his line with a Mountjoy heir. His line runs on to a fourth baron famed as a scholar and a friend to men of learning.
britannica-1911-northampton-massachusett:
Northampton is the subject of a city article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Northampton is a city and county seat in Massachusetts in the United States. It stands on a great river, north of Springfield. Its people numbered over nineteen thousand at the census of 1910. Its chief village is counted one of the prettiest in New England.

The article notes a mountain nearby that can be climbed by road and by a mountain railway. Its summit commands a grand view. The city holds a state hospital for the insane and a famed school for the deaf. It is also the seat of Smith College, a leading college for women. A charity fund left by a local judge supports schools and other good works across nearby towns. Its will was contested by his heirs but upheld by the state court in 1847.
britannica-1911-norwood-massachusetts:
Norwood, a township in Norfolk county, Massachusetts, is described in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It lies about fourteen miles south-west of Boston. Its people numbered 5,840 in 1900 and 8,014 in 1910. The township covers about ten square miles. The Neponset river runs through it. A railway links it with Boston and New York.

The article lists the town's library and its works. The Morrill Memorial Library held 12,000 volumes in 1909. Local works made printing ink and glue. Tanneries and an iron foundry also stood in the town. Three printing firms ran presses and binderies there. Norwood began as the South Precinct of Dedham. It became a township in 1872, with part of Walpole added.
britannica-1911-orleanists:
The Orleanists were a French political party born of the Revolution, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains their aim. The party took its name from the Orleans branch of the house of Bourbon. Those princes, sprung from the younger brother of Louis the Fourteenth, were its chiefs. The party ceased to stand apart soon after the third republic was set up in 1872.

The aim of the Orleanists can be put in one line. They sought a common measure between two things. One was the monarchical principle, rule by a king. The other was the rights of man, as set forth by the leaders of 1789. The entry points readers to the lives of the Orleans princes for the story. Those lives show how the princes came to head the party, and how its hopes rose and fell.
britannica-1911-palk-straits: Palk Straits is named in a 1911 Britannica article as the channel between the mainland of India and the island of Ceylon. It is named after Robert Palk, governor of Madras in the years 1755 to 1763. The straits lie north of the line of reefs called Adam's Bridge. The Gulf of Manaar lies south of that line. The two channels are joined by the Pamban passage. The short entry fixes the strait's place, its name source, and its links in a few lines.
britannica-1911-pamphlets:
Pamphlet is a word whose first trace in print stands in a famed book on the love of books from the middle ages. There it is used in a Latin dress for small works. In English it shows in the verse and prose of early poets, in each case set against book to mark a work of small size.

A will of a late age calls a short add on text by the same name, the 1911 Britannica entry says. In the next age the word fit single plays, poems, papers, and news sheets. Not till a later age did it take its modern sense: a short prose tract on a point of strife. The French form of the word came from English in time, for sharp short writs of attack.
britannica-1911-pandects:
Pandects is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a famed digest of Roman law. The name comes from a Greek word for a work that holds all things. The emperor Justinian had the work made in the sixth century. It was put in order in the years 530 to 533.

The digest runs to fifty books, each split into titles and laws. Parts were drawn from the works of thirty-nine jurists of old Rome. Two of them, Ulpian and Paulus, make up near half the whole. The work was named the sole source of non-statute law. Notes on it, and use of the old texts to clear up doubts, were banned.
britannica-1911-piarists:
Piarists are members of a Catholic order devoted to free schooling. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells the order founding and fall. Joseph Calasanza, a Spaniard, started the work at Rome. A brotherhood he formed in 1607 became a congregation in 1617.

The order took a fourth vow beyond the usual three. That vow bound them to teach youth without charge. Papal favor gave them the rights of the begging orders in 1622. Jesuit envy then cost Calasanza his post in 1643. Three years later the pope stripped the order of its rights. Those rights came back in steps over the next fifty years. The founder was made a saint in 1767. Their schools ran nine grades from first reading to rhetoric.
britannica-1911-pigments:
Pigments is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on the colouring matter used in paint. The word comes from a Latin term tied to painting. The entry first draws a line between pigments and paints. Paints are made from pigments by adding a vehicle or medium that carries them. Pigments and dyes are not the same thing either.

A pigment, in fact, does not dissolve in the vehicle it is mixed with, while a dye does dissolve. Pigments vary in how clear or solid they look on a surface. They should work with ease and not react badly with each other or with their vehicles. They should also stand firm under light and air. Any change a vehicle works in their hue should be one that can be reckoned in advance.
britannica-1911-pitcher-plants:
Pitcher plants are plants whose leaves bear traps in the shape of a pitcher, or are pitcher-shaped in form. The plant most meant by the name is Nepenthes. That genus holds near sixty kinds, native to the tropics of Asia and north Australia. One kind only is native to Madagascar. North Borneo is rich in kinds above all. They are shrubby plants that climb over the growth round them.

Nepenthes climbs by means of tendril-like growths of the midrib of the leaf, past the leaf tip. The pitcher forms at the end of that tendril. It is tube-shaped as a rule. Some kinds bear two forms of pitcher on one plant, a lower or ground form and an upper one. The article sets out the parts of the pitcher in its figures. It names the honey glands of the lid and the glands inside that digest prey.
britannica-1911-pozharevats:
Pozharevats is a town in Servia, in the Morava valley, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a gazetteer entry. The town stands four miles east of the Morava river and eight miles south of the Danube. Its steamer station, Dubravitsa, stands on the Danube bank with a custom house. That station serves in practice as the harbour of the town.

The town has no special industry of its own. It is the chief market of a wide and fruitful plain between three rivers. Those rivers are the Morava, the Mlava, and the Danube. Pozharevats is the capital of a department of the same name. It holds a prefecture, a court of justice, a college, and schools. A large modern penitentiary stands there, with parts for political offenders and for women.
britannica-1911-quincy-massachusetts:
Quincy, a city in Massachusetts, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It sits in Norfolk county, on Massachusetts Bay. The Neponset river parts it from Boston on the north. Fore river parts it from Weymouth on the south. Its people grew from 16,723 in 1890 to 32,642 in 1910.

Rail and electric lines serve the city. To a large degree, Quincy is a suburb where Boston folk live. The birthplaces of two presidents still stand there. The house of John Adams was built in 1681. The house of John Quincy Adams was built in 1716. The Stone Temple, a Unitarian church, is the burial place of both men. Quincy was also the home of Charles Francis Adams. John Adams gave the town his fine private library, as the article goes on to tell. Few small cities hold so much national memory.
britannica-1911-remonstrants:
Remonstrants was the name given to Dutch Protestants who held the views linked with Arminius after his death, as this 1911 Britannica article explains. In 1610 they put before the states of Holland and Friesland a remonstrance in five articles. Those articles set out where they parted from stricter Calvinism.

The first point held that the divine decree of choosing who is saved is conditional, not absolute. The second held that the Atonement was meant for all, not for a few only. The third held that man cannot by himself exercise a saving faith. The article presents these points as the core of the group's stand, which shaped a lasting split in Dutch church life.
britannica-1911-rickets:
Rickets is the subject of a medical article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Rickets is a disease of childhood marked by soft bones. It also shows poor feeding and weak growth. The name comes from an old English word for twist. A Greek based name links it to the spine, one of the first parts hit.

The article says signs show some months after birth, most often near the end of year one. Early signs include poor appetite, vomiting, and loose bowels. The child loses flesh and sweats much on the head in sleep. The bones grow sore to touch. In time the ends of long bones swell and the legs bend out or in. The trunk can also warp as the spine curves. Readers get a clear clinical picture of the disease.
britannica-1911-roads-and-streets:
Roads and Streets is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on made ways for travel. The two words name the chief kinds of route built by man. Roads link place to place for carts and for walkers. Streets are the roads that run through towns and villages. They are lined, more or less, by houses and other buildings. The article deals with how roads are made. It runs from the first great road makers, the Romans, to modern times.

Before the Romans, ways in Europe were mere tracks. Feet, hooves, and wheels wore those tracks into the ground. The word road came late into its present broad use. The text cites the New English Dictionary for its first use. That first use is traced to Shakespeare. The entry thus joins word history with the craft of building. It gives readers a frame for the long survey that follows.
britannica-1911-rockland-massachusetts:
Rockland, a township in Plymouth county in Massachusetts, is described in a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies about twenty miles south of Boston and covers about ten square miles. Its people numbered 5,213 in 1890, 5,327 in 1900, and 6,928 by the census of 1910. A rail line and an electric line between towns served it.

The article names boots and shoes and tacks as its chief goods. It notes a public library founded in 1878. Rockland became a township in its own right in 1874, having before that been part of Abington. Brief as it is, the entry fixes the place, its size, its growth, and its main trades at the start of the new century.
britannica-1911-somerville-massachusetts:
Somerville is a city of Massachusetts described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in Middlesex county, on the Mystic river, next to Boston, Cambridge, Medford, and Arlington. Its people grew fast, from about forty thousand in 1890 to more than seventy-seven thousand in 1910. Many of its folk were born abroad, most of all English-Canadians and Irish.

The city is a home and factory suburb of Boston and shares its water, sewer, and park systems. Its land is a patch of hills and vales along the Mystic. Sights and seats include a public library of 1872 with eighty thousand books, a city hall, a hospital, and two high schools. The worth of its factory goods in 1905 was near twenty-three million dollars. Slaughter and meat packing led the trades, with bleach works and finish works in train.
britannica-1911-state-rights:
State rights, a term in the study of politics, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the powers of rule held by each state in a federal union. In that sphere a state may act free from the central power. The text gives the United States as a key case.

When the states formed the union under the plan of 1787, they kept set rights for themselves. The central power must respect those rights by basic law. Only a change to that plan can cut them down.
