They stand recorded twice in the Pentateuch, in Exodus chapter 20 and Deuteronomy chapter 5, abridged in catechisms. 

God's finger wrote them on two stone tables, Moses received them amid Sinai's thunders, and they grounded Mosaic Law. Christ summed them in love of God and neighbour. He proclaimed them binding under the New Law in Matthew chapter 19 and the Sermon on the Mount, and deepened them, banning needless oaths like false ones and hatred like murder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophilanthr:
Friends of God and Man, a deist sect born late in the French Revolution, are the group described here. Legal rule of the Constitutional Church, worship of reason, and cult of the Supreme Being had left France, in practice, atheist and immoral. Disciples of Rousseau and Robespierre sought a new faith joining Rousseau's deism to Robespierre's civic virtue.

Chemin wrote their Manual, and Haüy lent his school for the blind as a first meeting place. The Convention gave them Sainte Catherine's little church in Paris, and growth stayed slow until Directory member La Révellière-Lépeaux took their cause. After the coup of 18 Fructidor left him master, their high tide came, with festivals, hymns, and moral lectures filling churches the Revolution had emptied.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trappists:
The common name for the Cistercians who follow the reform begun by Abbot de Rancé, born 1626 and died 1700, at the Abbey of La Trappe. Strictly there is no separate Order of Trappists: the name marks the Reformed Cistercians, as distinct from the Cistercians of the Common Observance.

De Rancé's reform revived the primitive austerities that commendatory abbots, political troubles and human inconstancy had let lapse across the order. After the Revolution scattered the monks, Dom Augustine led them through exile in several countries, including Russia and America. Napoleon's fall let them return to France and rebuild houses such as La Trappe and Aiguebelle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tritheists:
Heretics who divide the Substance of the Blessed Trinity, usually meaning a section of the Monophysites powerful in the second half of the sixth century. Their founder is said to be John Ascunages of Antioch. Their chief writer was John Philoponus, the great Aristotelian commentator, backed by the bishops Conon of Tarsus and Eugenius of Seleucia.

Deposed by their fellow provincials, Conon and Eugenius found a protector at Constantinople in Athanasius the Monk, grandson of the Empress Theodora. They refused to anathematize Philoponus in dispute before the patriarch John Scholasticus, and were banished to Palestine. A later medieval form of tritheism drew condemnation at Oxford.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trusts-and-be:
A legal exposition of the trust. It is defined as a right enforceable solely in equity to the beneficial enjoyment of property whose legal title lies in another. It implies two interests. The trustee holds the legal title, and the beneficiary, known as the cestui que trust, enjoys the benefit of the property.

A valid trust needs three essentials. They are a definite subject matter within the settlor's disposal, a lawful definite object, and clear words or acts devoting the subject to that object. The entry covers who may serve as trustee and the Statute of Frauds for trusts of land. It also covers the court's power to supply a trustee rather than let a trust fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uniformity-ac:
The Uniformity Acts were English statutes passed at different times in a vain effort to force one form of public worship on the whole realm. Once communion with Rome was broken, the entry argues, unity was lost, and every attempt was doomed. Catholics resisted the acts on one side and Nonconformists on the other. The first act, of Edward VI, imposed the Book of Common Prayer and one order of service on all churches in England and Wales.

Later acts confirmed, repealed, and revived that settlement through the reigns of Mary, Elizabeth, and James I. One act of 1549 abolished old service books and images, and later measures defined open prayer and punished clergy who strayed from the set forms. The entry walks through each statute, its penalties, and its fate, showing how Parliament tried to legislate unity and why the effort kept failing against conscience on both sides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-universalists:
Universalists are a liberal Protestant body found chiefly in North America, whose distinctive tenet is the final salvation of all souls. Belief in universal salvation had won favour in various churches long before, but this entry treats Universalism only as a separate denomination. Its historic creed is the profession adopted by the General Convention at Winchester, New Hampshire, in 1803.

That creed affirms that Scripture reveals God's character and mankind's duty, interest, and final destination, and that there is one God whose nature is love. From that love the body draws its hope that all souls will at last be saved. The entry sets out the denomination's doctrine, its organization, and its growth in America, noting how its hopeful teaching shaped its worship and its quarrels with stricter Calvinist neighbours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-use-and-abuse:
Amulets have served everywhere as safeguards against mishap, danger, or witchcraft, and as pledges of success in undertakings, though the word's origin is not firmly settled. Greeks knew them as phylacterion, periamma, and periapton, while Arabs and Persians called them talisman, perhaps from the later Greek telesma. Their variety bewilders: carved stones, bits of metal, figures of gods, and strips of paper or parchment bearing cryptic phrases, blessings, and curses.

Among Egyptians one class of amulets held primacy, the entry notes, and the survey runs through peoples and ages to the Christian use and abuse of such objects. It distinguishes lawful sacramentals from superstitious reliance on charms, and sets out the church's teaching on why a blessed object may be kept but never trusted as magic. A compact study of a habit as old as fear itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vestments:
Vestments are the garments clergy wear by church rule or custom when performing sacred ceremonies, above all Mass, then sacraments, blessings, the canonical hours, processions, and public prayer. The Latin rite's full list runs from amice, alb, cincture, maniple, stole. Chasuble to dalmatic, cope, mitre, pallium, gloves, and sandals, with the pope wearing the most elaborate and numerous set.

Priests at Mass wear amice, alb, cincture, maniple, stole, and chasuble, plus surplice and cope on other occasions; bishops add tunic, dalmatic, sandals, buskins, gloves, and mitre, and archbishops the pallium. The entry then traces each garment's history in four periods, noting eastern counterparts such as the epigonation, first a handkerchief called enchirion. Showing how, from the thirteenth century on, vestment history becomes largely a story of rubrics, embroidery, and materials.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-war-of-the-pe:
The War of the Peasants was the revolt of southern and central Germany's peasants in 1524 to 1525, whose causes remain disputed through religious and political prejudice. The prevailing view in the entry attributes it mainly to economic distress, not doctrine alone. Cities overshadowing the countryside, and precious metals from Peru, Mexico, and Germany halving money's value while prices soared, wool doubling in Thuringia and merchandise rising fivefold. Lords, instead of cutting leases or raising wages, taxed heavily, extended authority, increased serfs' services, and attacked market associations and hereditary leases.

Peasant demands, economic, social, and religious, sought lower interest, lighter compulsory service and penalties, restored commons rights of pasture, fishing. Hunting, election of pastors, and, since Christ made all men free, abolition of serfdom, while still obeying God-appointed authorities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-smits:
William Smits was a Flemish Franciscan Bible scholar whose Dutch Bible with notes ran to seventeen volumes. Born at Kevelaer in Gelderland in 1704, he died on 1 December 1770. He joined the Friars Minor in the Belgian province at eighteen and applied himself with striking success to biblical tongues and Scripture, rising to lector. From 1732 to 1744 he published Antwerp theses on textual criticism and chronology.

In one thesis Smits showed the Latin Vulgate largely faithful to the Hebrew original; in another he argued the Septuagint Greek text deserved preference over the current Hebrew. At Cardinal Archbishop Philip of Alsace's urging he undertook a full Flemish Bible, far more than a plain Vulgate rendering, with grammatical, literal, and critical notes. He finished only thirteen sacred books, issued from 1744 to 1767, and his pupil Peter van Hove carried the work on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zionists:
Zionists are followers of the movement to segregate the Jewish people as a nation and give it a national home in Palestine or elsewhere. Orthodox Judaism holds to a pure Zionism: return to Palestine, the Messias's coming, the overthrow of hostile powers by him, the Temple's restoration and worship, and the Messianic reign. Reformed Jews reject a return to Zion. The Frankfort rabbinical conference of July 1845 deleted ritual prayers for return and a Jewish state. The Philadelphia conference of 1869 defined the Messianic hope as all God's children united in confessing God's unity, and Pittsburg in 1885 repeated that idea.

Theodor Herzl gave the movement dignity, form, and permanence with his 1896 Judenstaat, won leaders like Zangwill, Nordau, and Marmorek, and by 1899 counted over 100,000 shekel-payers. Herzl died on 3 July 1904, and Nordau became president at the seventh congress in 1905.
chantecler-play-in-four-acts:
Edmond Rostand's verse play in four acts, Englished by Gertrude Hall, gives its stage to a farmyard. The cast list alone is a poem. Patou the dog, the Blackbird, and the Peacock appear. So do the Nightingale, the Grand-Duke, and the Screech-Owl. A carrier-pigeon, a wood-pecker, and hens of every colour follow. Chantecler the cock stands at the centre.

A prologue makes the audience listen before the curtain rises: the manager halts the lift, ear bent, while magpies, wooden shoes, sheep bells, and barking build the yard out of sound alone. Chantecler believes his crowing calls the sun, and the yard's flatterers and mockers test that faith. Rostand writes animals who speak like courtiers, wits, and lovers of France.
christmas-entertainments:
Alice M. Kellogg compiled a practical book of Christmas pieces for children aged five to fifteen. Everything in it is made to be performed. New songs are fitted to old tunes, so a school needs no new music. Fancy drills — a Christmas-bell drill, a snow brigade — give whole classes something to do in formation.

Acrostics spell out Santa Claus and Merry Christmas down the page. Motion songs come with numbered directions for hands, heads, and cradles. Tableaux pose Christmas pictures in stillness. Short plays, among them Mr. St. Nicholas by Kellogg herself, suit a school stage. Recitations are sorted by grade, from a youngest pupil's six lines on Saint Nick to grammar-grade pieces by Eugene Field and Lucy Larcom.
cromwell-a-drama-in-five-acts:
A verse drama in five acts on Oliver Cromwell, by Alfred B. Richards, fills this volume. Petter, Duff, and Company printed it at London, and the title page date reads MDCCCLII. Richards lists his other plays and poems on the title page, among them Croesus and Vandyck.

The cast sets Cromwell at the head, with Milton as his secretary. Ireton, Harrison, Bradshaw, and Ludlow stand among the Parliament men. Lady Cromwell, her daughter Elizabeth, and Florence Nevel lead the women. Roundheads, Cavaliers, soldiers, and crowds fill the stage. Talk of Rome, mobs, and one man's rise drives the verse. The play is a Victorian try at the great Puritan as a tragic hero.
doe-osti-17168022-data-and-ai-systems-fy:
Rafael Ferreira da Silva, Scott Klasky, Robert Patton, and Oak Ridge colleagues compile fiscal 2026 highlights of the lab's Data and AI Systems Section, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4963. The section works on the data and artificial intelligence foundations of scientific discovery. Its year spanned data engineering, learning systems, performance engineering, visualization, and workflow systems.

A note from the section head opens the volume, followed by project highlights from a long author roster. Release is under a Creative Commons Attribution license, with a preferred citation given in the front matter. The report serves as the section's public record of work delivered in 2026 across computing programs at the laboratory.
doe-osti-17197384-data-and-ai-systems-fy: Data and AI systems got their FY2026 highlights again, and this DOE report recaps the year's achievements. The pages showcase the wins. The stakeholders get their summary. The highlights were FY2026. The achievements were recapped. The summary was annual. The wins were showcased.
doe-osti-2574824-lamp-operational-concep:
Report LA-UR-25-27831, also numbered LAMP-SE-RPT-002, by Robert Garnett of Los Alamos and issued July 31, 2025, works out how a major upgrade changes daily operations at LANSCE. The LAMP project rebuilds the accelerator's front end. Aging Cockcroft-Walton injectors give way to new ion sources, low-energy transports, a radio frequency quadrupole, and a modern drift-tube linac.

New hardware means new operating patterns. The report walks through the present H-plus and H-minus delivery modes and the two new modes the upgrade creates, then traces startup and running sequences. A large share covers safety integration: the personnel protection and machine protection systems, and the radiation safety system beam plugs that guard entry into exclusion areas. Integration issues with the existing complex are flagged, and conclusions collect the operational changes operators should expect once LAMP is installed.
doe-osti-2575552-helium-bubble-physics-e:
Report LA-UR-25-28007, by J. I. Katz of Los Alamos and issued August 6, 2025, examines the helium bubbles that grow inside aging plutonium. Alpha decay steadily adds helium to the metal. New results from the MST-16 group show the bubble count rising only slowly, if at all, while the size spread shifts toward larger bubbles. Aged plutonium also foams when annealed at high temperature.

Katz attributes both behaviors to fast diffusion. After a few years of aging, fresh helium reaches existing bubbles instead of nucleating new ones. During heating, big bubbles grow at the expense of small ones, the classic Ostwald ripening pattern. Swelling follows because larger bubbles hold their helium at lower Laplace pressure, hence lower density. A simple theory is developed, and tests are proposed in aluminum alloyed with boron-10, where reactor neutrons raise the helium content in controlled steps.
doe-osti-2997097-high-energy-physics-net:
Energy Sciences Network report LBNL-2001696 records the High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review held from July to December 2024. Lead authors Jason Zurawski, Dale Carder, and Evangelos Chaniotakis gathered the data needs of the field's big experiments for ESnet, the Department's research network. Collider, telescope, and neutrino programs all ship data through the same backbone.

Case studies walk through each program's data centers and transfer patterns. The Rubin Observatory section details its United States Data Facility, where a prompt enclave processes images in near real time and feeds status back to the observatory control system. Alert pipelines turn fresh images into data products for the science community. Network planners use the gathered volumes, peaks, and timing needs to size links years before the data arrives.
doe-osti-2997224-high-energy-physics-net:
Energy Sciences Network's High Energy Physics Network Requirements Review, covering July to December 2024, was republished through the University of California in October 2025. Lead authors Jason Zurawski, Dale Carder, and Evangelos Chaniotakis, with many contributors, catalog how the field's experiments move data. ESnet, run by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, carries much of that traffic.

Experiment chapters quantify transfer patterns activity by activity. Belle II's showing in the DC24 data challenge reached 250 terabytes per day. That is more than six times the top rate expected at decade's end. No network bottlenecks have been seen since its move to the Rucio data manager in 2021. Staging campaigns, which happen once a year or less, rank second in volume but stay inside the sites. The review turns such records into capacity requirements for the next network build.
doe-osti-2998964-dune-nd-lar-2x2-demonst:
Vanessa Cerrone's Fermilab Italian Students Program final report, FERMILAB-TM-2906-STUDENT, covers tests of the ArgonCube 2x2 Demonstrator. The demonstrator is a medium-size prototype for the near detector of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment. Its four liquid argon modules must prove the modular design before the full detector sits in the NuMI beam at Fermilab, upstream of the older MINOS hall.

Cerrone's work split in two parts, supervised by Antonio Ereditato and Ting Miao. First came clean power: she built a real-time method to watch ground impedance at the Liquid Argon Test Facility, logging values to a database shown online. Quiet grounding keeps detector noise low. Second came quality tests of the light readout system after transport, checking that each unit still worked as rated. Two modules were under test during her stay, ahead of beam placement.
doe-osti-3006050-assessment-of-uranium-i:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-25/53, dated August 31, 2025, weighs the value of recovered uranium taken from used fuel of a once-through sodium-cooled fast reactor fed with HALEU. E. Hoffman, A. M. Bachmann, and N. Stauff of Argonne wrote it with A. Cuadra and C. Lu of Brookhaven. Fast reactors leave more fissile material in their used fuel than thermal reactors do, so the recovered uranium starts richer in uranium-235. Three minor isotopes set much of its worth.

Trace uranium-232 raises dose rates and so raises fuel fabrication cost. Uranium-234 and uranium-236, both richer in recovered uranium than in natural uranium, act as neutron poisons and force higher uranium-235 content to compensate. The report works through example fuel cycles, including down-blending for pressurized water reactor fuel and re-enrichment for fast reactor fuel, and prices each route in cost tables.
doe-osti-3006720-challenge-problem-1-pre:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-25/42 gives preliminary results for Challenge Problem 1, direct numerical simulation of transient flows. Alexey Burbasov, Igor Bolotnov, and Nam Dinh head the author team. The team modeled a sudden decay in driving pressure in a downcomer-like channel, like a loss-of-flow event, using the GPU-accelerated NekRS solver. They tracked Reynolds number, boundary-layer structure, turbulence statistics, and heat-transfer metrics through the transient.

Findings include steady thickening and eventual asymmetry of the velocity and thermal boundary layers as buoyancy slowed the flow. Turbulence profiles showed little memory lag at matching Reynolds number, but peak locations shifted toward the cooled wall. Eddy viscosity and diffusivity overshot on the cooled side, pushing turbulent Prandtl numbers below one. A transient Nusselt number rise, credited to wall-temperature inertia and residual eddy mixing, gave a temporary cooling margin above steady-state predictions.
doe-osti-3008084-solenoidal-fields-from-:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229199-2025-TECH, by Erdong Wang, Jyoti Biswas, and Eric Liu, dated December 2025, designs a focusing solenoid built from permanent bar magnets. It serves the low-energy section of a spin-polarized electron injector for the Electron-Ion Collider.

Quadrupole triplets normally focus that section, but their large footprint leaves no room for beam diagnostics. Rings of rectangular bar magnets, north poles facing the beamline, create the solenoid field with no power supply or cooling. Fields were computed with analytical formulas in Mathematica 14, and sliding the gap between rings tunes the focal length. The compact design frees space along the injector for instruments.
doe-osti-3008526-proposed-new-stella-2-t:
Argonne National Laboratory report by Tyler Sumner, Yeongshin Jeong, and Anton Moisseytsev, dated December 31, 2025, proposes new tests for the STELLA-2 sodium facility in Korea. STELLA-2 is KAERI's large-scale sodium thermal-hydraulic loop, built for the PGSFR sodium fast reactor concept, and its data validate reactor safety codes.

KAERI asked Argonne which tests to add in its 2026 campaign, aiming at system conditions earlier campaigns never reached. The proposals script the reactor vessel cooling system through options such as staying on, changing heat rejection to a set percentage, or tripping. Two tests would close one side of the cooling system to force lopsided cold-pool temperatures. The decay heat removal system stays off throughout, at KAERI's direction.
doe-osti-3023094-threat-hunt-guide-for-b:
Remy Vanece Stolworthy, Megan Jordan Culler, and James A Cerkovnik of Idaho National Laboratory wrote this threat hunt guide for battery energy storage systems, report INL/RPT-25-89299, dated December 2025. It grew out of rapid risk assessments the lab ran with energy organizations across the United States under a Department of Energy CESER initiative. Battery sites are now digital, networked, and often lightly watched.

The method is passive network monitoring: watch traffic without disturbing operations, learn normal device behavior, then hunt for signs of an intruder. The guide suggests starting at one representative site, placing sensors at spots such as the boundary between corporate IT and the operations network, and checking data capture before scaling fleet-wide. Tools such as the Malcolm traffic analysis suite are named.
doe-osti-3025314-fy25-ldrd-project-accom:
Elizabeth Wheeler compiled Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's FY25 LDRD project accomplishments in LLNL-TR-2017208, dated March 2026. Laboratory-directed research is the lab's internal portfolio of investigator-led projects, and an accomplishments volume gathers one year's worth of outcomes in a single reference. The entries span Livermore's missions, from stockpile science to energy and computing.

Much of the book is bibliography: publications, reports, and talks credited to each project. A run of entries on quantum optimal control, for instance, lists work on master equations for open quantum systems and gradient-based control of quantum testbeds. Presentations ran from Brown University to a 2024 computing conference in Lisbon. Readers mining the volume can trace a project's outputs without hunting through separate annual reports.
doe-osti-3364917-cyber-informed-engineer:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5T00-97232, by Sriharsha Etigowni and Richard Macwan and dated May 2026, works through use cases for a cyber-informed engineering requirements framework. The DOE program, run with Idaho National Laboratory, pushes engineers to design cyber risk out of energy systems at the drawing stage rather than bolting defenses on later. Requirements are the lever: what a specification demands, builders must deliver.

Use case material grounds the framework in concrete procurement language. Sample clauses cover junction box placement and ratings, conduit runs capped at 20 feet, breaker compatibility, and a ban on splices in designated runs. Writing security into such ordinary details is the point. The document shows specifiers how consequence-focused thinking becomes enforceable contract text for field equipment.
doe-osti-3366074-advanced-transmission-t:
A slide deck by Megan Jordan Culler and Alex Tylecote recaps supplier cohort workshops on advanced transmission technologies, the family of grid upgrades that includes dynamic line ratings and high-performance conductors. Utilities, vendors, and researchers compared notes on why proven hardware still struggles to deploy. The deck sorts the talks into five cross-cutting themes.

Institutional barriers outweigh technical limits, participants agreed: unclear roles and consultant-driven conservatism stall adoption. Integration points with utility control systems are the largest cyber exposure. Supply chain worry centers on long-term trust, especially foreign semiconductor dependence, with buyers asking for software and hardware bills of materials. Human-in-the-loop validation remains the critical control point, and vendor security steps such as penetration testing and signed firmware are becoming standard buying practice.
doe-osti-3371805-concise-guide-on-hydrog:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory guide PNNL-39015 gives ports a plain, compact entry point into hydrogen as a fuel and cargo. The guide walks through how hydrogen is made, moved, stored, and used, with the choices framed by what a port can buy and run today. Storage gets close attention, since ports must hold fuel on site for ships, trucks, and yard equipment.

Compressed gas storage suits small amounts, on the order of 1,000 kilograms or less, and is on the market now. Liquid hydrogen packs more fuel into less space, but chilling it to about minus 253 degrees Celsius costs energy and boil-off losses add up. Liquid organic hydrogen carriers, chemicals that hold hydrogen and release it later, round out the main options the guide weighs for port use.
doe-osti-3684050-carbon-tetrachloride-de:
Pacific Northwest report, dated August 2026, gives lab results on carbon tetrachloride breakdown in Hanford's 200-ZP-1 ground. Nine authors are printed, led by Christopher Bagwell, Guohui Wang, and Danielle Saunders. The solvent reached the aquifer from plutonium production discharges between 1955 and 1973. It sank through more than seventy metres of sediment into a large plume. Rules require its level to fall to a set low mark within one hundred twenty-five years.

Water alone showed no removal in lab batches, matching a decay half-life of centuries. The new finding is brighter: native microbes in site sediment broke the solvent down fast and nearly fully without oxygen. In one borehole, all three sampled depths degraded it, with half-lives near seven days. Low-oxygen pockets inside the aquifer hold the needed conditions. The team calls it strong support for natural attenuation at the site.
dreams-waking-thoughts-and-incidents:
William Beckford, the rich young author of Vathek, wrote his European tour as a set of letters dated 1780, and the hosted copy follows the 1891 Ward, Lock edition. The first letter, dated June 19, 1780, confesses his method at once: a mist hovers before his eyes, and he sees all places faint and hazy through it. He claims no vanity of exact remark.

Through Kent he dozes, opens his eyes near Canterbury to birch trees gilt with broom, and sinks back into dreams of choirs in native shades. Later letters cross the Alps, where white goats gamble on cliff edges at sunset and shake their beards at the party below. Beckford turns travel into reverie: palaces, music, and ruins pass like scenes in a theater of the mind. The book shows the Grand Tour remade by a dreamy, brilliant, and very rich young man.
early-reviews-of-english-poets:
John Louis Haney, a Philadelphia teacher and scholar, collected the first reviews of the English poets in a 1904 volume from the Egerton Press. A long introduction and a bibliography frame the pieces. Haney's aim is plain: let readers watch fame being made and unmade in the magazines of the day.

The contents run from Gray's Odes and Goldsmith's Traveller through Burns, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Scott, Byron, Shelley, Keats, Tennyson, and Browning. Each poet gets the notices that greeted the first books, from the Monthly and Critical Reviews, the Edinburgh, Blackwood's, and the Quarterly. A Byron piece hedges on his Ossianic verse, pleading small skill in that kind. Students of taste can see which judges praised Lyrical Ballads, which savaged Endymion, and how wrong the wise could be.
editorial-wild-oats:
Mark Twain laughs at his young newspaper self in Editorial Wild Oats, a set of sketches issued by Harper and Brothers in 1905. Six pieces fill the contents: My First Literary Venture, Journalism in Tennessee, Nicodemus Dodge — Printer, Mr. Bloke's Item, How I Edited an Agricultural Paper, and The Killing of Julius Caesar Localized.

The first sketch recalls a smart boy of thirteen whose first scribbling stirred a fine sensation in town. In the agricultural paper piece, Twain confesses his ignorance of farming while old readers hang on his words. One absurd passage instructs that the guano is a fine bird, to be imported not earlier than June and kept warm in winter. The relief on a listener's face, moonlight over a bleak landscape, greets each new pearl of nonsense. The set is Twain's own roast of green editors and the papers that printed them.
english-walnuts:
Walter Fox Allen compiles the case for a nut in English Walnuts, copyrighted 1912, telling what you need to know about planting, cultivating, and harvesting it. Allen gathered his material from many trustworthy sources, the United States Department of Agriculture among them. The foreword notes the tremendous interest then rising among owners of country estates.

The Persian or English walnut, he argues, rewards the grower past other nuts. Choice kinds fall clean and free from the shuck, frosts do the harvesting in October, and the trees prune themselves. An alkali sap keeps scales and pests away, and late blossoms dodge spring frosts. The book's tail carries nursery praise for named varieties, hickory-nut flavor and all.
essays-on-education-and-kindred-subjects:
Herbert Spencer argues that schools teach the wrong things in Essays on Education and Kindred Subjects, here in Everyman's Library, first published there in 1911. The front matter gives his life in brief: born at Derby in 1820, son of a teacher, railway work, then sub-editor of The Economist in 1848, dead in 1903. A select bibliography lists Social Statics and the Synthetic Philosophy.

The education essays ask what knowledge is of most worth and scour ornamental schooling. A kindred paper traces sculpture's slow separation from the wall in Egyptian art, read off the British Museum's cases. Spencer's system, from First Principles to the Principles of Morality, crowds the bibliography. Dent published the volume as Everyman number 504.
essays-on-russian-novelists:
Essays on Russian Novelists, by William Lyon Phelps, argues that Russia's greatness rests on its ideas and literature, not its fleets. Phelps opens with the Japanese war, which left Russia's navy destroyed, her armies beaten, her treasury empty, and her pride in the dust. Against that humiliation he sets a question for proud Americans: what have the two nations given the world's literature?

His first essay reads Russian national character through Russian fiction. Russia is old, he notes, yet her literature, so far as the world cares, begins in the nineteenth century, a twin of America's. The essays then take up the great novelists one by one. Phelps writes like a Yale professor lecturing general readers. He asks what each writer saw in the Russian soul. Peasants, officials, and seekers fill their pages, and he explains why. Criticism here is an act of introduction between two young literatures.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-the-acts:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on the Acts covers chapters I to XII in this part. Alexander Maclaren opens with The Ascension from Acts I. The Theme of Acts links the book's first verses to its close. The Forty Days and The Unknown To-Morrow follow.

Pentecost fills the next run, with The Abiding Gift and Peter's First Sermon. A Fourfold Cord and A Pure Church an Increasing Church use Acts II. The healing at the gate brings The Prince of Life. Stephen's story begins with Filled with the Spirit in chapter VI. Obedient Disobedience and Gamaliel's Counsel treat the first persecution. Maclaren reads Acts as the church's marching orders, full of witness and courage.
fairy-tales-from-the-arabian-nights:
Dixon's Fairy Tales from the Arabian Nights selects tales for young readers in a first series. E. Dixon edited the text from Galland's 1821 version, lightly abridged. His note, dated at Cambridge at Christmas 1893, says the edition suits boys and girls. The King of Persia and the Princess of the Sea opens the set.

Prince Beder and the Princess Giauhara follows as its sequel. The Three Princes and Princess Nouronnihar leads to Prince Ahmed and the Fairy. Prince Camaralzaman and the Princess of China comes next. The Story of Zobeide and The Story of the King's Son add shorter pieces. All seven voyages of Sinbad the Sailor close the volume. Dixon favors romance and marvel over the Nights' darker matter.
father-and-son-a-study-of-two-temperamen:
Edmund Gosse called Father and Son a study of two temperaments and swore in his 1907 preface that every part was scrupulously true. Gosse, son of the naturalist Philip Henry Gosse, grew up inside a strict Puritan household of Plymouth Brethren, where novels, holidays, and doubt itself were sins. The book records the boy's slow, secret emancipation as science and poetry opened doors his father's faith kept locked.

Names are changed, as the preface admits, and comedy mixes with the tragedy of a loving father and son ceasing to speak the same language. Gosse published the memoir anonymously; it became the classic account of Victorian religious childhood. Its calm, funny, devastating tone lets the facts accuse without a raised voice.
ferragus-chief-of-the-de-vorants:
Honore de Balzac's Ferragus, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation, opens a trilogy. With The Duchesse de Langeais and The Girl with the Golden Eyes, it forms The Thirteen. Balzac dedicates the tale to Hector Berlioz. His preface describes thirteen men banded in Paris under the Empire, sworn to one thought and never betraying each other.

Auguste de Maulincour follows a mysterious woman through midnight Paris and is marked for death by the brotherhood. Jules and Clemence Desmarets enjoy one completely happy day, foreboding it their last. Ferragus, a convict become secret sovereign, protects his daughter Clemence from the world. Balzac's Paris of passwords and hidden chiefs starts here.
fians-fairies-and-picts:
MacRitchie asks what stands behind the fairy tales of Scotland in Fians, Fairies and Picts. David MacRitchie argues that the small folk of legend were a real people of the past. The book is illustrated, and its frontispiece gives a plan of an underground gallery on South Uist. He builds his case from stones as much as from stories.

Earth-houses, the sunken stone galleries of the north, fill much of the text. MacRitchie cites the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland and its papers on such sites, from Barvas to the Hebrides. An appendix gathers plates from Captain Thomas's work on those structures. His claim links the Picts of history to the fairies and fians of tale, as one race seen at two removes. The book is a bold piece of folklore study, argued from spade and page alike.
for-luncheon-and-supper-guests:
Bradley's cookbook plans company meals around ten menus and more than a hundred recipes. The dishes suit Sunday night suppers, midday luncheons, high teas, afternoon parties, and automobile picnics. Tea rooms, lunch rooms, and motor inns are named as users too. She advised doing as much as possible the day before.

The recipes run to salads and their dressings in the sampled pages. Russian dressing mixes mayonnaise with chili sauce, pimiento, green pepper, and celery. Thousand Island is the same dressing with stiffly beaten cream folded in at serving. Alice Bradley, principal of Miss Farmer's School of Cookery, brought the book out in Boston in 1923.
four-early-pamphlets:
Godwin's first four pamphlets, all from his early career, are gathered here under one cover. A Defence of the Rockingham Party argues for their coalition with Lord North. Instructions to a Statesman, An Account of the Seminary, and The Herald of Literature complete the set.

The Herald looks back to the ancients for its standard of writing. Greek and Roman authors drew knowledge from the page of the universe, not only from books. Their noble freedom of mind stamped their work with originality, while modern copies grow feeble and unmarked. William Godwin published the first of these pieces in 1783, a decade before his fame in political philosophy.
g-f-watts:
Chesterton's G. F. Watts is a short critical study of the painter George Frederic Watts. G. K. Chesterton published it in 1904. The book carries a long list of photogravure plates: Hope, Mammon, The Minotaur, and The Court of Death among the allegories. Portraits include Tennyson, Browning, Mill, and Carlyle. Chesterton defends Watts against the general reaction of the age against allegorical art. That reaction, he argues, is the true bar to reading Watts fairly.

He asks what the charge against allegory rests on, and answers it point by point. The study is as much a defense of symbolic art as of one painter. It shows Chesterton's critical method in early form.
ghosts-a-domestic-tragedy-in-three-acts:
Henrik Ibsen set Ghosts in a rain-dark house on a Norwegian fjord, in R. Farquharson Sharp's translation. Widow Helen Alving is opening an orphanage built to launder the memory of her husband, a respected captain who lived in secret vice. Her son Oswald, an artist home from Paris, carries his father's disease in his body, and Pastor Manders brings the parish's respectability with him.

Across three acts the dead past takes the house: the captain's sins, a maid's daughter, a fire, and Oswald's final collapse toward the sun he begs to see. Ibsen meant ghosts as inherited ideas as much as inherited illness. The play scandalized Europe in the 1880s and still lands like an accusation against respectable silence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CivilRightsDivi: nsia-CivilRightsDivisionRay Civil Rights Division Ray: the made public government document on the Civil Rights Division and the Ray case. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PolygraphTests_: nsia-PolygraphTests Polygraph Tests: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Riots_Riots: Washington Post Potomac Magazine, October 13, 1968: the Potomac section, largely advertising content. The weeklies, preserved, complete, a single section, dated material, filed, an obscure item. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the press and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
During the Cold War, American agents scoured the globe for enemy hardware they could study. James E. David edited this briefing book, number 616, published in January 2018. Newly declassified documents fill in blanks on that secret search for foreign objects.

The haul ranged from captured MiG fighters to pieces of space junk. Each captured machine taught engineers how Soviet technology really worked, beyond what spies reported. The posting calls scavenging an underreported side of intelligence work. It is a useful corrective: some of the most valuable secrets of the Cold War were not stolen papers but physical objects, hauled home and taken apart.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico_F:
Mexico's Dirty War, decades of state violence against dissidents, went officially unexamined for fifty years. Kate Doyle and Claire Dorfman edited this briefing book, number 879, published in December 2024. It covers the country's first national truth commission and its monumental reports on that violence.

Government archives played an essential role in investigating past abuses, the posting notes. Declassified documents also reveal an American choice: Washington prioritized the stability of the Mexican regime over human rights concerns. The set pairs Mexico's late reckoning with the foreign support that helped delay it, a combination truth commissions rarely document so directly.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Launch on warning means firing nuclear missiles on the first warning of an enemy attack, before the incoming warheads land. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 674, published in June 2019, updating a 2001 posting. The policy was adopted in the 1970s and remains in effect.

Its danger is the false alert: a sensor error could trigger launch in minutes. A top defense official in 1978 called the policy dangerous, wrong, and ineffective. A Reagan directive, by contrast, aimed to leave Soviet planners with strong uncertainty about the American response. The set preserves an argument among insiders that has never been settled in public.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Prepa: United States Cyber Command began as a subordinate headquarters and grew into a full combatant command with its own operational force. A National Security Archive briefing book page presents documents tracing that path. They appear under the heading of preparing for computer network operations. They show how USCYBERCOM built, staffed, and trained the teams meant to fight in cyberspace. Only the page capture is preserved in this entry's evidence. The subject itself is foundational, since nearly every later American cyber operation descends from the force-building years these documents describe.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Silk_:
Silk Road was an online black market where drugs were sold for Bitcoin behind layers of secrecy. Federal agents shut it down in 2013 and 2014, and its founder, Ross Ulbricht, was arrested and prosecuted. A National Security Archive posting from December 2019 turns the lens around and examines the investigators themselves.

Two agents, one from the Drug Enforcement Administration and one from the Secret Service, became targets of corruption investigations tied to their work on the case. That twist made Silk Road a double story: a landmark cybercrime takedown and a warning about the temptations built into undercover work with digital money. Readers get the outline of the massive multi-agency hunt and the scandal that grew inside it, drawn from the released record.
great-violinists-and-pianists:
Ferris warns his readers at the start of Great Violinists and Pianists, copyrighted in 1881, that the title promises more than any small book can give. He has not tried to cover the whole field of executive music, he says. He chose only the artists whom all judges place at the very top, the landmarks in the history of music. Living performers are left out on purpose, since their rank is not yet settled.

Fiddlers of the line of Paganini and pianists of the line of Liszt fill the sketches. Ferris tells how each rose, what hearers praised in the playing, and what mark each left on the art. The facts are dressed in his usual warm, racy style. The book belongs with his Great Singers and Great Composers volumes, a parlor course in musical fame for the general reader.
hendershot-1928-press-accounts:
Lester Hendershot, an inventor from Pennsylvania, briefly stunned the press in 1928 with a motor that seemed to run on nothing. Six newspaper reports from that year are gathered here. Five come from the New York Times and one from the New York American, all from February and March.

The reports run from a test flight crowd that included Charles Lindbergh to the slow collapse of the claim. Backers from the Guggenheim fund soon backed away, and experts called the motor a trick. Read in order, the clippings show a free-energy sensation rising and dying in five weeks.
hobson-s-choice-a-lancashire-comedy-in-f:
Hobson's Choice, a Lancashire comedy in four acts by Harold Brighouse, was first produced in America. Its first English production came on June 22, 1916, at the Apollo Theatre, London. The printed cast lists Edyth Goodall as Maggie Hobson. Norman McKinnel played her father, Henry Horatio Hobson, and produced the play. The scene is Salford, Lancashire, and the period is 1880.

Three acts sit in Hobson's boot shop in Chapel Street. The fourth moves to Will Mossop's shop. Hobson is a widowed master shoemaker with three daughters and a love of the pub. Maggie, the eldest, refuses the future he plans. She chooses Will Mossop, his timid best workman, for a husband and a business partner. Brighouse builds the comedy on that choice. The title's phrase means no choice at all. Maggie turns it into the freest decision in the play.
honoring-parents: This short tract for children came from the Massachusetts Sabbath School Society, at Boston in 1851. It teaches the fifth commandment: honor your father and your mother. Cheerful, prompt obedience is the first way, it says. A story shows a second. Little Willy, at school, has his book snatched by a rude boy named Henry. Willy does not strike back or snatch in return. He asks in a coaxing tone and bears the loss with grace. That conduct, the tract says, honored his mother, though she never heard of it.
how-to-see-the-british-museum-in-four-vi:
W Blanchard Jerrold wrote this guide to the British Museum, at London in 1852. He parcels the vast house into four visits. The first tour is all zoology. Giraffe, walrus, rhinoceros, and hippopotamus lead the hoofed ranks.

Birds, reptiles, British beasts, and fishes fill out the first day. The second visit turns to minerals and fossils. Etruscan vases, spoils of Italian tombs, reward the antiquities rooms. Jerrold notes how those tombs vary in ornament with their owners' state. A visitor with four days and this book could face the museum without despair. It is a window on the house as Victorians first learned it.
imaginary-portraits:
Walter Pater invented a form in Imaginary Portraits: four studies of artists and thinkers who never quite existed as he shows them. A Prince of Court Painters reconstructs the young Watteau from a friend's journal at Valenciennes in 1701, all sketches, feast days, and early genius. Denys l'Auxerrois brings a medieval god of wine into a French cathedral town, with bloody results.

Sebastian van Storck follows a Dutch follower of Spinoza into cold, abstract devotion, and Duke Carl of Rosenmold ends the book in eighteenth-century Germany. Pater writes slow, jeweled prose, caring more for a temperament's inner weather than for plot. The portraits are really essays on kinds of beauty and belief, and they shaped a generation of aesthetic writers.
impressions-and-comments:
Havelock Ellis kept notes for years on random leaves, and Impressions and Comments gathers those brief records. In his preface he calls them loose pages from a journal, more personal than a bound book should be. He warns that blanks are left for the reader to fill. Autumn, he says, is the time to scatter them.

Short entries turn on life, thought, art, and small sights. One note recalls red roses on a verandah in Australia, seen forty years before. Others weigh how flowers move savage, craftsman, and poet alike. The book gives Ellis in flashes, one facet at a time.
in-kedar-s-tents:
In Kedar's Tents, by Henry Seton Merriman, carries an English hero into Spain in a 1909 London edition from Smith, Elder and Co. Merriman's contents move like a campaign map: One Soweth, Another Reapeth, then Like Ships Upon the Sea and Le Premier Pas, the first step. A chapter called Contraband admits the smuggling that runs under the story's politics.

At Ronda and in a Moorish garden the Spanish setting deepens, through a love letter and a war of wit to a city of discontent. Merriman wrote political adventure across Europe and its empires. Here he sets love and conspiracy in a Spain of garrisons, gardens, and mountain roads. The title borrows the psalmist's cry of dwelling far from home among strangers. The novel keeps that exile feeling under its intrigue. Its Englishman stands in uniform, in love, and in danger of choosing wrong.
irish-plays-and-playwrights:
Cornelius Weygandt surveyed Irish Plays and Playwrights in Boston in 1913. Chapters treat the Celtic Renaissance and the Abbey Theatre's players and audience. Yeats gets a full chapter, then Edward Martyn and George Moore. George Russell, Lady Gregory, and Synge follow in order.

Christy Mahon's eloquence to Pegeen is quoted from Synge's Playboy. Any girl, Pegeen says, would walk her heart out to meet his like for talk. Younger dramatists, from Colum to Ervine, close the survey. An appendix lists plays produced in Dublin by the Abbey company. Weygandt explains the revival to American readers.
island-nights-entertainments:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote these three tales of the South Seas in his last years, and the set came out in 1893. He lived then in Samoa, and the isles fill his pages with heat, trade, and old rites. The set's name plays on the tale nights of the Arabian Nights.

'The Bottle Imp' is the gem of the set: a man buys a bottle with an imp that grants all wishes. The catch is grim: who dies with the bottle in hand is damned for good. The rest hold the same mix of charm, dread, and the lore of the isles.
jacobs-incidents:
Harriet Jacobs published Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl in 1861, writing under the name Linda Brent. Jacobs had escaped North years before, but she hid her identity to protect others. Hers is the classic account of slavery as a Black woman lived it.

Jacobs tells how her master harassed her from girlhood and how she resisted. To escape him she hid for seven years in a tiny crawlspace above her grandmother's porch. From there she watched her own children grow below. The book exposed slavery's assault on mothers and families to a wide Northern audience.
kelly-miller-s-history-of-the-world-war-:
Kelly Miller's History of the World War for Human Rights is a 1919 history of the Great War, copyrighted by A. Jenkins. Miller was dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at Howard University. His subtitle explains why America entered the war, states the Allies' cause, and records the part the Negro took in army and navy. Official photographs show devices of modern warfare.

Miller had written Race Adjustment, Out of the House of Bondage, and many pamphlets on social questions. Contributions came from General Pershing, Frederick Drinker, E. A. Allen, and others. The history argues that Black soldiers' service proved their claim to full American rights. It is both a war chronicle and a civil rights brief, written while the ink was fresh.
lectures-on-popular-and-scientific-subje:
The Earl of Caithness delivered these lectures on popular and scientific subjects in many places. Trübner published the second, enlarged edition in London in 1879. The Earl was a fellow of the Royal Society.

Talks treat coal and coal mines, plus science applied to art. One lecture defends thrift: take care of the pence. Others cover the steam engine and past means of travel and news. Caithness writes for general audiences, not specialists. His volume shows how Victorian lords joined the public science movement. A lecture on communication traces roads, posts, and wires. Caithness treats invention as a story for every listener.
legends-of-the-madonna-as-represented-in:
Anna Jameson wrote Legends of the Madonna as part of her Sacred and Legendary Art series. Houghton Mifflin issued this corrected, enlarged edition at Boston in 1881. Publishers note that Jameson died before revising this edition herself.

She explains how artists pictured Mary across the centuries. Paintings, sculptures, and church images guide her chapters. Stories behind the images matter as much as the art itself. Jameson helped English readers learn to read religious pictures. Her warm, learned style made art history welcoming to newcomers. Her earlier Sacred and Legendary Art volumes stand behind it. Jameson treats painters as storytellers in line and color.
legge-the-chinese-classics-vol-1-confuci:
Confucius speaks in the Analects, the heart of the first volume of Legge's Chinese Classics, printed with the Chinese text. Short sayings and brief talks with disciples fill the book. Virtue, learning, good rule, and the good life form its steady themes.

Legge's Victorian version, fruit of years in China, opened the Master to the English world. Rulers hear that kindness and rite, not force, hold a state together. Students hear that learning begins with honesty about what one knows. The Analects shaped East Asian life for two thousand years, and Legge's labor remains a monument of the field.
lollingdon-downs-and-other-poems-with-so:
John Masefield published this poetry volume with Heinemann in 1917. He dedicates the poems and sonnets to his wife. Companion volumes include Dauber, The Daffodil Fields, and Philip the King. The Faithful, a play, shares the uniform edition list.

The opening poem counts life as beads of coloured days. The self, Masefield writes, is the string holding them. Lollingdon Downs gives the collection its title and landscape. Sonnets accompany the longer poems throughout the volume. The Faithful, his play, shares the uniform volume list. Dauber and The Daffodil Fields precede Philip the King there.
macmillan-co-s-general-catalogue-of-work:
Macmillan and Co.'s General Catalogue, dated December 1869, lists their books for sale. It covers history, biography, travels, and belles lettres. Each entry carries some short account of the critical notices it won. Names here include Gladstone, Guizot, Kingsley, Freeman, and John Morley.

A publisher's catalogue is a map of what one age read. Macmillan stood among London's most respected houses in 1869. Their list mixes sermons, scholarship, novels, and tales of travel. Prices and praise helped booksellers and readers choose new works. Today the catalogue serves historians of Victorian reading. It shows the taste of a book-buying public long vanished.
maggie-a-girl-of-the-streets: Crane's 1893 Maggie follows a Bowery girl's ruin. Naturalism grinds. The Tower library holds the full text. It maggied streets. Tenements crushed. Girl fell. Pity stared. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
make-your-own-hats:
Make Your Own Hats is a millinery manual by Gene Allen Martin. Houghton Mifflin published it in 1921, with drawings by E. E. Martin. Martin directed domestic arts at the Minneapolis Y.W.C.A. She also designed and taught hat-making for many students.

The first chapters cover equipment, materials, and velvet-covered frames. Frames of neteen, crinoline, and wire each get full treatment. Later lessons turn to shaping, trimming, and finishing hats at home. The book assumes a home sewer with patience and taste. It preserves the craft behind the grand hats of 1921. Modern makers still learn from such clear, careful manuals.
marjorie-s-three-gifts:
Marjorie's Three Gifts is a short story by Louisa May Alcott. Roberts Brothers' Boston edition here dates from 1899. Marjorie sits on the doorstep shelling peas into a bright tin pan. Roses peep at her through the porch lattice, and robins wish her happy birthday.

She hears none of it, for her thoughts are far away. Last night granny told her a fairy tale of gifts. A poor girl at her spinning received a good-luck penny from a Brownie. Then a fairy passed, with a gift of her own. Alcott lets Marjorie's birthday wish meet the old tale's magic. The Little Women author writes with her usual tender wisdom.
memories-and-portraits:
Robert Louis Stevenson gathered Memories and Portraits in a set of papers. Chatto and Windus printed this fine paper edition in London in 1912. He gave the book to his mother, in past joy and present sorrow.

His note says the papers hang together more than they seem. Memories of youth and portraits of the dead build one face. That face, he found, was his own young self, long lost. He was the first to be surprised by that turn, he admits. A steamer note, written within sight of Cape Race, dates the gift. Read in order, he urges, not dipped into at random.
men-women-and-boats:
Vincent Starrett edited this posthumous collection of Stephen Crane's stories and sketches. He gathered the pieces from out-of-print books and old magazine files. Some tales appear between covers here for the first time. The title was the editor's own choice, as his note explains.

The centerpiece is The Open Boat, Crane's celebrated tale of shipwrecked men at sea. Around it stand war sketches, city pieces, and early experiments like A Dark Brown Dog. The editor regrets that copyright problems forced out The Blue Hotel. For readers, the volume recovers minor Crane works that had nearly vanished from print.
men-women-and-ghosts:
Amy Lowell's book gathers narrative poems rather than lyrics, as her preface explains. She calls them stories, stretched to the widest sense of the word. Some are tales in scenes, while others make characters of air, clouds, and streets. The poems use the free rhythms of vers libre throughout.

Lowell says Debussy's piano music showed her how movement could shape a poem. She experiments with rhythm the way a musician varies tempo and theme. Poems like A Roxbury Garden try to copy the motion of rolling hoops and growing plants. The book shows an American modernist testing what free verse could do.
mercadet-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
Honoré de Balzac wrote this comedy in three acts, first staged in Paris in August 1851. The scene is a Paris house around 1845. Mercadet, a speculator, owes money to a crowd of creditors. His daughter Julie has a suitor, De la Brive, whose fortune matters greatly to the family.

Creditors like Goulard, Pierquin, and Violette press at the door from the first scene. Even the servants joke that their master is sure to drown. Mercadet schemes, stalls, and charms his way through each new demand. Balzac turns debt and speculation into fast, sharp stage comedy.
miscellaneous-mathematical-constants:
Simon Plouffe compiled this reference collection of mathematical constants at Simon Fraser University. Each number is computed to hundreds or thousands of digits. Entries range from one over pi squared, to five thousand digits, to the cosine of one at fifteen thousand digits. The file was downloaded from the Inverse Symbolic Calculator project's tables.

Named constants include Artin's, Catalan's, Champernowne's, and the Copeland-Erdos constant. Roots, exponentials, and zeta values fill out the list. The collection serves programmers and researchers who need exact digits for checking calculations. Plouffe later became known for formulas computing pi's digits, and this file shows his early precision work.
modern-religious-cults-and-movements:
Gaius Glenn Atkins, a Congregational minister and author, wrote this survey of America's new religions. His publisher's description lists the movements drawing crowds for two decades past. They include faith healing, Christian Science, and New Thought. Theosophy and spiritualism complete the set.

Atkins brought, his reviewers said, a firm grasp of Christian belief to the task. He wrote with clarity about movements many churchgoers found confusing or threatening. His other books ranged from Jerusalem's history to studies of the great mystics. This volume asks what needs the cults meet, and how the older churches should answer them.
mr-pim-passes-by-a-comedy-in-three-acts:
A. A. Milne wrote this comedy in three acts for the stage. The cast lists George Marden, his wife Olivia, and niece Dinah. Lady Marden, Brian Strange, and Carraway Pim complete the house party. The scene is the morning room at Marden House in Buckinghamshire.

Milne first staged the play in Manchester and then in London. A passing remark by Mr. Pim shakes the calm house. Old ties and young love are thrown into doubt. The mix-up is handled with light talk and neat turns. It shows Milne the playwright, years before his bear books made him most famous.
mrs-budlong-s-christmas-presents:
Rupert Hughes published this comic novel in 1912, set in the small town of Carthage. The story opens the morning after Christmas Eve. The whole house feels the ache of gifts given, missed, and received. Folks must smile and cry out that each gift is just right.

Hughes notes that Carthage folk are not rich, so gifts run small. Some are useless, and some are far too useful. Chapter titles promise schemes, foiled plans, and an amazing Christmas. Mrs. Budlong stands at the center of the giving and scheming. The book is a warm, sharp comedy about pride, love, and holiday gifts gone wrong.
music-as-a-language-lectures-to-music-st:
Ethel Home, head mistress of Kensington High School, gave these lectures to music students. Oxford's Clarendon Press issued the book in 1916. Her title claims music is a language to be taught with care. The first lecture treats the training of the music teacher.

Later lectures cover school programs, voice work, and the sol-fa method. Ear training, sight singing, rhythm, and dictation each get a chapter. She ends with harmony and first steps in composition. Home writes for teachers, not performers. Her plan shows how music was taught in British schools, step by plain step.
my-war-experiences-in-two-continents:
S. Macnaughtan's war memoir was edited by her niece after her death. John Murray issued it in London in 1919. The niece, Mrs. Lionel Salmon, shaped the letters and notes. A portrait by E. O. Hoppe fronts the volume.

The title promises war work on two continents. Macnaughtan, a novelist, went out to aid troops and the wounded. Her dedication follows a wish she had voiced herself. The book mixes letters, diary notes, and sharp witness. It shows the home front and the war zones through one tireless woman's eyes, kept in print by her family's care.
nasa-tm-19630006831-observational-astrop:
Theodore P. Stecher and James E. Milligan of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this paper. They gave it at the COSPAR meeting in May 1962. It reports star studies made from sounding rockets. Earth's air blocks ultraviolet light, so rockets carried the tools above it.

The paper opens by noting air is opaque below a set wavelength. Rocket flights caught ultraviolet spectra, the rainbow of starlight spread out. Observed light was checked against model stellar atmospheres. Light soaked up between the stars was part of the study. These short rocket hops opened a new window on hot stars before space telescopes flew.
nasa-tm-19650010094-scientific-explorati:
An address given on October 5, 1964, at Worcester Polytechnic Institute forms the core of this record. The speaker returned to Worcester for the institute's centennial convocation luncheon. Hugh L Dryden, NASA's deputy administrator, had been prevented from attending, the address notes.

Its subject is what the scientific exploration of space demands of education. A new field needs trained people, and schools must supply them. The speech speaks to that challenge in general terms for a general audience. It preserves how space leaders made the education case in public in 1964. Heard today, it also records the hopes and worries that space flight raised for schools at that moment.
nasa-tm-19660011717-ego-orbital-paramete:
H E Montgomery and S J Paddack, in Goddard's Theoretical Division, computed orbit data and heat inputs for the EGO satellite in April 1963. EGO was part of the Orbiting Geophysical Observatory family, called OGO in the catalog note. Their work gives orbital parameters over time, the spacecraft's changing angles, and the heat flowing into it from Sun and Earth.

Heat input decides a satellite's temperature balance in orbit. Designers need that input for each point of the path, not just an average. The authors present both their methods and their results. Other teams could then check thermal designs against real numbers, rather than rough guesses, for a large observatory satellite.
nasa-tm-19660028661-c2-swan-bands-in-com:
Ralph E. Stockhausen and Donald E. Osterbrock study comet light in this paper. Comets glow with bright bands of light from carbon molecules, called the C2 Swan bands. The authors ask how the molecules' vibration levels are populated when sunlight excites them, a process called fluorescence.

They calculate those populations two ways and get similar results. One way is a rough three-level shortcut; the other solves the balance equations for ten levels. Their excitation temperatures match published comet observations well. They also estimate the infrared glow from the same process in a bright comet, and find it small and hard to detect.
nasa-tm-19670012131-polarization-and-int:
Donald F. Heath, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in March 1967. It reports rocket measurements of hydrogen Lyman alpha light in the day airglow, the faint ultraviolet glow of the upper atmosphere. Heath measured both the light's intensity and its polarization, a measure theorists had flagged as key to the hydrogen problem.

A far ultraviolet polarization photometer with many channels recorded intensity and polarization against altitude for several emission features. These included the Lyman alpha line, atomic oxygen lines, and an unnamed glow at longer wavelengths. The instrument flew on an Aerobee 150 rocket launched from White Sands, New Mexico, on August 29, 1966. Partner experiments on the same flight measured direct solar Lyman alpha, broadband solar flux, and electron density and temperature.
nasa-tm-19670022480-pressure-and-heat-tr:
John O. Reller Jr. and H. Lee Seegmiller, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, measured what flight does to a Mercury capsule shape. Their memorandum, TM X-647, reports pressure and heat-transfer measurements on a model of the Mercury capsule, the first American crewed spacecraft. Knowing the heating on its blunt heat shield was vital to a safe return through the atmosphere.

The program spread across three kinds of facilities: wind tunnels, shock tunnels, and free flight. Separate sections describe the models and instrumentation used in each setting. Data reduction chapters treat the calibration of the air streams, chemical equilibrium in the flow around the model. Other chapters treat heat-transfer data reduction and collected flow visualization. Results and discussion then take up the stagnation region, the heat shield, and the rest of the capsule surface in turn.
nasa-tm-19670030839-station-contact-time:
F. O. Vonbun, of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, Texas, compiled this data paper in November 1964. It gives station contact times for Apollo orbits with variable launch azimuths. A contact time is the window during which a ground station can hear and talk to a spacecraft. Mission planners needed those windows in advance.

The paper presents graphs of contact times for the Apollo spacecraft in its parking orbits around Earth. Two orbit heights are considered, roughly two hundred and three hundred kilometers up. The graphs cover one to six parking orbits and show each ground station's windows as the launch azimuth swings across its full range. When a launch slips, the azimuth changes continuously with the delay. Vonbun hoped the graphs would help solve the tracking and communication tasks that such shifting orbits create.
nasa-tm-19680024113-variable-geometry-re:
Milton A. Beheim and Aaron S. Boksenbom of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52447, for an aeronautical sciences congress in Munich, Germany. They examine why jet inlets and exhaust nozzles for very fast aircraft must change shape in flight. A shape that works well above the speed of sound performs badly below it, they note.

Fixed shapes bring heavy pressure losses and drag at the speeds they were not built for. Lewis tests therefore compared round inlets first, with flat two-sided designs also prepared. The team varied how compression splits between outside and inside surfaces, and tried plug nozzles as well. They stress that results were still incomplete, so their conclusions stay tentative.
nasa-tm-19690010670-gamma-ray-astronomy-:
C. E. Fichtel, D. A. Kniffen, and H. B. Ogelman of Goddard Space Flight Center report gamma ray astronomy balloon results in this February 1969 paper, X-611-69-58. Balloons lift Goddard's digitized spark chamber telescope above most of the air. From that height it can catch gamma rays, the most energetic form of light, arriving from space.

The team reanalyzed data on the galactic center, hunting a possible line source in the galactic plane. Their value alone does not justify claiming a detection, they state, though it fits a satellite result. They also measured the atmospheric background glow from many angles. Upper limits on point sources fell below simple forecasts, and no positive point source evidence was found.
nasa-tm-19690030728-the-topside-ionosphe:
S. J. Bauer, R. E. Hartle, and J. R. Herman, of Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this October 1969 preprint, X-615-69-459. Their subject is the topside ionosphere of Venus and its interaction with the solar wind. Mariner V's two-frequency radio occultation experiment had watched the daytime ionosphere end abruptly. Venus has no strong magnetic shield, so the wind strikes that layer directly.

The authors picture solar wind magnetic fields piling up atop the conducting ionosphere. That magnetic obstacle, a kind of pseudo-magnetopause, raises a bow shock in the supersonic wind. Evidence came from both Mariner V and Venera IV. Using measured wind properties, they estimate the shocked gas and field buildup. Pressure balance at the cutoff, they show, fits the sharp electron density edge.
nasa-tm-19700022716-optimum-launch-traje:
Omer F. Spurlock and Fred Teren of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 astrodynamics conference in Santa Barbara, California. It finds the best launch trajectories for the ATS-E mission. ATS-E was an Applications Technology Satellite bound for a high orbit.

The authors obtained the optimum paths and present their analysis, steps, and results. Each path is computed from launch to insertion into the final orbit. Because the apogee motor was much smaller than the optimum size, the standard profile had to change. Their adjusted paths yield the greatest payload the smaller motor can deliver.
nasa-tm-19710012124-analytical-studies-o:
Theodore L. Felsentreger and James P. Murphy wrote this NASA preprint in March 1971 on luni-solar effects, the slow pulls of the Moon and Sun on artificial satellites. Those pulls gradually change a satellite's orbital elements, the numbers that describe its path. Predicting them matters for keeping spacecraft on station and for reading tracking data correctly.

The study works out perturbations in the orbital elements and compares them with effects from Earth's own gravity field. It then applies the analysis to real spacecraft: Relay 1, Telstar 2, and Relay 2. Separate sections treat shadow effects on Telstar 2, when Earth blocks the Sun's pull, and seasonal variations in Earth's gravity field. Figures track eccentricity and inclination changes for the Relay and Telstar satellites.
nasa-tm-19720017235-apollo-14-some-geoch:
Apollo 14: Some Geochemical Aspects reports the chemistry of Moon samples brought home by the Apollo 14 mission. The scan does not render its author names legibly. Apollo 14 was the first mission to visit an uplands region, away from the dark mare plains. Its landing site sat in the Fra Mauro Formation, debris thrown out by the impact that formed the Imbrium basin.

Chemical analyses covered five soil samples, three core samples, a soil clod, two breccia rocks, a basalt, and separated mineral phases. The samples proved strikingly uniform in chemistry, pointing to thorough mixing or uniform source rocks. The basalt could be matched by a mixture of about four parts soil to one part plagioclase. The authors found the samples chemically kin to Apollo 12 and 15 KREEP material, and suggested that mare basalts may represent fused cumulates.
new-arabian-nights: Stevenson's 1882 book of tales, led by the Suicide Club stories of Prince Florizel's wild nights in low London. Odd clubs, false names, and dark deeds unfold with the young writer's verve. These early pieces show him finding his voice, and they are still a pure joy to read.
night-must-fall-a-play-in-three-acts:
Emlyn Williams wrote Night Must Fall as a play in three acts, with performance rights held by his agent in London. A Lord Chief Justice appears before the play, in the Court of Criminal Appeal. The action then moves to Forest Corner, Mrs Bramson's bungalow in Essex, in the present day.

Mrs Bramson's niece Olivia Grayne and a man named Hubert Laurie join the household cast. A nurse, a cook, and a maid named Dora Parkoe fill out the house. Inspector Belsize and a man called Dan complete the list. Act one is an October morning. Act two falls twelve days later, then two days on. Crime hangs over the bungalow.
olympian-nights:
John Kendrick Bangs published this comic fantasy in 1902. Harper and Brothers issued it in New York and London. Bangs had written A House-Boat on the Styx before. The narrator reaches Mount Olympus in the first chapter. He seeks shelter among the old Greek gods.

An elevator boy and a valet serve modern comforts there. Golf links and a dining room update the ancient home. A chapter visits Aesculapius, the god of healing, as a doctor. Bangs mixes myth with modern American jokes and manners. The book is light satire for readers who know Olympus. Its humor stays playful rather than sharp.
on-nothing-kindred-subjects:
Hilaire Belloc wrote these light essays on small subjects. He dedicated the book to his friend Maurice Baring. The contents list essays on inns, ignorance, and advertisement. Other pieces treat a house, a dog, and tea. Trains, railways, and conversations in trains also appear.

Some essays turn grave, on a child who died. Others treat the return of the dead with wit. Belloc finds great truths inside trifles and daily scenes. Inns, lanes, and the human lot fill his pages. The book shows his paradoxical wisdom at play. Heads also treat a lost manuscript and a rich man's pain. A plea to take up one's pen opens the set.
pamela-giraud-a-play-in-five-acts:
Honoré de Balzac's Pamela Giraud is a play in five acts. Paris first saw it at the Théâtre de la Gaîté. The date was September 26, 1843. The scene is Paris during the Napoleonic plots. Louis the Eighteenth then reigned. The cast joins a general, a lawyer, and a wealthy merchant. Pamela herself is a poor working girl.

Act One opens in an attic and workshop. An artificial flower-maker works there by candlelight. The ceiling slopes so a man could hide behind it. Pamela sits at her work-table, discovered at her flowers. Joseph Binet sits near her. Balzac, the great novelist of money and ambition, builds his melodrama from that garret. A hidden man and a rich man's son will do the rest.
penelope-s-postscripts:
Penelope's Postscripts collects later travels of Kate Douglas Wiggin's Penelope Hamilton, in an edition published by Hodder and Stoughton in 1915. The contents list Penelope in Switzerland, in Venice, her prints of Wales, Penelope in Devon, and Penelope at home. The first piece opens in Geneva with her travelling companion Salemina.

Salemina, Penelope explains, is a charming spinster from Salem, Massachusetts, forever being asked if she is one of the P.'s of Salem. The postscripts keep the manner of the earlier Penelope books: bright letters home, full of hotels, sights, and affectionate teasing of fellow travellers.
phantom-airships-1909-1913-press-account:
Four newspaper accounts trace The Phantom Airship Waves of 1909-1913, gathered from the Library of Congress's Chronicling America. A landing reported on Caerphilly Mountain opens the British scare of 1909, when crowds scanned night skies for German raiders. An American piece blames mirages, and a Chicago aviator's supposed phantom is unmasked as himself.

The last item, from 1913, shows French troops seizing a Zeppelin at Luneville, proof of how seriously states took mystery aircraft. Together the pieces catch the mood before the First World War: new machines in the sky, old fears on the ground. They form the press record of the pre-war phantom waves.
podcast-joerogan-jYfAhupxaTs:
Rick Doblin returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1964, another lap in his long campaign. Doblin's MAPS organization had by then carried MDMA therapy through its final trials for PTSD. The finish line he had chased since the 1980s was in view.

He updates Rogan on the trial results, the regulators' questions, and what legal therapy would require of clinics. Rogan asks what could still go wrong. The episode is a hopeful progress report from the psychedelic movement's most patient man, and it pairs with his many other visits to form a full record of the cause.
political-pamphlets:
George Saintsbury edited this volume of Political Pamphlets for the Pocket Library of English Literature, published by Percival and Company in London in 1892. Saintsbury's series put short classics into portable volumes, and the pamphlet volume is a greatest-hits of English polemic: Halifax's Letter to a Dissenter, Defoe's Shortest Way with the Dissenters. The hoax that nearly got its author hanged, and Swift's Drapier's Letters, which defeated a coinage scheme and made Ireland a nation in print.

Burke's second letter on a regicide peace brings the volume to revolution, Sydney Smith's Peter Plymley letters add wit to the case for Catholic relief. Cobbett's letters to the journeymen and labourers close with radical thunder. Saintsbury, the great critical anthologist, chose pamphlets as literature, not just evidence: proof that the short prose broadside, written overnight, could outlast the books of centuries.
port-o-gold-a-history-romance-of-the-san:
Louis J. Stellman published Port o' Gold in 1922, calling it a history-romance of the San Francisco Argonauts, the forty-niners who sailed for gold. He dedicates the book to the city of his adoption and rebirth in a long poem that watches dawn break over her roofs and bay. Remembers her rising from the fiery torch, betrayed by greed and smirched by her sons' disgrace, to make herself a new and honored place.

Behind the dedication stands the whole epic: the gold discovery, the rush by sea. The instant city of gamblers, vigilantes, and dreamers, worked into fiction with real events under the plot. Stellman, a San Francisco journalist and photographer, wrote his city as romance because that is how she felt to him. The book keeps the Argonaut myth warm as the last survivors were dying.
recollections-of-bytown-and-its-old-inha:
William Pittman Lett published his recollections of Bytown and its old inhabitants at Ottawa in 1874, in verse. His introduction says the pieces began as private lines, not meant for print. Friends urged him to gather them in compact shape, and he changed his mind.

Lett states his aim plainly: to save from being lost as many names and events of Bytown's early days as memory could recall. He asks for no praise for polish of rhythm or measure, saying he aimed at truth. The town he recalls had grown, by his writing, into a city of nearly thirty thousand people.
recollections-of-the-late-william-beckfo:
